“You’re supposed to be on my side.”

“I am. I can agree with her as well.” He drew her in, and she leaned against him, and her eyes filled without warning. “She thought I didn’t care.”

“She knows now.”

“The twenty-first of December. A proper race. Our sponsorship, in daylight.”

“Then we’ll read the contracts before anyone signs anything.”

“Of course you’d say that.”

“I’d be a poor husband if I let you sign a sponsorship without reading the terms.”

“You’re a very annoying husband.”

“And yet you keep him,” said Chen Si. Then his face went quiet. “Your mother has registration numbers. By tomorrow night she won’t have the man who took the photograph. Nobody will hurt him. He’ll find he’s been offered a very good job a long way away, and that he’d like to take it.” He looked at her. “That’s what I want to do. I’m asking you.”

She looked back at him for a long moment. “Ask me again in the morning. If I still say yes, do it.”

“All right.” He turned her hand over in his. “She used Serafina because she knew you’d come. She was counting on you being too frightened to tell me.”

“She was right.”

He didn’t look pleased. He didn’t punish her for it either. “Next time, tell me before you go.”

“Next time I will.”

“And I won’t decide anything for you without asking. Especially when I think it’s necessary.”

She put her hand to his face, and he turned his head and kissed her palm.

“Thank you for waiting,” she whispered.

He kissed her then, slowly at first, his hand at her jaw, and then she moved closer and he pulled her into his arms and kissed her as if he’d been holding a question in his mouth for five hours and had decided, finally, not to ask it.

“I’m not angry that you were frightened,” he said against her hair. “I’m angry that she made you think you had to carry it on your own. That isn’t the same thing.”

He held her for a while. Then he looked at the clock.

“Have you eaten?”

She stared at him. “I’ve just told you my mother blackmailed me with my sister.”

“I heard. Have you eaten?”

She laughed, properly, for the first time since the photograph. “No.”

“Stay there,” said Chen Si, and went into the kitchen, and she heard him get out the rice.

Her phone buzzed.

Serafina: Don’t tell Mother about December yet.

Aurelia: I won’t.

Serafina: And thank you.

Aurelia: You don’t owe me anything. Just drive safely.

She put the phone down. Her mother had wanted a letter, and a smile, and a daughter who came when she was called. Instead she’d handed Aurelia a reason to stop keeping her sister a secret. On the twenty-first of December Serafina would race under her own name, and down the side of her car, in letters a foot high, would be Aurelia’s.

chapters.title: The Racing Team She Pretends Not to Fund
chapters.desc: Aurelia sells Fu Kang a watch from Geneva and follows his money all the way to his father’s name. She also learns to change a wheel and rebuilds her sister’s sponsorship deck in one night.
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t pretend to fund it any more.” “No. Now I pretend I’m not terrified.”
chapters.content:
Monsieur Aubert had not sold a watch to a man he disliked in thirty years. He’d made the rule after a collector tried to pay him with money that smelled of a minister’s missing millions. He’d made a second rule soon after: he didn’t sell to men who thought money made them interesting.

“Fu Kang, unfortunately,” he said, “appears to be both.”

It was the first Monday in November, in the back room of Aubert & Fils, which had stood on the same corner of the old quarter since before Aurelia was born. Pale walls, dark velvet cases, and a long-case clock that had run seven minutes slow for as long as she could remember. Between them on the table lay an old watch with a champagne dial and a movement so well kept it looked as if it had been made last week. Not the dearest thing in the room. Very nearly the rarest.

“He’s offered above the asking price,” said Monsieur Aubert.

“That doesn’t mean you should accept.”

“You’re advising me not to sell?”

“I’m advising you to sell it properly. A buyer whose name is checked. Clean papers. A documented sale through the usual channels. No odd payment instructions, no favours for go-betweens, nothing changed afterwards. And I’d like to know if he tries to change any of it.”

The old man looked at her over his glasses for a long moment, and then laughed softly. “Ah. You’re not selling him a watch.”

“Of course I am.”

“Naturally,” said Monsieur Aubert, and asked her nothing else.

She wasn’t going to manufacture anything. She only wanted to see what Fu Kang did when nobody made things convenient for him.

✦ ✦ ✦

Big Wu was not impressed by Aurelia Chen. He was impressed by people who could work, and he made sure she understood there was a difference.

“Again.”

“I just did it.”

“You did it badly.”

“That’s very encouraging.”

“Encouraging doesn’t tighten bolts,” said Big Wu.

Serafina’s team had two bays in the garage under the railway bridge, the one with a train over it every eleven minutes. It smelled of rubber and oil and the black coffee Big Wu boiled in a dented kettle by the office. He was enormous, and gruff, and wouldn’t hear the number four said out loud, and he’d agreed to teach her to change a wheel on the grounds that a sponsor who didn’t know what she was paying for was a sponsor who’d get bored.

“Check the jack.”

“Stable.”

“Now the wrench. Not like that. Put your weight there and you’ll slip and break your face.”

She moved her grip. The wheel came off and was checked and went back on, the nuts tightened in the right order, and Big Wu inspected it and grunted.

“Is that approval?”

“It’s not a complaint.”

“I’ll take it.”

“You shouldn’t.”

Across the garage Serafina, in a black team jacket with her hair cut short and ragged by her own kitchen scissors, looked up from a bonnet. “What are you staring at?”

“I’m supervising.”

“You’re changing wheels.”

“That too.”

“You’re sisters?” said Big Wu.

“Unfortunately,” said Serafina.

“She’s always been ungrateful,” said Aurelia.

“Good. You’ll both fit in.”

When he had gone to shout at somebody else, Serafina wiped her hands on a rag. “You don’t pretend to fund it any more.”

“No,” said Aurelia, tightening the last nut. “Now I pretend I’m not terrified.”

By the end of the first week she had blisters. By the end of the second she could do it without asking him to repeat anything. By the end of the third he’d stopped correcting her grip. He still complained, but now he complained while handing her the tools, which she counted as progress.

One afternoon Chen Si came down in a dark coat and shoes that had never been meant for a garage floor. Big Wu looked at him, and at Aurelia, and back.

“Your husband?”

“Unfortunately.”

“He’s too clean.”

“He’s always like that.”

Chen Si crouched beside her by the wheel. “Don’t,” she said. “You’ll ruin those trousers.”

“Is this the right position?”

“Are you testing me?”

“She’s better than she was,” said Big Wu. “Still slow.”

“Does she get that from you?” said Chen Si.

“Don’t encourage her,” said Big Wu.

When she stood up there was a black smear along her jaw. Chen Si took a clean handkerchief from his pocket and wiped it away, and Big Wu made a noise of profound disgust and told them both to go home.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the twenty-first of November Qian put a report on his desk at twenty to eight in the morning. Seven companies in three jurisdictions, and a chain of payments built so that nobody could read it as one movement. The first paid the second, the second the third, the third bought something through the fourth, and by the time the money reached the company that had bought Fu Kang’s watches its beginning had been washed off. But the pattern was there.

“Some of these companies do real business,” said Qian. “We haven’t treated everything as suspicious.”

“Good. And at the end?”

“Mr. Yuen thinks a private trust.”

“Whose?”

“We don’t know yet.”

“Then don’t guess.”

Four days later Qian came in with a single sheet and didn’t put it down at once.

“We have the trust. The register’s closed, but there’s a document from the sale that names who controls it.”

He laid it on the desk. Chen Si read the name twice.

Fu Jianguo.

He didn’t move for some time. Eleven years. Eleven years of rumours, and witnesses who remembered things differently once they were sitting in a formal room, and men who’d been at his father’s table and couldn’t recall his name. Enough to know what had happened. Never enough to prove it. And now here it was. Not a recollection. Not an old man who might die or change his story. A piece of paper with Fu’s name on it.

“How did we get it?”

“Through the records attached to the watch sale. It’s being checked. Mr. Yuen has counsel on the chain of custody.”

“We’ll be careful how we use it.”

“Yes.”

“Nobody contacts Fu. Nobody lets him know. Nobody goes near Fu Kang until the record’s complete. A copy to counsel. The original stays here.”

When Qian had gone he looked at the name in the folder for a long while. He’d imagined this moment for eleven years. He’d expected rage, or relief, or the hard satisfaction of finding the thing at last. What he felt was cold. A piece of paper couldn’t give him back his father, or his mother sitting by a telephone. But it could stop Fu Jianguo pretending he’d never touched them.

He picked up his phone.

Chen Si: Are you at the garage?

Aurelia: Yes.

Chen Si: Have you eaten?

Aurelia: Big Wu gave me half a sandwich.

Chen Si: That isn’t lunch.

Aurelia: It was a very large sandwich.

Chen Si: I’ll bring you something.

He closed the folder.

✦ ✦ ✦

Late on the last Thursday in November he found her at the big bench in the workroom over the shop, surrounded by drawings and a velvet mat strewn with tiny gold jump rings, trying to make a bracelet’s clasp behave.

“You’re working late.”

“So are you.”

“I brought dinner.”

“Then you’re welcome.” She held a ring under the lamp without looking up. “Do you know what’s wrong with this?”

“Not enough tension.”

“How do you know that?”

“I’ve watched you.”

“Watching isn’t knowing. The ring has to close completely without losing its shape. Force it and the metal loses its line. Leave it loose and the clasp fails.”

“Like a negotiation.”

“Please don’t compare my jewellery to your business. Jewellery’s honest. If a stone has a flaw I can see it. If a clasp’s badly made, it breaks. People are much more complicated.”

“Have you eaten?”

“In ten minutes.”

“You said ten minutes twenty minutes ago.”

“You’re keeping count?”

“Someone has to.” He stood behind her. “You’re rubbing your thumb.”

She looked down. She was. She hadn’t known.

“Only with you,” he said, before she could call him observant, and waited until she’d put the pliers down, and then took her face in both hands and kissed her.

Her elbow knocked the velvet mat. Gold rings scattered across the bench and one bounced off onto the floor.

“Look what you’ve done.”

“An unfortunate loss.”

“They’re gold.”

“I’ll replace them.”

“That isn’t the point. You interrupted my work.”

“I brought dinner.”

“That isn’t an apology.”

“No?” said Chen Si, and kissed her again. “Then I’ll keep trying.”

She laughed and took his lapels and pulled him down, and the rest of the jump rings waited.

✦ ✦ ✦

The sponsorship deck for Serafina’s team was due on the Monday after the first week of December, and by Thursday night Aurelia had two days left and forty pages to write, three notebooks, a laptop and a cup of cold coffee on the dining table. Serafina stood behind her chair.

“Do we really need forty pages?”

“Yes. You want serious sponsors.”

“I want somebody to pay for tyres.”

“Then we’ll need to explain why they should.”

The team. The driver. The car, matte black, number seven, which Serafina had already named Gilded. The calendar. The audience. What a sponsor got for their money, tier by tier. And a long section on safety, which Serafina frowned at.

“Everybody knows racing’s dangerous.”

“Exactly. So we show them we take it seriously.”

“You’re paying for all this?”

“I’m proposing the first sponsorship. The rest depends on who joins us.”

“You already pay for the team. Why do you keep doing that?”

“Doing what?”

“Helping me without making me feel I’ve had to ask.”

Aurelia looked at her sister. “Because I remember what it’s like to want something and have everybody ask what they’d get out of it. And because you’re a good driver.”

“Obviously.”

“Don’t become unbearable.”

“Too late.”

At twelve minutes to midnight Chen Si came down and found them arguing about the size of the name on the cover.

“She thinks mine should be bigger,” said Serafina.

“Tell her it should be smaller,” said Aurelia.

He looked at the page. “The name’s fine.”

“See?”

“You’re supposed to be impartial.”

“I’m not,” said Chen Si. “Have you eaten?”

“She made me eat,” said Serafina, getting up. “Goodnight, boss.”

“Don’t,” said Aurelia.

At sixteen minutes past one he woke to her side of the bed empty and went down and found her at the table again in the glow of the screen. She’d changed the cover and the budget and added a page on what the team could give a sponsor besides a sticker on a car.

“How many?”

“Thirty-eight.”

“Ten minutes.”

“Fifteen.”

“Twelve.”

“Thirteen.”

“Agreed.”

At twenty-nine minutes past one she saved it. Forty pages. TEAM AURELIA · SERAFINA SONG · NUMBER 7. She leaned back. “Done.”

He picked her up before she could reach for the coffee.

“Put me down.”

“You negotiated thirteen minutes. You’ve used them,” said Chen Si, and carried her upstairs.

✦ ✦ ✦

Fu Kang came to Da Gianni on the twelfth of December twelve minutes late. Aurelia was already at the corner table in dark green, with her hair pinned at the nape and a thin gold bracelet that had thirty-six jump rings in it. No sign of Chen Si. That was deliberate.

“Mrs. Chen. I was surprised to have your invitation.”

“I imagine you have a great many invitations.”

“Not usually from your side of the family.”

For the first few minutes they talked about watches, and he knew more than she’d expected. The history of the piece he’d bought from Monsieur Aubert, the old movement, which dealers lied and which only exaggerated. There was real feeling in it. She noted that, and put it away.

“Do you wear them?”

“Some.”

“And the rest?”

“Investment.”

“That’s an unromantic way to describe collecting.”

“Romance is expensive.”

“Only when you buy the wrong things,” said Aurelia, and waited until the waiter had gone, and put a slim folder on the cloth between them.

He didn’t touch it. She opened it herself. The bridge agreement. Then a note of his father’s demand: fifteen per cent, for Fu Kang.

His face changed. “Where did you get that?”

“From the people involved.”

“My father’s already discussed it with Mr. Song.”

“Your father’s discussed a great many things with Mr. Song. It became my family’s business when he tried to use my husband to get it.”

“Is this supposed to frighten me?”

“No,” said Aurelia. “It’s a chance to decide something before things become a good deal less comfortable.” She turned the page. The watch. The company that bought it. The seven companies above that, and the trust at the top of them. She didn’t pretend it proved more than it did. She didn’t need to. He stopped smiling.

“You’ve been investigating me.”

“I’ve been investigating what your father asked of my family. Your name turned up in the records.”

“What do you want?”

She put the agreement in front of him. “Your signature. As the man your father meant to hold that fifteen per cent. That you’ll take no share in the bridge you haven’t paid for, and that you’ll stand aside from the approvals.”

He stared at it. “You think you can make me sign this?”

“No. I think you can decide whether signing it is better than your father explaining to the people whose job it is to ask why his interest in a public bridge is hidden behind a watch company and a private trust.”

“You don’t know what you’re threatening.”

“I know exactly what I’m asking.”

He laughed shortly. “You’re your husband’s wife after all.”

Her eyes went cool. “No. I’m Aurelia Chen. My husband has no interest in your father. My father has already said no to him. I’m offering you a way to finish this without your family making a weapon out of my father’s bridge. If you refuse, it stays unsigned and blocked, and the documents go to the people who examine such things.”

She didn’t lean forward. She didn’t raise her voice. She waited.

After a long time, he picked up the pen and signed. Quick and sharp. He pushed it back across the table.

“Don’t mistake this for peace between our families.”

“I wouldn’t dream of it.”

“And don’t think my father will leave you alone.”

She stood and picked up her bag. “Then he’ll have to learn I’m not very easy to persuade. Good evening, Mr. Fu.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The signed agreement reached her father the next morning. He rang her while she was in the shop counting a parcel of loose sapphires, and for a moment he said nothing at all.

“Ba?”

“Fu Kang signed. How?”

“With a pen.”

“Aurelia.”

She laughed. “I spoke to him.”

“That simple?”

“Not quite.”

He laughed too, warm and unguarded, a sound she hadn’t heard from him in years. Then he was quiet. “Your mother told me you’d make trouble.”

“And what do you think?”

“I think she was right. I think you’ve made the right kind of trouble.” She heard him draw a breath, as if the next words had been waiting behind his teeth for some time. “You built something of your own. You kept it. You looked after your sister. And now you’ve helped your father without asking him for a single thing in return. I was wrong to think you were too young for these things.” A pause. “I’m proud of you.”

It didn’t land like a demand. It didn’t land like a bar she’d have to clear again tomorrow. It was just said.

“Thank you, Ba.”

“Come to dinner next week. Bring Chen Si. And Serafina.”

“I’ll ask them.”

“Take care of yourself, Aurelia.”

When she put the phone down her eyes were wet, and she didn’t notice Chen Si until his hand came to her waist from behind.

“How long have you been there?”

“Long enough.”

“Ba said he was proud of me.”

“He should have said it years ago.”

“Yes,” she said, and leaned back into his chest. “You haven’t asked how I did it.”

“I trust you.”

“That sounds dangerous.”

“It probably is,” he said, and turned her round and kissed her, softly, and then again when she reached for his lapels. “I’m proud of you too.”

“You’re always proud of me.”

“Yes.”

“Even when I make a mess?”

“Especially then.”

“That’s a very low standard.”

“It’s a very generous one.” He looked past her at the bench, at the drawings and the bracelet waiting on its mat. “How many rings left?”

“Eight.”

He took his coat off.

“What are you doing?”

“Helping.”

“You don’t know how.”

“Then teach me.”

She handed him the little pliers. “Carefully.”

“Yes, boss,” said Chen Si, and for the next half hour the most feared man in the city sat at his wife’s bench closing gold jump rings under a lamp, one at a time, without distorting the metal, while she watched him. He was patient. He was precise. He was, she admitted privately, very good at doing what he was told. When he’d closed the last one she inspected the bracelet under the loupe.

“Acceptable.”

“Only acceptable?”

“Don’t let it go to your head.”

“Too late,” he said, and pulled her in. Outside, the city went on into December, and in a garage under the railway bridge a matte black car with her name on the bonnet was being made ready for the twenty-first.

chapters.title: Sisters at a Racetrack
chapters.desc: Serafina wins the last race of the season with AURELIA on her bonnet. Chen Si goes up to the VIP lounge to have a word with her mother.
chapters.epigraph: “Don’t watch the car. Watch the gap. The car goes where the gap is.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Aurelia noticed at the circuit in the north, on the twenty-first of December, wasn’t the engines, though they came up through the soles of her shoes, and it wasn’t the crowd. It was the way eleven thousand people could all hold their breath at once.

She stood behind the glass of the hospitality box above the pit straight. Below her, four rows back on the grid, sat a matte black car. GILDED along its flank in thin gold. And across the bonnet, in clean gold capitals that anyone in the grandstand could read: AURELIA.

She’d approved the paint, the lettering, the sponsors’ placings, the photographs. She’d argued over the shade of gold until Big Wu threatened to hand her a brush. Seeing it here was different. Her name was on a racing car. Her sister was going to drive it.

“You’re doing it again,” said Chen Si beside her.

“Doing what?”

“Looking as if you’re about to give the car a performance review.”

“The left side of the lettering’s slightly lower.”

He looked at the car, and then at her. “You’re the only person in this building who could see that.”

“Which is why I’m the one checking.”

She’d been nervous since breakfast. She’d rearranged the same jewellery box twice and asked the driver three times about the traffic. Her hands were cold. He took them, opened his coat, and tucked both of them into his pockets with his own round them.

“Your hands are warm.”

“I know.”

“Very arrogant.”

“You married me.”

“An administrative error.”

“Then file a complaint,” said Chen Si, and kissed her forehead.

✦ ✦ ✦

Fifteen minutes before the start she went down to the garage. Serafina was by the car in a black suit with gold at the shoulders, helmet under her arm, braids tight to her head, with Big Wu at her elbow holding a clipboard as if he’d fight the whole circuit with it.

“You didn’t have to come down.”

“I’m inspecting my investment. Your left-side lettering’s crooked.”

“You’re joking.”

“Slightly.”

“It’s straight,” said Big Wu. “I checked it three times because you made me.”

Aurelia reached up and straightened the collar of her sister’s suit. She’d done the same thing every morning when they were small, to Serafina’s school blazer, before their mother came downstairs.

“Radio?”

“Yes.”

“Belts? Medics?”

“Aurelia. You’re doing it again.”

Serafina hugged her, hard, with the helmet between them.

“Drive your race,” Aurelia said into her shoulder. “Don’t think about the people watching. Don’t think about Mother. Think about the corners, and Big Wu shouting at you afterwards.”

“That’s guaranteed.”

“And remember the car’s yours today.”

“Not yours?”

“Technically,” said Aurelia, “I own the bonnet.”

Serafina laughed. “Don’t watch the car,” she said. “Watch the gap. The car goes where the gap is.” She pulled on her helmet, and stopped with the visor still up. “Stay where I can see you.”

“I will.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The lights went out at twenty to three, and the black car moved.

For the first seconds Aurelia couldn’t breathe. Gilded tucked into the first corner behind two others and held the inside line and didn’t take the gap on the outside.

“She’s holding back.”

“She’s placing herself.”

“She could have gone round the blue one.”

“Perhaps she doesn’t want to yet.”

“You’re very calm.”

“I’m not driving.”

“Neither am I.”

“Exactly,” said Chen Si.

Sixth. Fifth on the back straight. She didn’t know she was talking until she heard herself. “Come on. Come on, Sera.” Every time Gilded vanished behind the stands the space it left behind was unbearable. Every time it came back her eyes found it before anything else on the track. When she squeezed too hard he didn’t complain. When her fingers went cold again he rubbed them between his palms. Once he lifted her knuckles to his mouth, and she didn’t notice.

“She’s third.”

“Yes.”

“She’s third, Chen Si.”

“I heard you the first time.”

Second, on the straight, and the grandstand came to its feet. One car left in front, red, the championship leader, who’d been shutting the inside door all afternoon with a little more violence every lap.

On the last lap they came into the Needle, the hairpin at the end of the back straight, and the red car moved across to the inside as it had every time. Gilded stayed behind it.

“Why isn’t she going?”

Then she went. Not desperately. She waited until the red car had committed to its line and then took the outside, clean and late and certain, braking on the marker to the metre, and for one impossible second the two cars ran side by side round the hairpin, and then the black one came out in front.

The announcer’s voice broke. “SERAFINA SONG TAKES THE LEAD—”

The chequered flag came down. Gilded crossed the line first.

For a moment Aurelia just stared. She watched the car slow, the marshals waving, the garage below erupt. Then it reached her. Her sister had started from the fourth row and won.

The noise she made was half a laugh and half something else. Chen Si turned, and she was already crying, and he opened his arms and she walked into them. He held her with one hand at the back of her head and the other across her shoulders, and she sobbed. Not quietly. Not prettily. Not in the careful, rationed way she’d let herself feel things for twenty-four years. Around them eleven thousand people were shouting her sister’s name, and she cried into her husband’s coat as though the whole world had finally handed Serafina something she’d been owed since she was a child.

“Look at her, sweetheart,” he said.

On the track Serafina had climbed out and pulled her helmet off, her face scarlet, her braid coming down. She looked straight up at the box. She lifted both arms. Then she pointed at the gold letters on the bonnet, and then at her sister.

Chen Si watched his wife press her fingers to her mouth. He’d seen her face men down who thought they could frighten her. He’d seen her empty a room with one question. He’d never seen her like this, not trying to win anything at all, only happy because somebody she loved had.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the garage it was chaos: mechanics, officials, people who’d been shouting Serafina’s name for ten minutes and now wanted to shake her hand. Big Wu was blowing his nose and blaming the cold.

“Make way for the sponsor!” somebody yelled.

Serafina came at her at a run. “We won!”

“You won.”

“Did you see the Needle? Big Wu said I’d lose the place.”

“I said you were taking a risk,” said Big Wu.

“Same thing.”

“It is not the same thing.”

The gold A on the bonnet had a long black smear of rubber across it now. Aurelia looked at it.

“Perfect,” she said.

“You said it was crooked!”

“I’ve changed my mind.”

Somebody came through the crowd with a bottle of champagne. “Absolutely not,” said Aurelia. “Not until the medics have seen you and Big Wu’s been over the car.”

“You’re not my mother.”

“Thank God.”

Serafina laughed so hard she had to hold on to the wing mirror, and went off towards the medical bay, and for once in her life Aurelia didn’t follow. She knew her sister would come back.

✦ ✦ ✦

Vittoria hadn’t come down.

Aurelia saw her through the glass of the hospitality lounge upstairs, beside the windows, with a man Aurelia knew from a charity dinner years ago. Li Zhenhua. Neat, grey, with the ease of somebody used to being listened to. Her mother had introduced him once as an old friend of the family. He’d spent thirty years close to the traffic police. And at that dinner he’d looked at Serafina, who was seventeen, not with a stranger’s polite interest but with recognition.

Chen Si followed her eyes. “Who’s that?”

She told him.

“Stay with your sister,” he said.

“Where are you going?”

“To have a word with your mother.”

She caught his sleeve. “Not here. Don’t make a scene.”

He looked down at her hand, and back at her face, in the voice she knew meant he’d already decided. “I’ll speak to her. That’s all.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Vittoria turned from the window. “Mr. Chen. Where’s Aurelia?”

“With her sister.” He looked at the man in the chair. “Mr. Li.”

Li stood. “Congratulations on the race.”

“Why is he here?” said Chen Si, to Vittoria.

“I invited him. He’s interested in motorsport.”

“Then he’ll have recognised Serafina.”

“Of course he did. He knows the family.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

The lounge went quiet. Vittoria’s mouth thinned. “I thought it would be useful for someone who knows the authorities to see what sort of company Serafina keeps.”

“You brought him here to identify her.”

“I believe there’s a misunderstanding,” said Li. “Mrs. Song was concerned. I have friends in traffic enforcement. I was only asked to look.”

“At what?”

“Whether any of the cars or drivers were known to the police.”

“She’s registered. The circuit’s licensed. Every car here passed scrutineering this morning. There was nothing for you to look at, Mr. Li. I suggest you leave.”

Li looked at Vittoria. She said nothing. He picked up his coat and went.

“You think you can frighten me,” said Vittoria, when the door had shut.

“No.”

“Then what is this?”

“A warning. You sent Aurelia a photograph of her sister and told her you’d hand Serafina to the police unless she made me write to Fu Jianguo.”

“That was a family matter.”

“You made it mine when you used my name.”

“I was protecting the family.”

“You were controlling it.”

She lifted her chin. “You sound very like your father.”

Something changed in his face. A stillness round the eyes, no more. She’d meant to provoke him, and she had. He didn’t raise his voice. He didn’t move a step.

“Don’t use my father’s name to make a point you can’t defend,” he said. “Your daughter won a championship today. She has the right to stand beside her own car without being watched and named and threatened by someone you brought into the room. One more photograph. One more threat. One more attempt to use Serafina to force Aurelia. After that I stop being polite.”

“Is that a threat?”

“It’s the last warning you’ll have from me.”

At the door she said, “Aurelia will understand one day that I’m trying to protect her.”

He looked back. “She understands you perfectly,” said Chen Si.

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia was at the top of the stairs with her arms folded.

“How was your conversation?”

“Brief.”

“Did you frighten her?”

He considered. “A little.”

He told her about Li, and her face went hard. “I don’t want Serafina to know. Not today.”

“All right. There’s something else. Li’s nephew is in traffic enforcement. He’s been selling details of private cars to people with no business asking for them. We found him while we were looking for whoever took the photograph. His superiors have been told. He’s been moved to a post in the far west.”

“You arranged that.”

“Yes.”

“Did you have the authority?”

“No.”

“Then how?”

“Through people who do.”

Her voice dropped. “You can’t move people’s lives around because you’re angry.”

“He was selling information about private citizens.”

“Then he should be investigated and answer for it properly. Not shipped off because you decided so.”

His jaw set. For a moment she saw the old instinct in his face, the one that solved a problem by making it disappear. Then he looked at her.

“You’re right. It may have been deserved. That wasn’t mine to decide. I’ll have Qian put it back through the proper channels, and if the move was wrong it’ll be undone.”

“Thank you.”

She took his hand and turned it over. The thin white line across the palm. The pale shiny burn running from the heel of it up inside the wrist, that he always said came from the road.

“You’re very good at frightening people,” she said.

“Only when it’s necessary.”

“That’s what frightening people always say.” She kissed the scarred palm. “Come on. Serafina’s waiting.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Serafina was beside the car with a streak of grease on her jaw. She narrowed her eyes at them both.

“Where did you go?”

“Nowhere important.”

“That means somewhere important.”

“Congratulations,” said Chen Si. “You drove well.”

“Big Wu says I took too much risk at the Needle.”

“Big Wu’s probably right.”

“You’re meant to congratulate me.”

“I did.”

Then Serafina looked at his hand, where his cuff had slipped back and the scar showed. She looked at it for a moment. And without a word she put her own palm against his. Smaller, oily, with a red mark where the wheel had rubbed through her glove.

No speech. No apology for the getaway car. Just that.

“You’re family,” she said.

He looked at her. “I know.”

“Right.” She let go. “Photograph. All three of us. With Gilded.”

“Move,” said Big Wu, “you’re blocking the bonnet.”

In the photograph Serafina is grinning, and Aurelia is laughing, and Chen Si is looking at his wife instead of the camera, and behind them the black car carries her name in gold, with a stripe of rubber through the last letter.

✦ ✦ ✦

He drove them home himself. For a while she didn’t say anything, watching the lights run over the windscreen. Her hands weren’t cold any more.

“She really won,” she said.

“She did.”

“When we were small she used to line up toy cars on the kitchen floor and make me announce the winner.”

“Did she always win?”

“Always. Not because she was faster. She just wouldn’t accept any result she didn’t like.”

“That sounds familiar.”

“Are you saying I’m difficult?”

“I’m saying there’s a family resemblance.” He changed lanes. “You can look after her without choosing every turn she takes. And you can be proud of her without answering for whatever she does next.”

“That’s harder.”

“I know.”

She put her hand on his thigh. “Did you mean it? That you’d stop being polite?”

“Yes.”

“Don’t let her turn you into somebody you don’t want to be.”

He lifted her hand and kissed her knuckles. “I won’t.”

At the next red light she leaned across, and he turned to meet her, and kissed her, slowly, his hand moving from the wheel to her cheek, until the car behind them sounded its horn.

“You didn’t call me your queen today,” she said, as they pulled away.

“Did you want me to?”

“I’m observing its absence.”

“An important distinction.”

“Very.”

“Not today,” said Chen Si. “I’ve something planned for Christmas.”

“You’re terrible at surprises. You once had Qian deliver a present to the shop while I was standing next to him.”

“That was efficient.”

“That was ridiculous.”

“This will be better.”

“Drive faster,” said Aurelia.

“Why?”

“Because I’d like to kiss you without worrying about the road,” she said, and he laughed, and drove a little faster, and kept the words for Christmas.

chapters.title: My Queen Is Not a Title
chapters.desc: Aurelia wears a dress of gold to her mother’s Christmas party, and Chen Si calls her his queen in front of Fu Jianguo. Upstairs, in her old room, he makes her watch herself in the mirror.
chapters.epigraph: “She doesn’t need my name. She has her own.”
chapters.content:
The dress weighed four kilograms. Aurelia had weighed it herself, twice. The second time Enzo had taken the scales away and told her that if she was determined to carry a whole collection on her body she could at least stop checking whether it was four or four point one.

On Christmas night she stood in front of the long mirror in her dressing room and looked at it on her. Gold. Not champagne gold, not the warm yellow of an ordinary evening dress. Something deeper, almost molten under the lamps. Thousands of tiny gold elements fixed one by one to a structured silk foundation, overlapping like scales, so the light ran over her whenever she breathed. A close bodice. A restrained neck. A skirt that fell straight and opened a little at the back so she could walk.

Four kilograms of gold. Four kilograms of work. Four kilograms of the woman she’d spent years becoming.

“Well?” she said.

Chen Si was on the edge of the bed doing up his cufflinks, and had been watching her for some minutes without a word. He finished the second one and stood.

“Turn round.”

“I just did.”

“Again.”

She turned. He came up behind her in the glass, in black, his shirt very white.

“You haven’t said anything.”

“I’m looking.”

“At the dress?”

“No.”

He put his hands at her waist, very lightly, because of the work. “Can you walk in it? Sit? Climb stairs?”

“I designed it. I know how it moves.”

“Then I have no objections.”

“That was not the compliment I was waiting for.”

He looked at her for a long moment in the mirror. “I think everyone at your mother’s party will spend the night trying to decide whether that dress is made of gold, or whether you’ve talked the light into staying on you.”

“Better.”

“And I intend to stand very close to you all evening.”

“Because you’re proud of my dress?”

“Because I’m selfish,” said Chen Si.

✦ ✦ ✦

Vittoria’s Christmas party at the house on the Peak had never once in its history been asked to consider a budget. White roses and winter branches all the way up the drive. A tree in the hall as tall as the staircase, hung with crystal. An orchestra under a ceiling of warm lights. It wasn’t really a family gathering. There were too many associates and too many people whose invitations depended on what they were for. But the Song name was on the cards, and this year Aurelia had decided to come. Not because her mother had asked. Not to be forgiven. Because she wanted to.

When she stepped out of the car the guests nearest the door turned, and the dress caught the lights of the porch, and the talk around them faltered, and somebody said her name.

“You’re making an entrance,” said Chen Si.

“I walked through a door.”

“An expensive door.”

“Your observations are getting less intelligent,” said Aurelia, and took his arm.

A woman she knew from the trade came at her across the hall, the same woman who’d once offered her a price for her first collection so insulting that Aurelia had suggested she try something in plastic.

“Aurelia. You look extraordinary. Is that from the new collection?”

“It’s a private piece.”

“You must tell me when you make something like it.”

Chen Si stood at her side with one hand at the small of her back and didn’t say a word while she explained the dress: how the weight was spread, how the elements were fixed so the silk could still move. He didn’t answer anything for her.

“You must be very proud of your wife’s work, Mr. Chen.”

“I am,” he said, looking at Aurelia.

✦ ✦ ✦

Fu Jianguo was by the tree.

Dark suit, a glass of champagne, hair gone almost entirely silver. Age had softened the edges of his face and taken nothing from the authority he expected people to give him. Aurelia saw him first. Then Chen Si did, and for a moment the noise of the party seemed to draw back a long way.

Fu saw them coming. She watched something calculate behind his eyes. He lifted his glass an inch.

“Chen Si.”

Chen Si walked past him.

He didn’t turn his head. He didn’t slow. He didn’t so much as let his eyes rest on the man for the length of a breath. He walked past Fu Jianguo as he’d have walked past a pillar, with his wife on his arm, and kept going.

Aurelia felt the change in his body, small and absolute, through his sleeve. She looked back once. Fu had lowered his glass. For the first time that evening he looked as though he didn’t know whether to follow them.

She knew what it cost her husband to be in a room with that man. She also knew he hadn’t come here to give Fu Jianguo the gift of seeing him react.

Her father was in the drawing room with a group of men. He saw her and smiled. Not a large smile. Not the kind of public display her mother would have counted as enough. But real.

“You made this?”

“Yes.”

He looked at the work for a long time. “It’s beautiful.”

A man beside him turned. “Mr. Chen, I hear the bridge agreement’s been signed at last. That must have been quite a negotiation. Your influence certainly helped.”

“No,” said Chen Si.

The man paused.

“It was signed because Aurelia understood exactly what was being negotiated, what her father’s company needed, and what it could afford to give. She built the case. She dealt with Fu Kang. She got the signature. I helped where she asked me to. The credit is hers.”

“With the Chen name behind her, of course,” said someone at her father’s elbow, smiling.

“She doesn’t need my name. She has her own.”

“Impressive.”

“More than that.” His hand moved from her back to her waist, and his voice stayed level and carried exactly as far as the men round them. “She’s the most capable person in this house tonight.”

He looked at her.

“And she is my queen.”

It didn’t land like a claim of ownership. It didn’t land like a title he’d conferred on her. It landed like a thing he’d always known and had simply decided, tonight, to say aloud in her mother’s drawing room. For a moment she forgot where she was. His thumb moved once at her waist, and he turned back to the conversation as though nothing had happened. Somebody laughed, warmly. Somebody lifted a glass. Her father looked at her with pride, and with something very like relief.

“You’re using the title in public now?” she murmured.

“Only when it’s appropriate.”

“And who decides when it’s appropriate?”

“You do.”

“Good answer.”

Two hours later Fu Jianguo collected his coat from the hall, spoke a few words to a man from the finance ministry, and left. He hadn’t come near Chen Si again. He hadn’t congratulated Aurelia, or spoken to her father.

“Do you feel anything?” she said, watching the door close behind him.

“Nothing I want to give him.”

She slid her hand into his. “Then don’t. Come upstairs with me. My old room.”

His eyebrows went up a fraction. “Is that an invitation?”

“Don’t sound so pleased with yourself.”

“I’m trying not to.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The upstairs corridor was quiet, the orchestra muffled behind closed doors, fairy lights wound along the banister and a bank of white lilies on the landing. The dress made a soft metallic whisper with every step. At the last door she stopped with her hand on the handle and didn’t open it.

“Do you want me to come in?” he said.

“Yes.”

It hadn’t changed as much as she’d expected. The same ivory walls, the same cream curtains she’d chosen at seventeen, the long desk under the window, the carved mirror, and a bed that looked far too small to belong to the woman standing in the doorway.

“I haven’t been in here for years,” she said.

“Did you like it?”

“When I was younger. Now it feels like a room someone’s keeping for a girl who doesn’t live here any more.”

On the desk was a little wooden box. In it a few old hair clips, a broken bracelet, and a thin silver ring she’d worn at fifteen. She turned the ring in her fingers.

“I thought if I got far enough, she’d have to love me. Tonight she barely looked at the dress.”

“She looked at it.”

“How do you know?”

“I watched her watch you come in.”

Aurelia was quiet. “She used to draw dresses,” she said. “I found them in her wardrobe when I was little. On the backs of receipts and envelopes. Evening dresses, coats. They were beautiful. I’ve never told anyone that.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She went down to the landing for a moment to fetch her wrap from the cloakroom, and her mother was there by the window with a glass of champagne she hadn’t touched. Vittoria looked at the dress. For a second something passed over her face that Aurelia had no name for.

“You made it yourself?”

“Yes.”

“Four kilograms?”

Aurelia blinked. “Four.”

“That’s a great deal of metal to carry.”

“I designed it to spread the weight.”

“Of course you did.” A silence. Then, looking at the glass and not at her daughter: “I wanted to be a designer once.”

Aurelia had braced for a criticism. Too heavy, too much, too showy for a woman her age. She hadn’t braced for this.

“I know,” she said. “I found your sketches.”

Vittoria’s face changed. “You were too young to understand them.”

“I understood they were beautiful.”

Her mother looked away, somewhere a long way off. “My father said I’d never make a living. My mother said a woman needed a husband. I was told I had more important things to do.” A small laugh. “So I became very good at making other people do what I thought was best.”

Aurelia said nothing.

“When you opened your shop I thought you were being foolish. I thought you’d fail and come home.”

“You wanted me to give it up.”

“I wanted you to be safe.”

“Those aren’t always the same thing.”

They stood on the stairs with twenty-four years between them, none of it said. Then Vittoria asked, very quietly, “Do you think I could have done it?”

It was so unlike her that Aurelia almost didn’t recognise it for a question. She looked at the woman who’d measured her posture and her smile and her marks and made her believe love was a thing you could be examined for and fail.

“Yes,” she said carefully. “Talent doesn’t vanish because you stop using it. But you’d have had to want it enough to make it yours.”

Her mother didn’t answer.

“Goodnight, Mother.”

“Aurelia.” She stopped. “The dress is beautiful.”

“Thank you,” said Aurelia. It wasn’t an apology. It didn’t undo anything. It was something her mother had almost never said, and she left it where it was and went back up the stairs.

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Si had taken off his jacket and folded it over a chair. He met her eyes in the old mirror.

“Everything all right?”

“She told me she wanted to be a designer.” She came and stood beside him. “I think she spent so long regretting what she didn’t do that she couldn’t bear to watch me do it. Tonight she looked at my dress. Not like a mother. Like a designer.”

“Then perhaps for a moment she saw something she’d once wanted,” he said, and touched the gold at her shoulder. “May I help you out of it?”

“Carefully. Enzo spent three days on the back. If you break anything you can explain it to him.”

“I’d rather negotiate with Fu Jianguo again.”

She laughed and turned her back to him. He started on the tiny fastenings at her shoulders, slowly, and when one clasp wouldn’t come he stopped and asked her to turn a little, and in the glass she watched his face. The same concentration he gave a ledger, or a chessboard, or a problem he had no intention of leaving unsolved.

“You’re very serious.”

“This dress is expensive.”

“I made it.”

“That makes it more expensive.”

One by one the fastenings came undone. He helped her step out of it and laid it over the padded chair so that none of the work was folded or pressed. She stood in front of the mirror in her silk slip. Without the gold she looked smaller. Younger. The room behind her was still the room she’d grown up in.

He stood behind her with his hands at her waist. “Look at yourself.”

“Chen Si.”

“Not the dress. Do you know what I saw when you walked into that hall? A woman who’d made a thing nobody else could make, walking into a house where people once made her feel small, and not asking anyone to move aside for her.”

“Your queen?”

“Don’t look away.” He tipped her chin up with one finger. “You’re not my queen because I call you one. I call you one because I know who you are. You don’t need the gold. You don’t need that room downstairs to recognise you. You don’t need anyone.”

She turned round in his arms and loosened his tie.

“You’re very good at this.”

“At what?”

“Making me cry.”

“I’ll try to be less effective.”

“Don’t,” she said, and pulled him down by the tie and kissed him.

He kissed her slowly, one hand at her waist and one at the back of her neck, without any weight in it at all, and when she drew back for breath he rested his forehead on hers.

“Still all right?”

“Very.”

“Tell me if that changes.”

In the carved mirror they were his dark shirt and her pale silk and the old ivory room, the girl she’d been and the woman she’d become. For once she didn’t examine herself for flaws. She watched how he held her. He slid the straps of the slip off her shoulders and let it fall, and stood behind her with his mouth on the side of her neck and his hands on her bare skin, one spread over her stomach and one over her breast, and made her keep her eyes on the glass. “Look at yourself,” he said again, and she did, while his hand moved lower and her knees went, until she had to hold the edge of the dressing table and couldn’t look at anything. He took her to the narrow bed she’d slept in at sixteen and made love to her slowly in it, with her old curtains drawn and the music coming up through the floor, his weight on her and his eyes on hers, until she put her hand over her own mouth so the house wouldn’t hear. The gold dress lay over the chair. The orchestra played on downstairs. And in the room where she’d once dreamed of becoming someone worth loving, he loved her without asking her to become anything at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

Much later there was a knock.

“Miss Aurelia?”

Pina, who’d been housekeeper on the Peak since Aurelia was fifteen. Chen Si’s collar was open and his tie was somewhere near the dressing table. His mouth curved.

“Don’t,” said Aurelia, pulling on her robe.

“I’m not doing anything.”

“You’re smiling.”

She opened the door a few inches. Pina stood there with a small silver tray, and her eyes took in Aurelia’s face, and the room behind her, and the man in it, and her own face didn’t change at all. She was a sensible woman.

“Your father asks whether you’ll be coming down for dessert.”

Aurelia looked back once at Chen Si, then at Pina.

“No. Tell him I’m upstairs with my husband.”

“Of course, Miss.” A hesitation. “Merry Christmas.”

“Merry Christmas, Pina.”

She shut the door and stood with her hand on it.

“What?” she said. He was watching her.

“I like hearing you say it.”

“Say what?”

“Your husband.”

“Well,” said Aurelia, coming back to him, “he is.”

“Fortunately.”

Downstairs her family was eating dessert under the lights. Her mother would be speaking to guests. Her father might be wondering whether she’d come down after all. She wasn’t a little girl waiting to hear her name called. She wasn’t a daughter waiting to be approved of. She wasn’t a title, or a dress, or a business arrangement. She was Aurelia, and she was upstairs, in her husband’s arms, exactly where she wanted to be.

“Merry Christmas, my queen,” said Chen Si into her hair.

“Merry Christmas, Chen Si.”

chapters.title: A Snake in the Syndicate
chapters.desc: Someone parks a lorry across the coast road in front of Zhao’s car. Chen Si comes home with shaking hands, knowing Sun Wei sold his diary, and decides to go to Sun Wei’s New Year’s Eve dinner anyway.
chapters.epigraph: “Zhendong doesn’t brake.”
chapters.content:
At two in the morning on the Saturday after Christmas the coast road at Lantern Bay was empty. The sea was a dark, restless shape beyond the rail, and the lamps stood far apart, with long stretches of black between them.

Zhao drove with one hand on the wheel. Chen Si sat beside him. They’d spent the evening at the Docks over a shipment that didn’t add up, and it should have taken an hour, and Chen Si had stayed until one.

“You’re quiet,” said Zhao.

“I’m thinking.”

“That’s usually when somebody gets hurt.”

“You’re becoming sentimental.”

“I’m becoming sensible. There’s a difference.”

Then Zhao’s face changed. Headlights round the bend ahead. Too high. Too wide. Not moving.

A lorry was parked across the road on the diagonal, its trailer filling nearly the whole of their lane. There was a gap on the left wide enough for something small. Not for them, at this speed. And behind the lorry, a second set of lights came on. A car. Waiting.

“Down,” said Zhao, and didn’t touch the brake, and wrenched the wheel.

Chen Si’s hand hit the dashboard. The tyres screamed. The wing mirror struck the trailer and went, and metal shrieked down the whole of the passenger side, and one wheel dropped onto the gravel. Zhao caught it, and put his foot down, and forced the car through the gap before the lorry could roll forward. Something heavy hit the back of them. The rear window went white with cracks. Zhao didn’t look round. He drove. The road bent hard along the coast and the car slid on the loose stuff and found the tarmac again.

“How many?”

“One behind. I don’t know about the lorry.”

Chen Si’s phone was already at his ear. “Qian. Lantern Bay. The coast road, northbound. A lorry across it and one car behind us.”

“Are you hurt?”

“No. Send the nearest team. I want the lorry and its registration, the driver held and questioned, and nobody touching it until it’s been photographed.”

Zhao took the next bend so hard the seat belts locked, and the lights behind them dropped away and didn’t come back. For a few seconds there was only the engine and the sound of tyres on wet road. Then Zhao let out a breath.

“Well. That was rude.”

Chen Si looked at him. There was blood running down his brother’s right forearm from a cut the glass had made. Chen Si laughed, short and without any humour in it at all. Then he looked down at his own hands. They were steady. For now.

✦ ✦ ✦

The lorry belonged to a small haulier with three vehicles and a yard near the bay. By three its owner had been got out of bed. By four he was sitting under strip lights in an office at the Docks, sweating, while two of Chen Si’s people asked him why his lorry had been parked across a public road at two in the morning. He said it had been stolen. Then that the driver had taken it without asking. Then that he’d never seen the driver in his life.

Chen Si listened once, through the glass, without raising his voice.

“Find out who paid him. Question the driver. Write everything down. If he’s committed a crime, the police can have him once we’ve finished.”

“And the haulier?”

The man had contracts with three of their warehouses, a port subcontractor and two transport firms. He’d done business with Chen Si’s people for years.

“Cancel every contract we hold with him. Freeze everything we owe him pending a legal review. Tell every partner he has that he’s under investigation for his part in an attempt on my life.”

“That will finish him,” said Qian.

“He chose to put a lorry across a road with two men in a car coming round the bend,” said Chen Si. “Let him explain his business decisions to whoever paid him for them.”

The driver, when they reached him, said he’d been paid in cash in a multi-storey car park by a man he never saw properly. He remembered only that the man had sat in the back of a dark car and that, when he leaned forward to hand over the envelope, a pair of reading glasses had swung loose on a cord round his neck.

Zhao came in from the corridor with a bandage up his forearm.

“Go home,” he said.

“You’re hurt.”

“It’s a scratch. I’ve had it cleaned.”

“Then you go home.”

Zhao looked at him for a long moment. “She’ll be awake.”

It was the first thing anybody had said all night that made Chen Si move.

✦ ✦ ✦

The flat was dark when he let himself in, except for the tree in the corner, still lit, throwing soft gold over everything. Aurelia had fallen asleep on the sofa with a book open on her chest and the television muted and a half-drunk cup of tea gone cold on the low table.

He stood in the doorway and didn’t move.

He’d spent two hours making decisions. Who was responsible, who’d be questioned, which men would lose everything they had by morning. He hadn’t been frightened doing any of it. Not the way he’d been on the coast road, when the lights came round the bend. Because his first thought then hadn’t been about the Syndicate. It had been about the woman asleep on this sofa. The one who’d told him to drive faster because she wanted to kiss him. The one who’d cried at a racetrack because her sister won. The one who’d wake up expecting him to have come home.

He touched her shoulder. She stirred.

“Chen Si?”

“I’m here.”

She sat up and pushed her hair back and looked at him properly. Dirt on his coat. A graze along his jaw. One shirt cuff torn half off. “Why are you so late?”

He opened his mouth, and nothing came out.

“What happened?”

“A lorry on the coast road. Across it. Somebody tried to stop the car.”

Her face went white. “Who was in the car?”

“Zhao and me. It hit the back of us. I’m fine.”

“How did you get past it?”

“Zhendong doesn’t brake.”

She reached for his hands. That was when she felt it.

They were shaking. Not much. Not enough for anyone across a room to see. But they were trembling against hers, and she turned them over one at a time and looked at them, and stopped breathing.

They hadn’t shaken on the road. They hadn’t shaken on the phone to Qian, or in the office at the Docks, or while he decided to ruin a man. They’d started when he walked into his own home and saw her asleep, and understood how close he’d come to not seeing her again.

“Look at me,” said Aurelia. “You’re home. You’re here. You’re not on that road any more.” She pressed his palms flat against her chest. “Stay with me.”

He looked at her. His hands went on shaking. She put both arms round him and pulled him in, and he let her, and sat with his face against her shoulder and his hands caught between them, and she rubbed his back, slowly, over and over.

“Zhao?”

“Some glass. He’s all right.”

“Thank God.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was several minutes before he spoke again.

“Sun Wei.”

She drew back.

“Whoever put that lorry there knew exactly when we’d leave the Docks and which road we’d take. Three people know my evenings that well. Qian. Zhao. And the senior men who share the management calendars. Sun Wei sees them.”

“Sun Wei,” said Aurelia, very quietly. Then her face changed. “The grey saloon. September.”

His face went still.

“We never found out who hired the investigator. It turned up just after the furniture money started going missing. Somebody was watching me before we knew who was behind the account. Somebody who knew my shops, and my hours, and my car.” She stood up; the silk of her robe shifted round her legs. “He brought me orchids. He sat at our table every Sunday and passed the soy sauce.”

“We don’t know he hired the man himself.”

“But he gave them what they needed.”

“We have to find out exactly what he gave.”

She looked at him, and the rest of it came together in her face all at once. The calendars. The coast road. The grey car. The orchids.

“You were nearly killed.”

“I’m here.”

“You were nearly killed,” she said, and her voice broke on it, and she was crying, not quietly, so hard she couldn’t get a breath. He caught her. She pressed both fists against his chest.

“I was asleep. I was asleep, and you were out there, and I didn’t know.”

“You couldn’t have known.”

“I should have known something was wrong—“

“No, sweetheart. You did nothing wrong.”

He sat back down and pulled her into his lap, and she folded against him with her arms round his neck and her knees tucked against his hips, and cried into his shoulder, and he held her and let her.

When at last she lifted her face her cheeks were wet and her nose was red.

“Promise me something. Don’t ever make me find out about something like this from someone else. And don’t tell me you’re fine when you’re not.”

“I’ll try.”

“No. Promise.”

He wiped a tear off her cheek with his thumb. “I promise to tell you when I’m frightened.”

It seemed to cost him more than the graze on his face.

“Were you?” she said. “Frightened?”

He was quiet for a long time. Then he nodded.

She kissed him. It wasn’t gentle. It shook. It had everything in it she couldn’t say, and her hands went over his shoulders and his face and his hair as if she were checking him, piece by piece, for proof that he was real and breathing. He kissed her back as if the same fear had finally found somewhere to go.

“I hate this,” she said against his mouth. “I hate that there are people who can decide to put a lorry in front of your car.”

“I don’t want you to carry it.”

She laughed, broken. “Too late.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Her hands found his shirt buttons, still unsteady. He caught her wrist, gently.

“Look at me. You’re upset. We can stay like this. I can just hold you.”

“I want you to hold me.”

“I am.”

“Then don’t let go.” She touched his face. “I need to feel you here. Not on that road. Not in some office. Here.”

“Still yes?”

“Yes.”

There was no contract between them that night. No clause, no silk, no word agreed in advance, no title. Only a woman who’d woken to find her husband’s hands shaking, and a man who’d spent the night believing he might not come home to her. She got his shirt open and pushed it off him and put her mouth on his chest, over his heart, to feel it going, and he pulled her nightdress over her head and dropped it on the floor among the wrapping paper. They came together on the sofa under the lights of the tree, clumsy with urgency and with tenderness, her knees either side of his hips, his hands shaking on her back and then not shaking, stopping only to breathe and to touch and to make sure the other was still there. When she took him inside her she held his face in both hands and wouldn’t let him close his eyes. She moved slowly at first and then with no care for anything, the tree lights sliding gold over his skin, until she shuddered and pressed her forehead to his and felt him follow her with a sound like something breaking open. For a long time afterwards neither of them said anything at all, and outside the city stayed dark.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was nearly eight when she woke, lying on his chest under a blanket with one leg tangled in his. She lay still and listened to him breathe. Steady. Warm. Here.

He opened his eyes. “Morning.”

“How are your hands?”

He turned one palm up. She put hers against it. “Better,” he said.

She kissed the scar across it. Then his mouth.

“You’re checking.”

“Very thoroughly.”

His phone buzzed on the table. Neither of them moved. It buzzed again.

“Leave it,” he said.

“Your empire can survive ten minutes.”

It buzzed a third time and he reached for it.

Sun Wei: Mr. Chen, I heard there was an incident near Lantern Bay last night. I hope you and Mr. Zhao are both unharmed. These roads have become so dangerous. Please let me know if there’s anything at all I can do.

He showed her. Her face went perfectly still.

“How thoughtful.”

“He wants to know whether it worked.”

“Then shall we tell him you’re alive?”

“Not yet.”

She smiled without any warmth at all. “No. Not yet.”

It buzzed again.

Sun Wei: I’d hoped you and Mrs. Chen might join us for New Year’s Eve. I’ve booked the Pearl, as always. It would be good to put the difficulties of this year behind us and begin the new one on better terms.

“The Pearl,” said Aurelia.

“He’s inviting us to dinner.”

“Two days after somebody tried to kill you.”

“An unfortunate coincidence.”

She gave him a look, and he very nearly smiled.

“He wants to see whether you know,” she said. “Or whether you suspect him.”

“Yes.”

“Are you going?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

He raised an eyebrow. “Good?”

“Of course we’re going.” Her face had become almost pleasant. She picked up her own phone. “He’s booked the boat. It would be rude not to tell him what we’ll be drinking.”

“You’re choosing the wine. Already.”

“I’m choosing all of it.” She scrolled the Pearl’s list. “And I’ll have it delivered, and sealed, and counted, and I’ll keep the key.”

“You’re enjoying this.”

“Not in the least.”

“You look pleased.”

“Would you prefer I cried?”

“No.”

“Then let me choose.” She turned to him. “We’re going to dinner. We’re going to let him welcome us. And we’re going to find out exactly how much he’s sold, without letting him see that we know.”

He lifted her hand and kissed the inside of her wrist.

“My wife,” he said.

“Your very expensive wife.”

“Extremely.”

She leaned back against him. The tree was still lit in the corner. The phone lay on the table with the snake’s invitation glowing on it, and Aurelia, who had learned from her mother how to smile at a table full of people she despised, had already decided which bottles to open.

chapters.title: The Glass of Wine at the Harbour Dinner
chapters.desc: New Year’s Eve on a boat called the Pearl. She chooses the wine. She opens every bottle herself. At midnight he takes her glass, because he only drinks what he takes. Twenty minutes later, his hand starts to shake.
chapters.epigraph: “I’ll come home with you.”
chapters.content:
Aurelia bought forty bottles of wine. Not thirty-nine. Not forty-one. Forty.

She had them delivered to the Pearl three days before New Year’s Eve. Each bottle was checked against its invoice and resealed in front of the boat’s manager. The labels were photographed. The delivery notes were copied. The cellar was counted and signed for by two people who’d never been in a room with Sun Wei. And the key to it hung on a fine gold chain round her wrist.

“You do know most people just bring a bottle to dinner?” said Chen Si.

She was standing in the Pearl’s dining room on the last afternoon of the year, looking at the glasses on the long table. “Most people aren’t having dinner with a man who may have arranged to have their husband killed on Saturday.”

“That’s fair.”

“Don’t sound so pleased.”

“I’m pleased you have a plan.”

“I have several.”

The Pearl had been the Syndicate’s New Year’s boat for longer than he’d run it: an old teak motor yacht, long and low, refitted with a dining saloon for forty and a covered deck at the stern, moored off the harbour wall with a launch at the ladder. Sun Wei had booked it, as he did every year. He’d chosen the guests. He’d sent three messages since Lantern Bay asking after Chen Si’s health. Aurelia hadn’t answered any of them. She’d chosen the wine.

He took her hand. “You’re worried.”

“Of course I’m worried.”

“I won’t let anything happen to you.”

“That isn’t the same as promising nothing will happen to you.”

“I know.”

“Then don’t make promises you can’t keep.”

He lifted her knuckles to his mouth. “I’ll come home with you.”

It wasn’t quite a promise. It was the one she wanted.

✦ ✦ ✦

The guests came aboard after eight. Sun Wei met each one at the top of the gangway in a dark blue suit with his reading glasses on their cord, and a face of such warm concern it might have been practised in a mirror.

“Mr. Chen. I’m so glad. I was afraid you might still be shaken after that dreadful business on the coast.”

“I’m well.”

“Excellent. Excellent.” He turned. “Mrs. Chen. You look beautiful. I hope the wine was satisfactory?”

“Very.”

“Your choice, I believe? Then I look forward to it.”

His eyes went, for less than a second, to the gold chain at her wrist and the little brass key lying against her skin. His smile didn’t move.

She noticed through the first hour that he never once stood near Chen Si for more than a moment. He spoke to Qian. He greeted Zhao, whose arm was still bandaged under his sleeve. He congratulated a man from the port on his promotion. But each time Chen Si came into a conversation, Sun Wei found a reason to be somewhere else. It was almost elegant.

“He’s avoiding you,” she said.

“Yes.”

“Does he think you’re angry?”

“Probably.”

“Are you?”

“Would it help if I said no?”

“No.”

“Then yes,” said Chen Si, and ran his thumb over the back of her hand. “Stay close to me tonight.”

“I was planning to.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They sat down at nine, forty of them, and the Pearl slid out past the harbour wall with its engines barely audible under the talk. The city lay along the water in a long glittering line. Sun Wei sat at the far end of the table. Chen Si sat beside her. Zhao was opposite, beside Qian.

Sun Wei stood up with his glass and made a toast. To stability. To working together. To putting old disagreements behind them in the new year. Everyone lifted a glass. Chen Si lifted his water.

“Mr. Chen, no wine?”

“Not tonight.”

“Of course. After the coast road, one learns to be careful.”

“One does.”

“To a safer year,” said Aurelia, and the table echoed her.

She watched Sun Wei over the rim of her glass, and he wasn’t watching her husband. He was watching her. Her glass. Where she put it down.

At eleven she stood by the bar with Qian.

“All forty bottles,” he said quietly. “Every seal whole when the cellar was opened. Every bottle opened in front of whoever asked for it.”

“Good. Keep the rest unopened.”

Sun Wei was by the windows talking to the man from the port. His eyes went to the table. To her place. Then away.

“He’s watching my glass,” she said.

“I noticed. He hasn’t touched it.”

“Keep watching.”

She went back to Chen Si and didn’t tell him. Not to keep a secret. Because she wanted one more minute to understand what she was seeing.

“Come outside,” he said.

On the covered deck at the stern the harbour wind was less fierce. He’d brought her coat and he put it round her shoulders, and she leaned on the rail and looked at the lights on the water.

“When this is over,” he said, “I want to take you somewhere quiet.”

“That sounds suspiciously like a holiday.”

“It is.”

“With no telephone calls?”

“I’ll consider it.”

“Chen Si.”

“No telephone calls.”

“Then I want a good breakfast. And a bath. And a street full of jewellers.”

“Of course,” he said, and kissed her, once, softly, and they went back in.

✦ ✦ ✦

At two minutes to midnight the guests gathered at the long windows. Waiters went round with trays of fresh flutes, champagne poured that minute from the bottles Aurelia had chosen, opened at the bar in front of whoever stood nearest. A boy of nineteen in a white jacket put a glass into her hand. She looked at it. Sealed bottle. Opened in front of her. Poured in front of her. Nothing in it she could see.

Sun Wei came across the saloon.

“Mr. Chen. Mrs. Chen. A wonderful evening. May I congratulate you on the wine, Mrs. Chen? Perhaps your husband might be persuaded to try a little, now. It’s nearly midnight.”

The countdown began at the far end of the room.

Ten.

She hadn’t drunk from the glass. She didn’t have to offer it. She never had to, with him. Since the first night, since a beer on a step outside a paper-offerings shop, he’d taken her drink out of her hand whenever he wanted to annoy her, and he did it now, the way he always did, smiling.

Seven.

“I only drink what I take,” said Chen Si, and took the glass out of her fingers.

Five.

He drank.

One.

The saloon went up in cheering. Fireworks broke over the harbour, gold and red on the black water. He put the glass down on the sill and pulled her in.

“Happy New Year, sweetheart.”

“Happy New Year.”

He kissed her with his hand firm at her waist, and then again. “To another year.”

“To another year.”

She picked up the glass to finish it and saw it was nearly empty, and put it back down.

✦ ✦ ✦

At nineteen minutes past twelve his hand began to shake.

He was listening to Zhao. She saw him close his fingers. She saw the tremor come back. He looked down at his hand as if it belonged to somebody else.

“Chen Si?”

“Something’s wrong,” he said, very quietly.

She moved closer. The colour was going out of his face as she watched. He looked at her, and for the first time in the fifteen months she’d known him she saw something in his eyes that turned her blood to water. Not fear. Not yet. Confusion.

“Don’t,” he said under his breath, as her hand came up. “Not in front of them.”

His fingers closed on her wrist, hard. His breathing had gone shallow and wrong. And one part of her mind looked at his face, and another heard the party roaring round them, and a third, cold and quite separate, went looking for the reason.

Not the wine. She’d watched every bottle. Not the bottle. Forty people had drunk from those bottles and were laughing at the windows.

The glass.

The glass that had been put into her hand two minutes to midnight. The rim. Where his mouth had been. Where hers would have been, if she’d drunk first. And somebody had known, with absolute certainty, that she wouldn’t. Somebody who’d sat at their table every Sunday for three years and watched him take her drink out of her hand and laugh.

“Zhao,” she said, and her voice came out strange. “The glass on the sill. Nobody touches it.”

Zhao looked once and understood. “Qian.”

Across the room Qian was already moving.

Then she looked up, and saw Sun Wei by the windows, quite still, watching. If the room knew Chen Si had been poisoned, Sun Wei would know that she knew.

So she laughed.

A small, bright, silly sound that had no business anywhere near her husband’s grey face. “Honestly, Chen Si.” She pushed his hair back off his forehead. “You’re making a scene. My husband,” she said to the faces turning towards them, “has had far too much champagne.”

“He’s tired,” said Zhao, taking the other side of him.

She put her arm round his waist and her face against his shoulder and walked him through the guests as if they were leaving any party at all, laughing into his coat, her heart going so hard she could hardly hear.

Sun Wei took one step towards them. “Mr. Chen? Can I arrange—“

“No, thank you,” said Aurelia, smiling. “He’s fine. Just tired.”

The saloon doors opened. The cold came in off the water. The moment they were through, the smile went off her face as though she’d wiped it.

On the stern deck, out of sight of the windows, his knees went.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao caught him before he hit the boards and took him up over his shoulder in one movement and went down the ladder to the launch, in the dark, one-handed, with a bandaged arm, faster than she’d ever seen anyone move. She came down after them with her shoes in her hand.

“Put him down. Down.”

Zhao laid him on the padded bench. She knelt on the wet floor of the launch beside him.

“Chen Si. Open your eyes.”

Nothing. She pressed two fingers to his wrist. There was a pulse. Thin. Uneven. Wrong.

“Ring Dr. Ma.”

“Done. He’s coming to the marina.”

The launch’s engine roared and the Pearl’s lights fell away behind them. She held his hand in both of hers. She put his palm against her cheek. “Listen to me. You said you’d come home with me. You said.”

Then his whole body went rigid, and his hand slid out of hers.

She checked his wrist. She pressed harder. Nothing.

“No,” she said. “No, no, no—“

“Aurelia—“

“Ring him again!”

Zhao shouted their position into the phone and dropped on his knees on the other side of the bench and began doing what the voice on the line told him, and she put her hands where he put them, and the world narrowed to the space between her hands on her husband’s chest. She knew enough to know this was far beyond anything she could mend. She counted anyway. Without deciding to. In Italian, because it was the language he’d learned for her, the one he’d said lo prometto in, in a courtyard by a canal.

“Uno. Due. Tre.”

She thought of his coat on a balcony. Quattro. His king lying on its side on a chessboard. Cinque. His voice in her mother’s drawing room: She is my queen. Sei. “Chen Si.” Sette. “Please.”

At some point she realised she was crying. She didn’t stop counting.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dr. Ma was on the marina steps with a team and a trolley. The moment the launch touched they were aboard, and somebody’s hands took hers off his chest, gently, and somebody said, “Madam, we need room.”

“He’s not breathing.”

“We know. Step back, please.”

Dr. Ma had known Chen Si for ten years. He’d stitched him after nights that never went into any hospital record. His face now was nothing but professional. For one second his eyes met hers, and she understood exactly how bad it was.

In the ambulance she held his hand. It was cold. She held it anyway. At the hospital a nurse stopped her at the doors.

“Please wait here.”

“I’m his wife.”

“I know. We need to treat him.”

The doors closed. She stood in the white corridor. Her hands had begun to shake now. On the inside of her wrist was a red mark where his fingers had held her before he fell.

Zhao came up beside her with his bandage soaked through. “Qian has the glass. The bottle, the table, all of it photographed. The guests are being kept apart. The police have been called.”

“Sun Wei?”

“Still on the boat.”

“Good.”

“Sit down.”

“No.”

He didn’t argue. After a while she said, “He was looking at me. On the boat. He was trying to tell me he was still there.” And she cried again, not loudly, not the way she’d cried at the racetrack. Smaller and much more frightening, from somewhere words didn’t go. Zhao didn’t tell her to be strong. He didn’t tell her it would be all right. He stood beside her and stayed.

At sixteen minutes to two Dr. Ma came out and pulled off his gloves.

“He’s alive.”

The words didn’t reach her at first. Her knees went, and Zhao’s hand caught her elbow.

“His heart stopped in the launch. We got it going again. It’s a heart poison, from a plant, I think, and if he’d had a full glass he’d have died on that boat. We’ve given him the antidote. He hasn’t answered it well. He’ll be in intensive care. The next hours matter.”

“Can I see him?”

“Not yet.”

“Tell him I’m here,” said Aurelia.

✦ ✦ ✦

At two Qian rang. “The boat’s secure. The guests have been questioned. Sun Wei has asked three times whether Mr. Chen is conscious. He hasn’t asked about the wine. He’s asked about you.”

“Don’t tell him anything. Keep him on the boat until the police have finished. And don’t let him see that we know about the glass.”

She put the phone down. Zhao looked at her.

“You’re going back.”

“If Sun Wei sees me crying, he’ll know.”

He didn’t like it. He understood it. He picked up his coat.

At half past two she walked back up the Pearl’s gangway with her face washed and her hair put up again and her dress, by some miracle, uncreased, and the little brass key lying on its gold chain against her wrist. The guests had been kept in the saloon. Sun Wei turned from the window.

“Mrs. Chen. How is Mr. Chen?”

“Resting.”

“How terrible. I was so concerned.”

“I know,” said Aurelia. She walked past him to the table. Her glass was gone. The bottle was gone. Everything else was exactly where it had been. She turned back to him and smiled.

“Wasn’t it a lovely evening? Your arrangements were perfect. Happy New Year, Sun Wei.”

He looked at her for a moment. Then he returned the smile.

“Happy New Year, Mrs. Chen.”

She stood there, composed, while the city went on celebrating beyond the glass, with her husband behind a set of doors a mile away fighting to stay alive, and the man who’d tried to kill him three yards from her believing he still had charge of the night. She didn’t hate him loudly. She didn’t threaten him. She didn’t let her hands shake. She smiled, and for the first time in her life understood exactly what patience could cost, and decided not to waste a minute of it.

chapters.title: The Week He Couldn’t Get Out of Bed
chapters.desc: A private room on the ninth floor with no name on the door. A heart that won’t keep time. A rumour, by the second of January, that the Don is dying. And a woman in yesterday’s gold, running everything in his name.
chapters.epigraph: “Somebody has to.”
chapters.content:
By seven on the first morning of the year Aurelia had thanked Sun Wei three times. Once on the Pearl, when she told him her husband had drunk too much and needed his bed. Once when he offered a car. Once when he wished Chen Si a quick recovery, and she touched his arm and said he was very kind.

Then she’d gone down the gangway with Zhao, carrying the knowledge that the man who’d poisoned her husband believed she was still a gracious hostess.

Now she stood in a corridor on the ninth floor of a hospital that didn’t put names on its doors. No nameplate. No flowers. No list of visitors where anyone could read it. One of Zhao’s men at each end of the corridor, and a nurse at the desk under orders to let nobody through without Dr. Ma.

She was still in the gold-coloured dress she’d worn to dinner. The hem was creased. Her hair was coming down. She’d washed her face and redone it in the visitors’ toilet, and been sick there first, and there were still shadows under her eyes. She hadn’t slept. She hadn’t eaten. She’d spent the hours since the marina going between the emergency floor, the ward and the telephone, making sure the right people knew the right things and nobody knew anything else.

Dr. Ma came out of the room.

“His circulation’s steadier than it was in the night. He’s in and out. His rhythm hasn’t settled. We’re watching it every second.” He didn’t soften anything. “It’s a cardiac glycoside.
