A plant poison. It interferes with the way the heart beats. We gave him the antidote and at first he barely answered it. We only just got ahead of it.”

“Only just.”

“Yes. The next few days matter.”

“Will he live?”

“We’re doing everything we can.”

It wasn’t the answer she wanted. She knew better than to ask a doctor for a promise.

“Go in,” he said. “Briefly.” He looked at the creased dress and the shadows under her eyes. “And eat something, Mrs. Chen, before I have to give you a bed of your own.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He looked smaller in the bed. That was her first thought. The bed seemed too large round him, with the monitors and the line running under the blanket and the dressing on the back of his hand. His face was the colour of paper. His mouth was dry.

She pulled the chair close and took his hand. It was warm. That was something.

“Happy New Year,” she whispered.

His eyelids moved. Opened a little. For a moment he didn’t seem to know her, and then his eyes settled on her face and his fingers moved against hers.

“Hello,” she said.

“You’re...” It was hardly a breath. “Still... wearing...”

She looked down at the creased gold silk and laughed out loud, a small cracked sound in the quiet room. “I haven’t had time to change.”

He looked at her a little longer, and his eyes closed again. She kissed his knuckles and stayed till the nurse asked her to let him rest.

✦ ✦ ✦

At noon Zhao came up with a clean shirt, a coat and a paper bag of food she didn’t want, and found her outside the room talking to Qian.

“The Docks are waiting for you, Mrs. Chen,” said Qian.

“I’ll go.”

“Not in that,” said Zhao. “You haven’t slept. You haven’t eaten.”

“I’ll sleep later. I’ll eat later.”

She took one step towards the door, and another, and the corridor tilted under her. She put a hand out for the wall and her knees went before she found it. Zhao caught her and put her into a chair.

“I’m fine. I stood up too fast.”

“You’ve been standing for a day and a half.”

Her body had started to shake. The corridor, the white light, all of it went a long way off. He took off his coat and put it round her, and it smelled of tobacco and cold air and the leather of his car. Then he crouched down in front of her with his forearms on his knees and his bandaged arm across them.

“Listen to me. He’s alive. Dr. Ma has him. Qian has the Docks for the next hour. You don’t have to do everything in the same hour.”

“Somebody has to.”

“Yes. Not you, every minute.” He looked at her. “He’s going to need you awake when he wakes up.”

That was what did it. Her face crumpled. She pressed her lips together and tried to keep still, and Zhao didn’t tell her not to cry. He stayed there on his heels in front of her until she could breathe.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the afternoon of the first of January she took his desk.

Not his office. His desk. The one at the harbour office where Qian laid out each day’s papers and Chen Si made decisions that changed the lives of several hundred people. She sat behind it in a black dress borrowed from Qian’s wife, with Zhao’s coat over the back of the chair and, in the handbag by her foot, the small gun Zhao had put there that morning without a word. She didn’t know which of them it was. She only knew it was one of them.

The room was full. Men who’d worked with Chen Si for years along the walls. Men who’d come in later, when the business grew past the old harbour. They were used to Chen Si speaking. They were not used to her.

Director Ko cleared his throat. “Mrs. Chen, we understand Mr. Chen is unwell. Perhaps we should wait until he can attend.”

“He’s in intensive care.”

“We need to know whether it’s serious.”

“It is.” She folded her hands on the desk. “He has severe food poisoning. He’ll stay under his doctors until they’re satisfied. Until then everything already decided stands. Qian runs the days. Zhao has security and the Docks. Anything that needs Chen Si’s own authority comes to me.”

A man by the window frowned. “With respect, an organisation can’t run indefinitely without its head.”

“Then it’s lucky we’re talking about a short arrangement.”

“How short?”

“Until his doctors say.”

“That could be weeks.”

“Then you’ll manage for weeks,” said Aurelia, and opened the first folder. “Furniture.”

The room shifted.

“Sun Wei’s asked for a review of how furniture’s run,” said a senior manager. “He says recent difficulties have shown weaknesses in the arrangement.”

“Has he? Sun Wei’s also handled reports that are now under investigation. So nobody destroys any record, moves any reporting line, or shifts any person without my written say. Any attempt will be treated as interference.”

“Some of these decisions are urgent.”

“Then you should have made them before you started discussing whether my husband could run his own house.”

Nobody answered that. She went on for an hour. She asked questions and listened to the answers. She turned down two proposals and approved one emergency payment after Qian had checked the papers. She didn’t pretend to know everything Chen Si knew. When she didn’t know something, she asked. When somebody tried to use that against her, she asked a better question. By the end of it nobody in the room mistook her for a decoration in his chair.

“You did well,” said Zhao, when they’d gone.

“Did I?”

“Yes. Now go back to the hospital.”

“I will.”

“Now. He’ll ask for you.”

She put the folder down and stood up.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the evening of the second of January the rumour had a shape. The Don was dying.

It started with a careless remark from a man who said he knew a nurse. Then a message in a private group of shippers. Then a telephone call from somebody who hadn’t spoken to Chen Si in six months and wanted to know whether the organisation might welcome outside money. Some said heart attack. Some said poison. One version said he was already dead and they were hiding it until a successor was chosen.

Mr. Yuen brought it to her in the corridor.

“The earliest version I can find came through one of Sun Wei’s old finance men. He’s been telling people we’re vulnerable.” He paused. “And Sun Wei has called a meeting for the fifth. For continuity, he says. To reassure the senior partners.”

“Who’s invited?”

“Department heads. Two of the old representatives. The furniture managers.”

“Zhao?”

“No.”

“Qian?”

“No.”

“Me?”

Mr. Yuen hesitated. “No.”

Aurelia smiled. It wasn’t pleasant. “Then he’s misunderstood something.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That night Chen Si woke properly for the first time.

She was in the chair by the bed with Mr. Yuen’s papers on her knee and heard the small movement and looked up, and his eyes were open.

“Hello,” she said.

“You’re here.”

“Of course I’m here.”

“What time is it?”

“Nearly ten.”

“Work,” he said, and tried to move.

She put her hand flat on his shoulder. “Your house hasn’t fallen down.”

“Sun Wei?”

“We know. He’s called a meeting for the fifth.”

His eyes sharpened. He tried to lift his head from the pillow. She watched the muscles of his neck shake with it. Then his head fell back, and he lay looking at the ceiling, and his jaw set.

“I can’t,” he said.

“You don’t have to.”

“Can’t even—“ His voice went. She bent closer. “Lift my head.”

Then she saw a tear slide out of the corner of his eye and into his hair.

He turned his face away from her, as far as he could, which wasn’t far. Another one followed.

“Don’t look.”

“Look at me.”

“I can’t.”

She understood. Not the weakness alone. The humiliation of it. The terror of not being able to command his own body. Of being the man who could silence a room by lifting his eyes, lying in a bed unable to lift his head off a pillow.

She leaned over him. “Chen Si. You carried me when I couldn’t stand. You held me when I cried in your office over a chessboard. You sat with me while I was frightened. You never once made me feel weak for needing you.” She kissed his forehead. “Now it’s my turn. You don’t have to be useful to me. You don’t have to be strong. You don’t have to get out of this bed or make a single decision. You’re my husband. That’s enough.”

His face broke. She put her cheek down against his and stayed there until his breathing went quiet.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the third of January they let him stay awake longer. His rhythm was still unsteady enough that they watched it every minute, and the smallest movement wore him out. He hated all of it. He hated the monitors. He hated the nurse helping him sit up. Most of all he hated that every man in his organisation now brought their decisions to his wife.

“You’re working,” he said. “Here.”

“Yes.”

“Go home.”

“No.”

“Aurelia.”

“Chen Si.”

“You’re stubborn.”

“Your influence,” said Aurelia. “How do you feel? Pain? Dizzy?”

“A little. I know what Dr. Ma said.”

“Then don’t argue. You’re very hard to look after.”

“You’re doing it badly.”

“Would you like to file a complaint?”

“Yes.”

“Write it yourself.”

He tried to laugh and it hurt him, and she was at his shoulder at once.

“Did you eat?” he said, when he’d got his breath.

“Yes.”

“What?”

“Food.”

“What food?”

She sighed. “Soup. Rice. Something with vegetables in it.”

He lifted his hand off the blanket. It came up a little way and stopped, as if it had run out. She caught it and put it to her cheek, and his thumb moved on her skin.

“Come closer.”

She bent down. He tried to lift his head and couldn’t, and his face tightened, and she slid her arm under his shoulders and took as much of his weight as he could bear to let her.

“Please,” he said.

She kissed him. It was hardly more than a touch. His lips were dry and there was almost no strength in him at all, but he held on to her as hard as he could.

“Again,” he whispered.

“Greedy.”

“Your husband.”

She kissed him again, and stayed a little longer, and when she drew back his eyes were already closing.

“Stay.”

“I’m here.”

“Don’t go.”

“I won’t,” said Aurelia, and sat down in the chair, and he fell asleep holding her hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

At seven thirty-two that evening Qian forwarded a message.

Sun Wei: Given Mr. Chen’s condition, I think it important that we meet on the fifth to discuss continuity and keep the organisation stable. This is not a challenge to anyone’s authority. It is simply a responsible precaution.

She read it twice and looked at her husband, asleep, his hand on the blanket, the monitor keeping watch beside him. Then she typed.

Aurelia: I agree continuity is important. I will attend.

She put the phone face down. Sun Wei wanted the senior men in one room without Chen Si. He wanted to tell them the Don was dying and that the house needed a steady hand, and to be the reasonable man who’d volunteer his own. She thought of her husband’s hands shaking on Saturday night. Of him trying to lift his head and failing. Of the tears he hadn’t been able to hide.

She opened Mr. Yuen’s folder on the bedside table. On the first page was the list of everyone Sun Wei had invited. She picked up a pen.

He’d lent her his coat on a cold balcony. He’d let her sit in his chair without once asking her to prove she deserved it. Now she would hold his place until he could stand in it again. And on the fifth of January Sun Wei would find out that the man he’d tried to remove had left his wife behind: a woman who knew exactly how to smile at a dinner table, and exactly when to stop.

chapters.title: She Signs His Name
chapters.desc: Forty documents in three days. One forged signature, perfect. A transfer Sun Wei tries to slip through at midnight. And Enzo, at three in the morning, teaching her the last stroke.
chapters.epigraph: “Don’t make me use my wife’s privileges.”
chapters.content:
The first document came at seventeen minutes past eight on the third of January. The second came eleven minutes later. By nine o’clock Aurelia had twenty-one of them on the table in the little office off the ward that Dr. Ma had given her, a cup of coffee she’d forgotten, and a husband asleep through the wall under a white blanket.

“Your house is very needy,” she told the monitor.

He could talk for a few minutes now. He could drink water by himself. He could sometimes hold her hand. He couldn’t work, and his organisation had apparently decided that was an unacceptable inconvenience. Supplier approvals. A maintenance contract at the port. Two payrolls. Three renewals. A stack of agreements that needed his own signature by the end of the week.

She rang Qian. “Why are there twenty-one?”

“Several departments have been waiting for Mr. Chen’s approval. Some since December.”

“Then they’ve waited long enough.”

“His signature is required. Shall I bring them over for him to look at?”

She looked through the glass of the door at his bed. He was asleep with his head turned towards her and a small crease between his eyebrows, as if even unconscious he resented being ill.

“No,” she said. “I’ll look at them. Send me the papers behind every one. The original terms, every amendment, and the name of everyone who approved it. Do you remember who’s sitting at his desk, Qian?”

A short silence. “Yes, Mrs. Chen.”

“Good.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The first two days were a lesson in how much work could hide behind a single name. Some documents were simple. Some meant comparing three versions of one agreement, ringing Mr. Yuen, and asking Zhao about decisions made before she’d ever walked onto a balcony. She didn’t sign anything for him. Not yet. The things she could approve under the arrangement she’d announced at his desk, she approved. The ones that needed his own hand went into a separate folder, and the folder grew.

On the afternoon of the third, Qian brought her a revised list. “These can’t move without Mr. Chen. All twenty-one.”

“Does he know that everyone’s apparently forgotten how to breathe without him signing a piece of paper?”

The corner of Qian’s mouth moved. “I doubt he’d be surprised.”

“Give them to me,” said a voice from the bed. He’d been awake and listening.

She stood. “No.”

“I can read.”

“Congratulations.”

“Aurelia. I need to know what’s happening.”

“I tell you everything.”

“Not everything.”

“Because some things aren’t worth waking you for.” She went and straightened the blanket over his legs. “You’re allowed to be a patient for a few days.”

“I don’t like it.”

“I’ve noticed.”

“Twenty-one. Bring them here.”

She considered him, and put the folder on the table beside the bed. “Look at the first three.”

He opened it. He read slowly, and stopped once to close his eyes, and by the second page his breathing had begun to labour. She took the folder away.

“Enough.”

“I haven’t finished.”

“You’ve finished for today.” She kissed his forehead. “Don’t make me use my wife’s privileges.”

“Which ones?”

“The ones where I take your pen away.”

He shut his eyes. “Terrifying.”

“Good,” said Aurelia, and went back to the office, and began to think.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first time she’d copied his signature, it had been an accident. The afternoon at her counter in March, with the eleven pages between them, watching him sign each one. Not because she was interested in his handwriting. Because she was interested in his hands. Long, exact fingers. No wasted movement, no flourish, no hesitation, his name going down on the page with the same quiet certainty he brought into a room. Afterwards she’d found herself drawing the shape of it in the margin of her sketchbook, and laughed at herself, and done it again.

Over the months it had become a small private habit, a comfort when he was away. His name in the margins beside a measurement. On the back of a drawing. Once beside a little sketch of a black jade queen.

She’d never meant to use it.

She opened the sketchbook now on his desk and turned the pages. There it was, over and over. And on the page from the twelfth of March, beside a careful copy of the last line of his disclosure: I am choosing her exactly as she is.

Her throat tightened. She shut the book. Then she picked up his pen.

✦ ✦ ✦

At three in the morning Enzo arrived with two coffees and a paper bag of pastries and stopped in the doorway.

“What happened here? This isn’t work. This is a crime scene.”

“You’re dramatic.”

“I’m Milanese. It’s a professional requirement.” Then he saw the open sketchbook and his face changed. “Aurelia. Why are you practising Chen Si’s signature?”

“Twenty-one documents.”

“You’re going to sign his name. Without telling him.”

“He knows I’m doing his work. He doesn’t know about this.”

“Madonna.” Enzo sat down opposite her. “Why me?”

“Because you’ve spent forty years at a bench. You know when a line’s wrong before you know why.”

He took the book and looked at it for a long time.

“You have the character of it. You’re watching the letters and not the movement. Look at the end of his name. You hold on too long. And here, you hesitate.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you doing it?”

“Because I haven’t slept.”

He looked at her over the book. “That’s not what I meant, cara.”

“I know.”

He closed it. “Tell me what the documents are.” He listened to all of it. “And the alternative?”

“Contracts suspended. Payrolls late. Men using his absence to move things round.”

Enzo pushed the book back across the desk. “Then I’ll help you see what you’re looking at. But you know what you’re doing. And if it goes wrong—“

“I’ll answer for it.”

“Of course you will.” He sighed and picked up her pen. “Now stop trying to make his name beautiful.”

“It’s already beautiful.”

“That’s the problem. You’re admiring it. Every time he changes direction, he lets go. You keep holding on.”

He didn’t make it easy. He made her look. At half past three he took the book away. At twenty to four he made her start again. At four she said he was worse than a schoolteacher. At a quarter past he told her she was a terrible student. At half past four she stopped trying to copy every letter and began to understand how the whole thing moved, and he leaned back.

“Better.”

“Perfect?”

“No.” He reached across the desk and put his hand over hers. “You’re doing this because you’re frightened. If everything keeps moving, you don’t have to think about what happened on that boat.”

“He’s alive. He’s getting better. So I have work to do.”

“Then do the work. But remember you’re allowed to be frightened while you do it.” He pushed the paper bag towards her. “Now eat.”

“Is that a pastry?”

“Two.”

“I love you.”

“I know. I’m very lovable.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By the morning of the fourth she’d checked every paper behind every page, sent two amendments back, returned three agreements for clarification, and signed the rest. Qian came into the office at eight and found her behind the desk with her hair tied back and her sleeves rolled up.

“Are they ready?”

“Yes.”

He took the folder and turned the pages one by one and looked at every signature. His face didn’t change.

“All twenty-one. Mr. Chen signed them?”

“Yes,” said Aurelia.

It was a lie. A small one, perhaps. Still a lie.

“I’ll send them out,” said Qian, and went.

She sat alone afterwards and looked at the pen in her hand. She’d spent ten months building a marriage around the idea that neither of them would ever use the other’s name as a weapon. Now she’d used his to stop his world being taken apart round him. She felt relief and shame in exactly equal measure, and couldn’t separate them.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eleven forty-seven that night, sitting by his bed, she had a message from Qian.

Qian: Sun Wei has put in an urgent request to move eleven million offshore. He says it has to go before midnight to close a settlement.

She sat up and opened the request. A time-critical settlement. References to an arrangement she’d never seen. Two department managers had approved it. She rang Qian.

“They say they were told Mr. Chen had already agreed,” he said.

“Did he?”

“There’s no record of it.”

The clock said 11:50.

“Hold it.”

“Mr. Chen’s approval is usually—“

“Then it stays held. Qian, don’t release eleven million because a man has suddenly discovered the meaning of the word urgent.”

There was a letter attached, addressed to Mr. Tan at the bank that held the settlement account, saying that Chen Si had personally approved the transfer before he fell ill and wanted it made without delay.

She looked at it, and at the pen on the table beside her. She understood exactly what Sun Wei was doing. If the money moved tonight, he could say later that the Don had approved it beforehand. And if anyone asked, the papers would carry Chen Si’s name.

She rang Mr. Yuen. He answered on the second ring and read the file in silence.

“This isn’t supported by any existing agreement. And the letter—“

“Is false.”

“Do you have a written instruction from Mr. Chen?”

“No.”

“Then it has to be stopped by someone with authority.”

“Can Mr. Tan freeze it?”

“If he has a formal notice from the authorised representative.”

11:54.

“Send me the wording that’s legally enough to hold everything still. I’ll approve it.”

“Mrs. Chen, this is eleven million. We should be very careful.”

“I am being careful.”

“Then we’ll write down every step.”

At 11:58 she sent the letter. It wasn’t in Chen Si’s voice. It didn’t carry his name. It was an instruction from Aurelia Chen, acting under the authority she’d already recorded with the bank, telling Mr. Tan to freeze the transfer until the agreement behind it had been independently checked. She copied Mr. Yuen. She copied Qian. Then she rang Mr. Tan himself.

“I’ve received your letter, Mrs. Chen. It’s held.”

“Thank you.”

“I’ll need Mr. Chen’s confirmation before releasing anything.”

“You’ll have it when he’s well enough to give it.”

11:59.

At one minute past midnight:

Qian: Held. Mr. Tan has acknowledged your instruction. Nothing has moved.

She let out a breath, small, almost without sound, and sat down, and for several minutes did nothing at all. She looked at his pen. She held it between her fingers. And at last she let herself feel how tired she was.

At sixteen minutes past two Qian came back and found her asleep at the office desk with her head on her arm and his pen still in her hand. He’d never seen her sleep anywhere but beside him. He came in quietly and took the pen out of her fingers, and she stirred.

“Chen Si?”

“No, Mrs. Chen. It’s Qian. The transfer’s frozen. Go home.”

“There’s still—“

“Mrs. Chen.” He put the pen down on the desk, very gently. “He wouldn’t want you to fall over his paperwork.”

“He’s not here to tell me what he wants.”

“No,” said Qian. “But I think I know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the morning of the fifth, early, he was awake when she came in. Still pale. Clearer in the eyes than the day before.

“You were working,” he said. “At my desk. Till late.”

“How do you know?”

“Qian.”

“Traitor.”

“Come here.” He lifted his hand with visible effort. She caught it before he could strain and put it to her cheek. “How long have you slept?”

“Enough.”

He looked at her.

“Not enough,” she admitted. “Twenty-one documents were waiting for your signature.”

“Did you send them back?”

“No.”

“What did you do?”

She took a breath. “I signed your name. On every one that needed it.”

He looked at her for a long time. “Where are they?”

“Sent out.”

“And Qian took them?”

“Yes.”

“And didn’t notice?”

“No.”

“Neither did I,” said Chen Si. “Show me.”

She gave him the sketchbook. He turned the pages slowly, the practice signatures, the old ones, the notes in the margins, and stopped at the page from March with her copy of his disclosure beside his name.

“Since then?”

“Not seriously.”

“How often?”

“Chen Si.”

“Very well.” He gave the book back. “And?”

“The documents were urgent. And Sun Wei tried to push eleven million offshore last night before midnight, with a letter saying you’d already agreed. I had Mr. Tan freeze it. Under my own name. Mr. Yuen has every page.”

His eyes sharpened. “Good.” Then he looked at her face. “You expected me to be angry.”

“I signed your name.”

“On papers you’d read? That had to be signed? That you understood?”

“Yes.”

He lifted her hand, slowly, and brought her knuckles to his mouth. “You did what was necessary. But you didn’t have to become me to look after what’s mine.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

“I was afraid that if I didn’t keep everything moving, someone would take it.”

“Someone may try. But the house isn’t worth losing yourself over.”

“You’re very good at saying things you don’t practise.”

“Fair,” said Chen Si.

She kissed his forehead, and his cheek, and then, carefully, his mouth.

“Again,” he said.

“You’re supposed to be resting.”

“I am. I’m asking for one thing.”

She bent down again. He kissed her slowly with what little strength he had, his thumb moving once under her eye.

“You’re still very demanding.”

“Your husband.”

“Unfortunately.”

She put his pen on the bedside table. He looked at it.

“Keep it.”

“Your pen?”

“So you can sign your own name,” said Chen Si, and closed his eyes, and held on to her fingers.

She’d spent three days learning to make his name look like his. Looking at the pen now, she understood that she’d never wanted to replace him. She’d only wanted there to be a world still standing when he came back to it. She didn’t reach for the papers. She sat and held his hand until it was time to go to the Jade Hall.

chapters.title: The Board Meeting Without a Don
chapters.desc: A private room in the old town, twelve men, one empty chair at the head of the table. Sun Wei has prepared a speech about continuity. Aurelia walks in alone, in black, and sits down before he can give it.
chapters.epigraph: “And nobody mistakes my patience for not knowing.”
chapters.content:
At twenty to nine on the fifth of January, eleven men sat down in the Jade Hall.

The upstairs room had been built before most of them were born: dark wood, carved screens, a long table polished until it gave back the ceiling. The windows looked down over the old town, where shopkeepers were winding up their shutters and vans were squeezing down streets too narrow for them.

Twelve chairs. Eleven men. The twelfth chair, at the head, stood empty, and Sun Wei stood beside it in a charcoal suit and a dark red tie, with his glasses on their cord and a folder under his hand: a prepared statement, a proposed interim arrangement, and a list of the names he’d already decided would support him.

“Thank you for coming at such short notice,” he said. “We all know Mr. Chen’s condition. It’s severe. His recovery is uncertain. Some of you have been told otherwise, but I think we must face the situation honestly.” He paused. “Chen Si may not come back.”

One of the older men shifted. “Has the hospital said so?”

“The hospital has said he’s critically ill.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

“No. But it’s enough to make us think about the future. The Docks need direction. The shipping contracts need approval. Our partners need reassurance. Our people need to know who’s responsible.” He laid his hand flat on the folder. “I’m not asking anyone to forget Mr. Chen. I’m asking you to think about what happens if he can’t return. An interim council. I’d take the daily running of things until Mr. Chen’s situation is resolved.”

“Resolved how?” said a younger man.

“However it must be,” said Sun Wei, and opened his folder.

The doors opened.

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia Chen walked into the Jade Hall alone, in black.

Not the soft black of mourning, and not the hard black of a woman trying to look frightening. A tailored suit with a narrow waist and clean shoulders, trousers that fell exactly over her shoes, hair back, very little on her face. At her throat, on a thin gold chain that had parted near the clasp and been tied there with a single loop of silk thread, hung a small pendant.

Qian had brought her his things from the boat on New Year’s morning in a plastic bag: wallet, watch, a black jade queen, and, folded into a handkerchief in his inside pocket, the broken necklace from the bottom left-hand corner of her window, which he’d carried every day since March and never had mended.

Today she was wearing it exactly as it was.

The room went silent. Sun Wei’s hand stayed on his folder.

“Mrs. Chen.”

“Good morning, Sun Wei.”

He looked past her. “Where is Mr. Chen?”

“In hospital.”

Nobody stood. Nobody offered her a seat. She didn’t wait to be offered. She walked the length of the table, pulled out the chair at its head, the one he’d been standing beside, and sat down in it, and put a slim leather folder on the wood in front of her.

“Please,” she said. “Go on.”

Sun Wei recovered first. “This is a private meeting of the senior leadership. You weren’t asked.”

“I know.”

“Then you’ll understand our surprise.”

“Would you like to talk about my invitation,” said Aurelia, “or about the fact that you’ve been getting ready to take my husband’s chair while he’s still alive?”

A man at the far end coughed.

“Nobody’s taking anything. We’re discussing continuity.”

“How considerate. You’ve prepared a speech? Please don’t let me interrupt it.”

He closed the folder. “I think it would be more useful to discuss this privately.”

“No.” It came out quietly. “This is a meeting about the future of the house. You wanted twelve people in the room. You have twelve. Let’s begin.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The first was Mr. Sze. He’d run the northern route for eleven years: broad, a heavy gold watch, the habit of looking at whoever was speaking as if waiting for them to finish wasting his time.

“Your route beat its target by six per cent last quarter,” she said. “Well done. Your maintenance costs went up nineteen. Your second contractor’s been billing for repairs nobody did. The same invoices, under two company names.”

His eyes went to her folder. “Who gave you that?”

“Does it matter?”

“It does if you’re accusing me.”

“I’m telling you what the records show. You can explain them to Mr. Yuen this afternoon. If it’s a mistake, it’ll be put right. If it isn’t, I’d find a better explanation.”

She turned. “Director Ko. Your western route. The numbers are good.” He looked relieved. “Your brother’s company has had three contracts without tender. One was for replacement equipment. Two were ordinary maintenance at well above the market rate. I’d ask your brother about it before Mr. Yuen does.”

The third man. The fourth. By the fifth the room had gone very quiet. She didn’t raise her voice once. She didn’t need to. She went round the table and told each man his routes and his skims, his private arrangements and the small secrets he’d spent years persuading himself nobody could see. The manager taking gifts from a contractor. The route that was failing behind reports of steady growth. The senior man using warehouse staff to build an extension on his own house. The one who’d found his son a desk in a department he had no qualifications for. She had the figures and the dates and the names of who’d signed what, and she didn’t look at her notes once.

“How could you possibly know all this?” said Director Ko at last.

“I read the documents.”

“All of them? That would take weeks.”

“It took three days,” said Aurelia. “Shall I go on?”

Nobody answered. She went on.

✦ ✦ ✦

At some point Sun Wei had sat down. He sat with both hands on the table and his speech closed in front of him.

“Sun Wei,” she said at last. “You’ve been very concerned about continuity. You’ve talked to several men here about an interim arrangement. You’ve told them Chen Si won’t recover.”

“I said his condition was uncertain.”

“You said he might not come back. You’re very comfortable discussing my husband’s death.”

The room went perfectly still.

“I’m trying to protect what he built.”

“Then you must be relieved to hear he’s alive.” She took a single sheet from her folder and laid it on the table and slid it towards the men. A formal letter, in the house’s usual form, over Chen Si’s name, giving his wife full authority over operations, staff, money and decisions for as long as he was incapacitated. At the foot, his signature. The one she’d drawn in the margins of her sketchbook since March. The one on twenty-one documents Qian had accepted without blinking.

“From today,” she said, “I act for Chen Si.”

The men bent over it. Sun Wei didn’t touch it.

“Is it genuine?”

She met his eyes. “It is the authority I’m presenting to this meeting.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

“No,” said Aurelia. “It isn’t.”

A few men looked up.

“Mr. Yuen has the records,” she went on. “The departments already have what they need to keep working. Any question about the scope of it can go to counsel.”

“Chen Si is in no state to write a letter.”

“You’re right. He’s in no state to come to this meeting. He’s in no state to sit at his desk. He’s in no state to deal with men who mistake a hospital bed for a vacancy.” She let it sit. “But he isn’t dead. And until he can come back, you’ll deal with me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Mr. Yuen had said nothing since the meeting began. He sat at the far end of the table with his briefcase shut by his chair and the careful neutral face of a man who’d spent his life advising people who didn’t like surprises. Now he opened it.

“I’d like something put in the record. At eleven forty-seven on the night before last, an urgent request was made to move eleven million to an offshore account.”

Sun Wei’s fingers moved on the table. It was very small. Aurelia saw it.

“The stated purpose was a settlement. The agreement behind it doesn’t allow the payment. The letter attached to it, saying Mr. Chen had approved it before he fell ill, can’t be verified. Mr. Tan has frozen it.”

One of the older men looked down the table. “Was that your request, Sun Wei?”

“It was an operational payment.”

“Eleven million, at midnight?”

“The settlement window—“

“—was no reason to go round approval,” said Mr. Yuen.

“Who authorised you to look at it?”

“Mrs. Chen.”

“Everything becomes urgent,” said Aurelia, “when somebody’s about to be caught. Why did it have to go before midnight, Sun Wei? Why after hours? Why did you tell Mr. Tan my husband had approved it when there’s no record that he did?” Her voice softened. “Was it because you thought there’d be nobody left to ask?”

His hand trembled on the wood. This time every man at the table saw it.

The clock on the wall was suddenly loud.

Sun Wei looked at the transfer report, and at the letter of authority, and round at the eleven faces, and seemed to understand at last that the meeting hadn’t gone the way he’d planned. He’d come to announce a new order. He’d been handed a list of his own failures instead.

He pushed his chair back slowly and bowed his head.

“Forgive an old man,” he said, with the practised humility of someone who’d spent his whole life knowing precisely when to bow.

She didn’t bow back. “There’s nothing for me to forgive yet.”

“I’ve always respected Mr. Chen.”

“Then you should have respected his absence.”

He held her eyes for a moment, and she held his. Then he walked to the door. Nobody stopped him. Nobody went with him. He left the Jade Hall with his folder still on the table.

When the door had shut, nobody moved for several seconds. Then Mr. Yuen began to clap. Once. Twice. Aurelia turned her head. He stopped.

“I’m sorry,” he said. “It seemed appropriate.”

One of the old men laughed shortly. Another joined in. For a moment the room filled with uncertain, embarrassed applause.

“Please,” said Aurelia, and stood, and it stopped. “I’m not asking you to admire me. I’m asking you to do your jobs. Every department sends its accounts in for review. Every transfer outside the ordinary needs a written reason. Nobody uses my husband’s illness to make private arrangements.” She looked down the table. “And nobody mistakes my patience for not knowing.”

The meeting ended at twenty-eight minutes past ten. By a quarter to eleven the hall was empty.

She sat on for a few minutes in his chair. She’d expected to feel triumphant. She felt tired. The room smelled of good tea and old wood and the men’s cologne. She touched the necklace at her throat, and the little loop of thread caught on her fingertip, and she thought of his face on the pillow, and his hand struggling to hold hers, and his pen on the bedside table.

“Mrs. Chen?” Mr. Yuen was in the doorway. “Are you all right?”

“Yes.” He looked at her. She sighed. “Not particularly.”

“That sounds more accurate.” His eyes went to the chain. “His?”

“Mine first.”

“Then I suppose he has good taste.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At the hospital Chen Si had asked for her. Not over and over. He knew better than to wear himself out. But when Qian came in with a glass of water, his eyes had gone straight to the door.

“Has she finished?”

“Mr. Yuen rang. It went well. Sun Wei left.”

“On his own feet?”

“After Mrs. Chen had finished speaking.”

Chen Si let out a breath that might have been a laugh. “That sounds like her.”

“She showed them your letter of authority.”

“Which letter?”

“The one giving her full authority.”

A pause. “Did it work?”

“They all accepted it.”

“Good,” said Chen Si, looking at the window.

“Mr. Chen. She wore the broken necklace.”

Something changed in his face, very slightly. Qian had worked for him long enough to see it.

“Tell her to come in the moment she arrives.”

She came in at eighteen minutes past eleven, the jacket off, the black trousers and silk blouse, hair coming loose. He looked at her. She looked at him.

“How was the meeting?”

“Sun Wei gave a speech. I interrupted him. I sat in your chair. He was very unhappy. He suggested an interim arrangement. I told him you were still alive.”

“You’re enjoying this,” he said.

“You weren’t there.”

“I can imagine.”

She took his hand. It was warmer today. She let out a breath she hadn’t known she was holding.

“Did you miss me?” she said.

“Yes.” It came so fast she blinked. Then his eyes went to her throat.

“You’re wearing it.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because I wanted to.”

“Keep it on,” he said.

“You’re giving me instructions?”

“For now.”

“How long is for now?”

“Until I can take it off you myself.”

He lifted his hand, slowly, and touched the chain where it lay on her collarbone. His fingers could barely manage it. She caught his wrist and guided it, and he found the little loop of thread where the link had parted.

“I thought you’d have mended it.”

“You said you’d keep it broken.”

“I did.”

“So I wore it like this.”

“Then keep it,” said Chen Si. “Until I can take it off.”

She kissed him, gently, and felt how much it cost him to kiss her back, and how his fingers held on to her as though he were afraid she might go somewhere.

“Sun Wei’s out of the room,” she said, with her forehead on his. “The transfer’s frozen. The men have been told to send in their accounts. And nobody saw me cry.”

His thumb moved on her cheek. “You don’t have to win every room, Aurelia. You don’t have to be me. You’re allowed to be my wife.”

“Is that all?”

“No. You’re also allowed to be the woman who sat in my chair and reminded eleven men who they answer to.”

She laughed softly. “That’s a very specific compliment.”

“I’ve had time to think,” said Chen Si, and his eyes grew heavy, and she settled into the chair beside him, careful of the lines. He wasn’t strong enough to take the necklace off her. Not yet. But he’d asked her to keep it on, and she meant to.

chapters.title: The Traitor at the Table
chapters.desc: She invites the senior men to dinner on the forty-fourth floor. Eleven guests, a soup that takes eight hours, and a list of three names in her head before anyone picks up a spoon.
chapters.epigraph: “She never made enough for just one person.”
chapters.content:
The first name was Hu. The second was Wan. The third was Judge Lai. Aurelia had all three before breakfast on the eighth of January, and told nobody.

At eight she stood in the kitchen on the forty-fourth floor with a report in one hand and a wooden spoon in the other. Outside the glass the harbour was pale with winter haze, and the city looked almost peaceful from that height, its cranes and towers softened by the light. On the stove, on the lowest flame, a pot of broth had been barely moving for six hours. Chen Lan’s recipe said eight. Aurelia had begun it at two in the morning, an hour after Zhao rang from the ninth floor to tell her about the woman in the nurse’s uniform, and how close she’d got, and that she hadn’t got any closer.

She turned a page.

The glasses on the Pearl had been supplied by a catering firm called Golden Spoon, which had done a dozen of the Syndicate’s private functions over two years. Ordinary enough. The Pearl had hired them; Golden Spoon had brought the glassware; afterwards it had been washed, packed and taken away. Except that the delivery sheet didn’t match the inventory. A second collection had been made after midnight, and four pieces had been written off as broken before anyone could look at them. Attached to the report was a photograph of the man who’d signed for that second collection.

Mr. Hu.

She’d met him twice. Once at a shipping dinner, where he’d admired her necklace. Once at the opening of the second shop, where he’d sent a very good bottle of wine. A quiet man. The kind who never spoke unless there was something in it for him.

She rang Qian. “Everything about Golden Spoon and the Pearl. The original contract. The replacement records. Every payment to them in six months. And where Mr. Hu was on New Year’s Eve.”

She went back to the stove. Two hours more.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second name was in the money behind the poison.

Dr. Ma was careful with his words. A cardiac glycoside, he said; the findings were consistent with deliberate poisoning; the laboratory hadn’t finished. The investigation was slower. The first thread came from the glass. The second came from the payments.

A pharmacologist had received a run of fees through a company tied to the port liaison office. Consulting fees, on paper, for consulting nobody had ever done. The man at the port who’d signed every one of them was Mr. Wan.

She rang Mr. Yuen. “Can you show Wan knew what the money was for?”

“Not yet. I can show he arranged it. His authorisation’s on every payment.”

“Does the pharmacologist know who commissioned him?”

“We’re trying to find out. Mrs. Chen, there’s something else. He’s gone. His flat was empty when we got there last night.”

Her fingers tightened on the phone. “Find him. Somebody’s already tried to kill my husband twice. I don’t want to discover that the man who made the poison has decided to finish the job.”

“I understand.”

She stood very still for a moment. Then she checked the broth.

✦ ✦ ✦

The third name came from the woman in the nurse’s uniform.

She hadn’t been a nurse. She’d had a uniform, a forged pass, and a syringe already filled, and a sum of money she’d been promised that was enough to leave the city for good. She’d lasted forty minutes in a small room at the hospital with Mr. Yuen across the table from her and Zhao by the door with his knuckles wrapped in gauze. Then she’d said that the money had come from a man who worked for Judge Lai.

Lai Shun had spent twenty years moving between the bench and quiet advisory work for the old families. He’d been to several of Chen Si’s public dinners. He wasn’t a man who needed to raise his voice. He was a man who could make other people vanish behind paperwork.

“That’s a serious allegation,” Mr. Yuen had told her. “It’ll have to be supported.”

“Then support it,” said Aurelia. “Can you tie Hu to Wan?”

“Golden Spoon took four payments from a company connected to the port liaison office.”

“Do we know Hu knew what was on the glass?”

“Not yet.”

“Then we don’t accuse anyone in public until we have the records.”

“What do you mean to do?”

She closed the folder. “Invite them to dinner.”

He blinked. “All of them?”

“Eleven men.”

“Some of those men may have helped try to kill your husband.”

“I know.”

“Wouldn’t it be safer to have them questioned one at a time?”

“Perhaps.” She looked at the pot on the stove. “They’ve spent years believing they can sit at one table, smile at each other, and decide how much of the truth the rest of us are allowed to see. I’d like to watch what happens when they find out I know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The invitation went out that afternoon. Eleven guests. A private dinner on the forty-fourth floor. No wives, no assistants, no press. Mrs. Chen requests the pleasure of your company tonight. The evening will be private and informal. One man declined. She rang him herself. He came.

“Hu, Wan, and Judge Lai,” said Qian, looking at the list. “You’re certain?”

“Certain enough to ask them to dinner.”

“That isn’t quite the same thing.”

“No. Which is why Mr. Yuen will be at the table and Zhao will be at the door.”

“Does Mr. Chen know?”

“He knows I’m feeding eleven men. He doesn’t know which.”

“Shouldn’t he?”

“Would you like to wake him and tell him?”

“No, Mrs. Chen.”

“Neither would I.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d set the long table with ivory plates and dark green napkins and a low bowl of white camellias, no music, no extra staff. She wore plain black and the broken necklace with its loop of silk thread. At the far end she’d left one chair empty, and wouldn’t let anyone move it.

Hu came at twenty to eight and bowed a little. “Your home is beautiful. Mr. Chen must be pleased.”

“He is.”

Wan came ten minutes after, with a bottle, which she thanked him for and gave to the staff without looking at the label. Judge Lai came last: sixty-odd, silver-haired, with a pleasant face that made him seem far more approachable than he was.

“I was so sorry to hear of Mr. Chen’s illness.”

“Thank you.”

“He’s recovering?”

“He is.”

“That’s very good news,” said Judge Lai, and she smiled and showed him in.

By eight they were all seated. At ten past, the soup came.

It had taken eight hours. Clear and golden, ginger and dried scallop, the fish simmered until it fell apart and then lifted out so that only the cleanest flakes went back in. She hadn’t made it perfectly. She’d rung Enzo twice. She’d sent Qian across the city at four for dried tangerine peel. She’d ruined the first pot by letting it boil, and started again. The second was beautiful.

She stood at her place.

“Before we begin, thank you all for coming. These weeks have been hard. Chen Si’s illness has made things uncertain, and many of you have carried more than usual. I’m grateful.” She looked round the table. “I wanted to share something of his family tonight. This soup is his mother’s. Chen Lan’s. She made it for him when he was ill. I thought he might like it waiting when he comes home.”

“A lovely thought,” said Judge Lai.

Eleven bowls went down. Eleven spoons beside them. Nobody had lifted one.

“Before anyone picks up a spoon,” said Aurelia, and laid her napkin by her plate, “there are three things I’d like to talk about. Mr. Hu.”

He looked up.

“Golden Spoon brought the glasses to the Pearl on New Year’s Eve. Golden Spoon was also paid four times by a company connected to the port liaison office. Three were called equipment. The fourth was called replacement stock. And after midnight on the first, somebody collected four glasses from the Pearl and wrote them off as broken before they could be looked at. The man who signed for them was you.”

His face barely moved. “That’s an operational matter.”

“Perhaps. It’s an interesting one.” She turned. “Mr. Wan. Your office approved a series of payments to a pharmacologist. Consulting fees, for consulting nobody did. Your authorisation’s on every one. The pharmacologist has disappeared. The payments fall in the weeks before my husband was poisoned.”

Wan’s hand moved beside his bowl.

“And Judge Lai. Your name was given to us last night by a woman in a nurse’s uniform, who was stopped outside my husband’s room with a syringe in her hand. She said she’d been paid to finish what began on New Year’s Eve.”

Judge Lai folded his hands. “That’s a grave accusation.”

“Yes.”

“Do you believe it?”

“I believe it’s worth investigating.”

“Then perhaps you should leave it to the proper authorities.”

“That’s exactly what I mean to do.”

“Mrs. Chen.” He looked at her almost with pity. “You’re young. I understand you’re frightened for your husband. But fear and grief make people see patterns that aren’t there.”

“Chen Si isn’t dead.”

“I didn’t say he was.”

“You’ve all been behaving as if he were.” She looked at the empty chair. “That ends tonight.”

“And if you’re wrong?”

“Then the investigation will show it.”

“And if you’re right?”

“Then you’ll answer for what you did.”

“You should be careful,” said Judge Lai gently. “Your husband has spent many years building relationships. It would be a pity if you damaged them out of emotion.”

“You think I’m here because I’m emotional?”

“I think you’re hurt.”

“Of course I’m hurt.” Her voice was soft. “My husband was poisoned. His heart stopped in my hands on a boat. For three days he couldn’t lift his head. And someone sent a woman into his hospital with a syringe.” She leaned forward. “Do you think I ought to be calm about that? I am calm. That’s why you’re still sitting at my table.”

The silence was absolute.

At twenty to nine Zhao came in. He didn’t hurry. He walked round behind the chairs and stopped beside Hu with two of his men at his back.

“Mr. Hu.”

“Mrs. Chen, you can’t—“

“Please stand,” said Aurelia.

Hu looked at the door, and at Wan. Wan was already halfway up. “Sit down,” he hissed. “We can settle this—“

Zhao put a hand on Hu’s shoulder. Hu jerked away. “Don’t touch me.”

“Then get up yourself,” said Zhao. Hu got up. Wan followed, grey in the face.

Judge Lai stayed where he was. “Mrs. Chen, you’re making a serious mistake. You can’t have a judge removed from a private dinner on a frightened woman’s word.”

“No. But I can have you shown out while the evidence is kept safe and the right people are told.”

“You think your husband’s name protects you?”

She touched the broken chain at her throat. “No. I think the truth does.”

“Judge Lai,” said Zhao. “Get up.”

For a moment it seemed he’d refuse. Then he rose. The three of them were taken out one at a time. No shouting. No struggle. Only the sound of chairs on the floor and the door closing.

Eight men were left. Eight bowls. Eight spoons. One empty chair. The soup was beginning to cool.

“Please,” said Aurelia. “Eat.”

“After that?” said one of the old men.

“Especially after that.”

He lifted his spoon. The others followed. She waited until the first of them had tasted it, and saw his face change.

“This is Chen Lan’s?”

“Yes.”

“She used to make it when he was a boy.”

At the far end of the table Mr. Yuen hadn’t moved. He was looking into his bowl. He picked up the spoon and tasted it, and stopped, and his eyes filled. For a moment he looked ashamed of it. He bent his head and pressed his lips together, and the tears went over anyway.

“Did you know her?” said Aurelia.

“Many years ago.” He wiped his cheek with the back of his hand. “I was her husband’s lawyer. She used to bring this soup to the old office. Whenever anyone was ill. Whenever anyone had worked too long. She never once asked who deserved it.” His voice broke. “After he died, the boy used to bring her recipe book to my office and sit and read it in the corner. He said she’d written everything down so he wouldn’t forget.”

Chen Si had told her almost nothing about his mother. What she knew was made of absences: a telephone, a stopped watch, a house with nobody in it. She hadn’t known about the soup. She wished she had.

“She’d have been proud of him,” said Mr. Yuen.

“Yes,” said Aurelia. “I think so too.”

The eight men ate in a silence that wasn’t uncomfortable. It was something quieter: the silence of a room that has remembered something it had nearly forgotten. One of them asked for more. One thanked the kitchen. One, very quietly, asked for the recipe.

She didn’t mistake it for victory. Hu, Wan and Judge Lai weren’t convicted of anything. Their names would need records and witnesses and an investigation that could stand up. But they were no longer hidden among the others at the table. That was enough for one night.

✦ ✦ ✦

At a quarter past ten, when the last of them had gone, she filled a small container with the last of the soup and took it to the ninth floor.

He was awake.

“You’re late,” he said.

“Good evening to you too.”

“How many?”

“Eight.”

“From eleven.”

“Yes.”

“Hu. Wan. Lai.”

She stopped. “Mr. Yuen told you.”

“He told Qian. Qian told me. Eventually.”

“You’re not supposed to be running your house from a hospital bed.”

“I’m not. I’m asking about it. That’s different.” His eyes went to her throat. “You’re still wearing it.”

“Of course.”

“Did you serve the soup?”

“Yes. Mr. Yuen cried.”

He went quite still. She sat down beside him.

“He said your mother used to bring it to the old office. When anyone was ill. When anyone had worked too long.”

He looked at the window for a long time. “She did. She never made enough for just one person.”

“I think I’d have liked her.”

He looked back at her. “She’d have liked you.”

“How do you know?”

“You made her soup.”

She laughed, and her eyes were wet. “That’s a very low standard.”

“She wasn’t difficult to please.” He lifted her fingers and put his mouth to them, weakly. “Did you follow it exactly?”

“Almost. I had to ring Enzo. The first pot boiled.”

He smiled, small and tired and real. “She’d have forgiven you.”

She took the lid off the container and held a spoon of it to his mouth, and he tasted his mother’s soup for the first time in seven years, and closed his eyes.

“Thank you for making it,” said Chen Si, almost too softly to hear, and fell asleep holding her hand.

chapters.title: What She Does to the Traitor
chapters.desc: Not a gun. Not a knife. Not Zhao. Contracts, deeds, a frozen account, a forty-page file, and one suitcase. Quietly. Thoroughly. Completely. By breakfast, Sun Wei owns nothing but the clothes he is standing in.
chapters.epigraph: “You didn’t need a gun.”
chapters.content:
Zhao offered to kill Sun Wei on the morning of the ninth of January. He said it standing at the window of the room on the ninth floor, in the tone another man might use to offer to fetch lunch.

“Give me the word, Mrs. Chen.”

Aurelia looked up from the papers on her knee. Chen Si was asleep. The monitor kept its patient count beside the bed, and a thin winter light lay across the blanket and the back of his hand.

She put her pen down. “No.”

Zhao’s face didn’t change. “He sent the glass. Then he sent a woman with a syringe.”

“I know.”

“Then why should he leave this city breathing?”

“Because Si is lying in that bed with tubes in his arms,” she said, “and if I start, that’s who I am when he wakes up. I don’t want to spend the rest of my life wondering whether I turned into the thing I was trying to stop.” She looked at the window, at the grey harbour beyond Zhao’s shoulder. “And because it would be too easy. I want him to wake up tomorrow and find that nobody answers his calls. I want him to look at his accounts and see nothing. I want every man who used to stand when he walked into a room to understand there’s nothing left in his hands to give them. I want him to know exactly what he lost, and to have time to count it.”

Zhao considered that for a while. “That’s cruel.”

“Yes.”

“He might like it.” A tilt of the head towards the bed.

“He’d tell me to be careful. And then he’d ask what I needed.” She picked up her pen again. “I need you to keep him alive. That’s all.”

Something in Zhao’s shoulders let go. “That I can do.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Mr. Tan rang at twenty past ten. Sun Wei’s signatory rights had been suspended across every account held through the Syndicate’s banks, and nothing would be accepted under his authority until the review was finished. Then he cleared his throat in the way bankers do before a number.

“There are discrepancies in the books, Mrs. Chen.”

“How much?”

“Thirty-one million.”

She didn’t move.

“Over several years,” said Mr. Tan. “Some buried in operating costs. Some paid to companies that supplied nothing at all. We can already show a substantial personal benefit. The rest is still being reconciled.”

She thought of the warehouse men laid off last spring because the budget was suddenly tight, and the suppliers who had waited five months to be paid.

“Send everything to Mr. Yuen. And Mr. Tan, if anyone calls this an accounting discrepancy, correct them. It was theft.”

“Understood.”

By lunchtime, Sun Wei knew. He rang Qian, who didn’t pick up. He rang Mr. Tan, who told him what Mr. Tan had told her. He asked to speak to Mr. Chen, and was told that Mr. Chen was under medical care and receiving no one. Then he rang her.

She let it ring three times, and went out into the corridor so the voice wouldn’t be in the room.

“Mrs. Chen. My accounts have been restricted.”

“Yes.”

“You can’t do that without Mr. Chen.”

“I can.”

“Those accounts are twenty years of work.”

“Thirty-one million of work,” she said.

There was a silence long enough for a nurse to walk past and turn the corner.

“Those figures aren’t final.”

“Then you should have kept better records.”

His voice went lower, smoother, the voice he’d used across the Sunday table while he passed her the orchids. “You should be careful, my dear, about the accusations you make.”

“I haven’t made any. Not in public. I’ve sent the evidence to the people whose job it is to look at it.” She leaned her shoulder on the wall. “You keep telling me Chen Si would never have treated you like this. You’re right. Chen Si trusted you. That was your chance to deserve it.”

She ended the call and went back in. Chen Si had turned his head on the pillow and was watching her with half-open eyes.

“Who?” he said, hardly louder than breath.

“Nobody,” she said. “Go back to sleep.”

He didn’t believe her, but he slept.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ms. Fong came up to the forty-fourth floor the next morning. She was small and silver-framed, in a grey suit so neat it made people check whether they’d forgotten to sign something, and she had managed the Syndicate’s holdings for nearly twenty years without ever being photographed. Aurelia had met her twice. Both times Ms. Fong had said perhaps eleven words.

She put a folder on the desk. “The shareholding agreements.”

Sun Wei held no great block of anything. He held six founder’s shares, one in each of six companies, and those six small pieces of paper had given him a vote and a veto everywhere that mattered: the furniture importer, two freight firms, the warehouse company, the cold store, the property firm that owned his own office. Every agreement had a clause for misconduct. Mr. Yuen had spent the previous day reading them with counsel, and the answer was in the margin in his small, sloping hand. On a breach of trust, the shares went back to the company at the price set down in the original deed.

“One coin each,” said Ms. Fong.

Aurelia looked up.

“It was a formality, when they were written. Nobody expected it to be used.” Ms. Fong turned a page so the notices lay on top. “They’re prepared.”

“Will he dispute it?”

“He may.”

“Then let him.” Aurelia signed where she was entitled to sign, and Ms. Fong gathered the pages and squared them against the desk.

“How long has he held them?”

“Nine years.”

“Then I suppose nine years is long enough.”

Ms. Fong didn’t smile. But at the door, collecting her folder against her chest, the corner of her mouth moved.

The house was harder. Sun Wei lived on the eastern side of the city in a white villa with a view of the water, bought with his own money and a loan from a bank in which the Syndicate held most of the shares. The loan had a clause, as these things do, that let the bank call it in if the borrower was found to have defrauded an affiliated company.

“He can’t repay it,” said Mr. Yuen, on the phone. “Not from anything he can reach.”

“Then what happens?”

“Notice. Time to settle. If he can’t, the bank takes the property back through the ordinary process. Mrs. Chen, this must be the contract and nothing but the contract. If it looks like revenge, a court will treat it as revenge.”

“Then make sure it isn’t.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the eleventh of January, at a quarter past nine in the morning, she opened a new file. She closed it a little after midnight.

It was forty pages long, and it wasn’t a letter. There were no adjectives in it. It set out the thirty-one million and where each part had gone. The transfer he’d tried to push through at eleven forty-seven on the night of the third. The authority letter with Chen Si’s forged hand on it. The pharmacologist’s fees, and the man at the port who had signed for them. The catering firm, the second collection from the Pearl after midnight, the four glasses written off as broken. The woman in the nurse’s uniform, and the name she had given. The six shares, the loan, the clauses under which both were going home.

Every page had a source and every figure had a document behind it, and every conclusion was marked for what it was: established, supported, under investigation. Where the woman with the syringe had named Judge Lai, the file said that she had named him, and not one word more.

Mr. Yuen read it at her dining table with his glasses on the end of his nose. It took him an hour and a half. When he reached the end he went back to page twenty-two and read it again.

“You haven’t said he sent her.”

“We can’t show that he did. Yet.”

“Good.” He squared the pages. “I don’t think you’re being too thorough, if that’s what you’re going to ask me. I think you’re making it very difficult for anyone in this organisation to say afterwards that they didn’t know.”

“That’s the idea.”

“Who has it?”

She told him. The twelve men from the Jade Hall. The eight who had stayed and eaten the soup. Mr. Tan, Ms. Fong, Qian, Zhao. “And one to Sun Wei.”

He took his glasses off. “Why?”

“So he knows exactly why it’s all going.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Sun Wei had his copy at half past eight the next morning, in his office over the furniture showroom. The cover page carried nothing but his name and the date. By page twenty his assistant had come in twice and gone out again without saying anything. By page thirty he had stopped pretending it was an internal report. At page thirty-eight, where the six shares and the white villa were set out in two paragraphs, he picked up the phone.

She didn’t answer. Qian didn’t answer. Mr. Yuen told him, very courteously, that any further communication should go through his lawyers.

He threw the file across the room. The pages slid under the cabinets. For the first time in twenty years, nobody came running when he shouted.

She saw him that night, at eleven, at the old harbour office down on the docks. Not the Jade Hall, and not Chen Si’s study. A small room with a desk and two chairs and a window over the black water, where Chen Si’s father had once kept his first ledgers.

He came in still in his good suit. It no longer seemed to belong to him. He hadn’t shaved properly; there was a nick under his jaw. The reading glasses hung on their cord against his chest.

“You’ve gone too far, my dear.”

“Have I?”

“You’ve frozen my accounts. You’ve taken my shares. You’ve called in my house.”

“Under the terms you agreed to.”

“I gave this organisation twenty years.”

“And you spent them stealing from it.” She didn’t raise her voice. “You sent a glass to that boat. You paid men to move the money for it. You sold his calendar to the people with the lorry on the coast road. And when he lived, someone sent a woman into his hospital with a syringe. I can’t prove that last part. I’m not going to try tonight.”

For a moment something showed under the anger, something small and unpleasant, the face of a man doing sums.

“You can’t prove most of it.”

“Some of it is in bank records. Some of it is in statements. Some of it is still being looked for.” She closed the file. “But you’re not leaving this room with his money, or his shares, or a single one of the men who used to work for you. I didn’t take those things from you. You did that yourself.”

He laughed once, without any breath behind it. “He would never have done this.”

“No. He gave you twenty years. He gave you a seat at his table on Sundays, and his trust, and things you could never have built on your own.” She touched the necklace at her throat, the little loop of silk thread at the parted link. “Do you know what the worst of these twelve days has been? Not the boat. Not the hospital. Watching my husband try to lift his hand off the blanket, while men who’d eaten his food were already measuring his chair.”

“You don’t understand what I was under.”

“No,” she said. “I don’t.”

She pushed the envelope across the desk. He didn’t touch it.

“What is it?”

“Six coins. One for each share, at the price in your own agreements. That’s what they were worth in the end.”

He opened it. The coins slid into his palm and lay there, small and dull. His face went dark red, all the way to the hairline.

“You’re mocking me.”

“No. I’m paying you. Everything else you owe is with the lawyers.” She stood up. “There’s nothing to pack. Your accounts are frozen and the house belongs to the bank. You won’t contact the staff, or the senior men, or the suppliers, or anyone who has ever been paid by my husband. Zhao is downstairs. He’ll take you to the border.”

“Tonight?”

“Now.”

“And where am I supposed to go?”

“Anywhere,” said Aurelia, “that isn’t here.”

He stood for a long moment with the coins in his fist. Then he went down the stairs ahead of her, and Zhao opened the back door of the car without a word, and Sun Wei got in, in the clothes he was standing in.

She watched the tail lights to the end of the quay. She didn’t wave. Then she went back to the hospital.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao drove without the radio. For the first hour Sun Wei said nothing. Then he began.

“You should tell her this is unnecessary.”

“She knows what she’s doing.”

“Twenty years,” said Sun Wei, to the window. “Do you know what I did for this organisation?”

Zhao changed lanes. “I know what you did to it.”

At a petrol station an hour from the border he stopped and bought two bottles of water and put one on the seat beside Sun Wei.

“Why?”

“Because I’m driving,” said Zhao. “Drink.”

A little before four they reached the crossing. Zhao got out and opened the back door. There was no speech. He handed over the one document Sun Wei would need, and stood by the car with his hands in his coat pockets, and watched him walk towards the lights. Halfway there, Sun Wei stopped and looked back. Zhao didn’t move. Sun Wei turned and kept walking until the dark on the other side of the barrier took him, with six coins in his pocket and nothing else he owned except his shoes.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was getting light when Zhao came up to the ninth floor. Aurelia was outside the room with a paper cup of tea she’d forgotten to drink.

“Done?”

“Yes.”

“Did he make trouble?”

“Not much.”

She nodded and said thank you, and Zhao stood there for a moment as if he wasn’t sure what to do with his hands. Then he took one of hers in his. His palm was rough and scarred. He held it, briefly, not like a bodyguard and not like a man taking orders.

“He won’t come back,” Zhao said.

“I know.”

He let go and opened the door for her. “Go in.”

Chen Si was awake. He turned his head before she was through the door.

“You’re back.”

“Zhao told you.”

“Is it done?”

She sat in the chair beside him and told him, all of it, in order, the way she’d have told him the quarter’s figures. The rights, the shares, the house, the forty pages. The six coins. He listened with his eyes on her face, and when she said thirty-one million his mouth went hard, and then it eased again.

“You didn’t kill him.”

“Zhao offered.”

“I know he did.” A ghost of a smile. “Zhao tells me things.”

“That man needs to learn how to keep a conversation private.”

“Why did you say no?”

“Because I wanted him to understand what he’d done,” she said. “And because I didn’t want you to wake up and find I’d made a decision for you that you could never take back.”

He lifted his hand off the blanket. It cost him; she could see it cost him. She took it and laid it against her cheek.

“Thank you,” he said.

“You’d have done the same.”

“Perhaps.” His eyes moved over her face, slowly, as if he were reading it. “You’re terrifying. You know that? You walked into a room full of old men and made them sit down. You found the money. You found the ones who were measuring my chair. You took twenty years of a man’s little kingdom inside mine and you took it apart with paperwork.”

“Contracts. Deeds. A frozen account. Forty pages.”

He laughed very softly, and it made him cough, and she waited with her hand flat on his chest until it passed.

“You didn’t need a gun,” he said.

“No.”

She bent and kissed the inside of his wrist, just above the blue vein, and felt his fingers try to close on hers.

“Are you frightened of me?” she asked.

“Sometimes.” He watched her face fall a little, and went on. “Not because I think you’d hurt me. Because I know what you’ll do to anyone who comes near what you love.”

She kissed his wrist again. “Good. Then you know never to make me angry.”

“Noted.” His thumb moved on her cheek. “Have you eaten?”

“Chen Si.”

“Answer.”

“Half a sandwich.”

“That isn’t food.”

“I spent the night removing a man from your organisation. I didn’t have time to cook.”

“Then get well, and cook for me yourself.”

“I will.”

On the bedside table the black jade queen stood beside his pen, where she had put them on the first night so that he would see them whenever he woke. The investigations would go on for months. But Sun Wei was on the other side of the border with six coins and his shoes, and the chair at the head of the table was still waiting.

“My wife,” Chen Si murmured, and closed his eyes.

“Your terrifying wife.”

“My terrifying wife.”

She stayed until his breathing changed, with his fingers in hers and the broken necklace warm against her throat, and outside the window the harbour turned from grey to white.

chapters.title: His Brother Guards the Door
chapters.desc: Fourteen nights on a plastic chair outside a room on the ninth floor. A woman with a syringe. A woman who falls asleep on his shoulder at four in the morning. Zhao Zhendong has never had a sister. He finds out what it is like.
chapters.epigraph: “You’re a good brother.”
chapters.content:
Zhao Zhendong had brothers in everything but blood. Men who had stood beside him in bad rooms, men who had carried him out of worse ones. He had never had a sister. He found out what it was like on a plastic chair outside a room on the ninth floor, over fourteen nights in January.

It began on the first, when Chen Si’s heart still couldn’t hold its rhythm for more than an hour at a time. At midnight Zhao took the chair by the door. At six Qian came to relieve him. At midnight Zhao came back. Nobody asked him to, and nobody told him to stop, and by the fourth night the nurses had stopped asking whether he was staying and simply brought two cups of tea instead of one.

The chair was terrible. Hard grey plastic, a back that ended halfway up his spine, legs that shrieked on the floor if he shifted. It had been made for people waiting twenty minutes for a prescription, not for a man who meant to sit in it until dawn. He complained about it once, under his breath, at half past two on the third night, and the door opened and Aurelia came out in yesterday’s gold dress with a hospital cardigan over it.

“Would you like a cushion?”

“No.”

“A blanket?”

“Go back inside.”

“You’re very unfriendly.”

“You’re very awake.”

She went back in. Ten minutes later she came out with a cushion from somewhere, put it on the chair beside him and said good night, Zhao, and shut the door. He looked at it for a long time. Then he used it.

The nights found a shape. Twelve-fifteen, the nurse checked the monitors. One, tea. Around two Aurelia came out to stretch her legs, walked to the end of the corridor and back, and stood at the window with her arms folded as if she could keep the city away by looking at it. Three was the quietest hour. At four the sky over the harbour began to thin. The walls were not thick, and sometimes towards five he heard her talking in there, low, the way you talk to someone who is asleep. He never listened on purpose. She told Chen Si about the weather. She complained about the hospital porridge. She read him the day’s messages and argued with the ones she didn’t like, as though he were going to answer. Once she said, very quietly, Please come home soon, and Zhao looked down at his hands and stayed looking at them until the sun came up. He never told her he’d heard.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the seventh night Qian made her go home. She hadn’t slept in a bed since the boat, and she had eleven men to feed the next evening and a soup to make that took eight hours, and Qian, who had never in seven years raised his voice to anyone, stood in the corridor and told her that if she fell over on the forty-fourth floor in front of the senior men, it would be his fault and he would not forgive her. She went. She looked back twice.

At twenty to one a nurse came round the corner with a covered tray.

Zhao knew the night staff by then. He knew their faces and their shoes and the way each of them pushed the door. He didn’t know this one.

“Night shift,” she said, before he’d asked.

“Name?”

She gave him one. The photograph on her badge was very slightly out of focus.

“Which department?”

“Cardiology. I need to check Mr. Chen’s line.”

Zhao stood up. The tray tilted in her hands, and the cloth slid an inch, and he saw the syringe under it, already filled.

“Put it down.”

“I have an order.”

“Show me.”

She took one step back. He stepped between her and the door, and she turned and ran.

He caught her at the stairwell. The tray went down and something metal went skittering across the tiles. She fought harder than he expected, hard enough to tear the shoulder of his jacket, and when he pinned her wrist against the fire door she tried for her pocket with the other hand and he knocked it away and felt the skin go across his knuckles on the edge of the door frame. By the time security came running he had the syringe in his own fist, held away from his body, and her face against the wall.

“Who sent you?”

She said nothing. For the first time, she looked frightened.

“Nobody touches this,” he told the guard, and gave him the syringe as if it were a live round. “Call Mr. Yuen. Nobody asks her anything until he’s here.”

Then he went back and looked through the glass. Chen Si was asleep. The monitor hadn’t changed its count.

He rang the forty-fourth floor at five past one. She answered on the first ring, which meant she hadn’t been asleep either.

“He’s all right,” he said first, before anything else. “He didn’t wake. Nobody went in.” Then he told her the rest.

There was a silence on the line, the kind that has a person standing very still at the end of it.

“I’m coming.”

“No. Stay where you are. He’s asleep. I’m here. You’ve got a soup to make.”

“Are you hurt?”

He looked at his knuckles. “No.”

“Zhao.”

“A little.”

She breathed out. “Get someone to clean it. Properly. Not with tea.”

“Go to sleep, Mrs. Chen.”

She didn’t, of course. She rang off and went into the kitchen at two in the morning and began the broth on the lowest flame, and he sat back down on the cushion with his hand wrapped in hospital gauze, and they each kept their own watch, twenty floors and half a city apart.

✦ ✦ ✦

The nights were hardest after four. On the ninth night she was back in the chair beside the bed, and Zhao, getting up to stretch, saw her through the glass with her fingers wrapped round Chen Si’s hand, watching the drip. One drop. Another. Her lips were moving. She was counting. He could see where she’d bitten her lower lip raw.

Then Chen Si’s fingers moved, and she bent over him, and Zhao turned away from the glass, because it wasn’t his to watch. He learned what was said a long time later, from Chen Si, in a car, when neither of them was looking at the other.

“You’re counting,” Chen Si had said.

“Someone has to.”

“Stop.”

“I can’t.”

“Then count me.” A breath. “One husband.”

She had laughed, a small broken sound. “What’s two?”

“Hands.”

“You’re very bad at counting.”

“Three. You’re here.”

She stopped counting the drip after that.

At twelve minutes past four she came out into the corridor and stood in front of him as if she’d forgotten why she had come.

“Can I sit here?”

He moved his elbow off the second chair. She sat. Her eyes closed.

“You should sleep in there,” he said.

“If I sleep I might miss something.”

“You won’t.”

“I know,” she said, in the voice of someone who didn’t.

Her head tipped sideways. She straightened it. It tipped again. “Mrs. Chen,” he said. “Sleep.” She opened one eye and told him he was rude, and tried to sit up properly, and then without another word her head came down on his shoulder and stayed there.

Zhao went still. He could have called Qian. He could have fetched a nurse to walk her back inside. He could have moved. At half past four the night nurse came past, and he put one finger to his lips, and she smiled and went by on the sides of her shoes. At five Qian arrived, stopped dead, looked at them, and looked at Zhao.

“Don’t,” said Zhao.

Qian put a cup of tea on the table without a sound and went away again. At half past five Aurelia’s cheek slid against the seam of his jacket, and he shifted the collar so it wouldn’t mark her face. She murmured something. He bent his head. It was Chen Si’s name.

When she woke it was nearly seven. She looked at the corridor, and then at his shoulder, and then at her own hand, which had at some point taken hold of his sleeve, and sat up so fast her hair caught on his button.

“Oh, no.”

“Good morning.”

“How long?”

“Long enough.”

“Why didn’t you wake me?”

“You were asleep.”

She put both hands over her face. He stood and rolled his shoulder until it clicked. She watched him do it through her fingers, and then she lowered her hands and said thank you, and then, very softly, as if it had just occurred to her: “You’re a good brother.”

His face did something he didn’t give it permission to do. He picked up his jacket. “Go and eat breakfast,” he said, and walked away down the corridor, and she didn’t know that he carried the word around with him all that day, through the docks and the bank and the cold store, the way a man carries a stone in his pocket that he keeps touching to make sure it’s still there.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came back after midnight on the eleventh with forty pages in a folder and sat down beside him without being asked.

“Done?” he said.

“Done.” She put the folder on her knees. He was turning his hand over, looking at the gauze, and she was looking at his other palm, at the old white line across the middle of it.

“Si has one of those.”

“Yes.”

“He told me once it was from the road.” She waited. “It wasn’t, was it?”

Zhao looked at the door of the room for a long while.

“Block C,” he said. “He was sixteen. I was fifteen. It isn’t a place you leave through the gate. There was a riot one night, and he’d been planning for months, and he knew a way down into the drains. Half a kilometre in the dark, water up to here.” He touched his chest. “I’d been cut. I couldn’t do much. He held me up the whole way. Kept talking. I told him to leave me, and he told me to stop wasting his time.”

She laughed under her breath. “That sounds like him.”

“It wasn’t funny then.” He rubbed his thumb along the old scar. “When we came out there was a doctor in the old town who’d stitch anyone, if you paid. Three days, he kept me. We had nothing. On the third day Si went out and came back with a book. His father’s. A very old book, four hundred years old, the only thing of Chen Rong’s he still had that was worth anything. He put it on the doctor’s table, and the doctor looked inside the cover, and that was the bill paid.”

She was very quiet.
