“He tried to buy it back, later. It had gone through three hands by then. Somewhere overseas. He never found it.” Zhao looked at the floor. “He doesn’t talk about it. He didn’t want you to think he’d lost something for me.”

“He didn’t lose it for you,” she said. “He chose you. That’s not the same thing.”

Zhao looked at her for a long moment. Then he nodded, once, and they didn’t speak again until the nurse came.

He didn’t sit in the chair on the twelfth. On the twelfth he drove Sun Wei to the border in the middle of the night and left him on the far side with six coins and his shoes, and Qian took the door. Afterwards Zhao counted it anyway. Thirteen nights on the chair and one on the border road, and as far as he was concerned that made fourteen.

At nine on the morning of the thirteenth, from the corridor, he heard her on the phone to Enzo.

“A very old book. From 1592, I think. It belonged to Chen Si’s father.”

A long pause.

“No. I don’t know the title.”

Another.

“I know it isn’t a necklace, Enzo. Find me someone who knows where to look. And don’t tell Chen Si.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the fifteenth, the morning they were letting him go home, Chen Si came out of the room in a wheelchair for the first time. A nurse pushed it. Qian walked beside it carrying a bag of medicine as though it were a briefcase of bearer bonds. Aurelia came behind with her hand on the back of the chair. Dr. Ma had allowed ten minutes outside the door, provided nobody let Mr. Chen do anything at all.

Zhao stood up.

Chen Si looked at him, and then at the plastic chair, and then at the cushion on it.

“That looks uncomfortable.”

“It is.”

“Why didn’t you ask for another?”

“Because you were in there.”

Chen Si didn’t answer that. He nodded at the second chair. “Sit.”

“Mr. Chen—“

“Sit down, Brother.”

Zhao sat. Chen Si held out his hand, slowly, because his arm was still heavy, and after a moment Zhao put his palm against it. The two old white lines crossed. Chen Si closed his fingers.

“You stayed,” he said.

“Of course.”

“You didn’t have to.”

“Yes,” said Zhao. “I did.”

Aurelia looked from one of them to the other and said, “You’re both impossible,” and neither of them disagreed. A man who had once held another up through half a kilometre of black water. A man who had sat outside a door for fourteen nights, give or take a border. And between them, with her hand on the back of the wheelchair, the woman who had somehow become the middle of both their lives.

Later, when Zhao had gone to bring the car round, she settled Chen Si for the last half hour before they left and bent to kiss him, briefly, a reward for sitting up. He caught her fingers when she drew back.

“Again.”

“You’re tired.”

“One more.”

She kissed him again, and he followed her a fraction when she pulled away, and she laughed against his mouth and told him he was supposed to be resting.

“I am,” he said. “Help me.”

Out in the corridor Zhao sat down on the cushion one last time to wait for the nurse’s signature. The night nurse, going off shift, brought him a cup of tea he hadn’t asked for. Through the glass he could see the two of them, her forehead against Chen Si’s, his hand in her hair. The chair was still terrible. He found he didn’t mind it. Somewhere in the last fourteen nights, without asking anyone, he had been given a sister.

chapters.title: A Laptop, a Gun, and a Very Tired Co-Ruler
chapters.desc: His first night home. He wakes at three in the morning and she is in the chair beside the bed, asleep sitting up, with a laptop on her knees and a gun on the table and his necklace at her throat. He finally understands what he married.
chapters.epigraph: “Just you, in this bed, not dying.”
chapters.content:
Chen Si came home in a wheelchair, and disliked it from the first yard.

Not because it was uncomfortable, although it was, and not because the drive from the hospital to the private entrance took forty minutes in the afternoon traffic, although it did. He disliked the way everyone looked at him. Qian pushed the chair as if it were full of eggs. Zhao walked beside it with a bag of medicine and the face of a man prepared to break the arm of anyone who suggested the journey had been too much. In the lift, the security man who had ridden up and down with Chen Si for four years kept his eyes on the floor numbers with great concentration, the way you avoid looking at a man who has been crying.

Aurelia walked in front, and opened the door herself.

The flat smelled of cedar and cold stone, and of the white ranunculus she had put in the hall that morning. Everything was where he remembered it. Except the stack of folders on the dining table, which hadn’t been there before. And a laptop on the sofa, open. And his wife, who looked, now that he could see her in their own light instead of under hospital strip-lights, as though she had not slept properly for a very long time.

She crouched in front of the chair. “How does it feel?”

“Like being returned by kidnappers.”

“You’re welcome.”

He took her hand and held it, his thumb on the inside of her wrist, until Dr. Ma, who had insisted on coming to see the bedroom for himself, cleared his throat.

“I’d like everyone to hear the instructions once more.”

Chen Si closed his eyes. Aurelia looked delighted.

“Rest. No business, no meetings, no screens for longer than half an hour. The heart is recovering, but it tires, and when it tires it misbehaves. The medication exactly as written. Monitoring twice a week.” Dr. Ma turned to Aurelia. “You will make sure of all of this.”

“I will.”

“And no sexual activity,” said Dr. Ma, in the voice of a judge handing down a sentence, “until I have examined him again and cleared him.”

Qian looked at the ceiling. Zhao found something urgent in the medicine bag.

“For how long?” said Chen Si.

“Until I say otherwise.”

There was a short pause in which Aurelia’s shoulders began to shake. Chen Si turned his head and looked at her. He knew precisely which clause she was thinking of, and so did she, and she pressed her lips together so hard they went white, and failed, and laughed out loud in front of the cardiologist.

“I am serious, Mrs. Chen.”

“So am I,” she managed. “Completely.”

“My wife,” said Chen Si, to nobody, “has become very powerful.”

“She was powerful before you married her,” said Dr. Ma, and left.

✦ ✦ ✦

Getting him into bed took three people and more patience than he possessed. He could stand for a few seconds if someone held his arm, and after that his legs began to shake in a way that had nothing to do with him. Aurelia kept a hand at his waist while Qian and Zhao lowered him against the pillows. He hated every second of it. She knew, and said nothing, and pulled the blanket over his knees and put another pillow behind his back, and when he said he didn’t want another pillow she left it there anyway.

“Stay,” he said.

“I’m not going anywhere.”

She meant it. But her eyes went to the laptop on the sofa as she said it, and then to her phone, and he noticed. He noticed that she had sat down in the one chair from which she could see both the bedroom door and the window. He had spent fifteen days in a bed unable to do anything but hold her hand. He was home now, and his wife was still waiting for someone to come through the door.

Zhao took over the lobby without telling anyone. He walked the entrances, spoke to the building’s security chief for twenty minutes, checked the private lift and put two men on the service door. Then he went into the kitchen, and when Aurelia came looking for him he was standing at the stove with a wooden spoon.

“Congee,” he said, before she could ask.

“You can make congee?”

He gave her a flat look. “He’s been eating hospital food for fifteen days.”

She leaned on the counter and watched him for a minute. Then she reached past him and turned the flame down. “Lower. It’ll catch.”

“Thank you.” He stirred. “Go upstairs.”

“Save me some.”

He pointed the spoon at her. “Your husband isn’t the only one in this building who needs watching.” And because he was Zhao, he said nothing else, and she went.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eleven, Chen Si fell asleep. At midnight she was still awake. At one, Mr. Yuen rang twice about the pharmacologist, who had been found in a rented room near the bus station and was talking. At half past one she went through the latest reconciliation from Mr. Tan. At two she read the building’s security log, line by line. At a quarter past she sent Qian a message about the Jade Hall. At half past she opened the ledger again.

At three o’clock, Chen Si woke.

The first thing he saw was a pool of yellow light by the window. The second was his wife, asleep in the chair beside it.

She was sitting upright. Her head had tipped to one side and her hair had fallen across her cheek. The laptop lay open on her knees, its screen dimmed but still showing a spreadsheet, and her right hand rested on the keys with a pen caught between two fingers. On the little table beside her was a glass of water, a slice of toast with one bite out of it, and a pistol.

His eyes stopped on the pistol. Then they went to her throat.

She was wearing the broken necklace. Her own necklace, really: the one from the bottom left-hand corner of her shop window that she had given him in March without mending it, the one he had carried folded in a handkerchief in his inside pocket ever since. Qian must have brought it to her from the boat with his things. She had tied the parted link with a loop of silk thread. It lay against the collar of her sleep shirt and moved when she breathed.

He looked at her for a long time. The laptop. The ledger. The gun. The necklace. His wife, asleep sitting up, because apparently she had decided that being unconscious was no excuse for stopping work. And he understood, with a clearness that made his chest ache in a way that had nothing to do with the poison, exactly what he had married. Not a woman who waited for him to come home. A woman who had kept his whole world standing while he couldn’t lift it, and had forgotten she was allowed to put it down.

“Aurelia.”

She didn’t stir. The laptop began to slide. He reached for it, slowly, because his arm was still lead from the shoulder down, and caught the edge before it fell. The movement woke her, and she came upright all at once, already looking at him.

“What is it? Are you in pain? Do you need—“

“Come here.”

“One minute. I just have to send—“

“No.”

Something in his voice stopped her. She closed the laptop. Then she looked at the table and saw what he’d seen.

“Security,” she said.

“On the table.”

“Within reach.”

“Come here,” he said again, and this time she did.

She sat on the edge of the bed. He put his hand up and touched the skin under her eyes, where the shadows were. Her face had got thinner. There was a cut on one knuckle he didn’t know about, ink down the side of her first finger, a bruise going yellow on the inside of her wrist. He ran his thumb over the bruise.

“How long have you been sleeping in chairs?”

She looked at the window. “A little while.”

“How long?”

“Sixteen nights,” she said. “More or less. Since the boat. I lost count of the days, so I counted nights instead.”

He shut his eyes. When he opened them she was watching him carefully.

“Don’t do that,” she said.

“Do what?”

“Blame yourself. I can see you starting.”

“I left you with all of it.”

“You didn’t leave. Someone tried to kill you.” Her voice wobbled, just slightly. “I was afraid that if I slept, something would happen and I wouldn’t know.”

“Something did happen,” he said. “And you were there. When I woke up, you were there. When I couldn’t speak. When I couldn’t lift my hand. I knew, every time.” He moved his thumb on her wrist. “You kept me alive in every way there was.”

“I didn’t do enough.”

“Aurelia.”

“I couldn’t stop it. I couldn’t make you better. I couldn’t—“

“Stop,” he said, quite gently, and she stopped, and a tear came down her face, and he wiped it off with the side of his thumb. She bent until her forehead rested on his.

“Come to bed.”

“The accounts—“

“Can wait.” He gave her a tired, almost helpless smile. “Please.”

That did it. Getting in beside him was a careful business. She was frightened of the wires taped under his shirt, frightened of his ribs, frightened, he could tell, of his heart, and she asked about all three, and he said still attached about the last one, and she gave him an exasperated look and lay down against his side. He got his arm round her, not as far as he wanted to.

“Sleep.”

“I should check the—“

“If I need you, I’ll wake you.”

“Promise?”

“I promise.”

It took less than five minutes. Sixteen nights of fear and paper and counting the drip came down on her all at once, and her fingers curled into his shirt, and she was gone. Chen Si stayed awake. He looked at the necklace rising and falling at her throat, and he kissed her hair, and towards dawn he slept too.

✦ ✦ ✦

At seven Zhao came up with a thermos and knocked once. When nobody answered he opened the door an inch.

The laptop was shut on the table. The pistol had gone back into its case. Chen Si was awake against the pillows with his wife asleep on his arm.

“Quiet,” said Chen Si.

Zhao looked at her, and at the clock. “Since when?”

“Three.”

“Good.” He put the thermos down and turned to go.

“Brother.” Zhao stopped. “How long was she sleeping in that chair?”

“Sixteen nights.”

“She told you?”

“I was sitting outside the door.” Zhao’s voice was perfectly flat. “She slept when she couldn’t keep her eyes open. Sometimes in there. Sometimes on my shoulder. Some nights she woke every twenty minutes to look at the screen.” He glanced at her again. “She was afraid to leave you.”

Chen Si’s fingers moved in her hair. “Thank you,” he said. “For the door. For her.”

“You’re my brother,” said Zhao, and went out.

She slept for eleven hours. When she woke it was dark outside, and for a moment she didn’t know where she was. Then she felt his chest under her cheek, rising, and his hand in her hair, and lifted her head.

“What time is it?”

“Nine.”

“At night?”

“At night.”

She sat up far too quickly. “Your medicine—“

“Taken.”

“Did you eat?”

“Zhao’s congee. Twice.”

“Did Dr. Ma—“

He caught her hand. “You slept.”

She stared at him. Then her face gave way into a smile. “That feels illegal.”

“We’ll keep it between us.”

He touched the necklace at her throat. She had worn it every day, she said; she’d put it on in the hospital the morning Qian brought it, and hadn’t taken it off since, not even in the shower.

“Why?”

She looked at him as if the question were stupid. “Because it was yours.”

“Everything I have is yours.”

“Don’t say things like that. I don’t want everything you have.”

“What do you want?”

She leaned down and kissed his forehead. “You,” she said. “Just you, in this bed, not dying.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning Zhao brought congee and a typed list, and put both on the table. Two men on the main entrance. One on the service lift. A visitors’ list, a rota, a code word that changed every Monday.

“You made a roster,” said Aurelia.

“Yes.”

“How long are you planning to stay?”

“Until I’m satisfied.”

“With what?”

“Everything.” He put the bowl in front of Chen Si. “All of it.”

“That’s a lot,” said Chen Si.

“You’re recovering.”

Chen Si looked at his wife for help. She smiled at him sweetly. “Listen to your brother.” Zhao gave her a look of real approval, and waited until Chen Si had swallowed the first spoonful, and went.

When the door had closed Chen Si put his spoon down and took her hand and turned it over and kissed the palm.

“Co-ruler,” he said.

“What?”

“That’s what you are. Not just my wife. When I couldn’t sit at the table, you took my chair. When I couldn’t sign, you signed. When the men decided I was dying, you made very sure they understood the house still had someone at the head of it.” He looked at her. “And you didn’t turn into me. You stood next to me. All the years I spent building something that might outlive me, I never once thought about what it would mean to have someone who could keep it alive without becoming its prisoner.”

“You’re making it sound very grand.”

“It is grand.”

“You’ve been poisoned. Your judgement may be impaired.”

“Possibly.” He didn’t smile. “I want a twelfth clause.”

She raised an eyebrow. “The contract has eleven. Clause eleven says it runs ten years, and at the end of them the Wife may rewrite every word of it. Not the Husband. The Wife.”

“I know. I read it every week in the hospital. Qian brought it in a folder.” He held her eyes. “So I’m not writing it. I’m asking you to keep it in mind. That neither of us carries the house alone. That if one of us can’t stand, the other takes the chair, and when the first can stand again, they sit at the table together.”

“And if neither of us can stand?”

“Then we sit on the floor together.”

A small smile came and went. “That’s your legal wording?”

“Mr. Yuen can make it worse.”

“Don’t you dare.” She looked down at their hands for a long time. Then she said, “Three conditions. Neither of us gets to disappear into work when the other needs them. Neither of us makes decisions about the other’s life and calls it protection. And you don’t get to pretend you’re fine when you’re not.”

“That last one may be difficult.”

“Then practise.” She took a pen off the tray, and the back of the discharge sheet, and wrote on it in red, Clause 12: we sit at the same table. To be considered, March 2029. A., and folded it, and put it in the drawer of his bedside table. “There. It’s in the drawer. Ask me again in nine years.”

He laughed, and it made him cough, and she put her hand flat on his chest and waited.

That evening, after Zhao had done his rounds and Dr. Ma had rung to check the numbers, she put a glass of water within his reach and sat on the edge of the bed, and then she leaned down and kissed him.

It wasn’t like the little kisses on the ninth floor, the ones that were half checking he was still warm. Nobody came in to read a monitor. Nothing beeped. It was a proper kiss, the first since the boat, slow and certain, her hand on his cheek, his fingers going carefully into her hair. When she drew back, he followed her an inch.

“Dr. Ma said no.”

“I know.”

“Don’t look at me like that.”

“I’m not negotiating.”

“You are. You’re negotiating with your eyebrows.” She touched his mouth with her thumb. He kissed it.

“I missed you,” he said.

“I was right there.”

“I know you were. I missed you anyway.” He had missed her arguing with him across a dinner table, stealing his chair, kissing him in the middle of a sentence to win it. He had missed her having a life outside a hospital room and a thousand opinions about his. He had missed her being his wife and not his nurse.

“I’m still here,” she said. “I’m not going anywhere.”

She lay down beside him. The laptop stayed shut on the table across the room. The pistol stayed in its case. For the first time in sixteen nights she slept without one eye on the door, and he held her hand under the blanket and didn’t count anything at all.

chapters.title: He Is Weak for Six Weeks
chapters.desc: No stairs. No work. No anger. No sex. He hates every minute. She makes him eat. And on the forty-second day, when Dr. Ma finally says yes, the Wife reads clause nine very carefully, and finds a way to make sure he doesn’t lift a finger.
chapters.epigraph: “I didn’t marry your strength, Chen Si. I married you.”
chapters.content:
Recovery, Chen Si discovered, was a humiliating business, and it began with the stairs.

“No,” said Aurelia.

She was standing at the foot of the staircase that went up from the living room to the study, holding a cup of warm water. He was standing beside the wheelchair with one hand on the banister.

“I can manage.”

“Dr. Ma said no stairs.”

“He said I should avoid unnecessary exertion.”

“Stairs are unnecessary. There’s a lift.”

Behind him, as if it had been listening, the little private lift that ran between the two floors of the flat chimed and opened its doors. Chen Si said nothing at all. Aurelia smiled at him with enormous sweetness and said, “After you,” and he went, and he hated her, and he loved her, and he was beginning to suspect the two feelings had become impossible to separate.

The second humiliation was work. On his third morning home he asked Qian for the reports. Qian brought them. Aurelia took them out of Qian’s hands on the way past and put the whole folder on the far end of the dining table, eleven feet from the nearest thing Chen Si could reach.

“Give them back.”

“No.”

“They’re mine.”

“Your heart is yours too. Dr. Ma still gets to tell you what to do with it.”

He turned to Qian, who was standing between them with the expression of a man who had been trained for knives and ambushes and had never once been trained for this.

“Tell my wife I need the reports.”

Qian looked at Aurelia, and then at the ceiling. “Madam has already reviewed them, Mr. Chen.”

“Clause twelve,” said Aurelia, picking up her teacup. “I know it’s in a drawer. I’m applying it early. You can’t only use it when it suits you.”

When Qian had gone, she came round the table and kissed the top of his head and told him to be a good patient, and he told her he wasn’t a patient, and she said he was the worst patient Dr. Ma had ever had and that Dr. Ma liked her better. After she’d gone downstairs to her own calls, he rang Qian and asked, in a low voice, whether there was any way to fire a cardiologist. Qian said he would look into it. Neither of them believed him.

✦ ✦ ✦

The third humiliation was food. Chen Si had never in his life been a man who needed reminding to eat; he ate when he was hungry and stopped when he wasn’t, and he didn’t think meals worth conversation. But the poison had done something to his appetite. Some mornings the smell of anything made him sick. Some evenings he looked at a plate and felt nothing but tired.

Aurelia did not accept this.

On the first morning she put a bowl of congee in front of him. He said he wasn’t hungry. She said three spoonfuls. He said no. She said five, which he pointed out was not how bargaining worked, and she said it was when you were bargaining with a man who had the appetite of a sick sparrow. He pushed the bowl away. She looked at it, and pulled her chair closer, and picked up the spoon.

“Open.”

“I’m not a child.”

“I know. Children are more co-operative.”

He turned his face to the window. She didn’t argue. She didn’t scold. She put the spoon down and sat there looking at him with an expression that was neither anger nor disappointment, and that was worse than either.

“You’re going to make yourself ill,” she said quietly.

“I am ill.”

“Then help me get you better.” She picked the spoon up again. “Please.”

He opened his mouth. She fed him one spoonful, then another. By the time the bowl was half empty his face was a study in misery, and she wiped a drop from the corner of his mouth with her thumb and told him he was doing very well, and he called her a sadist, and she said, “Your wife,” and gave him another.

She fed him for four days. She varied it according to what he could keep down: plain, then with shredded chicken, then ginger, then a little white fish. On the third day he set his jaw and wouldn’t open his mouth at all, and she waited, and then said, “Fine,” and began to eat out of his bowl herself. He watched her take two spoonfuls. On the third, he reached for it. She moved it out of his reach.

“Oh,” she said. “Suddenly hungry?”

On the fourth day a spoonful slid off the edge and landed on his white shirt, and he looked down at the stain and then up at her with such outrage that she lost all control of her face and laughed until she had to put the bowl down. He watched her bent double over the table. Then, without meaning to, he laughed as well. It was short and quiet and it left him out of breath, and she was beside him at once with her hand on his chest, still laughing, wet-eyed, and he caught her wrist and said, “Feed me another,” and for the first time he finished the bowl.

✦ ✦ ✦

The nights were harder. In the day she had calls and papers and staff and the endless work of keeping the Syndicate running without letting every small fire become a blaze. At night there was the quiet, and his heartbeat.

For eleven nights she counted it.

Dr. Ma had told her not to. The monitor patch on his chest sent its numbers to a screen in the next room and to the clinic, and it would wake the whole building if anything went wrong. She understood that perfectly. She lay with her head on his shoulder and her hand flat over his heart and counted anyway. Sometimes she got to a hundred. Sometimes she lost her place and started again. Sometimes she woke out of a dream with her palm already pressed against him before she knew she was awake.

On the fifth night he caught her hand in the dark. “What are you counting?”

She was quiet for a while. “You.”

“You don’t need to.”

“I know. I like hearing it.”

He kissed her hair. “Then listen.”

On the seventh night he woke and she was sitting up, her hand still on his chest, her eyes open in the dark. On the eighth he told her to sleep, and she did, for forty minutes, and then her hand found him again. On the eleventh she counted until she fell asleep. He lay awake a long time after, looking at her fingers spread over his ribs as if she had decided that if she held his heart carefully enough it would never try to leave her again. He wanted to tell her she could stop now. But he knew something about fear. It doesn’t leave because someone tells it to. So he put his hand over hers and let her keep it there.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the end of January she had learned that running a criminal organisation from a dining table while nursing a husband who hated being nursed was not, in most ways, very different from running a jewellery business. The main difference was that the jewellery business had fewer people trying to poison him.

Mr. Yuen came on a Tuesday with three folders and laid them in front of her. Chen Si was on the sofa in the living room, ten feet away, pretending not to listen.

The pharmacologist had told the police everything. The fees through the port liaison office had been arranged by Mr. Wan, as the file said. And the money that had paid Mr. Wan had come, through two companies and a cold store, from Sun Wei. Judge Lai had resigned from two boards and was saying nothing through three lawyers.

“And Mr. Hu’s route,” said Mr. Yuen. “Still suspended. His men want to know who they work for.”

“Mr. Ngai,” said Aurelia.

Mr. Yuen opened his notebook. “That’s a great deal of responsibility.”

“I know. He can inherit the work. He doesn’t inherit the man.” She turned a page. “And from this quarter, your share is doubled.”

He looked up over his glasses. “That isn’t necessary.”

“It is. You did your job for three weeks while everyone else in this organisation was busy wondering whether my husband would live long enough to sign anything.”

“I’d have done it regardless.”

“I know,” she said. “That’s why it’s doubled. Now go and find out where Judge Lai’s money went.”

From the sofa Chen Si said, without opening his eyes, “She’s right about Ngai. Give him the route. Keep the accounts under review until the investigation closes.”

“And the share, Mr. Chen?”

“Her decision.”

When Mr. Yuen had gone, he called her over. She came and sat on the arm of the sofa.

“You gave Yuen double.”

“He’ll take a holiday at last.”

“I wasn’t worried about the money.”

“What were you worried about?”

He reached for her hand. “That you were doing it all alone again.”

“I’m not.” She kissed his temple. “You’re here, criticising from the sofa.”

“And if I weren’t?”

“Then I’d still be here.” He didn’t like that answer, and she knew it, so she added, “But I’d rather have you next to me,” and his face eased.

✦ ✦ ✦

The worst day was the twenty-fourth day. He tried to walk from the bedroom to the living room without waiting for anyone, and made it halfway down the corridor before his legs began to tremble in long slow waves, and she came round the corner in time to catch him. He hated that she had to. He hated the sweat at his temples and the shake in his knees and the way his own body had stopped taking orders. She got him to the sofa and brought him water. He didn’t take it.

“Are you angry with me?” she asked, crouching in front of him.

“No.”

“With Zhao?”

“No.”

“Dr. Ma?”

A pause. “Possibly.”

“That’s fair.”

“I should be better by now.”

“You’re better than you were yesterday.”

“It isn’t enough.”

“It has to be,” she said. “You don’t have to be the man who walked onto that boat. You just have to be the man who gets up tomorrow.”

He looked at the floor. “I hate needing help. I hate you watching me need it.”

“I don’t mind watching. I mind that you think being loved means being useful.” She lifted his hand and kissed the knuckles. “I didn’t marry your strength, Chen Si. I married you.”

He was silent for a long time. Then he put his hand round the back of her neck, the way he used to, and brought her face down to his and kissed her. It wasn’t much of a kiss, by his old standards. There wasn’t much strength in it. There was nothing uncertain about it either.

“Eighteen more days,” he said against her mouth.

She drew back. “What?”

“Day forty-two. The next assessment.”

She stared at him, and then she understood, and started to laugh. “You’re counting.”

“Apparently it’s catching.”

“He didn’t promise anything on day forty-two. He said he’d look at you.”

“I know. I’m very motivated.”

She put a fingertip on his lips. “Behave.” He kissed the fingertip.

✦ ✦ ✦

She hadn’t marked day forty-two on any calendar. She didn’t ask Qian to arrange anything. Chen Si remembered, of course, and so, it turned out, did Dr. Ma, who on Tuesday the eleventh of February listened to his chest for a long time, took his pressure twice, made him walk the length of the clinic corridor and back while he watched with his arms folded, and read the numbers off the monitor with his lips pursed.

“Progressing,” he said at last. “Still weakness. The medication continues. Activity goes up gradually. No lifting, no sudden effort, no return to a full working day.” He looked from one of them to the other. “And as for intimacy.”

Chen Si became very still. Aurelia folded her hands in her lap.

“You may resume it. Gradually. If there is chest discomfort, dizziness, breathlessness that isn’t ordinary, palpitations, you stop. You do not treat this as permission to run a marathon.”

“Thank you,” said Chen Si.

“Don’t thank me as if I’d given you a medal. If I see you back here because you’ve been trying to prove something, I will tell everyone in this city why.”

“I’ll make sure he behaves,” said Aurelia.

Dr. Ma looked at her. “That, Mrs. Chen, is what concerns me.”

They were quiet in the car. He had his hand over hers on the seat between them, and he watched her looking out of the window, smiling at nothing.

“What?”

“You’re cleared.”

“Gradually.”

“With restrictions. No lifting. No proving anything.” She turned and kissed his cheek. “Welcome back.”

“Thank you for waiting.”

“I wasn’t waiting for you to turn into someone else,” she said. “I was waiting for you to come home to yourself.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening she went into her dressing room and came out with a scarf.

Not silk from one of her own collections. Old cashmere, soft as breath and faded at the edges, the colour of milky tea. Her grandmother had worn it on cool evenings in Milan. Chen Si put out his hand and touched it.

“Your grandmother’s.”

“Yes.” She took the marriage agreement out of the drawer of her bedside table, where it lived, eleven pages in her red ink, his signature at the bottom of each. She found the ninth clause and read it aloud. “All matters of intimacy shall be under the direction of the Wife, until she says otherwise.” She looked up. “Still agree?”

“Yes.”

“Still comfortable?”

“Yes.”

“The word?”

“Milan,” he said. “And in Milan, Rotterdam.”

“Good husband.” She put the agreement down. “I want your hands here.” She touched his wrists. “Not because you can’t move them. Because you trust me not to ask for anything you don’t want to give.”

He looked at her for a long moment. Then he held his hands out, wrists together.

She wound the scarf round them loosely, with room to spare, and tied it to the dark wooden post at the head of the bed with a knot a child could have undone. She checked his fingers, and his shoulders, because of his ribs, because of his heart. She asked if it was too tight and he said no, and she asked if he could get free and he turned his wrists and showed her he could, and she said good, and then she leaned over him and looked at his face for a while without doing anything at all.

“Tonight,” she said, “you don’t have to do one single thing.”

He didn’t move his hands. That was the whole of it, in a way. He had spent six weeks being lifted and turned and fed and told, and hating all of it, and now she was asking him to lie still, and he found that when it was her asking, and when it was this, lying still was the easiest thing in the world. She kissed his forehead, his eyes, his jaw. She took her time over his mouth. She unbuttoned his shirt slowly, one button and then a long pause and then the next, and laid her palm flat on his chest the way she had every night for eleven nights, and this time she didn’t count. His breath caught. She lifted her head and looked at him, and he said, “Don’t you dare stop,” and she laughed, low, and didn’t.

She was careful with him, and she was not gentle, and the difference was entirely hers to decide. She kissed her way down the scar where the wires had been and undid his belt and took the rest off him and let him watch her undress at the foot of the bed, slowly, piece by piece, until his wrists pulled against the cashmere. She stopped and waited, her mouth an inch from his, until he let them go slack again, and she smiled, and went on. When she straddled him and took him inside her she did it so slowly he shut his eyes, and she told him to open them, and he did. She set the pace and kept it there, low and steady, her palm on his heart to feel it, until he was saying her name in a voice she hadn’t heard since before the boat. Only then did she let go, and so did he.

Afterwards the scarf lay folded on the bedside table and his hands were free, one of them spread over the small of her back. She lay with her ear against his chest.

“Anything hurt?”

“No.”

“Dizzy?”

“No.”

“Breathing?”

“Sweetheart,” he said. “I’m all right.”

She lifted her head and searched his face once more, and then put it down again.

“You read clause nine very carefully,” he said, after a while.

“I wrote it.”

“You still checked.”

“Contracts should be respected.”

He laughed, very softly. “I thought I was marrying a woman who had to come first. I didn’t know I was marrying the one who’d sit beside me for forty-two days, and count my heart, and take my chair, and then tell me to lie still while she loved me.”

“You make me sound very noble.”

“You’re not. You’re stubborn, and difficult, and terrifying, and often unreasonable.”

“Often?”

“Always.” He kissed her nose. “And mine.”

She lifted an eyebrow. “By choice.”

“Always by choice.”

She put her cheek back on his chest. For forty-two days she had been careful with his heart. Tonight, for the first time since the boat, she let him hold hers.

chapters.title: The Word Is Milan
chapters.desc: The danger is over. He is safe. She is fine. She is fine for nine days. On the tenth, in the middle of the boutique, holding a champagne flute for a client, her hands stop working. She says the word for the first time, and it isn’t in bed.
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t have to earn being frightened.”
chapters.content:
For nine days, Aurelia was fine.

She went back to the boutique on a Tuesday, the fourth of February, in a camel coat and the broken necklace, and rejected three settings by eleven because the proportions were wrong. On Wednesday she corrected a supplier’s invoice to the last decimal and sat through the Harbour Road managers’ meeting and made a decision about the spring stock that Mr. Yuen, when he heard of it, called unusually ruthless. On Thursday she laughed at Chen Si for taking the lift. On Friday she had lunch with Serafina, who ate both their desserts and talked about engine mounts for an hour. On Saturday she slept until ten. On Sunday she took him to the flower market, slowly, his arm through hers, and spent twenty minutes arguing with a florist about the difference between blush and dusty rose while he leaned on a pillar and watched her with his hands in his coat pockets. On Monday she went back to work. On Tuesday she held his hand at the clinic while Dr. Ma said gradually, and that night she did not count his heart. On Wednesday she bought a pair of shoes she didn’t need.

Nine days. She was working, eating, sleeping, laughing, kissing her husband, complaining about the damp. The fear had become something behind her. It belonged to the ninth floor and the boat and the weeks of counting the gaps between his heartbeats, and those were over. He was home. He was safe. She was fine.

On the tenth day, in the middle of her own boutique, holding a champagne flute for a client, her hands stopped working.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was a perfectly ordinary afternoon. A private viewing for a woman who had bought two pieces from the very first Harbour Road collection and had come back to commission earrings for her daughter’s wedding. The room smelled of white roses and beeswax. Lily was laying out the last tray. Enzo was in the workshop at the back, arguing with one of the bench men about a clasp.

“The setting is very restrained,” Aurelia was saying, a necklace across her palm. “I wanted the stones to have room.”

“You’re always so particular.”

“I have to be.” She reached for the glass on the silver tray beside her, to give it to her client.

Her fingers were supposed to close round the stem. They didn’t.

She tried again. Nothing. Her hand hung in the air above the tray, an inch from the glass, and she could see it, the narrow stem catching the light, the tiny curved reflection of her own fingers in the bowl, and they would not move.

“Aurelia?”

Someone laughed by the door. Somewhere behind her a glass was put down on a counter with a small, hard sound.

And she wasn’t in the boutique. She was on the stern of the Pearl, with the deck moving under her shoes and the fireworks breaking green over the harbour, and his weight was coming down on her shoulder, and she was laughing for the guests, laughing with her face in his collar so that nobody would see what his face was doing. She could feel how cold his hand was. She could see the glass rolling on the boards.

Her breath caught, and didn’t come back.

The flute began to rattle against the tray. Her client reached out to steady her, and Aurelia flinched so hard that the glass went over and burst on the stone floor, and the sound of it broke something open. She took a step back. Another. Her heart was going so fast it hurt. There wasn’t enough air in the room. She pressed her hand flat against her breastbone. Not here. Not now. I have a client. People are watching. I’m Aurelia Chen and I don’t—

Her knees went.

Enzo came out of the workshop, saw her face and stopped. “Everyone,” he said, in a voice she had never heard him use, “please go through to the salon.” Lily had the client by the elbow before he’d finished the sentence.

The phone was in Aurelia’s pocket. She could feel it against her hip. She knew who she needed. Her fingers wouldn’t do it. Then, all at once, they would, and the screen swam, and she found the top of her list and pressed.

It rang once.

“Sweetheart?”

“Chen—“ Her voice cracked in half.

“I’m here. Where are you?”

“I can’t—“

His voice changed. Not louder. Narrower. “Are you hurt?”

“No.”

“Is anyone there who shouldn’t be?”

“No.”

“Where are you?”

“The shop.” She dragged in a breath that didn’t reach anywhere. And then, almost too quietly for the phone to carry, she said the word.

“Milan.”

There was a silence on the line. Not a dropped call. The silence of a man who had heard something he had been waiting years to hear and had hoped never would.

“I’m coming,” said Chen Si.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was in the study on the forty-fourth floor with Qian, going through the short list of things Dr. Ma allowed him to touch. When she said it he stood up so fast that the chair rolled back into the shelves.

“The car,” he said. “Harbour Road. Now.”

Qian took one look at him and was already dialling. Chen Si went to the lift and stood in front of it and watched the little light over the doors say twelve, and fourteen, and fifteen, coming up so slowly, and he turned away from it and opened the stairwell door.

“Mr. Chen—“

“Take the lift. Have the car at the door.”

“Your heart—“

“I know.”

Forty-four floors. He hadn’t run them since before the boat. He should not have run them now. He knew exactly what Dr. Ma would say and exactly what his body would put up with and exactly where the line was between wanting something and being a fool about it, and he ran anyway.

By the sixth floor his chest had tightened. By the tenth his breathing had a rasp in it. On the fifteenth he had to stop and hold the rail for three seconds with his head down. Then he went on. He wasn’t thinking about the stairs. He was thinking of her in a room full of people with her hands not working. He was thinking about the word.

The safe word wasn’t a pretty clause she had written in red because she liked the idea of having the last say. It was a promise. If either of them said it, everything stopped. No questions first. No argument. No explain. And she had said it, not in bed, not in a game, not laughing, but because something in her had finally become too heavy to carry and she hadn’t had any other way to tell him.

On the twenty-first floor his vision greyed at the edges, and he held the rail and breathed, and went on. Somewhere around the thirtieth his phone rang. It was Qian. He answered without stopping.

“Where are you?”

“Stairs.”

“Mr. Chen, the car is—“

“Call Dr. Ma.”

“Sir—“

“Call him, Qian.”

He came out into the lobby with his jacket open and his hair in his eyes and his hand pressed for one second against his chest, and the car was at the kerb with the door open, and Qian was standing beside it with his phone to his ear and the face of a man reporting a crime.

✦ ✦ ✦

The client had gone. The salon was empty. Lily was on her knees by the door, sweeping the glass into a dustpan, and she looked up at him and pointed through to the back.

Aurelia was on the workshop floor. She was sitting against the side of the bench with her knees drawn up and one hand over her mouth. Enzo was crouched an arm’s length away, not touching her, talking very low in Italian. He looked up.

“She’s here,” Enzo said, and moved aside.

Chen Si didn’t rush at her. He didn’t take hold of her. He got down, carefully, onto one knee in front of her, and held his hands out palms up between them.

“Sweetheart.”

She looked up. Her eyes were very wide. She was breathing in short, shallow catches, as if the air were being rationed.

“Can I touch you?”

She nodded. He took her hands. They were ice. He folded them between his.

“Look at my face. Don’t try to breathe properly. Just do what I do.”

He breathed in, slowly, and out. She tried, and it came too fast, and he shook his head a little and said, “That’s all right. Again.” He counted it under his breath. One, two, three, out. One, two, three. She shut her eyes. “Keep them open for me,” he said, and she opened them.

It didn’t get better at once. Her chest still hurt and her fingers still shook and every few seconds her eyes went round the workshop as if she wasn’t sure it would stay there. He didn’t tell her nothing was wrong. He didn’t tell her to calm down. He didn’t tell her she was safe before she could believe it. He knelt on the stone floor and told her what was true.

“You’re in the workshop. It’s Thursday afternoon. Enzo’s here. Lily’s sweeping up. The glass is broken and nobody is angry with you. I’m here.”

Her eyes filled. Then she saw his face properly: the grey under the skin, the sweat at his temple, the way his own breath was still coming hard.

“Your heart.”

“Mine’s being looked after,” he said. “Right now I’m looking after you.”

She began to cry. Quietly, tears running down while she went on trying to breathe.

“I ruined the viewing.”

“No.”

“I broke the glass.”

“I’ll buy you another. A crate.” She made a small broken sound that was almost a laugh. And then she whispered it again, as if she needed to be sure he’d heard it the first time. “Milan.”

He shut his eyes for one second, and pressed her hands flat against his own chest. “I heard you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was twenty minutes before she could stand, and he didn’t hurry any of them. Enzo brought water. Dr. Ma, on Qian’s phone, was not pleased to learn that his patient had run down forty-four floors, and even less pleased to hear that his chest had tightened on the way.

“Mr. Chen. I would like you to stop making my work difficult.”

“I understand.”

“You understand, and you did it.”

Chen Si looked at his wife. She was still holding his hand. “Yes.”

Aurelia took the phone out of his fingers. “Dr. Ma. I’m sorry.”

“Is the chest pain easing, Mrs. Chen?”

“I don’t have chest pain.”

“You do. It’s easing?”

She thought about it. “Yes.”

“Then you are both coming to me now. You, because of what has just happened. Your husband, because apparently he has decided that stairs are a sport.” A pause. “And Mrs. Chen. You did right to ask for help.”

There was no dramatic finding. Chen Si’s heart had not done anything new, though Dr. Ma told him in some detail what it might have done and that he was not, under any circumstances, to do that again. Aurelia’s symptoms were those of a panic attack. It could come, Dr. Ma said, weeks after the danger had passed; the body can stay at its post long after the mind has been told to stand down. She asked whether it would happen again. He didn’t promise that it wouldn’t. He said these things took time and that people mattered, and he wrote a name on the back of a prescription pad, Dr. Ho, and a number.

It was late when they got home. She went straight into the bedroom and sat on the edge of the bed and looked at her hands. They were steady now. She opened and closed them. Once, twice. Then she pressed the palms together hard, as if they might try something.

He came in a few minutes later in a soft shirt, his hair still damp where he’d washed his face, and stood in front of her.

“May I?”

She nodded. He sat beside her.

“I thought I was fine,” she said. “I really thought I was. I went back to work. I saw Serafina. I slept. I laughed. Most days I didn’t even think about the boat.”

“That doesn’t mean it wasn’t still hurting.”

“I don’t understand why today.”

“Because it was today.” He turned her hand over. “You don’t have to earn being frightened. You don’t need a reason that would satisfy a committee.”

“I was holding a glass. And I couldn’t move my hand. It was so stupid.”

“No.”

“I felt ridiculous.”

He lifted her hand and kissed the palm. “You said the word. You trusted me enough to use it.”

“I didn’t want you to hear it. I didn’t want you to worry.”

He stared at her, and a small disbelieving laugh came out of him. “Aurelia. You rang me with the safe word. What was I supposed to do? Finish my meeting?”

She laughed too, weakly, and he kissed her forehead.

“When you wrote that clause,” he said, “you weren’t choosing a word for decoration. You were promising that neither of us would ever have to pretend. That’s all it’s for. That’s what it did.”

“I thought I’d use it to make you stop something.”

“You did,” he said. “It still counts.”

She looked at him for a long moment. Then her face broke, and she bent forward into his chest, and this time she didn’t try to hold any of it together.

It came out of her all at once. Not the quiet, careful tears she’d let herself have on the ninth floor while he was too weak to do anything about them. These came from much further down. She clutched his shirt in both fists and cried as though the deck were still moving under her.

“I thought you were dead.”

“I know.”

“I saw you stop breathing. I kept thinking, what if I hadn’t walked you out of the room? What if I hadn’t noticed? What if I’d let you drink it and smiled—“

“Stop.”

“I couldn’t make your heart go. I couldn’t make you wake up—“

“Aurelia.” He waited until she lifted her face. “You did not fail me. You were frightened, and exhausted, and you kept me alive while somebody was trying very hard to take me away from you. You did not have to do it perfectly.”

She cried harder. He drew her into his lap, carefully, mindful of how little strength he had, and she folded into him, and he held her with one hand moving slowly over her hair.

“Let it come,” he said. “You’re home. You’re not on the boat.”

“I scared you.”

“Yes.” She went still. He kissed her temple. “Because I heard that word and knew you were hurting. And because I love you.”

Much later, when she was lying against him and the crying had worn down into slow, tired breaths, he said, “Dr. Ma wants you to talk to someone.”

“I know.”

“You don’t have to know what to say before you go.”

“What if I can’t talk?”

“Then don’t.”

“What if I cry?”

“Then cry.”

She was quiet for a long time. “I don’t want to go alone.”

“You won’t.”

“You can’t come in if I don’t want you to.”

“Then I’ll sit outside.”

“And if I change my mind?”

“Then I’ll come in.”

She nodded slowly against his chest. “We’ll ring tomorrow.”

At two in the morning he woke. She was asleep beside him, her hand resting on his chest, not counting. He lay and looked at it. He remembered her writing the word into the agreement on the twelfth of March, in red, in her neat hard capitals: MILAN. The city of her grandparents, where in May they would marry. A word that would stop everything. He had understood the principle. He had not understood how much it might cost her to use it. Today she had said it in the middle of a room full of people, with her hands gone and her breath gone, before she could explain a single thing. And he had heard her. That mattered. He thought it might be the thing that mattered most.

She stirred. “Chen Si?”

“I’m here.”

“Go back to sleep.”

“Yes, sweetheart.”

The danger was over. He understood now that surviving it wasn’t the same as being untouched by it. In the morning they would ring Dr. Ho. He would drive her, and he would sit outside, and if she ever needed to say Milan again he would stop everything. Every time.

chapters.title: The Collection Called “Balcony”
chapters.desc: A year after the boat. Therapy on Tuesdays. A florist from the Walled City married to her brother-in-law. And a collection about the worst night of her life, which she models for exactly one person, piece by piece.
chapters.epigraph: “Now I know you.”
chapters.content:
On the first Tuesday, Aurelia wore a black suit.

Not because Dr. Ho had asked anyone to dress for her. Because the jacket had hard shoulders and the trousers fell exactly right, and in it she felt she could walk into any room on earth and negotiate her way back out. She stood in front of the mirror for ten minutes on the third of March. Then she changed her earrings. Then she changed them back.

Chen Si, in the doorway, looked at the two pairs on the dressing table. “They’re the same.”

“They are not remotely the same.”

He picked up the smaller ones. “These. They don’t argue with the jacket.”

She studied them for a long moment, as if he had said something mildly offensive, and then put them on.

Dr. Ho’s rooms were on the fourth floor of a quiet building near the botanical gardens, pale walls, two armchairs and a sofa, a window full of old trees. Aurelia didn’t like it. She didn’t like that the room had been arranged for people to sit and talk. She was very good at talking. She wasn’t at all sure she was any good at being listened to.

He walked her to the door. “Here or outside?”

“Here.” She looked at the door. “What if I don’t know what to say?”

“Then say that.”

She went in. He sat down on the waiting-room sofa and didn’t take out his phone. He sat with his hands loose between his knees and waited.

Fifty minutes later she came out with a headache.

“Strange,” she said, before he could ask. “Not bad strange.” In the lift she said, “She asked me what I remembered. I told her about the glass. Then she asked me what I felt just before, and I said I didn’t know, and she said that was all right, we had time.” She looked at the lift doors. “Can we get something sweet?”

They got something sweet. It became the shape of Tuesdays. He drove her every week. Some weeks she talked on the way, and some she watched the city go by with her hands in her lap. He never asked what had been said. He never asked whether she’d cried, or whether she was getting better. At red lights he reached across and took her hand, and sometimes he kissed the knuckles and sometimes he just held them. On the fourth Tuesday she turned her hand over and laced their fingers together. On the sixth she brought a book. On the ninth she fell asleep in the passenger seat on the way home, and he parked under the building and sat beside her in the dim garage for twenty minutes with the engine off, until she opened her eyes and asked him why he hadn’t woken her, and then whether she had drooled, and he said a little, and she said his name in a voice of real horror, and he kissed her hand and admitted he was lying.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the third Tuesday he wasn’t there in the morning.

“Zhao’s getting married,” he’d said the night before, putting his cufflinks in the dish. “Tomorrow. The registry. I’m his witness.”

She sat up in bed. “Zhao is getting married? To whom?”

“A florist.”

“Which florist?”

“A very good one.” And he had gone into the bathroom and shut the door, and she could hear him laughing.

At twenty to one on the seventeenth of March, as she was locking the workroom drawer before Dr. Ho, her phone went. He was outside a restaurant somewhere, she could hear traffic, and he was enjoying himself far too much.

“It’s done. No, I didn’t forget the ring. Actually,” and she heard the smile turn wicked, “she’s right here. You remember Elowen Lin?”

Aurelia shrieked. She heard it come out of her and couldn’t stop it. Lily, at the counter downstairs, dropped a roll of tissue paper.

Elowen Lin. Who had sat two desks along from her for four years. Who had come second to her two years running, and in the third year had taken first place from her, and the student council after it, and in between they had both wasted a frankly embarrassing amount of energy on the same boy, a senior who had preferred physics to either of them. Aurelia had not spoken to her since the day the results went up.

The phone changed hands. “Hello?”

“Elowen Lin,” said Aurelia, in her sweetest voice. “He told me Zhendong was marrying a florist. He didn’t tell me which florist.”

“Aurelia.”

“Congratulations. I’ll come and see your little shop. Soon.”

It came out sounding exactly like a threat, which was how she’d meant it, more or less. Elowen said lovely in a voice that could have frozen the harbour and gave the phone back.

“Something you want to tell me?” said Chen Si.

“Nothing at all,” said Aurelia, and found she was smiling so hard it hurt.

She went on the Thursday, in a pale pink cashmere coat and pearls and enormous sunglasses, because there are some entrances that have to be made properly. The shop was a narrow bright room near the old Walled City, full of buckets and green smells. Elowen was trimming white roses at the counter. She looked up, put the knife down and said “Aurelia Song” in the tone of a woman identifying a pest.

“Chen,” said Aurelia cheerfully. “Aurelia Chen, now.”

It took perhaps three minutes for the argument to pick up exactly where the last school bell had cut it off, as if nobody had been away. Small, though. It’s a flower shop, not an exhibition hall. Aurelia told her that their husbands were brothers, by oath, which with those two was worse than blood, and that it meant they would be seeing each other at every birthday and New Year and festival and random Sunday for the rest of their lives, and Elowen looked at her for a long moment and asked whether it was too late to get divorced, and Aurelia nearly dropped a vase.

By half past twelve she had taken off the pink coat and was sitting behind the counter with a cup of tea as if she had been coming there for years. Before she left she put the cup down, and for a moment the game went out of her face.

“Can I tell you something? Properly. Not to win.” She turned her ring on her finger. “The people who want to hurt men like ours don’t go away. They get patient. And sooner or later they work out that the easiest way to a man nobody can touch is the woman he goes home to. Keep a bag packed. Know two ways out of every room you sit in. Learn which of his men you’d trust with your life, and then make him prove it.” She smiled, and it was almost kind. “And when he tells you something is nothing, it isn’t nothing. Remember that.”

“Is that what you do?”

“Every day,” said Aurelia, and then, because it was intolerable to have been sincere for that long in front of Elowen Lin, she got up and went to the display and said, “Now. My label’s showing in June and I need flowers. Nothing with leaves.”

“Flowers have leaves.”

“An unfortunate design flaw.”

Elowen did the flowers in June. They argued about peonies for three weeks. On the night, every single one opened exactly on time, and Aurelia never told her so.

✦ ✦ ✦

By April Aurelia had stopped wearing suits to Dr. Ho’s. She brought a notebook instead, and sometimes wrote in it before she went in and sometimes didn’t open it. Dr. Ho never asked for more than she had ready. They talked about the boat and the ninth floor and the champagne flute. About the way she had learned, without noticing, to watch everyone’s hands when they were holding a glass. They talked about her mother: about the years of trying to become someone Vittoria might finally look at, and the difference between being good at things and being safe. Sometimes they talked about nothing that seemed to matter at all, the smell of rain on Harbour Road, a difficult client, Serafina stealing her shoes when they were nine and seven and wearing them to climb the garden wall.

She found that she could say a frightening thing out loud without being swallowed by it. She also found that some weeks were harder than others. There were Tuesdays she left that room lighter than she’d gone in, and there were Tuesdays she sat in the car afterwards and cried with her forehead against the window. He learned not to ask which kind it had been. He put his hand out, palm up, on the seat between them, and she took it when she wanted to.

In May he went for his own follow-up. His strength was coming back, and with it most of his work, and Dr. Ma said that was acceptable provided Mr. Chen stopped pretending he was twenty. Chen Si found this deeply insulting. Aurelia found it the funniest thing she had heard all year, and said so in the lift, and he asked whether she would prefer to walk home, and she said absolutely not, and in the car, when he leaned over to do up her seat belt, she held his face and told him he was doing well, and he said so was she.

✦ ✦ ✦

By August the new collection had started, and it started with a coat.

Not a real one. The memory of one. His, on a balcony on the Peak in October, the night she had walked out of her father’s birthday dinner rather than let her mother see her cry. She remembered the weight of it on her shoulders. The warmth, which wasn’t heavy and wasn’t dramatic; just enough to make a cold night slightly less cold. It had smelled faintly of cedar and rain. She remembered his voice, out of the dark beside her, asking whether she would let him kiss her, and thinking quite clearly that she had just met a man who was going to be the most inconvenient thing in her life.

The memory had changed shape over the years. At first it had been about being seen. Then about being chosen. Then about the strange, frightening business of letting somebody stand next to her without asking her to become smaller to fit. Now, eight months after the boat, she wanted to make something out of it. Not a memorial. Not a confession. Something people could wear.

On the first page of a new sketchbook she wrote BALCONY. Under it: Eleven pieces. Camel gold. Warmth without weight.

It took her into September. A collar that curved the way cloth falls over a shoulder. Earrings one fraction longer than the other, unbalanced and somehow right. A bracelet that was a single warm line. A ring with an open setting so the stone sat in the air. A pendant with a whole small architecture hidden behind its plain face. Camel gold for all of it; not yellow, not rose, something quieter with a muted depth to it, like good wool. Champagne diamonds, pale cognac ones, a few warm sapphires. Nothing that arrived in a room before the woman wearing it.

She and Enzo argued over every millimetre. He challenged her proportions and she challenged his settings. They changed the bracelet clasp three times. Paul, the young pattern-cutter who had come to them the year before from a house in the north, held the prototypes up to the lamp for hours without complaint while she squinted at them, and stayed late twice when a clasp wouldn’t sit. At one point Enzo held up the collar and said, “This is too sentimental.”

“It’s jewellery.”

“It’s a love letter.”

“Then stop reading it,” said Aurelia, and took it back.

Chen Si noticed the secrecy. The workroom door shut when he came up the stairs. The sketchbook that slid under a pile of invoices. He didn’t ask. He had learned that some things were worth waiting to be shown. But one night in September he came up to the workroom at one in the morning and found her asleep at the bench with a pencil still in her hand and a curved piece of gold lying beside her wrist, and he picked it up, very carefully, and turned it to the light.

“Don’t,” she said, without opening her eyes.

He put it down. “I didn’t see anything.”

“You were holding it.”

“I was looking at it.”

“That’s seeing.” She put the piece in a velvet pouch and stood up and pushed him out ahead of her and locked the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t announce it. No launch, no invitations, no press. She asked him to come upstairs at eight on a Sunday evening, the thirteenth of September, and dress, but not too much, and when he asked whether this was a trap she said possibly.

The lights in the living room on the forty-fourth floor were low. A long table stood in front of the window, and on it, in a row, were eleven velvet boxes. She was standing beside them in a plain black dress, her hair pinned up, and she wasn’t wearing a single piece of jewellery. Not even her rings.

“My new collection,” she said.

He looked at the boxes, and then at her. “What’s it called?”

She touched the first one. “Balcony.”

She watched him understand. Then she opened the box. The collar lay inside, curved, the colour of a coat.

“May I?” he said.

She nodded, and turned, and he stepped behind her. His fingers were warm on the back of her neck. The gold settled on her collarbone with a weight she had chosen herself, gram by gram. In the black window their reflections stood together over the lights of the city.

She opened the second box. He took out the earrings and put them on her one at a time, his knuckles brushing her jaw. The third was the bracelet; he fastened it round her wrist and turned her hand over to see the clasp sit. The fourth was a ring, and he slid it onto her finger as if there might be a question about it. He took his time over each. He asked before he touched her hair. He checked every clasp against her skin. When the pendant caught on the neckline of her dress he stopped and freed it, and she watched his face in the dark glass, and he wasn’t looking at the jewellery the way a buyer would. He was looking at the woman wearing it.

At the eighth box he paused with the bracelet in his hand. “Why camel?”

“Because of your coat.”

He looked down at the gold in his fingers.

“I remembered how warm it was,” she said. “Not heavy. Not much. Just enough that the night felt less cold. I wanted all of it to feel like that.”

He fastened the bracelet, and opened the ninth, and the tenth. The eleventh was the plainest. A single curved line of camel gold with one small champagne diamond at its centre, which didn’t sparkle at all until she moved, and then caught the light like something remembering itself.

He held it a long time before he put it on her.

“You were angry that night,” he said.

“I was furious.”

“You were trying not to cry.”

“I was not going to cry.”

“I know.” He fastened the clasp. “You were cold.”

“I was angry.”

“You were also cold.” He laid his hands on her shoulders, over the gold, and looked at her in the glass. “I never wanted to fix you,” he said. “You weren’t broken. I didn’t give you the coat because you needed rescuing. I gave it to you because you were cold. And because I wanted to stand next to you for a bit longer.”

Her eyes filled. “I thought you saw me, that night.”

“I did.”

“And now?”

He turned her round and put his palm against her cheek. “Now I know you.”

She leaned into his hand, and he kissed her forehead, and then the corner of her eye, and then her mouth, and for a while neither of them was looking at the window.

Later she sat at the dressing table and he took it all off again, piece by piece, in the order he had put it on, and laid each one back in its box. When he reached the last necklace he stopped.

“Keep it.”

“It’s part of the collection.”

“Then make another,” he said, and fastened it again.

She didn’t intend to keep any of them. They would go into the catalogue. They would be photographed and priced and sold, and other women would wear them to other dinners and bring their own nights to them, and that was what jewellery was for. But the first time all eleven had been worn together, it had been for one person. The man who had put his coat round her shoulders on a balcony. The man who had once confused protecting someone with knowing what they needed, and had learned, slowly and against his own nature, that love has to ask.

She closed the last box. He stood behind her and asked if she was finished.

“Carry me,” she said.

He raised an eyebrow. “Eleven metres.”

“Exactly eleven.”

He bent and lifted her, carefully, and she laughed and wound her arms round his neck and told him he was getting stronger and that Dr. Ma would approve, and he told her not to tell Dr. Ma. Eleven metres was a long way from a balcony. That night, for once, neither of them needed rescuing.

chapters.title: The Paris Show
chapters.desc: Six days before the presentation, a rival house shows a coat-collar necklace that is hers, line for line. Someone sold her sketches. Her atelier is in pieces. She has three nights. He is in the front row, and does not look at his phone.
chapters.epigraph: “Not everything important has to be seen by everyone.”
chapters.content:
The necklace appeared on a Friday morning, the twenty-sixth of February, while Aurelia was drinking her first coffee at the kitchen counter. Enzo sent the photograph with no greeting and no explanation. Just the image, and under it four words.

Tell me I’m wrong.

A model under the white lights of Delorme’s private presentation in Paris, the night before. Round her throat, a collar in warm gold whose curve followed the collarbone and then rose, softly, towards the shoulders, the way cloth falls. Aurelia put her cup down. She enlarged the picture. The front was very slightly asymmetric. The single stone sat just off the breastbone in an open setting she had spent three weeks of August getting right. She enlarged it again, until the pixels broke, and looked at the clasp.

Not similar. Not in the spirit of. Hers.

The second photograph was a bracelet. The third, a pair of earrings, one fractionally longer than the other.

“How many?” she said, when he answered.

“Four I can see.”

“Only four?”

“So far.”

She stood up so fast the stool went over. “Get the workshop on a call. Nobody touches the original drawings. Nobody deletes anything. I want the dated sketches, the bench records, every prototype, every invoice for every gram.”

“I’m already doing it.”

She looked at the picture again. Delorme hadn’t borrowed an idea. They had taken her work line for line, and shown it to buyers and the press six days before she was due to show it herself. She picked up the coffee. It had gone cold. She drank it anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Si found her in the study that evening with Delorme’s presentation open on the laptop and three of her own August sketches laid beside it on the desk, and her earrings still on though she had changed out of everything else. She turned the screen towards him without a word. He looked once, then again. His expression barely moved, but something behind his eyes went very still.

“Your show is in six days,” he said.

“I know.”

He looked at her, and she folded her arms.

“Don’t.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“You’re going to tell me to cancel.”

“I was going to ask whether you want to.”

She held his gaze, and then her shoulders came down an inch. “No.”

“All right.”

“They took the collar. The bracelet. The earrings. Even the open setting on the pendant. I have the files. I have the bench records. I can prove they copied me. I can’t prove who gave it to them.”

“Qian’s looking.”

She turned round. “Since when?”

“Since Enzo rang me this morning.”

“Without asking me.”

He accepted that. “Yes.”

“I would have told you to look. Next time, ask me.”

“You’re right,” he said, at once, so plainly that it took the fight straight out of her, and she looked away at the window. He put his hand lightly against her back.

“Do you want me to leave it to you?”

“No. I want you to help me find out. And Chen Si.” She looked at him. “Don’t frighten anyone on my behalf.”

The corner of his mouth moved. “I’ll try to be disappointing.” He kissed her forehead, and turned the laptop back round. “Show me what they took.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Qian’s report came the next afternoon. The leak was in the atelier.

Paul, the pattern-cutter who had come to them nearly two years before. Not a senior man. He didn’t see every collection. But he had held the Balcony prototypes up to the lamp for hours, and he had been in the room for every fitting, and he had stayed late twice when a clasp wouldn’t sit. Forty thousand had gone into his account in November through a firm in Lyon that did no business with anyone, and the bank records were already with Mr. Yuen.

“He’s admitted it,” said Qian. “His sister’s been in hospital since the autumn. Long treatment. The bills.”

Aurelia’s pencil stopped. “He told you that himself?”

“Yes.”

“Where is he?”

“Downstairs.”

Paul looked smaller than she remembered. He stood in front of her desk with his hands clasped and couldn’t lift his eyes past the edge of it. She didn’t ask him to sit.

“How long?”

“Madam, it was only—“

“How long.”

“Since November.”

“The drawings?”

“Yes.”

“The measurements?”

“Yes.”

“Photographs?”

He hesitated. “Yes.”

“You knew what this collection was,” she said. “You worked on it. You saw how many times we changed the settings. You knew which pieces were finished and which weren’t. You held them for me under the light.”

“I’m sorry.”

“Your sister’s illness doesn’t explain why you sold my work.”

His face crumpled. “I know.”

She looked at the man who had stood at her elbow at the bench; whose hands she had trusted with her best work because they were steady and patient. “You’re dismissed. Your access is cancelled. You won’t come into the atelier again. The lawyers will write to you.”

“Madam, please, my sister—“

She opened the folder. “Finance will settle her hospital bills directly with the hospital, against the hospital’s own invoices. Her treatment won’t stop because of what you did.”

He stared at her. “Why?”

“Because she didn’t sell my sketches.” His eyes filled. She didn’t soften her voice. “Don’t mistake it for forgiveness.”

When he had gone she sat very still for a while. She had thought the worst of it would be anger. It wasn’t. It was knowing that someone had stood close enough to see what mattered to her, and had decided to sell it anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

They landed in Paris on Monday, the first of March. The presentation was on Thursday.

The pieces were safe in the hotel’s strongroom. But Delorme had shown their copies first, and the photographs were everywhere, and half the commentators were calling the two collections strikingly similar while the other half were asking, in that tone, which house had got there first. That evening Aurelia answered Enzo, the atelier manager, Mr. Yuen and the event organiser. She approved the revised running order. She told everyone they would go ahead. Then she went into the bathroom and shut the door.

Alone, her hands began to shake.

She put both palms flat on the cold marble. The room was very quiet. And she was back in the boutique a year ago, the champagne flute, the glass breaking on the stone, her fingers hanging over the tray refusing her. Her chest tightened. Not again. She shut her eyes, and Dr. Ho’s voice came to her, unhurried, the voice of a woman with all afternoon.

You don’t have to force it away. Notice where you are. Notice what is happening now.

She opened her eyes. The bathroom. Paris. Monday night. A hotel towel folded over a heated rail. She breathed in slowly, and out. Her hands were still shaking. Five things she could see: the mirror; the tap; white freesias in a glass; the folded towel; the narrow line of diamonds on her finger. Four she could feel: the marble under her palms; the silk of her blouse; the floor through her stockings; the ring against her skin. She breathed. It didn’t go away. But it loosened, the way a knot does once you find which strand to pull.

“I’m here,” she told the woman in the mirror, and opened the door.

Chen Si was sitting on the end of the bed. He didn’t ask why she had been in there so long. He held out his hand, and she crossed the room and took it, and he drew her down beside him.

“Better?”

“A little.” She leaned on his shoulder. After a while she said, “I’m angry. I’m hurt. And I don’t want them to win.”

He kissed her hair. “Then don’t let them.”

She sat up and looked at him. His face was calm. Not because he thought it was easy. Because he thought she could do it.

“Come to the workshop,” she said.

“Now?”

“Now.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The organisers had given them a room on the floor below the presentation hall: four benches, magnifying lamps, velvet trays. Enzo was there, and two senior bench men who had flown out with the pieces, and the eleven pieces of Balcony laid out on black cloth. She went to the middle bench and picked up the collar.

“We’re changing the presentation. We show the inside.”

One of the bench men frowned. “The inside is plain.”

“Not by Thursday.” She turned the collar over under the lamp. “Every piece gets an engraving.”

Enzo understood first. He looked at Chen Si by the door, and back at her. “His?”

“Not his handwriting. The lines.” She took a pencil and drew on the back of a running order. A curve. “The railing.” Another. “The edge of the stone balustrade, where I was holding it.” A long soft line. “The way the coat fell over my shoulder. The shape of the doors behind us. The old ironwork.”

“Inside every piece?”

“Every piece.”

“Even the earrings?”

“Especially the earrings.”

Enzo began, slowly, to smile. “That’s going to be very difficult.”

“Then we have three nights.”

They worked through all three. The engravings weren’t decoration. They were small and quiet and you would never see them unless you took the piece off: a line beneath the collar, a curve along the inside of the bracelet, a pattern tucked into the pendant’s setting, a short run of strokes under the clasp of each earring. Not pictures of a balcony. The memory of one. She checked every cut under the loupe. Enzo adjusted the depth. The bench men worked with a patience she would think about for years. Chen Si stayed. He didn’t try to take over anything. He brought food when they forgot to eat and turned the heating up when the room went cold at three and sat beside her when she needed to stop for five minutes and moved away when she needed to concentrate.

At two on the first night she found him turning the bracelet over in his fingers.

“Do you recognise it?”

“The railing.” He touched the next line. “And this?”

“The fold of your coat.”

He looked at her. “You remember that?”

“Of course I remember. Do you remember what you said?”

“I asked whether you’d let me kiss you.”

“That was very forward.”

“I was being clear.”

“You were trying to get kissed.”

“Also true,” he said, and she touched his cheek, and went back to the bench.

On the second night he put a cup of tea beside her at three in the morning and said, “Drink,” and she said in a minute, and he said now, and she gave him a look and drank it. He picked up the bracelet again. Inside, the gentle curve of the rail was broken by one short, narrow stroke.

“What does that mean?”

“The place I was holding the balustrade. And this is the coat over my wrist.” She took it back from him. “The first time you gave me something without asking me to explain why I needed it. People will see the gold. They won’t see this unless they take it off.”

“That’s the point?”

“Not everything important has to be seen by everyone.”

He looked at her for a long moment, and then kissed her forehead and told her to go to bed. She said after this piece. He said Aurelia. She said one. He sighed and said one, as if he had been haggled down in a market.

The third night was the hardest. The last necklace had the narrowest inner surface of them all, and the line had to follow it without weakening the setting. Enzo looked at it under the lamp for a long time.

“We may have to simplify.”

“No.”

“Cara, the surface is tiny.”

“I know.”

“The piece has to hold.”

She looked again. He was right. You couldn’t force a line onto gold that didn’t have room for it; that was the first thing she had ever learned at a bench. She picked up her pencil. “Keep the railing. Take out the door.”

“And the coat?”

“One curve.”

He smiled. “Better.”

At dawn on Thursday all eleven pieces lay on the velvet. Chen Si came up behind her and put his hands on her shoulders and asked if she was finished, and told her to sleep, and she said not yet, there was a show.

✦ ✦ ✦

The room on Thursday the fourth of March was full: buyers, editors, collectors, the people from the big houses who come to every presentation to see what they will have to worry about. Delorme’s director was in the second row. She had seen his name on the list, and she didn’t intend to look at him. She stood backstage in black with the first collar on her collarbone, and Enzo fastened the clasp and asked if it sat comfortably, and she looked out through the gap in the curtain.

Chen Si was in the front row in a dark suit. His phone was in his inside pocket. He hadn’t taken it out once. When he saw her looking he gave her one small nod.

She breathed in, and stepped into the light.

The first model came out in the collar, and the gold caught the light, and then she turned.
