They had changed the whole presentation to show every piece from every side: the models wore their hair up off the nape, turned their wrists at measured moments, let their hands fall open. And on the great screen behind the runway, as each one turned, the camera went close, and the audience saw the inside. The engraved lines. A railing. The edge of a coat. The curve of a door.

A second piece. A third. Each with its own small hidden memory under the gold.

They hadn’t changed the collection to hide the likeness. They had changed it to show the one part of it nobody could have copied.

She didn’t look at the director. Not once. At the end the models came back together, all eleven pieces, and the room held its breath for one beat, and then the applause came. She stepped out and bowed, and when she straightened her eyes met his across the second row. He wasn’t smiling. He was looking at the last image on the screen, the railing cut inside a collar. Then he gave her a small nod. Not an apology. Not an admission. An acknowledgement. She returned it. It was enough.

Backstage Enzo hugged her hard enough to lift her off her heels and said, “You did it,” and she said, “We did,” and he shook his head and said, “You did,” and then she saw Chen Si coming through the crowd.

He didn’t hurry. He came straight through it, his eyes on her, and stopped in front of her.

“Beautiful.”

“The collection?”

He touched the bracelet on her wrist. “You.” He turned her hand over so the inside of the bracelet showed, the little line of the railing, and bent his head and kissed it.

“You’ll get lipstick on the gold.”

“I’ll accept the consequences.”

“Did you watch?”

“Every second. I was in the front row. I wanted to see you.”

She kissed him then, among the rails of clothes and the models taking off their shoes. Not a polite kiss. A grateful one, a proud one, the kiss of a woman who had been frightened and gone out under the lights anyway. When they came apart he rested his forehead on hers and said she had been magnificent.

“I know,” said Aurelia.

He laughed out loud.

✦ ✦ ✦

The hotel room was quiet when they got back. She put her shoes by the wardrobe. He took off his tie. For a while neither of them said anything. Then she took off the bracelet and turned it over in her palm, and held it out to him, and he traced the line inside with his eyes.

“You put me inside every piece.”

“I put the memory inside them. The memory belongs to me. You happen to be in it.”

“Very generous.”

She laughed, and stepped closer, and said his name. Then she said, “Otherwise.”

His face changed. Not much. Just enough for her to see him recognise it: the word from the end of the ninth clause, the one that handed it over to him.

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

He pushed a strand of hair off her cheek. “Anything you want me to know?”

She thought about it. “Don’t rush. And don’t try to prove anything.”

“I have no intention of proving anything.”

“Good. I want you.”

He kissed her slowly, his hand at her waist, hers finding the back of his neck. Neither of them hurried. He took off her earrings first and laid them beside the bracelet on the table, and she undid his cufflinks, and they stopped more than once to kiss in the middle of it. He stopped once, his mouth against her shoulder, to ask if she was all right, and she answered by pulling him down onto the bed. He undressed her the way he undid clasps, slowly, and put his mouth to every inch he uncovered, her breasts, her stomach, the inside of her thighs, until she was gripping the sheet. When he moved inside her he took his time, deep and unhurried, and when she arched against him and said his name he said hers back like an answer.

Much later, in the dark, she touched his face. “Do you remember the balcony?”

“Yes.”

“The coat?”

“Yes. I remember the woman wearing it.”

She leaned into him, and when the last of the lamplight went out on the bracelet, neither of them was in any hurry to leave the other behind.

chapters.title: Her Parents Ask for Tickets
chapters.desc: After Paris, everyone wants to see the collection in Asia. A letter arrives in her mother’s handwriting asking for two seats. Aurelia sends them. In the back row. Then her father comes to the front anyway.
chapters.epigraph: “Keep it as long as you like.”
chapters.content:
The letter came on a Tuesday, the eleventh of May, on cream paper folded precisely into thirds, by a courier who had been told to get a signature. Aurelia knew the hand before she opened it.

Dear Aurelia,

I hear the Balcony collection is to be shown here in June. Your father and I would be grateful if you could arrange two seats for us. We would like to attend.

Vittoria

She read it twice. Her eyes stopped on the same word both times. Grateful.

Enzo, examining a pair of earrings at the other end of the counter, looked up. “Bad news?”

“No.”

“Good news?”

She thought about it. “I don’t know.”

He came and read it over her shoulder. “She asked.”

“She did.” Aurelia folded it back along its own creases. “She didn’t ask how I was. She didn’t ask if I wanted her there. She didn’t say a word about the collection. She said they’d be grateful for two seats.”

“Perhaps that’s all she knows how to say.”

It was an uncomfortable possibility, and Aurelia didn’t like him for raising it. She had spent too many years making her mother’s excuses for her, turning cruelty into concern and absence into some complicated form of love. But a letter had come. A request had been made. And for once in her life, Vittoria hadn’t demanded anything.

She pulled the seating plan for the June show across the counter. “Two tickets.”

“Where?”

She put her finger on the back row. Row R. There was a pillar in the middle of it, a fat old iron one left over from when the hall had been a customs shed, that hid a good third of the runway from anyone sitting behind it.

“That,” said Enzo, “is not a generous seat.”

“No,” said Aurelia. “It isn’t.” She picked the two places directly behind the pillar. “Send them.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Si found the letter that evening beside her sketchbook in the study, read it, and put it back exactly where it had been. She was on the sofa with one leg tucked under her and the seating plan on her knee.

“Row R,” he said.

“Yes.”

“Behind the pillar.”

“Yes.”

He sat beside her. “Do you want them there?”

“I don’t know.”

“Then why send them?”

“Because she asked.” She turned the plan so he could see. “They’ll see the collection. Not every detail. Enough. And if they don’t like the seats, they don’t have to come.” She put her head on his shoulder. “I don’t want to punish her. I just won’t put her in the front row because she has finally decided to come to something.”

“Then don’t.”

She lifted her head. “You’re not going to tell me to be the bigger person?”

“No. You’ve already decided. You don’t need me to turn it into a lesson.”

She looked at him for a moment, and then said he was becoming quite good at this, and he asked at what, and she said at not being irritating, and he said that was an impressive achievement and she shouldn’t expect it to last.

✦ ✦ ✦

Paris had made Balcony something people argued about, and by the time the June show was announced there were more people wanting seats than there were seats. Buyers wanted to see the pieces in the hand. Editors wanted the engravings explained. Collectors who had never come to anything of hers were ringing the shop for private appointments. The show was to be in the old customs hall on the waterfront, the runway running towards the tall harbour windows. Aurelia fought to keep the room small. She wanted people to see the work, not the spectacle. The list grew anyway.

Two days before, Elowen sent a message.

Elowen: Zhendong says he is family and family has a permanent right to your front row.

Aurelia: The front row is for people who can appreciate jewellery.

Elowen: Then I suppose I’ll sit there alone.

Aurelia: Bring peonies. I’ll reconsider.

On the morning of the show the atelier had been going since six. The pieces came across the harbour under escort, and every one was checked against its condition report and looked at under the light and set in its case. Aurelia went from table to table. She had slept badly. Not because of the collection.

Chen Si was by the entrance with the event director, in black with a dark tie, half his attention on the conversation and half on the room. As she passed he caught her hand.

“Eat something.”

“I’ve eaten.”

“What?”

“Coffee.”

“That’s a drink.”

“An ambitious one.”

He looked at her. She sighed and admitted there was a sandwich in the dressing room. He said half. She asked whether he was negotiating her lunch now. He said he was negotiating her ability to stay upright until the last model had gone back through the curtain. When she came out of the dressing room there was a small plate on the worktable with the other half of the sandwich on it and a glass of water beside it, and he was talking to the director again with an expression of complete innocence. She shook her head. She ate the other half.

Elowen arrived at eleven with an armful of pink peonies, still tight, a few just beginning to open, in a pale blue dress with her hair low on her neck. Zhao came behind her looking like a man who had been talked into a garden party at gunpoint.

“You’re late,” said Aurelia.

Zhao looked at his watch. “We’re early.”

“Late by my standards.”

“I chose the ones that will open by tonight,” said Elowen, and handed her the flowers, and Aurelia, who had planned to be ungracious, found she couldn’t.

“They’re perfect.”

“Where am I sitting?” said Zhao.

“Front row.”

He looked at her with deep suspicion. “Why?”

“Because Elowen is.”

Elowen took his hand. “Come along, husband,” she said, and Zhao’s face did a thing Aurelia had never once seen it do in front of a Syndicate man, and he went where he was led.

✦ ✦ ✦

The audience came in an hour early, and the room filled slowly. Aurelia stood behind the curtain with Enzo and the running order. She hadn’t looked at Row R yet. She knew exactly where it was, and which two seats, and where the pillar stood.

“You’re doing the thing,” said Enzo.

“What thing?”

“Reading the same page without reading it.”

“I’m checking the schedule.”

“Of course,” said Enzo, and then his face changed. “They’re here.”

She didn’t ask who. Song Weiren and Vittoria had come in together. Her father in a dark suit; her mother in cream, with a necklace at her throat Aurelia recognised from a collection she had made at twenty-one. They spoke to the usher. Vittoria glanced at the runway, and then at the plan in the usher’s hand. He pointed to the back. Aurelia watched her mother look at the pillar. Vittoria said something quiet. The usher nodded. They walked to the back of the room and sat down behind the iron.

Aurelia let out a breath she hadn’t known she was keeping. “Let’s begin.”

The lights went down. Balcony opened with the collar, as it had in Paris, warm gold and champagne stones and pale sapphires, the curve sitting on the model the way it had been meant to sit on her. Aurelia stood behind the curtain and listened to the music and watched the room lean forward. And then, between the second model and the third, she saw her father.

He wasn’t in Row R any more. He was standing in the side aisle, looking towards the front.

Vittoria was still in her seat.

Weiren said something to the usher, who gestured, politely, at the back. Weiren shook his head and went on walking. He didn’t go to the reserved seats. He didn’t ask anyone to introduce him. He walked down the side of the hall in the half-dark until he reached the front, and Zhao, who noticed everything, shifted along by one place without being asked, and Elowen looked up, smiled, and moved her bag off the empty chair beside her. Weiren sat.

Her father had never been a rebel. He was a man who avoided arguments he didn’t need, who let Vittoria speak first and decide first and, more often than not, end the conversation first. And he was sitting in the front row. Where he could see. Where he could read every detail. Where he could look at his daughter’s work without a pillar in the way.

Aurelia turned her back on the curtain before anyone could see her face.

The last necklace came out near the end, the plainest one, the single curved line with its one stone. The model turned, and the screen went close on the inside, the railing cut into the gold, and Weiren leaned forward with his elbows on his knees. He wasn’t looking at the model. He was looking at the necklace. Aurelia knew that look. It was the one he used to wear at the dining table when she was small and he was trying to understand a drawing, really understand it, before he said anything at all. He looked at the engraving. Then he looked up at the stage, where she had come out to take her bow.

Their eyes met. He smiled. Not the polite smile he used at family dinners. Not the careful one he wore when Vittoria was watching him. A real one. Something in her chest that had been clenched for a very long time came loose. She bowed with the team, and the applause rose round her, and when she looked again he was still smiling.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards the room filled up with talk. Buyers took Enzo into corners. Editors wanted fifteen minutes. The director brought two collectors over. She answered every question. She thanked the bench men by name. She didn’t look at Row R, not until the crowd began to thin out towards the doors, and then she did.

Vittoria was still there, standing beside the seats with her programme folded in one hand. Weiren was nowhere near her.

“Mother.”

“You did well,” said Vittoria, in exactly the voice she used for everything. “The pieces are very well made.”

“Thank you.”

“Your father went to the front.”

“I saw.”

“He didn’t ask me.”

“Perhaps he wanted to see.”

Vittoria’s mouth tightened. “He could have seen perfectly well from where we were put.” She looked down at the programme. “Your father was very impressed.”

“He’s welcome to tell me himself.”

“He’s gone to speak to someone.”

Aurelia understood. She didn’t ask whether her mother was disappointed, or offer better seats next time. She said, “I’m glad you came,” and something uncertain crossed Vittoria’s face, quickly, like a bird across a window. Then she nodded, said they should go, and walked out. She left the programme on the chair.

Weiren found her by the harbour windows with his jacket over his arm.

“Papa.”

“There you are.”

“You weren’t supposed to move.”

He laughed softly. “I know.”

“Your seat was behind a pillar.”

“I noticed.” His smile faded a little. He looked down at his hands. “I should have been on the balcony.”

She went very still.

“That night,” he said. “My birthday. When your mother stood up and told everyone the shop would close in January. I saw your face. I saw you go out. I knew why.” He lifted his eyes. “I didn’t follow you because I didn’t want another argument. That isn’t the same as having had no choice. I let you stand out there alone because I thought keeping out of it would keep the peace. It didn’t. It only meant you were the one who had to carry it.”

Her eyes had begun to sting.

“I’m sorry,” said Weiren. He didn’t hurry to fill the silence after it. He let the apology stand there between them, on its own, as if it had a right to. “You were my daughter. I should have gone out to the balcony.”

For years she had wanted him to say something like that. Not a speech. Not an explanation. Only that she had been hurt and that he had seen it. She stepped forward, and he opened his arms, and she went into them. He held her carefully at first and then, when she put both arms round him, tightly.

“I waited for you,” she said into his shoulder. “I thought you might come.”

“I know.” His hand moved over her hair. “I’m sorry I didn’t.”

For a moment she wasn’t the woman with two shops on Harbour Road, who had sat at the head of a table of frightened old men and taken a collection to Paris. She was his daughter. And this time her father had come to find her.

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Si found her a little later by the last case. She told him her father had apologised.

“How do you feel?”

“As if I don’t know what to do with it.”

“You don’t have to do anything with it tonight.”

“That’s what you always say.”

“Because it’s usually true.” He stood beside her and looked at the necklace. “He should have gone out to you.”

She turned. “You’re not going to defend him? Not even a little?”

“No.” She laughed through the last of the tears, and he touched her cheek. “An apology doesn’t change what happened. It can still mean something. Let it mean what it means.”

The programme was still on the chair when she went back for her bag. She picked it up. Under the printed paragraph about Balcony, in her mother’s hand, someone had written seven words, and underlined them.

Keep it as long as you like.

No signature. Nothing on the back. She stood with it for a long time. She couldn’t tell whether it was an offering, or a concession, or only another of her mother’s ways of saying something without having to say it out loud: about a collection, or a necklace, or a shop on Harbour Road that had once been sentenced to close in January. She didn’t know. She didn’t make herself decide. She folded it carefully and put it in her bag.

The harbour road was almost empty when they drove home, and he drove. She sat with her shoes off and the programme in her lap and the city lights going over the windscreen.

“My father came to the front,” she said. “He left her there.”

“He chose his seat.”

She laughed. “That’s one way to say it.” She opened the programme and held it out, and he read the seven words at a red light, and handed it back without comment.

“Nothing?” she said.

“What would you like me to say?”

“I don’t know.”

He took her hand. “Then I won’t decide for you.”

She looked at him for a moment. Then she leaned across the console and kissed him, hard. His hand came up to her jaw. The light went green. Behind them someone tapped their horn, once, politely, and neither of them moved. When she pulled back, breathless, she said, “Green,” and he said he had noticed, and kissed the corner of her mouth once more before he looked at the road.

Keep it as long as you like. She didn’t know what her mother meant. She didn’t know whether tomorrow would bring another letter, or another silence, or another small cruelty dressed up as advice. But her father had walked to the front. And Chen Si was driving her home. For tonight, that was enough.

chapters.title: He Takes a Day Off
chapters.desc: For the first time in eleven years, he switches off his phone at midnight and does not switch it back on. Nobody in the Syndicate knows what to do. She has planned the day. It involves a chess board, a bucket of ice, and rules.
chapters.epigraph: “Tomorrow, you belong to me.”
chapters.content:
At two minutes to midnight on Friday, Chen Si was answering an email. At one minute to, he was answering another. At midnight Aurelia reached across the desk and took the phone out of his hand.

He looked up. She held it just out of his reach.

“Good evening, Mr. Chen. Do you know what time it is?”

He glanced at the clock. “Midnight.”

“Excellent. You can still read a clock.” She put the phone into a small velvet box she had brought in with her, one of the long flat ones from the shop meant for a bracelet, and closed the lid on it. “Your day off has started.”

“I have a meeting at eight.”

“Not any more.”

“Aurelia.”

“It’s a coffin,” she said, tapping the box. “For your professional obligations.”

He reached for it. She put it behind her back. He said he needed to make one call, and she said Qian had his instructions, and he began to say he needed to check something, and she said his name, once, and he stopped. She sat on the edge of the desk and crossed her legs and looked at him with the expression he knew very well: the one she wore when she had already decided, and was only waiting to see whether he meant to make the evening difficult.

“When did you last take a whole day off?”

“Recently.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“A few months ago.”

“Zhao says eleven years.” She watched his face change, very slightly. “He says you answered a call from the docks while a doctor was stitching your arm. He says that was a quiet week.”

“Zhao exaggerates.”

“Does he?” She leaned in. “One whole day where you don’t answer a single call, or read a single report, or decide a single thing for anyone. When?”

He looked at her. She smiled.

“Exactly. Tomorrow, you belong to me.”

His eyes warmed. “Only tomorrow?”

“Don’t be greedy.” She slid off the desk with the box and went to the door. “Sleep well. You have a very demanding day ahead.”

“What’s in the box?” he called after her.

“Your freedom,” said Aurelia. “You’re welcome.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At a quarter past twelve Qian received a message.

Aurelia: Chen Si’s phone is with me. He is not to have it back until tomorrow night.

Qian read it twice. He looked across his own dark office at nothing in particular. In nine years he had always known what the right answer was. He rang Zhao.

“What?”

“Madam has confiscated the boss’s phone.”

There was a silence. Then Zhao laughed, a sound Qian heard perhaps twice a year. “Good.”

“Good?”

“She says he’s taking the day off?”

“Yes.”

“Even better.” A pause, in which Zhao seemed to work out the consequences. “Then who’s answering the calls?”

“You are,” said Qian, “apparently.”

“Do you know what to do?”

“No.”

“Neither do I. So we’re both having a terrible day.”

By eight o’clock the Syndicate had discovered that its head could not be reached. The first call was from the docks. Zhao said the boss was unavailable, and when would he be available, and Zhao said tomorrow. The second was two department heads in a quarrel over a warehouse; Zhao listened for thirty seconds and then said that if they needed a grown man to tell them to stop behaving like children he could arrange that, and hung up. The third was a senior man who insisted it could only be discussed with Mr. Chen personally. Zhao put him on speaker so Qian could hear, said the boss was taking a day off, and the senior man said, “That’s impossible.” Zhao rubbed his forehead. “Apparently not.”

By ten the messages had started. Is the boss ill? Has something happened? Should we postpone? Is this a test? Zhao wrote one message to the senior group and sent it.

Zhao: The boss is alive. He is unavailable. Behave accordingly.

“That was rather direct,” said Qian.

“I learned from the best,” said Zhao, and turned his phone face down on the desk.

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Si woke at nine, which hadn’t happened since he was a child. Aurelia was already dressed and standing by the bed with two cups of coffee and a folded card. On the front, in her hand: CHEN SI. DAY OFF. Inside, a list.

9.30 Breakfast. 10.30 Chess. 12.00 Lunch. 2.00 Unscheduled activities. 6.00 Dinner. After dinner: no business.

“Unscheduled activities?”

“Confidential.”

“Do I have a choice?”

“No.”

“Then why give me a schedule?”

“So you can admire the organisation that has gone into ruining your life.”

He laughed. She handed him his coffee, and smoothed the crease between his eyebrows with her thumb, and told him that today he was allowed to be useless. He said that was a cruel thing to say to a man. She said he was allowed to be useless and handsome, and he said that was better, and she kissed him and told him to get dressed.

They had breakfast on the terrace, congee and steamed buns and cut fruit and tea, enough for three people, and she made him eat more than he wanted. He sat opposite her in a dark sweater with the sleeves pushed up. There was no phone anywhere. He looked, she thought, almost peaceful. Then she caught him glancing through the glass doors at the study.

“You’re thinking about work.”

“No.”

She looked at him.

“Perhaps a little.”

She put a piece of steamed bun on his plate. “Think about that instead.”

They talked for an hour about things that needed no decision at all. A new clasp Enzo had finally passed. The flowers Elowen had sent on Wednesday for no reason. Whether the bird that sat on the terrace railing every morning was the same bird. It was unfamiliar. It was rather lovely.

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past ten she brought out the black jade chess set, and beside it a little stack of folded cards.

Rule one: each piece you capture is a point. Rule two: whoever has fewer points at the end of a game pays a forfeit. Rule three: no arguing with the referee.

“Who’s the referee?”

“Me.”

“Convenient.”

Rule four: forfeits are not negotiable.

“What are the forfeits?”

“You’ll find out,” said Aurelia.

The first game took eleven minutes. He took her bishop. She took his knight. He took her rook. She took his queen, and he stared at the board, and then at her. “You moved that pawn three turns ago to open the diagonal.”

“You’re very observant.”

She unfolded a card. Compliment the referee. Sincerely. He said she was the most beautiful woman in the room, and she said too easy. He said she was the cleverest, and she said flattery. He thought about it, and said she was the only person alive who had ever made him hand over his phone without a fight, and she laughed and said better.

The second game was harder. She was quick; he was patient. He took the centre and pinned her queen and backed her into a corner, and she frowned at the board, and then moved a knight he hadn’t been watching and took his rook out from under him.

“How?”

“You’re distracted.”

“By what?”

“Me.” She took another piece. “That should be a crime.”

The card said: Tell the referee something you have never told her. He was quiet for a while, looking at the board and not at her.

“When I was eighteen,” he said, “I used to sit in the car outside my mother’s flat for half an hour before I went up. Every time.”

Her face softened. “Why?”

“I didn’t want her to see how tired I was.”

“Did she know?”

“She always knew.”

She reached across the board and put her hand over his. “Next time you miss her,” she said, “tell me. Don’t sit in the car.”

He turned his hand over under hers. “All right.”

By noon he had lost four pieces and one argument about whether a pawn could be promoted on a Saturday, and she had won three forfeits: a sincere compliment, a confession, and a kiss, which had been her reward for taking his queen a second time. He said this was an unfair distribution of prizes. She said he should improve his strategy. At lunch he came up behind her at the counter and put his hands on her waist and asked how long she had been planning this. Since Zhao told her, she said. He kissed her cheek and said thank you. She turned round in his arms and asked what for.

“For making me stop.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At two o’clock she brought out an ice bucket.

He looked at it and said, “No.”

“You haven’t heard the rule.”

“I know enough.”

Beside it she set a shallow silver bowl of water, a folded towel, and a card. Rule five: the loser of the next game surrenders one hand to the winner’s mercy. He said that sounded suspicious. She said he was suspicious of everything. He said that was experience.

She won in eighteen moves. He studied the board, and looked up at her, and held out his hand.

“Both,” said Aurelia.

He held out both. She dipped her fingertips in the iced water, and took his right hand, and turned it over, and touched a sliver of ice to the inside of his wrist. His fingers flexed. She smiled and asked if he was sensitive there, and he said not particularly, and she drew the ice slowly up the inside of his forearm to the crook of his elbow, watching his face the whole time, and he watched hers back. She traced the edge of it across his palm and let it melt between their two hands. The water ran down his wrist. She bent and caught a drop of it with her mouth.

He breathed out, very carefully. “May I bargain?”

“Already?”

“Thirty seconds. Your hand. Let me hold it without you moving away.”

The teasing went out of her face. She put the ice back in the bowl and laid her hand in his. He closed his fingers round it and moved his thumb across her knuckles, once, and again. He didn’t say anything. He just held it. There was something in the way he asked for such small things that disarmed her every time: a minute, a touch, a little time with nobody demanding anything of him. When the thirty seconds were over she didn’t take her hand back.

“That was longer,” he said.

“I know.”

He lifted her palm and kissed it.

“You’re supposed to be losing,” she said.

“I am. I have excellent consolation.”

At four they went back to the board. She had changed into a soft dress; he had given up on the sweater and rolled his sleeves to the elbow. He was winning, and he knew it, and he knew she knew it.

“You’re being smug.”

“I’m playing chess.”

“Smugly.”

He moved his rook. “Check.” She looked at the board for a long time, and moved her king, and smiled at him, and he looked at the position for several seconds. Then he reached out, picked up his king, and laid it down on its side. Then he swept his arm across the board, and the pieces went everywhere.

“Chen Si! You were winning.”

“I know.” He was already reaching for her, and she laughed as he pulled her across the corner of the table and into his lap, with black jade rolling under the chairs.

“Then why surrender?”

“Because I’ve had enough chess.”

“You’re a terrible loser.”

“I didn’t lose. I resigned.”

“You ruined the board.”

“I’ll buy you another.”

“That isn’t the point. The point is that I was going to win.”

He kissed her. “Then you won,” he said, and she tried to look annoyed and couldn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

By six the light had gone. They had walked in the roof garden, and eaten, and spent an unreasonable amount of time arguing about whether chess pieces could be arranged on a shelf by height, which she won. He had not asked for his phone once. He had not wandered towards the study. Somewhere in the afternoon she had started to believe he might actually be enjoying it.

She found him at the bedroom window and he said, “Come here,” and she went. He put his arms round her and they watched the last of the daylight go off the harbour.

“Are you bored?”

“No.”

“Thinking about the Syndicate?”

He looked down at her. “Not particularly.”

“Good.” She leaned back against him. Then she said, very quietly, “Otherwise.”

He understood. His face changed, and softened. “Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

“Anything different?”

She shook her head. “Just you.”

“Then you have me,” he said.

At first they talked, lying on top of the covers in the dark. About Paris, and the June show. About the peonies. About Zhao’s increasingly desperate attempts to answer the Syndicate’s phones, and the senior man who had asked if it was a loyalty test, and Zhao telling him that if it was, he had just failed it. Chen Si laughed until he had to put his arm over his eyes.

Later they stopped talking. He kissed her slowly, the way you do when there is no meeting at eight, his hand flat on the small of her back, and she unbuttoned his shirt and put her palm on his chest and felt his heart going under it, strong and steady and quickening. There was no schedule. Nobody was waiting outside the door. He took her dress off over her head and laid her back on the covers and kissed down the length of her, unhurried, until she was the one who couldn’t keep still. When she pulled him up he came into her slowly, and stayed there, barely moving, his forehead on hers, until she laughed and dug her heels into the backs of his thighs and told him there was no meeting at eight. The city lights came on below the window one district at a time, and neither of them reached for a lamp, and when it took her it took her slowly, the way the whole day had, and he followed her down with her name against her throat.

She fell asleep with her cheek on his shoulder. He stayed awake a little longer, looking at her: the woman who had taken his phone, and made him play chess, and given him an entire day in which he did not have to be anyone’s answer.

✦ ✦ ✦

At ten to midnight he asked for it back. She fetched the velvet box from the study and opened the lid. Forty-three missed calls. Seventy-eight messages.

“Oh,” said Aurelia, over his shoulder.

“Zhao has been busy.”

Instead of opening any of them, he wrote one.

Chen Si: How did it go?

The answer came at once.

Zhao: How did it go? The docks are still there. The men are still idiots. I am considering retirement.

Chen Si smiled. He typed again.

Chen Si: Same day next month.

Aurelia burst out laughing. “You’re making it a monthly arrangement?”

He put the phone face down on the bedside table. “Apparently.”

“Without me confiscating it?”

He considered. “That may be negotiable.”

She climbed into his lap, and he held her. Outside, the city went on without him. The docks worked. The men argued. Qian filed the reports and Zhao answered the calls. For one whole day the Syndicate had survived without Chen Si, and Chen Si, who had spent eleven years believing everything would fall apart the moment he stopped holding it up, had found out something rather important. The world could wait.

His wife, in any case, had already booked next Saturday.

chapters.title: The Necklace She Makes for Him
chapters.desc: It isn’t jewellery. It’s a tag. Plain gold, on a plain chain, with three lines engraved on it in her hand, for a man who has spent his whole life waiting to be taken down the stairs.
chapters.epigraph: “Then I’ll always leave the light on.”
chapters.content:
At six in the morning on the sixth of January, Chen Si was standing outside a door that no longer existed.

He knew it was the dream. He knew because the corridor was too long and the walls were the wrong green, and because the clock over the stairwell had stopped at three minutes to six, and because his father was alive.

Chen Rong stood at the end of the corridor in his old grey coat. His hair was combed. The watch was on his wrist, the one with the cracked glass that would stop at six and never go again, the one his mother would keep on his side of the bed for six years. He looked younger than Chen Si remembered him, younger than he had any right to look. He looked tired.

“Si.”

Chen Si tried to move. His feet wouldn’t.

Behind his father, two men were coming up the stairs. Their shoes struck each step in a slow, even rhythm. His father glanced back at them, and then at his son.

“Go home.”

“Father—“

“Go home, Si.”

The men reached the landing. One of them held a folded paper. The other had his hand inside his coat. Chen Rong looked up at the clock. It said six.

“Don’t make this harder.”

This time Chen Si managed one step. His father smiled at him, the small smile he had used when Chen Si was a boy and had broken a glass in the kitchen: not angry, not frightened, almost apologetic. Then the men took him by the arms. Chen Si reached out and his fingers caught the sleeve of the grey coat, and for one moment he had it. Then the cloth slid through his hand, and the stairs took his father down.

He woke with his fist closed round nothing.

The bedroom was dark. His breathing was even, because he had taught it to be, but his heart was going much too fast. Beside him Aurelia slept on her side with one hand under her cheek. He got up without waking her and went into the bathroom and washed his face and stood looking at the mirror until the dream began to lose its edges. It never went altogether. Fourteen years, and still the corridor came back, and the watch, and the shoes on the stairs, and six o’clock. Sometimes his father said nothing at all. Sometimes he told Chen Si to run. Sometimes Chen Si reached the stairs before it ended, and found the door at the bottom locked. He had never once brought his father home.

When he came back to bed she was awake. She hadn’t turned on the light. She lifted the blanket. He lay down, and she moved close and laid her palm flat on his chest, where his heart was still settling.

“Your father?”

He nodded in the dark. She didn’t ask him to tell it. She stayed there with her fingers moving slowly on his shirt.

After a while he said, “It was six.”

She understood. She kissed his chest, just over his heart. “You’re here now. And I’m here.”

His hand found hers under the blanket. She held it until he slept.

✦ ✦ ✦

At nine she went to the atelier. Enzo was bent over a new setting with his loupe in his eye, and looked up.

“You’re early.”

“I need your help.”

“That sounds expensive.”

“Not this time.” She put a small sheet of paper on the bench. On it she had drawn a rectangle. No stones. No setting. No border. A plain tag with a hole at the top for a chain.

“A pendant?”

“A tag.”

“For a suitcase?”

She gave him a look. “For my husband.”

His face changed. He picked up the drawing and turned it towards the window. “How plain?”

“Very.”

“How big?”

“Big enough to read. Small enough to sit under his shirt and not show.”

“Gold?”

“Warm gold. Nothing on it.”

“Then why are you bringing it to me? I could have one of the bench men cut it in an afternoon.”

“Because I want to make it,” said Aurelia. “Myself. I haven’t made anything with my own two hands since the forty-one sapphires. Designing isn’t the same.”

He looked at her for a moment. “You want me to watch?”

“Yes.”

“You want me to do it for you?”

“No.”

“Good,” said Enzo, and moved his stool aside.

She worked slowly. She cut the blank from a sheet of eighteen-carat stock with the jeweller’s saw, the blade so fine it sang, and filed the edges herself, and then the corners, rounding each one until there was nothing left anywhere that could catch on skin or cloth. Enzo corrected her grip once, two fingers on her wrist, and then left her alone. She drilled the hole and countersank it and finished it with a burnisher until it was as smooth inside as out. She polished the whole small rectangle until it held a soft warm light rather than a shine. The chain was plain and strong, a close curb, nothing anyone would look at twice. It wasn’t a thing for a shop window. It would never be photographed for a campaign, and no collector would ever ask to see it in a private appointment. It wasn’t meant to be admired. It was meant to be worn, every day, until it went soft at the corners.

“Are you engraving it?” Enzo asked.

She took a folded piece of paper out of her pocket and gave it to him. Three short lines, in her own hand. He read them, and looked at her over the top of the paper.

“That’s rather good.”

“I know.”

He laughed. She set the tag in the engraver’s ball vise and turned it to the light and picked up the graver. She hadn’t cut letters by hand since she was nineteen. Her hand was steady. She cut one line at a time, checking the depth and the spacing before she went on, tilting the vise a few degrees for every curve, brushing the bright little curls of gold away with a sable brush. When she finished, she held it up.

If found. Call her. She will come.

Enzo read it again, and then he looked at her for a long moment.

“He’ll keep this until he dies.”

She ran her thumb along the edge. “That’s the idea.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He came home at half past five and found her in the bedroom by the dresser, holding a small box.

“What have you bought?”

“Nothing.”

“That looks like a box.”

“Your powers of observation remain remarkable.” She put it on the dresser and opened the lid. “Come here.”

A plain gold chain. At the centre, a small gold tag. He looked at it for a long time without touching it.

“What’s this?”

“Something I made.”

He picked it up. The tag lay in his palm, still warm from her hand. He turned it over and read the three lines. Then he read them again, and his thumb stopped under the first.

“Do you like it?”

He swallowed. “Why?”

She came close. “Because you keep dreaming that you’re too late.” His fingers closed over the tag. He started to say that wasn’t it, and she said his name, and he stopped. She put her hand on his wrist. “I know you can’t go back for him. I know. But I can give you something to carry home.”

It was so plain. No diamonds, no setting, no clever work that would make a stranger stop and look. Three lines in her handwriting. He had spent his whole life among things that could be taken away from him: money, territory, men, his father’s name. Even the memory of that morning was something he couldn’t hold without losing it again. And his wife was standing in front of him holding out a small piece of gold that said she would come. Not if he won. Not if he was useful. Not if he managed to keep everyone safe. If he was lost.

At six exactly she fastened it round his neck. She stood behind him and lifted his collar and the clasp clicked shut, and the tag slid down under his shirt and lay against his skin over his breastbone. He didn’t move. When she came round in front of him his eyes were wet, and he turned his face a little to the side.

She didn’t pretend not to see. She put her hand on his cheek. He tried to smile, and it didn’t hold, and one tear went down, and then another, and he bent his head. For a man who had spent fourteen years refusing to let anybody see what that morning had done to him, the silence was very nearly unbearable. She put her arms round him. His forehead came down on her shoulder, and he cried without making a sound, and she held him, one hand on the back of his head and the other flat on his chest, over the tag.

“I couldn’t bring him home,” he said.

“I know.”

“I tried.”

“I know.”

“I was supposed to—“

She drew back far enough to look at him. “No. You were fifteen. You were his son. You were not supposed to save him from everything.” She wiped his face with her thumbs. “You don’t have to keep going back to that staircase to prove you loved him.”

He looked at her for a long time. Then he bent and pressed his face into her palm, and she kissed his forehead, and he held her there while the clock on the dresser turned over to twenty-three minutes past six, and neither of them mentioned it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later he sat on the edge of the bed with the tag out of his shirt, turning it over and over between his fingers. She was taking off her earrings at the mirror.

“You’ll wear a hole in it.”

“Did you make all of it yourself?”

“With Enzo watching.”

“That’s still yours.” He ran his thumb over the letters. “Why a tag?”

She came and sat beside him. “Because I didn’t want to make you something beautiful that you’d feel you had to keep in a box. I wanted something you could wear every day without an occasion. And because you spend your whole life making sure everyone else gets home.” She touched the chain. “Somebody should make sure you do.”

His eyes softened. Then he caught her round the waist and pulled her down onto the bed, and she laughed in surprise and said his name, and he rolled her under him with one hand braced by her shoulder and the other on her face and kissed her. Not carefully. Not as though she might break. With everything he had been holding behind his teeth since six that morning, and she answered him in kind, her hands in his hair, the little gold tag swinging out of his open collar and lying in the hollow of her throat between them.

When he lifted his head his forehead stayed on hers.

“I’ll come home,” he said. “Every time.”

“Don’t make promises to the universe.”

“I’m not. I’m making one to you.” He kissed her again. “I will always come home to you.”

She held his face in both hands. “Then I’ll always leave the light on.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At New Year, in the first days of February, Zhao noticed the chain.

They were all on the forty-fourth floor after dinner, round the long table, the remains of a fish and a great deal of wine. Elowen had brought flowers. Qian had brought his wife and a bottle of something very old and both had been made to stay and drink some of it. Zhao had brought nothing, on the grounds that his presence was itself a generous contribution. Aurelia was pouring tea when Chen Si reached across her for the pot, and his collar shifted, and the gold tag showed for a second against his throat.

Zhao’s eyes went to it the way they went to a car parked in the wrong place. “What’s that?”

Chen Si looked down. “My necklace.”

“I can see that it’s a necklace.” Zhao leaned forward. “Let me see.”

Chen Si looked at Aurelia. She nodded. He lifted the tag out of his shirt and let it lie in his palm, and Zhao read it, and his face changed, and he read it again. Then he looked at Aurelia.

“You made this?”

“Yes.”

He turned it a little on Chen Si’s hand with one finger. No stones. No decoration. Only the words.

“You wear it every day?”

“Yes,” said Chen Si.

Zhao nodded slowly. Then, with complete seriousness, he said, “I want one.”

There was a short silence. Elowen laughed. “You’re not lost.”

Zhao looked at his wife. “Neither is he.”

Aurelia put the teapot down. “The same words?”

Zhao thought about it for a long time, longer than anyone at the table expected, so that the laughter went out of the room. Then he shook his head.

“No. Something that says someone will notice if I don’t come back.”

Elowen’s smile went soft. She reached across the corner of the table and took his hand. “I would notice,” she said.

Zhao looked at her for a long moment and said nothing at all, which from Zhao was a speech.

“I’ll make you one,” said Aurelia.

“Good.” He sat back.

Chen Si tucked the tag inside his shirt again and looked down the table at his wife, and she smiled at him. Under the warm light of the dining room sat two men who had spent most of their lives expecting to be left on a staircase, at a table with the people who had every intention of noticing when they came home.

chapters.title: Her Father Falls
chapters.desc: Shenzhen. Leverage. Four towers nobody will buy. Permits that won’t come. In eight weeks the Song Group goes from the second-richest family in the city to a story in the newspapers. Her father calls her at two in the morning. Her mother does not.
chapters.epigraph: “Go and get your father.”
chapters.content:
The first tower was supposed to sell in April. The second was supposed to follow in May. By June the Song Group had four unfinished towers in the new district across the bay, three banks asking for their money, and a bridge approach that had become worth a great deal to everyone except the family that had paid for it. By July, nobody wanted to buy any of it.

Aurelia read the report twice and put it down on the dining table. “How much?”

Mr. Yuen took his glasses off. “It depends whether you mean the loans, the guarantees, or what they lose if the towers sit empty.”

“All three.”

He told her. She went quiet.

Across the table Chen Si was reading something else. He hadn’t said a word since Mr. Yuen began. He wasn’t going to, and it was deliberate.

The Song Group had been in trouble before. It had survived bad bets and political quarrels and Vittoria’s very expensive insistence on looking like a family that had never needed to sell anything. This was different. The new district had been built on confidence: four towers, a promise of tenants, and the bridge approach that would tie the whole district to the business corridor along the bay. Everything rested on the bridge. Then the permits stopped moving. The banks became impatient. The buyers melted away. And Fu Jianguo, who had been sitting very still for four years waiting for the Song Group to weaken, began to let people feel his weight.

“He hasn’t bought the debt,” said Aurelia.

“He doesn’t need to,” said Mr. Yuen. “His people sit on the committees that sign the bridge. Every buyer in the city knows it. Nobody will touch the towers while the permits are in his drawer.”

Four years ago her father had refused to give Fu’s son fifteen per cent of that bridge, and a few months later Aurelia had sat across a table at Da Gianni and watched Fu Kang sign away even the share he’d already had. Fu Jianguo had not forgotten. He didn’t like to destroy a man outright. He preferred to leave him one last choice, and then make sure both doors opened into his own house.

“How long?” she said.

“At this rate? Two months. Perhaps less.”

She sat back. Chen Si turned a page. He didn’t look at her. Not because he wasn’t listening. Because he knew she would look at him when she wanted to know what he thought, and until then he would wait.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first week of May the banks called in the short loans. The second week the board met in emergency session at night. The third week a buyer walked away from the second tower with his deposit. By June the newspapers had started using words like collapse and distress and dynasty, and Aurelia didn’t read them. She read the contracts. She had Mr. Yuen pull every guarantee her father had signed in five years. She had the lawyers go through them line by line. She asked for independent valuations of all four towers and the bridge, separately, by firms Fu had never paid.

She didn’t ask Chen Si to make the banks wait. She didn’t ask him to ring Fu. She didn’t ask him to buy the towers. He knew she was refusing to ask. He also knew she was waiting for something, and he didn’t know what, and he didn’t ask that either.

One evening in June, after an hour on the phone with the Song Group’s finance director, she stood at the kitchen counter staring at a plate she hadn’t touched. He sat down across from her and pulled the plate closer. Steamed fish, ginger, spring onion. He had taken every bone out himself, and broken the flesh into small pieces, the way Uncle Fan did, the way he had for her on the first night in the basement behind the furniture market. He put a piece in her bowl.

“You haven’t offered to buy the towers,” she said.

“No.”

“Why not?”

“You haven’t asked me to.”

“You could. Buy the debt. Make the permits move. Have it settled before the morning editions.”

“Possibly.”

“You’re not going to?”

He reached over and took a shred of ginger off the corner of her mouth with his thumb. “Do you want me to?”

There it was. The question she had been walking round for six weeks. She wanted her father saved. She wanted the Song Group to survive, and the towers off the front pages, and the bridge back on the city’s plans where it belonged. But she didn’t want Chen Si to buy her father’s future and hand it to her like another present. She didn’t want to find out, ten years from now, that the only reason her family still had a name was that her husband had decided it should.

“I don’t know yet.”

He nodded. “Then I won’t.” He put another piece of fish in her bowl. “Eat first.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In the third week of June Fu Jianguo’s photograph appeared in the business pages. A private dinner with property men. The caption called him a possible partner in the bridge approach.

“He’s enjoying this,” said Aurelia.

“Yes.”

“He wants my father to come to him.”

“He’ll offer a rescue,” said Chen Si. “At whatever price he thinks your father will be desperate enough to pay.”

“He won’t get the bridge.”

He looked at her for a long moment. “All right.”

“That’s all?”

“What would you like me to say?”

“Something encouraging.”

He reached for her hand. “You’ll find a way.”

“And if I don’t?”

“Then we’ll find out what can be saved.”

It was so simple that it hurt. She held his fingers. “I don’t want to lose him.”

“I know,” said Chen Si.

By July the losses couldn’t be hidden any more, and the banks sent valuers to the house on the Peak.

They came on a Monday morning with clipboards and assistants and the careful faces of people told not to look too interested. Aurelia arrived halfway through the first room. A man was measuring the carved rosewood cabinet that had held her mother’s porcelain since before she was born. Another was standing in front of the painting over the landing, a misty river under mountains that had hung there since she was a small girl.

“What are you doing?”

The senior man turned. “Mrs. Chen. We act for the secured lenders. We’re assessing the movable assets in the security schedule.”

“That painting isn’t security.”

“It’s on the schedule.” He showed her. The painting had been listed as collateral six years ago. At the bottom of the page was her father’s signature.

For a moment she couldn’t move. Then she handed it back. “Go on. But nothing leaves this house without an inventory, an independent valuation and written confirmation from the lenders. And I want a copy of every page.”

She walked through the rooms. The house felt strange. She had sat on the floor under that painting while her father worked at the dining table with his sleeves rolled up and his reading glasses pushed into his hair. The vases had come back from a trip to the coast she could barely remember. Now they were numbers on a sheet.

She found Weiren in his study, standing at the window with his hands behind his back.

“You signed the schedule.”

“Years ago.”

“You didn’t tell me.”

“I thought we’d settle the loans before it came to this.” He stopped. For the first time she saw how tired he was, and under the tiredness something worse. He was ashamed.

“Why didn’t you call me?”

He gave a small smile with nothing in it. “Because you’re my daughter. I didn’t want you to see this.”

“You should have let me see it.” She touched his arm. “Don’t sign anything else unless Mr. Yuen has read it. And don’t agree to anything Fu offers you.”

“I haven’t.”

“Don’t.”

“I won’t.”

She kissed his cheek and told him to ring her if the men came back, and left quickly, before he could see how much the clipboards in the hall had frightened her.

✦ ✦ ✦

The call came at a quarter past two in the morning on Tuesday, the twenty-fifth of July.

Chen Si woke first. Her phone was buzzing on the bedside table, and the screen said Papa. He turned and put his hand on her shoulder and said her name, and then, “Your father,” and she was sitting up before he’d finished.

“Papa?”

For several seconds there was nothing. Then breathing. Not the even breathing of a man who has rung by mistake. Uneven. Careful. As if he were trying to make himself very small.

“I’m sorry,” said her father.

“What’s happened?”

“Nothing.”

“Don’t tell me nothing at two in the morning.”

A pause. “I didn’t know who else to ring.”

Her chest went tight. Chen Si was already sitting up.

“Where are you?”

“The office. I couldn’t sleep.” He breathed out. “I signed the wrong things, Aurelia. The guarantee. The extension. I thought the bank would give us another month. They won’t.”

She got up and went to the window. “How much?”

He told her. She shut her eyes.

“The houses,” he said. “The flats. Everything your mother—“

“Listen to me.”

“I thought I could put it right. I thought if I could only get the bridge moving—“ His voice went.

She gripped the edge of the dresser. “You’re not going to put it right on your own at two in the morning.”

A long silence. Then, very quietly: “I don’t know what to do.”

It was the first time in her life she had heard her father say it. Not I’ll handle it. Not it’s complicated. Not don’t worry about it. Only that he didn’t know. She turned and looked at Chen Si. He had his trousers on and was reaching for a shirt, and his eyes met hers, and he didn’t ask what she had decided. He waited.

“Are you alone?” she said into the phone.

“Yes.”

“Have you eaten?”

“No.”

“Have you been drinking?”

“Water.”

“Stay where you are. I’m coming.”

“Aurelia, you don’t have to—“

“I’m coming.” And then, because she heard him begin to say it again: “Don’t apologise for ringing me.”

When she put the phone down he was dressed and holding her coat. She took it.

“I need to go.”

“I know.”

“I don’t know what I’m going to do when I get there.”

“You don’t have to know yet.” He turned up her collar and smoothed it with his fingers, and kissed her, a quiet, steady kiss that didn’t ask her for anything. “Go and get your father.” He put the car keys in her hand. “Qian will have Mr. Yuen ready by morning. Nobody calls the Song Group until you say so.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The Song building was dark except for her father’s floor. He was behind his desk with his jacket over the back of the chair and his tie pulled loose and a glass of water half finished next to a stack of paper. He looked up when she came in and for a moment he seemed embarrassed, as if she had caught him in his underwear.

“You came.”

“Of course I came.” She put her bag down and pulled a chair round to his side of the desk. “Show me.”

He hesitated, and then gave her the first file. She read it. Then the next, and the next. Guarantees, extensions, revised repayment schedules, letters from three banks, some signed before the trouble was public and some after. She read every page. After twenty minutes he said she didn’t have to stay. She said she knew. He said it was late. She said she knew. He said she had her own business. She turned a page and said she knew, and he stopped.

At half past three she asked for fresh water. At four she rang Mr. Yuen and asked him to be at the office at eight. At a quarter past four she went down to the vending machine in the lobby and came back with two sandwiches in plastic triangles and made her father eat half of one. He looked at it with faint disgust and took a bite.

“You’re very like your husband,” he said.

“He’s a terrible influence.”

He smiled a little, and then his face fell. “I’m sorry I let it get this far.”

She put her own sandwich down. “Papa. Look at me. You made decisions. Some of them were wrong. Some you made because you trusted people who didn’t deserve it. We’re going to work out what can be saved and what can’t.” She waited until he was really looking. “But you are not the company.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

He didn’t answer. She reached across the desk and took his hand, and his fingers closed round hers, and for a moment he looked as though he would cry. Instead he squeezed, once, and held on.

At five the sky began to pale. She stood at the window and looked down at the empty streets: a delivery van crawling through a junction, a cleaner unlocking the glass doors of the bank across the road. Behind her, her father had fallen asleep in his chair with his head to one side. She took his jacket off the back of it and laid it over his shoulders. Then she sat down at his desk and opened a new notebook and wrote at the top of the first page: THE BRIDGE.

Under it she made a list. Not of things to buy, and not of people to frighten. Of things to understand first. What the bridge was actually worth, on its own. What was owed against it. Which permits were waiting, and on whose desk. What the engineers said. Whether the bridge could be cut loose from the four towers and stand by itself. What had been promised to the contractors and the shopkeepers along the approach road, who had borrowed against it too.

She didn’t know whether it could be saved. But she knew it couldn’t be saved by pretending the Song Group was still the family it had been eight weeks ago. She looked at the old man asleep in his chair. He had spent his whole life building things. She was not going to let Fu Jianguo decide that the only ending left was to stand there and watch them come down.

At 5:42 she picked up her phone.

Aurelia: I’m going to save the bridge.

The answer came a minute later.

Chen Si: Then I’ll help you understand what you’re buying. The decision stays yours.

Aurelia: I know.

Chen Si: Have you eaten?

She looked at the half sandwich.

Aurelia: Don’t start.

Chen Si: I married you. I reserve the right.

She laughed out loud, softly, in the grey light, and put the phone down and went back to the files.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday afternoon an envelope came to the shop. No courier this time, no signature, no crest. A small plain envelope with her name on the front in her mother’s hand. Inside it was a key. Old brass, gone dark at the edges, with a yellowed paper label tied to it with thread, and a card.

Morning room. Bureau. Third drawer.

Nothing else.

She knew the morning room. She knew the bureau: dark walnut on slender legs, under the tall window, the one piece of furniture Vittoria had kept when she changed everything else in the house. Aurelia hadn’t opened any of its drawers since she was a girl. She rang her mother. There was no answer. She sent a message, What is this key for?, and waited, and nothing came back. Enzo was waiting for her to approve a sample. Mr. Yuen had sent three documents marked urgent. She put the key in her bag.

That evening Chen Si found her at the dining table turning it over in her fingers.

“Your mother?”

“She sent me a key. And where it goes. Nothing else.”

“Do you want to open it?”

“I don’t know.”

“Then you don’t have to tonight.”

“What if it’s important?”

“Then it’ll still be important tomorrow.” He took the key and put it back in her palm and closed her fingers over it. “Whatever is in that drawer, you can decide what to do about it after you’ve seen it. Not before.”

For the first time in days she let herself lean back. Her father was asleep at home. The bridge was still in trouble. Fu Jianguo was still waiting. And her mother, who had not rung her in eight weeks of headlines, had sent her the key to a drawer she hadn’t opened since she was a child.

“Will you come with me?” she said.

“Of course.”

She put her head on his shoulder, and he kissed her hair, and the key lay warm in her closed hand.

chapters.title: Six in the Morning
chapters.desc: A locked drawer her mother never opened in front of anyone. Eleven bankers around one table. And a lane in the Western District at six o’clock, where two people stand side by side and watch a grey man walk down his own steps.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m hungry.”
chapters.content:
The key turned in the third drawer on the following Thursday, at ten in the morning, with her mother out at the hairdresser’s and Pina holding the morning-room door. For a second Aurelia thought it had snapped. The brass resisted, and then gave with a small dry click, and the drawer slid out on its old runners.

A folder of dark green leather, worn at the corners, tied with a thin ribbon. Under it, a bundle of newspaper cuttings with a faded blue ribbon round them.

The room smelled of old wood and the jasmine tea her mother drank there.

“Do you want me to read it first?”

“No,” she said. “It’s mine to open.”

He stepped back. She untied the ribbon.

The first letter was dated the summer of 2018. The second was a year later. The third was three weeks old. All three were in the same neat, almost courteous hand, on the paper of a government office, and all three were signed by Fu Jianguo. He wrote about the bridge. About the Song Group’s future. About opportunities that would benefit both families. And then, halfway down the second page of the first letter, the language changed. He wanted a percentage. And he wanted the Song family to consider a marriage between his son and their elder daughter.

Not an introduction. Not a dinner. Her name was written out in that neat hand as if it were one more asset on a schedule.

She put the letter down. Chen Si’s face had gone very still. “May I?” She gave it to him. He read the paragraph, and his jaw tightened, and he read the date.

“The summer before the balcony,” he said.

Under the letters was an envelope in her mother’s writing, dated the day after the first one arrived. Vittoria’s notes were short and exact.

He thinks the Song family is frightened enough to agree. He mentioned Fu Kang twice. I told him my daughter is not a bargaining instrument. He told me I should be practical.

And under that, in darker ink, pressed so hard the nib had scored the paper:

I threw my drink at him.

Aurelia read the sentence three times. Then she turned the page. There was more. Dates and names. Who had been in the room when Fu came, and what he had said, and what documents he had put on the table. Notes from a lunch with an old lawyer who had once defended Chen Rong. Vittoria had written down every meeting for five years. She hadn’t agreed to anything. She had refused, and she had kept the evidence, and among it, in a plastic sleeve, was a photocopy of a trust deed with Fu Jianguo’s own signature at the bottom: the same trust Qian had found at the end of the money for Fu Kang’s seven rare watches, four years ago, with no name on it but a company’s.

“Why didn’t she tell me?” Aurelia said.

“I don’t know,” said Chen Si.

The last thing in the drawer was the blue-ribboned bundle. She untied it. Newspaper cuttings, magazine pages, reviews. Vienna at nineteen. The Harbour Road opening. The forty-one sapphires. Paris. Every review she could remember, and some she couldn’t. And in the margins, in her mother’s hand, notes.

The stones are too heavy for the setting.

Good eye for proportion.

Too much gold. She should have held back.

The Paris engraving was clever.

Under the headline of the Vienna piece there was a short red line, and beside it, in the margin, a single word.

Mine.

She turned the next one over. The same word. And the next.

Her throat closed. It wasn’t an apology. It didn’t undo the years of corrections and silences and humiliations, or her mother’s fingers on the back of her neck at fashion shows until she held her head exactly so. It didn’t make the woman who had threatened her with a photograph of her own sister at an illegal race into someone safe. But it was proof of a thing Aurelia had never been allowed to see. Her mother had been watching. She had kept every small win. Even when she wouldn’t say a word about any of them.

Aurelia sat down in the chair by the bureau. Chen Si crouched beside her.

“I don’t know what to do with this.”

“You don’t have to know what it means today.”

“She wrote that word.”

“Yes.”

A tear went down her face, and he wiped it off with his thumb. “One thing at a time,” he said.

She nodded, and put the letters and the notes and the deed back in the green folder and tied the ribbon. “These go to Ms. Fong.” She looked at the blue ribbon in her lap. “These, I’m keeping.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Ms. Fong came to the forty-fourth floor that afternoon, and Mr. Yuen joined by video, and they went through every sheet. The deed was the important thing. It put Fu Jianguo’s own name at the end of the money that had bought Fu Kang’s watches; until now there had only been a trail of companies, and a trail can always be said to lead somewhere else. The letters were different. They showed a vice-minister writing to a private family on his office paper to ask for money in return for a bridge, and offering to take their daughter in part payment.

“They must be kept exactly as they are,” said Ms. Fong. “Certified copies. A record of every hand they pass through. Counsel reads everything before anything goes anywhere.”

“Then send them to the commission.”

Ms. Fong looked at her over her silver frames. “This will put a great deal of light on your mother.”

“My mother kept them because she knew exactly what he was. I’m not going to bury them to save his reputation.”

“Then I’ll arrange it.”

When Ms. Fong had gone, Aurelia went to Chen Si at the window. “Will it be enough?”

“Enough to open an investigation. Not enough to know what happens.”

“Then we do the next thing,” she said. “The bridge.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The eleven bankers came on the Tuesday. Nearly all had the careful faces of people who had spent thirty years watching beautiful projects fail. Between them they held every loan the Song Group had left, and the decision on whether anyone would ever lend against the bridge again.

Aurelia stood at the head of the table with Mr. Yuen on her right and Ms. Fong’s documents in front of her. Chen Si wasn’t in the room. He had offered. She had said no. The proposal had to stand on its own legs, and with him in the room they would have looked at him instead of the numbers.

The proposal was simple to say and hard to do. The bridge approach would be cut away from the four towers and treated as a separate project. Not one more coin would be borrowed against the bridge to cover the towers’ losses. And against the new loan, Aurelia Chen would pledge her three shops. The first one on Harbour Road. The second, two hundred metres along. The flagship.

A banker looked up from the valuations. “All three? That’s a considerable risk.”

“I understand.”

“Why should we believe the bridge can be finished?”

“Because the bridge isn’t the towers.” She turned to the engineers’ report. “The towers were financed on what somebody hoped tenants would pay. The bridge carries traffic that’s already there. The independent assessment is on page four.”

“And the permits?”

“I’m not asking you to pretend they’re certain. I’m asking for a structure that lets the bridge go forward without new borrowing being used to hide old losses.”

The man at the far end tapped his pen on the table. “And in return, three jewellery shops.”

She met his eyes. “In return, I put something real behind it.”

She didn’t mention Chen Si. It wasn’t that kind of meeting.

“If this fails,” said the first banker, “you lose all three.”

She looked down at the photographs of the shops. She remembered the second-hand counter she had bought for Harbour Road, and the first necklace she’d sold, and the mornings opening the shutters before the street was awake. She had built them with her own hands. She wasn’t offering them lightly. She was offering them on purpose.

“Yes,” she said.

It went on for four hours. She agreed where they were right and refused where they weren’t. By the end nothing was settled. But nobody had walked out, and they agreed to begin a formal review of the structure.

“You held the room,” said Mr. Yuen, gathering his papers. “You didn’t give them one answer they could use against you.”

Through the glass wall she could see the car park in the afternoon sun, and Chen Si leaning against the car. He hadn’t come in. He hadn’t rung to ask. He had waited. She went down the steps and he straightened when he saw her.

“Well?”

“They haven’t agreed. They listened.”

He opened the passenger door. She didn’t get in. She took hold of the front of his jacket and kissed him against the side of the car, and after a second’s surprise his hand settled on her waist, and she kissed him again, slower.

“Good meeting?”

“Exhausting.”

“Then why are you smiling?”

“Because you’re here.”

“I said I would be,” said Chen Si.

✦ ✦ ✦

The commission took its time through August. There were interviews, and three weeks in which the newspapers could tell something was happening and couldn’t find out what. Fu Jianguo went on appearing in public. He spoke at a property conference about the future of the bay corridor, and looked entirely comfortable.

Chen Si watched the interview in his study with the sound low. Aurelia stood behind his chair.

“Does it bother you?”

He turned it off. “Yes.”

“Are you afraid?”

It wasn’t a question anyone asked him. He looked down at his hands. “Not of him.” He turned his watch on his wrist. “I’m afraid of afterwards. I’ve imagined it for fifteen years. I know what I want him to lose. I know what I want him to understand. I don’t know what happens when I don’t have to think about him any more.”

She sat on the arm of the chair. “Then we’ll find out.”

“Together?”

“Together,” she said, and he turned her hand over and kissed the palm.

✦ ✦ ✦

They came for him on a Saturday at six in the morning, the second of September, a month after the papers had gone in.

She woke before the alarm. It was still dark. Chen Si was sitting on the edge of the bed, already dressed. Not a suit. Dark trousers and a plain shirt, buttoned at the wrists.

“Is it today?”

He nodded. The clock said 5:18. Neither of them spoke for a while. Then he looked down at himself.

“I don’t know what to wear.”

She stared at him. “What?”

“I don’t know what one wears.” His face was composed and his shoulders were straight, but his hands weren’t still. For fifteen years he had imagined this morning. He had never once imagined what he himself would feel.

“You’re not going to a wedding, or a funeral,” she said. “Wear what you’ve got on.” She took his hand.

“What if I feel nothing?”

“Then you feel nothing.”

“What if I feel too much?”

“Then I’ll be there.”

“What if it isn’t what I thought it would be?”

She lifted his hand to her mouth. “Then it doesn’t have to be.” She touched the gold tag under his shirt. “If found, call her. She will come. I’m here.”

He shut his eyes. Then he bent and put his forehead against hers. “All right.”

Fu Jianguo lived in an old stone house in the Western District with a narrow front door at the top of a flight of granite steps. They stood across the lane in the grey light, by the wall of the house opposite. There were no reporters. There was only the lane, and two cars, and four men in plain jackets who had gone up the steps at a minute to six. She had taken his hand at the car and he had not let go.

At six o’clock the door opened.

Fu Jianguo came out in pyjamas, a grey dressing gown thrown over them, his hair flattened on one side from the pillow. His face was white with fury. Fu looked up the lane, and saw Chen Si, and for a second his face went blank, almost puzzled, as though he were trying to remember where he had seen him before. Then it hardened.

“Chen Si.”

Chen Si said nothing. Fu’s eyes went to Aurelia.

“Your family has made a very serious mistake.”

“No,” she said. “You made yours.”

“You think this changes anything?” said Fu, to Chen Si.

For fifteen years Chen Si had carried this man down a staircase in his head. He had imagined shouting. He had imagined asking him why, and making him look, and making him say it. Standing in the lane with the light beginning to touch the granite, he found he had no words at all.

They took Fu down the steps. One. Then another. The slap of his slippers on the stone was unmistakable. Chen Si’s hand tightened round hers. Fu looked back once over his shoulder. Then he was put into the car and the door shut on him. A grey man in a grey dressing gown, at six in the morning, walking down his own steps. No speech. No last bargain. Nobody running to help.

She had expected relief, perhaps. Satisfaction. Instead his eyes had gone far away. The man he had waited fifteen years to see go down the stairs had gone down them, and his father still wasn’t coming home. He looked at the empty doorway, and at the steps, and then he bent his head. He didn’t cry. Not there. But when he turned to her she saw the boy in the dream corridor with a sleeve sliding out of his fingers, and she put her arms round him, and he held her hard enough to hurt.

“I thought I’d feel different,” he said.

“I know.”

“I thought—“

“I know.” She kissed his cheek. “Come and have breakfast with me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Uncle Fan was still setting out bowls behind the counter when they came down the basement steps behind the furniture market. He looked at Chen Si, and then at Aurelia, and asked nothing. He pointed at their table. “Sit.”

Tea, and fish congee, and steamed buns. “Eat before it goes cold,” said Uncle Fan.

Chen Si stared at the bowl for a long time. Then he picked up the spoon and tasted it. Then another spoonful, and another, and after a while he looked down at the bowl with mild surprise.

“I’m hungry.”

Aurelia smiled and touched his wrist and said, “Then eat,” and he did, all of it, and when Uncle Fan came back with the teapot and said “More?” he nodded, and Uncle Fan put a second bowl in front of him without a word. They ate breakfast. And for the first time in fifteen years Chen Si didn’t spend the morning waiting for six o’clock to be over.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the second Saturday of September, Aurelia went to see her mother.

Vittoria received her in the morning room. The brass key lay on the table between them. The third drawer was open. The green folder was gone, and the blue ribbon was in Aurelia’s own safe. She set a small velvet box down beside the key. Vittoria opened it. A Balcony bracelet in camel gold with a fine line of champagne diamonds, and inside the clasp, cut so small you needed to know it was there, the line of a railing.

“It’s beautiful,” said Vittoria.

“Thank you.”

Her mother looked at it a long time. “The engraving was clever. In Paris.”

“Enzo thought so too.”

A silence. Then: “I should have told you.”

“About Fu?”

“About the letters. What he asked for.”

“Yes.”

“I thought I could manage it.”

“You did manage it,” said Aurelia. “You should still have told me.”

Vittoria nodded. For once she didn’t explain herself. She looked at the bracelet, and then she said, very quietly, “Thank you.” It wasn’t an apology. Not quite. But it was something her mother had very rarely offered without a condition fastened to the back of it.

Aurelia pushed the box towards her. “It’s yours.”

“Why?”

She thought of the drawer, and the letters, and the word written in the margins again and again. She thought of the woman who had hurt her for twenty years, and the woman who had thrown a glass of wine in a vice-minister’s face rather than let him bargain with her daughter. Both were real. Neither cancelled the other.

“Because I wanted to give you something I made,” she said. “Not because I owe you anything.”

Vittoria’s fingers went still on the gold. “I understand.”

At the door, her mother said her name. Aurelia turned. Vittoria was holding the bracelet against her wrist.

“You looked very happy in the photographs.”

“I was.”

Vittoria looked at her for a long moment. “Good,” she said. It was a small word. Aurelia let it stay small, and went out without asking for more.

Chen Si was waiting by the car with his hands in his pockets. “How was it?”

“Not perfect.”

“All right?”

“Yes.” Before she got in she reached under his collar and found the little gold tag and ran her thumb over the letters, and he caught her hand and kissed it.

“Coming home?”

“Always,” she said, and this time, when they drove away from the house on the Peak, she didn’t look back.

chapters.title: Number One, By Her Own Rules
chapters.desc: 2024. A collection called “Seconda”, made from every second place she ever came. A prize in Geneva that nobody from Asia has ever won. Her parents in the front row, and a daughter who does not look for them once. And afterwards, in a hotel suite above the lake, a medal on a ribbon and a man who is not allowed to touch it.
chapters.epigraph: “Because I don’t need to rename the past to be proud of what I made out of it.”
chapters.content:
The shoebox was under the winter blankets, at the back of the wardrobe, in the room where she had slept until she was twenty.

Aurelia found it by accident. It was October, and the house on the Peak was being emptied for the bank. The painting over the landing had gone in August, the rosewood cabinet in September. Her father was living in the small flat near his office. Her mother had taken a set of rooms on the other side of the hill and said she preferred them. In a fortnight the gates would be locked and the keys handed to a man from the lenders, and Aurelia had come up to fetch her old design books before anyone could put them in a skip.

Her room was mostly as she had left it. On the bare desk stood a photograph of her at seventeen holding a certificate, with the face of a girl who had been made to stand there. She was looking for a sketchbook when she saw the box.

The lid was faded and soft at the corners. No label. Inside were medals.

Silver, and silver-coloured, and certificates folded neatly in half. She knew every one of them. The children’s piano competition at nine: second, and the silent train home afterwards with her mother looking out of the window. The regional young designers’ prize: second. The young jewellers’ showcase: second. The national design prize she had entered at sixteen, where the judges had praised her drawings at length and given the award to somebody else: second.

Second. Second. Second.
