She picked one up. The ribbon had frayed. She remembered coming home with it in her coat pocket, pretending not to care, and her mother on the telephone in the hall, who had barely looked. She turned it over. On the back, in her mother’s hand, in pencil, there was a date. She turned over another. A date. And another.

She sat down on the floor.

Every second place she had ever been given was in that box. Not thrown away. Not lost. Kept. At the bottom lay a small folded note, addressed to nobody.

She was always so close.

She read it twice and put it back. Then she sat for a long time with the medals spread round her knees on the carpet. She didn’t feel healed. Her mother had kept the evidence of the almosts. That wasn’t the same as saying she was proud. But Aurelia couldn’t stop looking at them. She had spent so much of her life thinking second place was a thing to wipe out. Her mother had kept every one.

She took the box home under her arm, and left the design books in the wardrobe.

✦ ✦ ✦

Enzo did not like the idea. He liked it even less once she had explained it.

“You want to melt them?”

“All the medals.”

He looked into the box. “These aren’t all the same metal, cara. Some of this is sterling. Some of it is plated brass that’s been pretending to be silver for twenty years. You can’t throw it all in one crucible.”

“Then we sort it.”

“And the base metal?”

“Out. We keep what’s real.”

“And if the colour is ugly?”

“Then we make it beautiful.”

He laughed. “Brava.” He took off his glasses and turned a medal between his fingers. “How many pieces?”

“Eleven.”

“Of course eleven,” said Enzo.

It took the best part of a year. They called it Seconda. Not Second Best. Not Almost. Seconda: the second place, the second attempt, the second time she had stood up after being told someone else had done it better. Every medal went under the analyser first, and the readings went into a ledger Enzo kept in his own hand, page by page, as if it were evidence. The plated ones were stripped and their silver recovered and the brass under it set aside. The sterling was refined. What came out was cast in small test bars and alloyed, very carefully, with a little of her own gold, batch after batch, until it behaved the same way twice. Aurelia insisted on doing the first pour herself, in a leather apron, with the fume hood roaring.

The metal that came out of it was unlike anything either of them had worked. Pale, with a muted warmth under the silver, a depth that shifted between grey and gold as the light moved. It was beautiful because it hadn’t started as one perfect thing. It had been made out of a great many imperfect histories.

Eleven pieces came out of it. A collar. Long earrings. Three rings. A cuff. A brooch. A pendant. Two bracelets. And one narrow, sculptural ornament for the hair. Each carried a small trace of one of the old medals: a raised rim, a scrap of stamped laurel, the ghost of a ribbon slot. Nothing copied. Everything transformed. One of the rings was almost severe in its plainness, a thick band with a single irregular ridge along the inside where a medal’s edge had been. She liked that one best.

In the middle of October, Chen Si found her on the atelier floor at midnight with the first finished pieces laid out on a cloth round her like a game of patience.

“Have you eaten?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

“Food.”

He waited. She looked up at him and told him he was becoming very difficult. He said Qian maintained he had always been difficult, and crouched beside her, and picked up the plain ring.

“What’s this one called?”

“Second. Not Seconda. Just Second.” She took it from him. “It’s the one I came second with most often. The piano.”

“And now?”

“Now it belongs to me.”

He kissed her forehead and said good. She asked if that was all, and whether he wasn’t going to tell her she was the best, and he said she was the best at being Aurelia, and she said that was a terrible answer, and he said it was an accurate one, and gathered her loose sketches into a pile and told her to come to bed in five minutes. She said ten. He said seven. She said deal.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the spring of 2024 nobody in the atelier was asking whether Seconda would be ready. They were asking where it would go. Aurelia knew. The Prix de Genève was among the oldest prizes in the jewellery world, old enough that certain houses treated it as an institution rather than a competition, and no designer from Asia had ever won its highest distinction. She told nobody she meant to win. She simply sent it in.

When the letter came, Enzo opened it, and read it twice, and said her name in a strange voice.

“Shortlisted,” he said.

She took the letter and read the first line and the second, and for a moment nothing in her face moved. Then she smiled. “Good.”

“Good?”

“I’ll celebrate when we win.”

Enzo threw a polishing cloth at her.

In August she sent two front-row tickets, one to her father and one to her mother. She addressed the envelopes herself and put in a card that said only I’d like you to be there. She didn’t ask whether they would come. Her father answered that evening.

Weiren: I will be there.

A few minutes later:

Vittoria: Thank you for inviting me.

Aurelia put the phone down. She didn’t ask what her mother thought of the work, or whether she thought it could win. She had stopped turning her work into a question that needed her mother’s answer.

Elowen bought her own ticket. She paid full price through the official office, chose a seat near the front, and sent a photograph of the receipt.

Elowen: Full price. No special treatment.

Aurelia: I’d have got you one.

Elowen: I know. That’s why I didn’t ask.

Then a photograph of her hand with the fingers crossed.

Elowen: For luck. Also I’m bringing flowers.

Aurelia: You can’t bring flowers into the judging hall.

Elowen: Then I’ll bring them afterwards.

Aurelia saved the photograph of the crossed fingers.

✦ ✦ ✦

Geneva in October was clear and cold, the lake flat as pewter. The exhibition hall was large and bright, with the kind of hush that makes people lower their voices without being asked. Seconda stood in the middle of her display: eleven pieces, eleven histories, eleven things that had once been handed to her as consolation, made into objects that wanted looking at.

The jury spent nearly an hour at her stand. One examined the alloy under a loupe. One asked about the medals. The third asked why she hadn’t kept them as they were.

“Because I didn’t want to build a shrine to the things I didn’t win.”

“Then what did you build?”

“Everything I brought away from those rooms. The work. The disappointment. The discipline. The people who helped me get up. The parts of myself I had to rebuild every time someone told me I was nearly good enough.” She paused. “And the fact that second place isn’t a permanent address.”

He looked at the collar for a long time. “Then why call it Seconda, and not First?”

“Because I don’t need to rename the past to be proud of what I made out of it.”

On the night of the ceremony she wore black and no jewellery at her throat at all, only a small pair of her own gold earrings. Chen Si adjusted the fall of her sleeve as they waited to go in, and said she was cold, and she said she was fine, and he gave her a look, and she smiled and said not everything was a problem he needed to solve. He offered his arm.

Her parents were in the front row. Her father upright, his hands folded on his programme; her mother in dark blue, composed. Elowen and Zhao were a little further along. Elowen saw her and crossed her fingers openly, both hands. Aurelia took her seat. She didn’t look at her parents again. Not once.

There were speeches, and introductions, and prizes in other categories. Then the last category. The presenter spoke about the history of the prize and the standard of the year and the extraordinary quality of the shortlist. Chen Si’s hand lay on the armrest beside hers. He didn’t touch her. He knew this one had to belong to her.

The presenter opened the envelope.

“The Prix de Genève is awarded to Aurelia Chen, for Seconda.”

For a second she didn’t move. Then the sound came up round her. Enzo made a noise that was nearly a shout. Elowen was on her feet clapping with both hands over her head. Her father was standing. Her mother was standing. Aurelia stood. Chen Si stood first, and then stepped back out of her way, and she walked past him to the stage.

She didn’t look for her parents’ faces. She didn’t need to.

The medal was heavier than she had expected. The presenter put it in her hands and said something about the first designer from Asia ever to receive it, and she heard the words go out over the room and come back. At the lectern the lights made the audience a dark shape. She found Enzo. Then Elowen. Then Zhao. Then Chen Si, standing at the front, very calm, his eyes much too bright.

“Seconda began with a shoebox,” she said, and a ripple of laughter went through the dark. “It was full of medals that weren’t the ones I wanted. They were the ones I had learned to live with. For a long time I believed that coming second meant I had failed to become something. That if I worked harder, if I were better, if I finally stood in the right room, someone would look at me and tell me I was enough.” She rested her fingers on the medal. “In the end I realised I had been asking the wrong question. I didn’t need to make the past disappear. I needed to decide what I would make out of it.”

She thanked the jury, and the atelier, and Enzo, whose face had become suspiciously damp, and the bench men who had poured and rolled and cut that strange metal for a year. Then she looked at the front row.

“And I want to thank someone who has never once asked me to win. He has watched me lose, and fail, and come second, and he has never made me feel that I had to be first to deserve to be loved.” The hall had gone quiet. “Thank you for never asking.”

He bowed his head. Only slightly. She saw it.

Afterwards Enzo hugged her until she complained about her ribs. Elowen cried and pretended it was hay fever. Zhao told her the collection was excellent, which from Zhao was an hour-long speech. Her father came and looked at the medal in her hand, and then at her.

“I’m proud of you.”

“Thank you, Papa.”

Her mother stood a little way behind him and didn’t push forward. She waited until Aurelia turned to her. “Congratulations.”

“Thank you.”

Vittoria looked past her at the cases. “All eleven?”

“All eleven.”

“They’re beautiful.”

“I know,” said Aurelia. Her mother’s mouth moved as though it might smile. Then she stepped back, and Aurelia didn’t follow her.

✦ ✦ ✦

The hotel suite looked over the lake. She put her earrings on the dressing table and the medal on the desk, still on its ribbon. He stood at the window in his shirtsleeves, watching the lights on the water.

“You’re quiet,” she said.

“You thanked me. For something I never thought was a sacrifice.”

“That’s why I thanked you.” She stood beside him. “I used to think that if I came second, people would love me less. I don’t think that any more.”

“Good.”

“You’re not going to say you’re proud of me?”

“I’m very proud of you.”

“More.”

He laughed and said her name, and she said more again, and he took her face in his hands. “I’m proud of the woman who made those eleven pieces. I’m proud of the girl who kept entering competitions after she came second. I’m proud of the woman who stood up there tonight and didn’t look round once to see whether anyone had decided she was worth something.” He kissed her forehead. “And I loved you before any of it.”

She kissed him, and he kissed her back, and then he stopped and looked over her shoulder at the desk.

“Your medal.”

“Don’t touch it.”

“I haven’t.”

“Don’t even think about touching it.” She picked it up and laid it carefully on the bedside table, and then went to the bedroom door and put both hands flat on the frame on either side and looked at him across the room.

“No kissing,” she said. “No touching. Until I say otherwise.”

He stayed exactly where he was. “All right.”

“You’re not going to ask why?”

“No.”

She smiled, and walked backwards into the room. He followed as far as the threshold and stopped there. She let him stand. She looked at him for a long time, enjoying the stillness in him.

“Do you know what I like about you?” she said. “When I tell you to wait, you wait.”

“You’re my wife.”

“That doesn’t explain it.”

“No,” he agreed. “It doesn’t.”

She lowered her hand. “Otherwise.”

He came to her. She set the pace for a long time, undressing him herself and then letting him undress her, his mouth on her breast and her throat and lower, until she pulled him onto the bed and over her. Then she gave it to him, and meant it, and he took her slowly and then hard, her legs round him, until she cried out against his shoulder. The medal stayed on the bedside table, untouched, catching a little lamplight off the lake.

In the morning she woke to find him dressed and sitting on the edge of the bed, looking at it.

“Don’t.”

“I haven’t done anything.”

“You’re thinking about it.”

“I was wondering whether it would be appropriate to congratulate it.”

She laughed and pulled him down by the collar and kissed him. Then she picked up the medal and put it in his palm. “Only because you asked.” He held it very carefully, as if it might be hot.

“Number one,” he said.

“No.” She took it back. “Number one, by my own rules.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The message came three days later, when she was back at the bench with the first drawings for whatever came next.

Vittoria: I am very proud of you. I always was.

She read it once and then again. She didn’t answer. Enzo was asking about a clasp, and she answered him, and approved the sample, and worked until the light went. Only later, when the atelier was empty and the bench lamps were off, did she pick the phone up again. She thought of the shoebox, and the pencilled dates, and the note. She was always so close. She thought of the woman who had kept every second place and the woman who had made second place feel like a personal failing. Both were her mother. She could take the message without pretending the rest hadn’t happened.

Aurelia: Thank you, Mama.

She didn’t add anything else. She put the phone in her bag and switched off the last light and went down to the street, where Chen Si was waiting by the car.

“My mother says she’s proud of me,” she told him, as he pulled out into the traffic.

He took her hand across the console. “Are you glad?”

“Yes.”

“Does it hurt?”

She thought about it. “A little.” Then she leaned over and kissed him. “But it doesn’t decide anything any more.”

chapters.title: Renewing the Contract
chapters.desc: Ten years to the day. Clause eleven says she may rewrite every clause. She has been drafting for a year. He has been preparing for longer, and he has a counter-offer, and a pen, and a book that cost a back-room doctor three days of stitches.
chapters.epigraph: “You only have to keep asking.”
chapters.content:
The first draft went into the bin in November. The second lasted until Christmas. The third survived New Year’s Eve and was thrown out on the second of January because Aurelia decided clause seven had become far too generous to her husband. By February she had stopped numbering them. By March, Chen Si had started collecting them.

He found the latest in the wastepaper basket beside her desk on the morning of the twelfth: twelve pages, red ink, whole paragraphs struck through so hard the nib had nearly torn the paper. When she came back from the bathroom he was sitting in her chair with it spread on his knees.

“You’re reading my rubbish.”

“I’m reading your proposed amendments. Clause eleven. You’ve made either party able to ask for a revision without having to give a reason.”

“It’s in the bin.”

“An unfortunate place for a legal instrument.” He turned a page. “And you’ve struck out in the event of a material change in circumstances.”

“It was vague.”

“It was. I’m not surprised. I’m impressed.”

She held out her hand. “Paper.”

He gave it to her. She squared it against the desk. “You weren’t supposed to see that one.”

“How many have there been?”

“None of your business.”

“Nine?”

“Chen Si.”

“Ten?” He watched her eyes narrow and laughed and stood up and kissed her forehead. “You’ve been asking Mr. Yuen about matrimonial property and the legal meaning of joint authority since last March. I didn’t ask. You said you’d tell me when it was ready.”

“You’re very irritating.”

“So I’ve been told.”

She put the draft into a folder. “Today. Eleven o’clock. The shop.”

“Should I bring a pen?”

“Bring two.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The first shop on Harbour Road was closed to customers that morning, the display lights down, the staff given the day. The counter had been cleared of everything but a cream folder, a fountain pen and twelve pages. She stood behind it in a dark suit with her hair pinned back and the small gold earrings he had given her on their first anniversary.

He came in at eleven exactly. No flowers. No jewellery box. A black leather document case, which he put down beside her folder.

“A counter-offer?”

“Naturally.”

“Of course you have.”

He pulled out the chair on the customer’s side and sat. For a moment they looked at each other across the glass. Eleven years ago he had stood at this counter with a letter proposing that her shop become a convenient pipe for his money. She had sent it back covered in red ink and made him a partner on her terms instead. And ten years ago today, at eleven twenty-nine, at this same counter, she had given him eleven pages and he had signed every one.

She opened the folder. “Clause one.”

She read the first eleven aloud. Some had been tightened. Some had grown. Her business was still hers and his still his, and neither could take the other’s through marriage. Property stayed separate unless they chose otherwise in writing. What was shared was listed, and could be listed differently. Friends, and hours, and a room each. No family, his or hers, had any say. The press stayed outside. Money stayed open between them. Privacy stayed private. Nine was still nine: all matters of intimacy under the direction of the Wife until she said otherwise. Ten was still the word, and the word was still Milan, and it still meant stop, without argument and without anyone being made to pay for it afterwards. Eleven was still the one that mattered most. The marriage went on because both of them chose it, and for no other reason. Not money, not reputation, not fear, not the convenience of other people.

When she finished he looked down at the pages. “You’ve made the way out plainer.”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

“You’re not going to argue?”

“Do you want me to?”

“No.”

“Then no.” He uncapped his pen. “Clause twelve?”

She slid the next page across. The heading read Clause 12: Equality and Co-Rule. Pinned to the corner, with a small gold paperclip, was a sheet of hospital discharge paper folded in four, gone soft at the creases, with nine-year-old red ink on the back. We sit at the same table. To be considered, March 2029. A.

He looked at it for a long time. “You kept it in the drawer.”

“You asked me to keep it in mind. I keep things.”

The clause was longer than the others. Neither of them would be subordinate to the other in their marriage or their house. Neither would be the final authority because of wealth, or family, or title. Every large decision about the life they shared would be made by both. Each kept full authority over their own work. Neither would be asked to give up ambition, or name, or independence, to make room for the other’s position. And at the bottom:

The parties acknowledge each other as equals and co-rulers of the life they have chosen to build. Neither is the other’s subject. Neither is the other’s possession.

“Co-rulers,” he said. “Not queen?”

“Do you have a problem with that?”

“No. You’ve taken the title out.”

“I’ve taken the ladder out.”

“You’re still my queen.”

“Chen Si.”

“Privately.”

She leaned on the counter. “Ten years ago your note on the back said you were choosing me. I want this one to say we’re choosing each other. Not that you protect me. Not that I belong to you. Not that I have to earn a place next to you. I don’t want to stand behind you, and I don’t want you standing behind me.”

He read the last sentence once more and signed beneath it. “Agreed.”

“That was easy. You’ve just given up your crown.”

He put the pen down. “I never needed it. You were never beneath me.”

For a moment she had no answer at all. Then she smiled and said that was just as well, because she would have been extremely difficult to manage, and he said he had noticed. He opened his case. Inside was a single sheet folded in half. She laughed out loud.

Clause 13: The Unpriced Gift.

“Once a year,” he said, “one of us gives the other something. An object, an afternoon, a promise, a piece of work. It has no price. It can’t be sold, swapped or valued. Neither of us may ask what it cost, or what it’s worth.”

“You’ve written a legal clause about giving me a present.”

“I thought you’d appreciate the paperwork.”

“You’re ridiculous.”

“Will you accept it?”

“Yes,” said Aurelia, and he signed, and turned the page round, and she signed under him. Thirteen clauses. Ten years, and the beginning of whatever came next.

“There’s one more thing,” he said. “Not a clause. Come home.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The safe was in the study, behind a panel in the shelves that opened with a key and a code. She knew what was in it: their papers, the original agreement, the Numero Uno drawings, the first Balcony sketches, a few pieces she never wore outside the flat, and the trays of loose diamonds she had bought over the years and never found the right reason to set. He opened it and lifted out one velvet tray, and then another. Under the diamonds lay a long flat parcel in dark blue cloth whose knots had been tied and retied many times. He put it on the desk and undid them.

A book. Large, the leather dark and worn soft, the title on the spine almost rubbed away. She leaned closer and read it, and looked at him.

“Journey to the West?”

“Fifteen ninety-two.”

She knew. Zhao had told her, nine years ago, outside a room on the ninth floor: a very old book, the only thing of Chen Rong’s still worth anything, put down on a back-room doctor’s table in the old town to pay for three days of stitches.

“How?”

“You.” He touched the cover. “You put Enzo’s dealer on it in 2020, and he put my father’s name on every list in the trade from here to Lisbon. In 2023 it came up in a private collection being broken up in Porto. The provenance said Chen, so the dealer rang the Chen he knew. He didn’t know it was mine. I paid what was asked and had it examined, and I brought it home.” A faint smile. “And put it under your diamonds.”

“Six years. Under my diamonds.”

“It was the safest place in the building.”

“Did Zhao know?”

“From the day it came. He promised not to tell you.”

“That man is impossible.”

“He said you should see it when I was ready to say what it meant.”

She opened the cover, very carefully. On the flyleaf, faded brown, in a hand she had never seen, a name: Chen Rong. She touched it with one fingertip.

“I didn’t tell the dealer whose it had been,” said Chen Si. “I didn’t want the price to turn into a conversation about my father.” He looked at the name. “I wanted to give it to you on a day that mattered.”

“Why give it to me? It’s yours.”

“Because you were the one who told me I didn’t have to keep going back to that staircase to prove I loved him. I couldn’t bring him home. I could bring this.” He was quiet. “I don’t want it in a safe. I don’t want it treated like something I’ll lose if anyone sees it. I want it on a shelf in our house. I want to read it again.”

She was crying, and smiling. “Then we will.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening she took the old black silk out of her drawer and laid it on the bed. He looked at it.

“Is this in the contract?”

“Not yet.” She picked it up. “Sit.”

He sat on the edge of the bed. She stood in front of him and asked whether he remembered clause nine, and he said every word, and she asked for the word, and he said Milan, and she said good and asked whether she might, and he said yes. She tied the silk over his eyes, checking that it wasn’t tight, and put his hands in his lap, and told him to stay.

“Yes, sweetheart.”

On the bedside table were ten small cards. Ten years. Ten things he had done that she had never properly counted. She sat down facing him and picked up the first.

“One. You learned my coffee order before you knew I’d ever have dinner with you.”

He smiled under the silk.

“Two. You asked the girl at the coffee shop to stop drawing hearts on my cup.”

“She was very enthusiastic.”

“Three. You took the bones out of my fish when you were too tired to see.”

“A sound investment.”

“Don’t interrupt. Four. You waited, every time I said not yet. Five. You sat up at two in the morning for thirty-seven nights learning Italian down a phone line so you could marry me in it. Six. You gave me back the black jade queen. Seven. You sat outside Dr. Ho’s door every Tuesday for two years and never once asked me what I’d said.” He had gone quiet. “Eight. You let me build my own business and never once tried to make it a room in yours. Nine. You came home.”

His fingers moved in his lap.

She looked at the last card. She had written it the night before. “Ten. You let me lose. At chess, when I did it on purpose, and you knew, and let me. To Evangeline, five rounds in a row. In every room in my life where I came second before you were there to watch. You never once made me feel better by pretending I hadn’t. You let me be angry. You let me be ordinary.” She took his hand. “And you loved me anyway.”

His hand closed on hers. For a while he said nothing. Then: “I have ten of my own.”

“Of course you do.”

“I’ve been counting since the first year.”

“Tell me.”

“Not yet. I want to give them to you properly.”

“You’re very competitive.”

“I married you.” She laughed and kissed his forehead and untied the silk. He opened his eyes and looked at her without speaking, and then he caught her wrist and kissed the inside of it.

“You’re allowed to touch me now,” she said, and put her hands on his shoulders. “Otherwise.”

“Sure?”

“Yes.”

He kissed her, and drew her down onto the bed, and took the silk from her hand and tied it over her own eyes instead, gently, and asked if she minded, and she said no in a voice that made him smile. Then she couldn’t see anything, and had only his hands and his mouth to go by, on her throat, her breasts, the inside of her thighs, slow and familiar and in no way tame, until she was arching off the sheet and asking him for it in two languages. When he finally gave it to her she wrapped herself round him and held on, blind and laughing and then not laughing, with thirteen clauses on the desk and his father’s book on the table by the window where he could see it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Past midnight, with her head on his shoulder, he said, “There’s something else I haven’t told you.”

“Another secret?”

He reached into the drawer of the bedside table and gave her a sheet of paper, folded small, handled so often the creases had gone white. She unfolded it. Italian. She read the first line, and frowned.

“This isn’t modern Italian.”

“No.”

“It’s Milanese. Old Milanese.” She had heard him speak a little of it, in August five years ago, to Signor Bruno outside a café with a pack of cards on the table. She had never seen him write a word of it. “How long?”

“Seven years.”

“You already knew enough for the vows.”

“Enough to surprise you. Then I wanted to understand more.” He took the page back and folded it. “I wanted to write something that belonged to nobody but us. May I?”

She nodded. He touched her cheek and began to speak. It came slowly. His accent wasn’t right. Once he stopped to find a word, and once he corrected himself, but he didn’t stop. It was soft and old and close, and in it he talked about a balcony, and a woman who wouldn’t cry in front of strangers, and a coat lent with no promise attached, and a girl who had believed she had to come first to be loved, and a woman who had become his equal and his partner and the one person he trusted to tell him when he was wrong. Then he took her hand, and gave her the last of it in plain words.

“I choose you again. Not because you’re mine, and not because you stand beside me, and not because we’ve spent ten years learning how to stay. Because you are still the person I want to meet every morning. And if you change, I’ll learn you again.”

He looked almost embarrassed. “Did that make sense?”

She was laughing and her eyes were full. “Mostly. You made one mistake.”

His face changed. “Where?”

“At the end. You don’t have to learn me again.” She kissed him. “You only have to keep asking.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning the renewed agreement lay on the counter at Harbour Road, thirteen clauses, two signatures under each. At the bottom of the last page she had added a line by hand. Renewed by choice. Subject to revision. No ownership implied. He read it, and picked up the pen, and wrote under it: And chosen again, every day.

“That isn’t legally necessary.”

“I know.”

“Then why write it?”

“Because I wanted to,” said Chen Si, and leaned across the glass and kissed her.

At home the safe was shut. The book was no longer under the diamonds. It stood on the shelf in the study between his mother’s recipe book and the black jade queen, where anyone who came in could see it.

“Ten more years?” she said.

“Only ten?”

“Don’t be greedy.”

He took her hand. “Then we’ll renew it again.”

“Every year.”

“Every year,” he said, and neither of them needed a clause for it.

chapters.title: The Woman Who Sets the Price
chapters.desc: Epilogue. October. The house on the Peak, bought at auction by a woman who did not tell anyone she was bidding. A party for her father’s seventieth. The same balcony. A different coat. And the same man, standing at the end of it in the dark.
chapters.epigraph: “To the woman who sets the price.”
chapters.content:
The house on the Peak had stood empty for eight years.

For the first three, people still called it the Song house. After that they called it the old Song house. By the sixth year the newspapers had stopped mentioning it at all. It had passed from the lenders to a bank, from the bank to two holding companies in turn, and from the second of those to an auction room, where it had been knocked down on a wet afternoon in December 2023 to a company nobody had heard of, which turned out on inspection to be owned, entirely, by a jeweller on Harbour Road.

Aurelia had never told anyone she was bidding. Not her father, not her mother, not Serafina. Not Chen Si, either, although he had found out within the month, when a document needing her signature arrived at the office with the address on the front. He had read the auction notice, and the date, and then looked across the desk at his wife.

“It’s a good property,” she had said.

He hadn’t asked anything else. He knew what it meant. She hadn’t bought it to rescue the Song family. She had bought it because she remembered a house that had once been hers, even if nobody in it had known how to make it feel like home.

She had spent eight years putting it back. Not rebuilding it into something nobody would recognise. Restoring it. The staircase mended, the old stone cleaned, the garden dug over and planted again, the tall windows taken out pane by pane and put back true. The ballroom ceiling brought back, square foot by square foot, to the blue it had been when her grandfather bought the place. The dining table was the original; the chairs had been recovered. The balcony doors had been rehung and the railing stripped and polished. And the morning room had its bureau.

That had taken longest. Vittoria’s bureau, dark walnut with fine brass fittings and drawers lined in green velvet, had been sold on its own and gone to a dealer in Lucerne. Aurelia had found it in a sale catalogue in 2027 and bought it back without giving her name. She had the missing handle remade by hand. She had the scratches left alone. Some things didn’t need to be made new to be worth bringing home.

Tonight the house would be full again.

“You’re telling them tonight?” Chen Si was in the bedroom doorway of the flat, fastening his watch. She was at the mirror with an earring.

“At the party.”

“Your father will want to know why you didn’t tell him.”

“I wanted to surprise him.”

“He’ll want to know why you bought it.”

“Because I wanted it.”

“That may not satisfy him.”

“It satisfies me.” In the mirror she watched him come up behind her and straighten the back of her collar.

“You look beautiful.”

“I know.”

“And so modest.”

“Twelve years of marriage have taught you to appreciate my best qualities.”

“Thirteen since the balcony.”

“You’re getting old.”

“You’re welcome to trade me in.”

“At this price?” She turned in his arms. “Overpriced.”

“Still worth it.” He kissed her, carefully enough not to touch her lipstick, and offered his arm.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao came first, with Elowen, who was carrying white peonies and wearing a dress the colour of warm champagne. He stood in the hall and looked round it slowly.

“Not bad.”

“That’s all?”

“Good staircase.”

“He’s been admiring the staircase from the car for five minutes,” said Elowen.

“It’s well built.”

“You’ve said so three times.”

“Because it’s true,” said Zhao, and kissed Aurelia’s cheek, and went in to look at it from closer up. Elowen held out the peonies and said not to tell Zhao, he thought the garden had enough flowers already, and Aurelia said she had put them somewhere he would have to look at them all night.

Serafina came next, late, on Qin Haozhen’s arm, with her hair up in a style that had very obviously taken an hour to look as if it had taken five minutes. She said traffic. Aurelia said she lived twenty minutes away. Serafina said traffic could happen in twenty minutes. Then she stopped in the hall and looked up at the landing, and at her sister.

“You actually bought it.”

“Yes.”

“Without telling me.”

“You’d have told Papa.”

“I might have.”

“You absolutely would have.”

Serafina laughed and hugged her hard and stepped back and said she was unbelievable, and then, to Qin, “She’s been talking about this house for years. Not out loud. She does the thing where she says she doesn’t care and then remembers every crack in the plaster,” and Aurelia sent her to find Zhao.

Song Weiren came a little before seven, alone. She went down the front steps to meet him. He was in a dark suit; his hair had gone almost white. He looked older than at the last family dinner, but steadier, too, as if something in him had finally been set down. He stopped at the gate and didn’t speak. He looked at the house, and then at her.

“Why are we here?”

“Happy birthday, Papa.”

“The house,” he said.

“Come in.”

In the hall his steps slowed. He looked at the staircase, and the banister, and the stone floor, and put his hand flat on the wall by the window.

“The crack. It was here.”

“It’s still there. I didn’t want to erase everything.”

He went up the stairs slowly with her a few steps behind. On the landing he stopped by the old window and looked down into the hall, and then he bowed his head, and his shoulders moved. She went to him. He tried to say something and nothing came. He put one hand on the banister and the other over his eyes.

“You bought it,” he said at last. “Our house.”

“The house,” said Aurelia.

“Why?”

“Because I remembered it.”

His face went. And then he put his arms round her: not politely, the way a man holds someone at a party, but the way a man holds the one thing he thought he had lost for good. For a moment she was a daughter, and nothing else. Not the woman who had saved a bridge, or held a room of bankers, or won a prize in Geneva. His daughter, on a landing, in the house she grew up in.

✦ ✦ ✦

Vittoria came twenty minutes later with a small bag and a composed face. Her eyes went round the hall: the painting, back over the landing, which Aurelia had found in 2025 in a sale of a dead man’s collection; the staircase; the floor. Then she saw the bureau through the open door of the morning room, exactly where it had always been, and stopped.

“You found it,” said her mother.

“Yes.”

Vittoria went in and ran her fingers along the walnut. “The handle.”

“Remade.”

“And the scratches?”

“I left them.”

Vittoria opened the third drawer. The green velvet had been repaired, but in one corner the old stain was still there. She closed it, and for a moment didn’t seem able to speak. Aurelia took a key out of her pocket: the old brass one, cleaned, its head worn smooth.

“For the bureau,” she said. “And the house.”

Vittoria looked at it and didn’t take it. “Why?”

“Because you kept everything in that drawer.”

“Not everything.”

“Enough.”

Her mother’s fingers closed round the key. And then, without any warning at all, she stepped forward and put her arms round her daughter.

Aurelia went perfectly still. She couldn’t remember the last time. Before the competitions, perhaps; when she was small enough to be picked up. Never once since without an audience, a photographer, a correction folded into it. Vittoria’s arms weren’t strong. Her scent was the same as it had always been. Aurelia could feel the tremor in her mother’s breathing. For a second she was sixteen again, holding a second-place certificate, waiting to be told it was still something. She didn’t become sixteen. She didn’t forget anything. But she let her mother hold her.

When Vittoria let go she kept one hand on Aurelia’s arm. “Thank you.”

“You’re welcome.”

It wasn’t forgiveness for everything. It wasn’t a promise that anything would be different. It was a beginning small enough to be real.

✦ ✦ ✦

The dining room was full by eight. Zhao and Elowen in the middle of the table, Serafina and Qin beside them, Enzo with a present he swore wasn’t jewellery although it was in one of his own boxes. Qian at Chen Si’s elbow murmuring about something that could, it turned out, wait until Monday. Mr. Yuen telling Weiren a story about a judge they had both disliked thirty years ago. Aurelia went round the table making sure everyone had eaten and her father wasn’t drowning in attention. Chen Si watched her from the other end. When she caught his eye he lifted his glass an inch.

Then Weiren stood up, and the room quietened.

He looked round at the people in his house. His house. He seemed to hear the word only after he had thought it. He put his hand on the back of his chair.

“Thank you for coming. Some of you remember this house. Some of you remember my fifty-seventh birthday in it. That night my wife made a toast, and I stood beside her and lifted my glass. It was about people who had done well, and made good decisions, and knew how to look after a family name.” He stopped. “I didn’t look at the person who had just walked out of the room. I saw her go. I knew why. And I stayed at the table. That was my failure.”

Aurelia looked down at her plate.

“Tonight I want to make a different one.” He lifted his glass towards her. “To the woman who came back for this house. Who saved what could be saved, and built what nobody gave her, and decided for herself what anything was worth.” His voice got stronger. “To the woman who sets the price. To my daughter.”

The whole room stood. She stayed in her seat for one second longer than she should have. Then she stood too, and looked at her father, who was smiling with tears running into his collar, and raised her own glass.

“To Papa,” she said. “And to the house. Thank you all for coming home.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, when they had all drifted out into the garden with their coffee, she went upstairs on her own. The balcony doors were open. The night air was moving the curtains. She stepped out and put her hands on the cold rail.

The city lay below her, glittering, the harbour black between its lights. She remembered the first time she had stood exactly here. October. Her father’s birthday. Her mother at the foot of the staircase, telling two hundred people that the Harbour Road shop would close in January. Swallowing the humiliation whole because she would not cry where anyone could see. And a man in black gloves arriving at her elbow out of the dark, with a coat, and a quiet voice, and a question that had sounded almost impossible.

The door opened behind her. She didn’t turn round. “You’re late.”

“Qian had a question.”

“Qian always has a question.”

He came and stood beside her. He was carrying a coat. Charcoal, soft wool, a little longer than the one he had put round her shoulders thirteen years ago. He shook it out.

“You’re cold.”

She looked at it. “Again?”

“Again.”

She turned her back to him, and he put it round her and settled the collar against her neck with both hands, and his hands stayed there a moment longer than they needed to.

“New coat.”

“Yes.”

“Expensive?”

“Reasonably.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“Very,” he said.

She laughed. “You’re getting better at this.”

“At buying coats?”

“At knowing when to lend them.”

“I’ve had practice.”

Over his shoulder she saw that her mother had come into the bedroom behind them, perhaps for her bag, perhaps only to see where her daughter had gone. Vittoria wasn’t hiding. She had seen them. And Aurelia felt the old instinct rise in her the way it always had: to step back, to make the moment smaller, to stand as if she had been caught at something she shouldn’t be doing.

She didn’t move.

Chen Si’s hand came to rest at her waist. He didn’t look at Vittoria. He looked at her. “May I?”

“Yes,” said Aurelia.

He kissed her on the balcony where they had met, under the same sky, with the house lit up behind them and the city below. Not in a hurry, and not for anyone watching. Her fingers curled into the lapels of the charcoal coat, and she kissed him back. When they came apart he rested his forehead against hers and asked if she was happy, and she said very, and he said good.

She didn’t turn round to see her mother’s face. She didn’t hide the kiss, or ask whether it was approved of. She stood with her husband, in the coat he had given her, on the balcony of a house she had bought and mended with her own money and her own hands. And for the first time in her life, the balcony wasn’t somewhere she had gone to get away. It was hers.

✦ ✦ ✦

When they came down, her father was at the foot of the stairs. He looked at the coat on his daughter’s shoulders, and then at Chen Si.

“Still lending her coats?”

“She still gets cold.”

“Then keep doing it,” said Weiren.

“Are you two deciding my wardrobe now?”

“No,” said Chen Si.

“I wouldn’t dare,” said her father.

From the dining room Serafina shouted that Zhao was trying to convince everybody that this staircase was better made than the one in his own house, and Zhao said that it was, and Elowen said he had been saying it for twenty minutes. Aurelia shook her head. “Family,” she said, and Chen Si held out his hand, and they went down the last steps together.

At the bottom she looked back once. The house was full of people. The bureau was in the morning room. Her father was laughing. Her mother was holding the key. And the balcony doors stood open to the night.

She hadn’t gone back to the life she had once had. She had built a different one. A house is not a family. A title is not love. Being first had never been the price of belonging. She had learned to set the price herself, and then, at last, she had learned that some things were never for sale.

chapters.title: Floral vs. Jewelry, Round Forty-One
chapters.desc: A charity lunch. One centrepiece budget. Two women who were first and second at school, and who have not stopped keeping score. Their husbands sit at the end of the table and say nothing, which is the most dangerous thing either of them can do.
chapters.epigraph: “Because I meant it.”
chapters.content:
The charity lunch had one budget for centrepieces. One. Mrs. Leung had made this clear in the invitation, in the follow-up letter, and in an unfortunate telephone call in which she had used the phrase a friendly creative competition four times. Aurelia had disliked her immediately. Not personally. Professionally.

“One budget,” said Mrs. Leung, on the third Saturday in May, standing between the two women in the ballroom of the yacht club with her hands clasped. “One winning design. The guests will vote.”

Elowen smiled politely. Aurelia smiled politely. At the far end of the long table, Chen Si and Zhao exchanged a look and said nothing at all. They had both learned that silence was the only sensible contribution a husband could make when two women who had come first and second at school were given a shared objective and an audience.

“Flowers,” said Elowen pleasantly, “are naturally suited to a centrepiece.”

“Jewellery is naturally suited to being looked at.”

“Flowers are alive.”

“Gold lasts longer.”

“Flowers have scent.”

“Some people find scent overwhelming.”

Elowen’s smile sharpened by a degree. “Some people have no imagination.”

“Some people,” said Aurelia, “have no resale value.”

At the end of the table Zhao reached quietly for his water. Chen Si looked at the chandelier. Round forty-one had begun.

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia’s pieces came first, in twelve flat cases carried by two of Enzo’s bench men. They were not arrangements. Each was a low sculpture of gold wildflowers on a base of brushed champagne gold: the small weeds of the Walled City, the kind that grow between old paving stones and in the cracks of walls nobody repairs. Chickweed in tiny clusters. Star-shaped blooms no bigger than a fingernail. Wild grasses, each blade beaten thin enough to tremble when someone walked past the table.

And in the centre of every one, a thistle.

She had made those herself, at night, for a month. The bracts were chased one by one so that each caught the light differently, and the spiny head was done in gold without being softened into anything harmless. It was beautiful, and it would hurt you if you weren’t careful.

Elowen stood in front of the first one for a long moment. “That’s a thistle.”

“Yes.”

“Not exactly the prettiest flower.”

Aurelia adjusted a blade of grass. “It isn’t trying to be.”

Elowen looked at her, and then smiled. “Interesting.”

“Thank you.”

“That wasn’t a compliment.”

“I’ve decided to take it as one.”

Across the room Chen Si leaned towards Zhao. “She’s pleased.”

Zhao was watching Elowen look at the thistle. “Your wife?”

“Yours.”

Zhao sighed. “I know.”

Elowen’s arrangements were exquisite. She had chosen wildflowers too, but hers were living: pale yellow blooms and loose white clusters and long trailing green, in shallow grey ceramic bowls she had thrown herself on a borrowed wheel. They looked as if someone had picked up a corner of a hillside after rain and persuaded it to sit nicely at a formal lunch.

Aurelia examined them with her head on one side. “Very pretty.”

“Thank you.”

“Quite a lot of green.”

“Flowers tend to come with leaves.”

“An unfortunate design limitation,” said Aurelia, and Elowen laughed, and then stepped closer and lowered her voice.

“Can I tell you something? Zhendong has been correcting my arrangements all morning.”

Aurelia blinked. “What?”

“He doesn’t say a word. He looks at a stem, moves it three centimetres to the left, and walks away.” At the far end of the room Zhao was talking to Chen Si with the expression of a man who had never done anything wrong in his life.

Aurelia turned slowly, and looked at her own table. Chen Si was standing beside one of her thistles. As she watched, he put out one finger and moved a single blade of gold grass. About three centimetres. To the left.

She turned back. “Chen Si does that.”

Elowen’s eyes widened. “He does?”

“He once rearranged my whole window while I was on the phone. He said the visual weight was wrong.”

“Was it?”

“That,” said Aurelia, “is not the point.”

They both pressed their lips together. They both looked at their husbands, who were now standing side by side between the two tables, contemplating the centrepieces with the grave attention of men inspecting a cargo manifest.

“Do you think they discuss it?” whispered Elowen.

“Absolutely.”

“Do you think they have opinions?”

“Unfortunately.” At the end of the table Chen Si moved another stem. Aurelia shut her eyes. “Forty-one rounds,” she said.

“Forty-one,” said Elowen, very contentedly.

✦ ✦ ✦

The voting began after the fish. Every guest had a small card and a pencil and was asked to choose. Aurelia stood by her table with her arms folded. Elowen stood by hers with the serene confidence of a woman who had grown flowers for twenty years and knew precisely what they did to people in a warm room. The cards went into a silver bowl. Mrs. Leung took them away to be counted, and came back with the face of a woman who has been given something interesting to announce.

“Well! We have an extraordinary result. Ninety-nine for the floral arrangements.” Elowen smiled. “And ninety-nine for the gold.”

Aurelia blinked. A tie. A perfect tie. She looked at Elowen. Elowen looked at her. Then, slowly, they both turned their heads towards the end of the table. Chen Si was examining his cuff. Zhao had become very interested in the yachts in the marina.

“There are,” said Mrs. Leung, consulting the last two cards in her hand, “two spoilt ballots.”

Aurelia held out her hand. “May I?”

Mrs. Leung hesitated, and passed them over. The first was in Chen Si’s handwriting. One word.

Mine.

The second was Zhao’s. The same word, in heavier pencil, as if he had pressed hard to make sure.

Mine.

Both women turned. Both men looked up. Neither man looked remotely ashamed.

“That isn’t a vote,” said Aurelia.

Chen Si considered this. “I didn’t say it was.”

Elowen held up Zhao’s card. “Neither is this.”

“Agreed,” said Zhao.

“Then why did you write it?”

He looked at her. “Because I meant it.”

Elowen opened her mouth, and shut it again, and went faintly pink to the ears.

Aurelia folded Chen Si’s card in half. “You’re both disqualified.”

“From the competition?” said Chen Si.

“From speaking.”

Zhao nodded. “That’s fair.”

Mrs. Leung, after a short consultation with her committee, divided the centrepiece budget into two equal halves and gave each half to the children’s ward in the name of the opposite team, which was, everyone agreed afterwards, the cleverest thing Mrs. Leung had ever done.

✦ ✦ ✦

The drive home was silent for about four minutes. Then Aurelia turned in her seat.

“One hundred and ninety-eight people. And they couldn’t decide.”

“Apparently.”

“Forty-one rounds and it ends in a tie.”

“You made something beautiful,” said Chen Si. “So did she. Perhaps a tie is right.”

“You’re taking her side.”

“I’m not taking anybody’s side.”

“You’re supposed to be my husband.”

“I am.”

“Then you should be furious.”

He glanced at her. “Would you like me to be?”

“Yes.”

He nodded gravely. “I’m furious.”

She narrowed her eyes. “You’re not.”

“No.” He reached over and ran his thumb across her knuckles. “Sweetheart, you made a gold thistle. You won.”

She tried not to smile, and failed, and leaned over the console and kissed him hard, and he caught her by the waist with one hand and laughed against her mouth. When she sat back she was still frowning on principle.

“Don’t think this means I accept the tie. Next time I’m making forty-one flowers.”

“I’ll make sure Zhao doesn’t vote.”

“Your handwriting is atrocious.”

“You kept the card.”

“Evidence.”

“Of what?”

“Your appalling judgement,” said Aurelia, and put the folded card in her bag.

At home there was a small parcel on the hall table, wrapped in brown paper and tied with green thread. A card said For the winner. Inside, between two sheets of archival paper, was a single tiny sprig of real chickweed, pressed flat, and under it, in Elowen’s neat hand:

Forty-one to thirty-nine.

Aurelia stared at it. Then she laughed out loud. On the back, smaller:

I only count the rounds I actually won. You know the score.

She picked up her phone.

Aurelia: You are an insufferable woman.

Elowen: Thank you. I learned from the best.

Aurelia: The thistle was better.

Elowen: The chickweed is alive.

Aurelia: Mine will outlive yours.

Elowen: Yours can’t grow.

Aurelia looked at the screen for a long moment. Then she typed.

Aurelia: Round forty-two.

Across the room Chen Si looked up from his book. “What’s wrong?”

“Nothing. I’m planning a competition.”

He closed the book. “Should I be concerned?”

“Very.”

He held out his arm and she went and sat against him with the pressed sprig still in her hand. He kissed her temple.

“Did you win?”

“No.”

“Did Elowen?”

“No.”

“Then perhaps you both did.”

“That’s a very diplomatic answer.”

“I’ve had practice,” said Chen Si.

Before bed she put the chickweed in a small frame and stood it on the shelf beside one of the gold thistles, which she had kept back from the children’s ward for exactly this purpose. One living. One lasting. Both beautiful. And neither woman prepared to give up a single point. Round forty-two was coming, and Chen Si and Zhao would be very wise to stay out of it.

chapters.title: He Has Never Been Late. Today He Was Late.
chapters.desc: Seven o’clock. A dinner reservation he made himself. Seven-fifteen. Seven-thirty. His phone goes to voicemail. Zhao’s phone goes to voicemail. For forty minutes, Aurelia Chen finds out exactly how much of her is still sitting in a corridor outside an ICU.
chapters.epigraph: “Thirty-one minutes late.”
chapters.content:
At twelve minutes past six on a Thursday, Aurelia received a photograph of a dress. Deep emerald silk, a soft neckline, a fitted waist. Elegant, quiet, and far too expensive to be sent casually.

Chen Si: Wear this tonight.

Aurelia: Why?

Chen Si: Because I like it.

Aurelia: You’ve never seen me in it.

Chen Si: I have an imagination.

Then, a moment later:

Chen Si: And Elowen doesn’t own the colour.

She laughed out loud in the empty workroom. At lunch Elowen had worn a beautiful green dress and made the error of announcing that green was her colour, and Aurelia had pointed out that colours were not property, and Elowen had suggested Aurelia was merely jealous. Apparently Zhao had reported this across the city within the hour.

Aurelia: You’re taking my side?

Chen Si: Always.

Aurelia: Even when I’m wrong?

Chen Si: Especially when you’re entertaining.

Dinner was at seven at a small place over the water that he had booked himself, which he never did. He had said he would collect her at a quarter to. At 6:42 a message came.

Chen Si: Running behind. Go at seven. I’ll meet you there.

She put on the green dress. She was at the restaurant at seven. He wasn’t.

At a quarter past she rang him. Voicemail. She rang again. Voicemail.

At 7:22 she rang Qian, who answered on the first ring and sounded as though he were standing in a wind. “Madam.”

“Where is my husband?”

A pause. “I’ll find out.”

“That isn’t an answer, Qian.”

“No, madam.”

At half past she rang Zhao. Voicemail. She looked at the phone. Zhao did not ignore calls. Not hers. Not ever. She rang again. Voicemail.

The host came over and asked whether she would like something while she waited. She said no. He asked whether she would prefer a quieter table. She said no. The door opened, and a couple came in laughing, shaking rain off an umbrella. Not him.

At 7:34 the soft music in the room became unbearable. At 7:36 she stopped pretending to read the menu. At 7:39 she remembered the ninth floor.

The white corridor. The smell of the hand gel. The grey plastic chair. The terrible stillness of a monitor when it stops making the sound it is supposed to make. His hand lying on the blanket with no strength in it. His lips with no colour. A doctor saying something to her that she couldn’t hear because she was watching the bed, waiting for it to move. Counting his heartbeat in Italian, under her breath, uno, due, tre, because Italian was the language of her grandmother’s kitchen and nothing bad had ever happened in it. How many times she had said his name. How none of it had been enough to wake him.

Her fingers had gone tight round the phone. She rang him again. Voicemail.

Her throat closed. She stood up so suddenly that the chair went back with a scrape, and the host came hurrying.

“Madam?”

“My car.”

“Of course.”

She already had her bag. Her mind had started building the possibilities with perfect, ruthless efficiency, the way she built a cost sheet. An accident. An ambush. A lorry across a lane. The coast road at Lantern Bay at two in the morning, with glass in Zhao’s arm. She had been there before. She could be on that road in twenty minutes if the tunnel was clear—

The door opened. A man came in breathing hard.

His shirt was torn at the shoulder. There was mud along one leg of his trousers to the knee. A shallow cut by his hairline. His hair looked as though he had dragged his hand through it many times. Chen Si. Alive.

For one second she couldn’t move. Then she crossed the restaurant, and he had barely turned before she had his face in her hands and was kissing him. Hard. Not a greeting. Not a careful kiss. Forty minutes of fear, and anger, and relief, and the need to feel him breathing against her mouth. He caught her round the waist. When she let go she was shaking.

“Thirty-one minutes.”

His face changed. “Aurelia—“

“Thirty-one minutes late.”

“I know.”

“Your phone.”

“Broken.”

“Zhao’s phone.”

“His too—“

“Don’t.” She put her forehead against his chest. For a moment the restaurant wasn’t there. He held her with one hand on the back of her head.

“I’m sorry.”

She swallowed. “Are you hurt?”

“No. Nothing serious.”

“Then why are you covered in mud?”

“An unfortunate incident.”

“That isn’t an explanation.”

“Car accident,” said a voice behind him, and Zhao came in, only marginally cleaner.

Aurelia closed her eyes. “You’re alive too.”

“Disappointingly.” He held up both hands before she could start. “It rained. A van came round the bend on the wrong side and the car went into the ditch. We had to climb out. The phones went into the water. Then we had to get the car out, because there were things in the boot that can’t be found by a recovery lorry.”

“You could have borrowed a phone.”

“From whom? The ditch?”

“You could have sent someone ahead.”

“Because—“

“Enough,” said Chen Si, and touched his arm.

Zhao looked at Aurelia. Something in his face softened. “I’m sorry, sister.”

That did it. Her anger went out of her all at once, and she nodded, once. “Sit down. Both of you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The food came forty minutes later. She hadn’t let go of his hand under the table. He had washed his face in the restaurant’s cloakroom and put on a clean shirt that Qian had produced from somewhere in nine minutes, and the cut at his hairline had been cleaned and closed with two thin strips. He ate quietly. She watched him. After a while he put his fork down.

“You’re still frightened.”

She looked at her plate. “I was going to drive the coast road.”

His hand tightened. “I know.”

“I thought it was happening again.”

He moved his chair closer. “I’m here.”

“That doesn’t mean it can’t happen.”

“No.” He didn’t tell her she was being unreasonable. He didn’t promise that nothing would ever happen again; he had never once lied to her, and he wasn’t going to start in a restaurant. He lifted her hand and kissed the knuckles. “I should have found a way to reach you. I should have known how long it would take. And I should have told you not to wait if I couldn’t come.”

“Yes,” she said, to all three.

“I’ll do better.”

She let out a long breath and leaned against his shoulder. “You’re still paying for dinner.”

“Of course.”

“And dessert. And the emotional damages.”

He kissed her temple. “Name your price.”

“Don’t tempt me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Outside, before they got into the car, he opened the rear door and reached in, and she heard a small sound. A thin, indignant mew.

She looked down. There was a soft carrier on the back seat, and in it a kitten. Grey, very small, round-eyed, with an expression of profound dissatisfaction at the whole evening. Chen Si opened the door of the carrier and the kitten put its head out and looked at Aurelia and complained again. It had a white patch under its chin and four white toes on one front paw.

She crouched in the green dress on the wet pavement and held out her hand. It sniffed her fingers, and then climbed onto her palm.

“Do you remember Topolino?” said Chen Si.

She looked up. Topolino. The small grey cat who had slept on the end of her bed when she was young, before the house on the Peak became a place where she learned to keep everything quiet. He had died the winter she was sixteen, and she had cried in the laundry room so nobody would hear, and the only person who had come to find her was Pina.

“How do you know about Topolino?”

“You told Pina,” he said. “Last week. You were asleep. You asked her where Topolino was. You said you wanted her to bring him upstairs. You said you hadn’t seen him for a long time.”

Her face changed. She looked down at the kitten in her hand.

“I thought you might like a cat again,” said Chen Si.

“So that’s where you were. Before the ditch.”

“There’s a woman out past the reservoir who breeds them. The van came round the bend on the way back.”

“Did you choose him?”

“I chose him because he was grey.”

“That’s your entire selection criterion?”

“He seemed suitable.”

The kitten climbed up her wrist into the crook of her elbow and settled there. She looked up at her husband with her eyes wet. “You bring me a cat after making me wait thirty-one minutes?”

“I thought it might improve my position.”

“You think you can buy your way out of this?”

“No.”

“Good,” said Aurelia, and stood up and kissed him, and kissed him again, and the kitten mewed between them.

They were still in the car when Zhao sent a message.

Zhao: Does it have a name?

She looked at Chen Si. “Topolino.”

He smiled. “Good.”

Zhao: Elowen says it has a sister.

Aurelia: What?

Zhao: White. Very pretty. I may have taken her.

“Zhao adopted the sister,” said Aurelia. “Without asking Elowen.”

“He’ll ask.”

“After?”

“Probably.”

Her phone rang. Elowen.

“Your husband brought you a kitten.”

“Yes.”

“And mine has brought me one.” A pause. “I’ve decided to call her Ritardo.”

Aurelia blinked. “Why?”

“Because your husband was late, and mine was responsible. Tell Chen Si I expect an apology for both of us. And tell Zhendong she’s sleeping in our room tonight and he can sleep where he likes.”

Aurelia was laughing so hard she couldn’t answer. Chen Si shut his eyes. “That’s unfair,” he said, to the roof of the car.

✦ ✦ ✦

At home, Topolino was given a warm round bed beside her reading chair, which he ignored, climbing into her lap instead. Chen Si watched from the doorway.

“He’s chosen you.”

“Obviously.”

“Should I be jealous?”

“Yes.”

He came and crouched beside the chair. The kitten put out one tiny paw and caught the cuff of his clean shirt. He looked down at it, and very carefully offered one finger, and the kitten wrapped both front paws round it and held on.

“Look,” said Aurelia. “He likes you.”

“I’ve been replaced.”

“Temporarily.”

He kissed her forehead, and her cheek, and the corner of her mouth. “Tomorrow there’ll be a second phone in every car. Zhao carries a spare. And if we’re ever held up, someone rings you before you’ve finished your first glass of water. Every time.”

She nodded. “Thank you.”

He touched her face. “Tonight, I’m here.”

The fear hadn’t gone altogether. It never did, just because someone came home. But his hand was warm on her cheek, and the kitten was purring against her stomach like a small engine.

“You’re still late,” she said.

“I know.”

“Thirty-one minutes.”

“I know.”

“You’ll be hearing about it for a long time.”

“I expect nothing less.”

At 11:47 Zhao sent one last message.

Zhao: Ritardo has settled in. Elowen says she likes her better than me.

Chen Si: Sensible cat.

Zhao: I hope your wife is still angry.

Chen Si looked across the room. Aurelia had fallen asleep on the sofa with one hand curled protectively beside Topolino.

Chen Si: She is.

Zhao: Good. You deserve it.

He put the phone away. Then he lifted his wife, kitten and all, and carried them upstairs. For the first time all evening he was not late, and in the morning, before anything else, he would remember to call.

chapters.title: What the Don’s Assistant Puts Up With
chapters.desc: Qian has worked for Chen Si for twelve years. He has two drawers of antacids, a spreadsheet titled “Clause Nine Scheduling Conflicts”, and a theory that the most dangerous man in the city is completely, catastrophically, embarrassingly in love. A week in his life.
chapters.epigraph: “Because I have a very difficult job.”
chapters.content:
Qian Yu had worked for Chen Si for twelve years. He had survived two attempted takeovers, one poisoning, a lorry across the coast road, and six weeks in which his employer insisted he was perfectly capable of running the Syndicate from a hospital bed. He kept two drawers of antacids. He had a medical insurance policy he had never expected to use so often. And on his laptop, in a folder of its own, he kept a spreadsheet titled CLAUSE NINE SCHEDULING CONFLICTS (INTERNAL).

He considered it his finest professional achievement. His second finest was still being employed. His third was not having strangled either of his employers. Yet.

Every morning at exactly 7:44, Chen Si opened a photograph on his phone. Qian knew because he had watched it happen for six years. It wasn’t a remarkable photograph. Aurelia at her bench in the workroom over the shop, in a white shirt with the sleeves rolled up, her hair clipped carelessly at the back of her head, a small smudge of polishing compound on one cheek, laughing at something out of the frame. She didn’t know it existed. Chen Si had taken it from the stairs one afternoon while she was too busy arguing with Enzo about a hinge to notice him. Qian had once asked whether he should move it into the secure personal archive. Chen Si had looked at him. “No. It stays here.” Qian had understood that, too.

At 7:44 on Monday, the photograph came up. At 7:45 the phone went back into the inside pocket. At 7:46 Chen Si said, “Rotterdam,” and Qian looked at the clock and accepted that another week had begun.

✦ ✦ ✦

The Rotterdam call on Tuesday morning was important. Three senior partners on the screen, two men from the bank in the room, and a lawyer who had flown in from Geneva the night before and was visibly regretting it. At 10:18 Chen Si was halfway through a sentence when the office door opened and Aurelia walked in.

She wore a cream blouse and dark trousers and the expression of a woman who had already decided the meeting was over. Qian stood up. “Madam.”

“Hello, Qian.”

Chen Si looked up, and his face changed. Not much. Enough. She came round the desk and bent and said something too quietly for the microphone. He muted it.

“Your tie,” she said.

“It’s fine.”

“It’s crooked.”

“Then fix it.”

Qian looked at the ceiling. Aurelia straightened the tie. Chen Si’s hand settled at her waist. She said something else, and he smiled, and then she kissed him. Qian turned to the window. He was a professional. He had twelve years of experience. He would not look.

The call stayed muted for four more minutes. When Chen Si finally unmuted it, his tie was crooked again, and one of the partners in Rotterdam said, rather carefully, “Mr. Chen, are we continuing?”

Chen Si adjusted his cuff. “Yes.”

Qian opened the spreadsheet and typed: Tue: Rotterdam delayed by domestic matter (tie). No further action.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Wednesday at two, Aurelia appeared beside his desk. “Qian. I need a favour.”

He closed the spreadsheet instantly. “Of course, madam.”

“How many free days does Chen Si have next month?”

“Define free.”

“Not working.”

“That,” said Qian, “is a theoretical category.”

She smiled. “Could you find twenty-six hours together?”

“Twenty-six?”

“Yes.”

“May I ask what for?”

“A dental appointment.”

He blinked. “A twenty-six-hour dental appointment?”

“Very complicated dentistry,” said Aurelia, and left.

At 2:17 his phone rang. “Qian. Clear twenty-six hours next month. Together.”

Qian closed his eyes. “May I ask the reason, Mr. Chen?”

“Dental.”

“Understood.”

“And don’t put it in the shared calendar.”

“Naturally.”

He put the phone down and opened the spreadsheet and created a new tab. DENTAL (26-HOUR). He entered two names, and sat back in his chair, and looked at the ceiling for some time. There were things a man could bear. There were others that required the second drawer.

At half past four his own assistant came in with a folder, and stopped behind his chair. “Mr. Qian, what’s this spreadsheet?”

“Nothing.”

“It says Clause Nine Scheduling Conflicts.”

“Internal.”

“Why are there three hundred and eighty-six entries?”

He took the folder out of her hands. “Because I have a difficult job.”

She was still looking at the screen. “Why are sixty-one of them dentist?”

Qian shut the laptop. “Because I have a very difficult job.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday at 11:52, lunch arrived. Not at the office canteen; at Chen Si’s private dining room down the corridor, in a covered clay pot wrapped in a quilted carrier. Qian knew the smell before he lifted the lid. Grouper soup. Ginger. A little spring onion. His mother’s recipe, out of the book Qian’s own wife had kept safe in a drawer for six years until there was someone to give it to. There was a card on top.

You forgot lunch again. Eat properly. A.

Qian carried it in and put it on the desk. Chen Si was back on with Rotterdam. Qian said “Mr. Chen,” very quietly, and Chen Si raised one finger without looking. Qian pointed at the pot. Chen Si looked, and stopped talking in the middle of a word. One of the Rotterdam partners went on for several seconds before he understood that the head of the Syndicate was no longer listening to him. Chen Si picked up the card and read it.

“Reschedule,” he said.

“Sir, they’ve been waiting since—“

“Tomorrow.”

“Of course.”

The screen went dark. Qian stood very still. In twelve years he had never once seen this man hang up on Rotterdam for soup. He had, in fairness, seen him walk out of a planning meeting because his wife had sent a photograph of a broken clasp. He looked at the pot, and the card, and briefly considered adding a column headed SOUP-RELATED INTERRUPTIONS. He decided against it. A man had to have standards.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday at ten past six, a message arrived on Chen Si’s phone.

Aurelia: I’m downstairs.

Chen Si read it and stood up at once. Qian looked at the pile on the desk. “Sir, the revised report—“

“Tomorrow.”

“The bank—“

“Monday.”

“The—“

“Qian.”

“Yes, sir.”

“Thank you,” said Chen Si, and walked out.

Qian followed at a respectful distance as far as the lifts. The doors opened. Aurelia was inside, and looked up as he stepped in.

“Finished?”

“For today.”

He caught her round the waist and kissed her. The doors began to close. Then they opened again, because a young man from the legal department was standing outside with a file, and had pressed the button, and was now frozen with his finger still on it. Chen Si didn’t move away at once. Aurelia, however, laughed against his mouth.

“Your colleague.”

Chen Si glanced round. “Get in.”

The young lawyer looked as though he had been invited into a cage. Qian stepped forward. “Perhaps the next lift.”

“Yes. Of course. Thank you.”

The doors closed. Qian stayed in the corridor and looked at the ceiling. Twelve years. Three hundred and eighty-six conflicts. Sixty-one dental appointments. One Don who could make a room full of armed men go quiet by putting down a teacup, and who would walk out of any meeting in the city the moment his wife said she was downstairs.

He went back to his desk and opened the spreadsheet and added a column: LIFT DELAYS. Then he shut it. It was Friday. He deserved a weekend.

✦ ✦ ✦

At two minutes past seven he found a small box on his desk. He assumed it was a courier delivery. It wasn’t. It was wrapped in dark green paper and tied with a thin gold ribbon, and his name was on the card in a hand he knew.

Inside lay a pair of gold cufflinks. Plain and heavy and beautifully finished, with the soft warm sheen of something made rather than bought. One was engraved DENTAL. The other, THANK YOU.

Under them was a second card.

For every appointment you have invented, every meeting you have moved, and everything you have so politely pretended not to see. We know exactly how good you are at your job. Aurelia & Chen Si

Qian sat down. He read it twice. Then he looked at the closed door of the office down the corridor. For twelve years he had served a man who was feared from the docks to the hills. A man who could make senior partners wait three hours without an explanation, and who had once walked into a room, listened to a single sentence, and decided the future of a whole division before the speaker had sat down. And that man’s wife had made him a pair of cufflinks that said Dental.

He put them carefully back in the box. He opened the laptop. The spreadsheet was still there. 386. He considered, for a moment, deleting it. Then he remembered the twenty-six hours next month. He added one final line.

Fri: compensation received for extraordinary scheduling demands. Continued employment recommended.

He saved the file and closed it, and for the first time in twelve years, alone in the office at seven on a Friday night, Qian Yu laughed out loud.

At 7:44 the next morning Chen Si would open the photograph again. Qian knew it. He also knew that Aurelia would almost certainly interrupt the schedule before nine. He had already restocked the second drawer. A man had to be ready for anything, working for the most dangerous man in the city. And his wife.

chapters.title: Blood Brothers Go Anniversary Shopping
chapters.desc: Two of the most feared men in the city. One shopping centre. Three hours before closing. Zhao’s anniversary is on Friday and he has bought nothing; Chen Si’s was on Sunday and he has bought nothing either.
chapters.epigraph: “I’d choose you again.”
chapters.content:
At three minutes past five on a Wednesday in March, Zhao Zhendong discovered that his wedding anniversary was on Friday.

He had known this, technically, for a year. He had known it the two years before that as well. The difficulty was that he had not bought anything. He stood in Chen Si’s office holding his phone and looking at the calendar on it as if it had personally betrayed him.

Chen Si looked up from his papers. “What’s wrong?”

“My anniversary.”

“Congratulations.”

“Friday.”

“Yes. The seventeenth. I was there.”

“I haven’t bought anything.”

Chen Si went back to his papers. “Then buy something.”

Zhao stared at him. “That’s why I’m here.”

Chen Si looked up again. For a moment neither of them spoke. Then Zhao said, with the grim seriousness of a man reporting an assassination plot, “I need your help.”

Chen Si put down his pen. “With what?”

“Shopping.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At 5:47 two of the most feared men in the city walked into the big shopping centre on the east side of the harbour. Zhao looked deeply uncomfortable. Chen Si looked mildly inconvenienced. They had three hours until closing.

“Where do we start?”

Chen Si glanced at the directory board. “Jewellery.”

“Why?”

“Women wear jewellery.”

“Elowen wears flowers.”

“Flowers die.”

“She likes them.”

“Then buy flowers.”

“I can’t give her flowers for our anniversary. She sells flowers.” Zhao opened his mouth to say something else, shut it, and muttered, “I hate shopping.”

The assistant in the jewellery shop came towards them with a bright smile, took one look, and lost about half of it. “Good evening. Can I help you find something?”

“His wife,” said Chen Si.

“Of course. What does she like?”

“Flowers,” said Zhao.

“Books,” said Chen Si.

Zhao turned. “How do you know?”

“You told me. At dinner. She reads in the bath until the water goes cold.”

Zhao thought about it, and nodded. The assistant brought out a tray. Zhao picked up a bracelet and said it was too thin; it would catch on her secateurs. A necklace: she’d get it caught in a bucket. A ring: she already had one, and wore it on the wrong finger because she liked it heavy. He picked up a second bracelet and asked the assistant, quite seriously, whether it would survive somebody changing a tyre. The assistant looked at Chen Si for help.

“You’re buying for a woman who married you,” said Chen Si. “She already knows what she’s getting.”

“That isn’t helpful.”

“It’s meant to be.”

They left without buying anything.

At 6:21 Zhao stopped in front of a bookshop, and went in, and Chen Si followed. Zhao went straight to the classics, as if he knew where they were, and took down a handsome bound edition of Journey to the West, and opened it at random, and began, quietly, to read aloud. His voice was slow and a little rough, but it was steady, and he didn’t lose his place.

Chen Si watched him. After a few lines Zhao stopped. “What?”

“Nothing. You read now.”

Zhao looked down at the page. “Yes.” He turned it. “Elowen likes listening. She says I used to rush the words, as if somebody was going to take the book away. I read her the monkey king last month. Took me three evenings.”

“You read to her?”

“Most nights.” He frowned. “Not every night. Most.”

Chen Si nodded and looked away at the shelves. He was thinking of a top bunk in Block C, a battered paperback with the cover torn off and the spine held together with tape, and a fifteen-year-old who could only make out one word in three, listening to him read in the dark so nobody would hear. And of another copy entirely, very old, which he had once put down on a back-room doctor’s table and never seen again.

Zhao put the book back. “I’ll buy her something she can use.”

“Shears.”

Zhao blinked. “What?”

“She runs a flower shop.”

“She has shears.”

“Not old Kyoto shears. There’s a dealer on the second floor who has a pair in the window. Hand-forged. A hundred years old. The handles have been rewrapped.”

Zhao looked at him for a long time. Then, slowly, he smiled. “That’s actually a good idea.”

Chen Si looked faintly offended. “I occasionally have them.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At 6:48, on the way to the shears, Chen Si stopped in front of an antique print dealer’s window. In it was an old map. He went in. Zhao followed, with a paper bag holding a book Elowen had mentioned wanting.

The map was dated 1890. It showed the harbour district in fine faded ink: the waterfront, the old warehouses, the narrow streets that had since vanished under the modern city, and climbing up the hill behind them in delicate hatching, the road to the Peak. Chen Si leaned close. He found Harbour Road, running along the old shoreline. He found the bend where, a century later, a shop would have a broken necklace in the bottom left-hand corner of its window. Then he followed the road up the hill with his eyes until he found the place where a house would stand, with a balcony on its east side, where a woman would one night refuse to cry in front of two hundred people.

“Original printing,” said the dealer at his shoulder. “Very well kept.”

Chen Si asked the price, and the dealer told him, and he nodded. “I’ll take it.”

“For Aurelia?” said Zhao.

“Yes.”

“Your anniversary was Sunday.”

“I know.”

“Didn’t you already give her something?”

“No,” said Chen Si. “I told her it was late.”

Zhao looked at him sideways. “Then why are you smiling?”

Chen Si said nothing.
