Three nights before, Aurelia had fallen asleep with her cheek on his shoulder while he read. Some time after one she had moved, and her fingers had curled into his shirt, and she had said, quite distinctly, I wish we’d never met. He had gone still. He had looked down at her. Her eyes were shut. She frowned in her sleep. Then she said, I want to do it all again.

He hadn’t slept properly since. He had replayed the first sentence for three nights and refused to let the second one comfort him. He knew the past had not always been kind to her; he knew there were parts of it she would have been glad to skip; he knew he had no right to ask her to be grateful for every page of their history. But the thought that she might want to rub out the day on the balcony had lodged somewhere under his ribs and stayed there. He had thought about asking her. He hadn’t wanted to make her explain something she had said asleep. So he had been unable to decide on a present for five days, and then he had seen the map. He wanted to ask her something else instead. If she could begin again, would she choose the same road twice?

By a quarter past seven they were outside on the pavement. Zhao had the shears, the book, and a packet of green tissue paper. Chen Si had the map, wrapped flat in brown paper under his arm.

“That wasn’t so bad,” said Zhao.

“You nearly interrogated a shop assistant.”

“She was showing me the wrong things.”

“You asked whether a bracelet could change a tyre.”

“It was a reasonable question.” They walked to the car. “We should do this again. Next year.”

“No.”

“Birthdays.”

“No.”

“New Year?”

Chen Si opened the car door. “Get in.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday morning Aurelia found the map in the dining room, laid flat under glass in a plain walnut frame, with a card propped against it that said Five days late. Happy anniversary.

She stopped. “Chen Si?”

He was at the table pouring tea. “Happy anniversary.”

She went to the map. Her eyes moved over the old streets and stopped at Harbour Road, and then followed the hatched road up the hill, the way his had, until it reached the place where the house would one day stand. She looked at him.

“1890?”

“Yes.”

“Original?”

“Verified.”

She looked at him for a long time, and then she remembered, and smiled. “You heard me. Three nights ago. I was talking in my sleep.”

He put the teapot down and didn’t answer.

“I said I wished we’d never met.” His face tightened, very slightly. She turned round. “I wasn’t finished.”

“I know. You said you wanted to do it all again.”

“I wasn’t wishing we had never met. I was wishing I could have the whole thing twice.” She came towards him. “The balcony. Your ridiculous business proposal. Uncle Fan’s fish. The chess. Your terrible Italian.”

“My Italian is excellent.”

“Your Italian was dreadful.”

“Four years of study.”

“And still dreadful.” She put her hand on his cheek. “I wanted to meet you again. Even knowing everything that was going to happen.”

He caught her hand. “You’d choose it again?”

“Every time.”

He looked at her for a moment without moving. Then he put one arm round her waist and lifted her clean off the floor and kissed her, and she laughed against his mouth and said his name.

“Again,” he said.

“What?”

“Say it again.”

She wrapped her arms round his neck. “I’d choose you again.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, across the city, Elowen unwrapped a pair of Kyoto shears in green paper, with an aged wooden handle bound in new cord and a blade so fine it seemed to cut the light. Under them was the book, and on the flyleaf, in heavy careful pencil, an inscription.

For the woman who listens to me read, even when I lose my place.

She read it twice and looked up at her husband. “You remembered.”

“I remembered.”

She kissed him, and lifted the shears out of their box, and her face changed. “Oh, Zhendong.” Then she turned them over and looked at him with narrowed eyes. “Did Chen Si help?”

Zhao hesitated. “Yes.”

“I knew it.”

On Sunday Aurelia received a photograph. Elowen, holding the shears in one hand and a small bunch of narcissi in the other.

Elowen: Round thirty-three. Mine.

Aurelia: The map is an 1890 original.

Elowen: My shears are a hundred years old.

Aurelia: Mine has historical significance.

Elowen: Mine can cut things.

Aurelia looked across the sofa at Chen Si, who was reading. “Your brother’s wife is being unreasonable.”

He didn’t look up. “Then she’s probably right.”

She gasped. “You’re taking her side?”

“I’m staying married.”

She threw a cushion at him. He caught it without looking up from his book. Her phone buzzed again.

Elowen: Thirty-four next year?

Aurelia: Don’t make me buy you better shears.

Elowen: Don’t make me plant a better garden.

Aurelia put the phone down. Chen Si held out his hand and she took it, and leaned against him, and looked up at the map, which was now on the wall where she could see it from anywhere in the room.

“Do you know what I like best about it? It proves the road was there before us. Both of them. The shop and the house. And we still found each other on it.”

He kissed her hair. “Next time I’ll find you sooner.”

“You were late enough the first time,” said Aurelia, and across the city, at that same moment, Zhao was reading the monkey king aloud to his wife for the second time.

Neither man had any intention of admitting that anniversary shopping had been a pleasant experience. Neither wife believed them for a second.

chapters.title: She Loses at Mahjong to the Quiet Sister
chapters.desc: Aurelia Chen has not lost a game of mahjong since she was nineteen. Elowen’s quiet sister has not said more than eleven words to her in five years. One Lunar New Year, one table, four players, and a husband standing behind his wife’s chair who is enjoying this far too much.
chapters.epigraph: “You laughed.”
chapters.content:
The Lin house in the Walled City had hosted the first night of the New Year for as long as anyone at the table could remember. It had never, until that night, hosted a mahjong disaster.

“Four players,” announced Lin Jian, tipping the tiles out onto the green baize of the old square table with a sound like hail on a roof. “No arguing about the rules.”

“Who would argue?” said Aurelia.

Elowen, on the sofa beside Zhao, looked at her.

“Fine,” said Aurelia. “No unnecessary arguing.”

Round the table: Aurelia, Raiden with his glasses pushed up into his hair, his wife Jia cracking her knuckles, and Evangeline, Elowen’s youngest sister, the quiet one. In five years of birthdays and festivals and random Sundays, Aurelia had heard Evangeline say perhaps eleven words. She was polite, and watchful, and very nearly impossible to read. Aurelia liked her. She also had no idea at all how to play against her.

Chen Si stood behind Aurelia’s chair. Before the first hand she took off her three rings, as she always did at the Jade Hall on Thursday nights, the diamond band and the pale sapphire and the old gold signet, and put them in his palm without looking round, and he closed his hand over them.

“Are you playing?” she asked him.

“No.”

“Good. I don’t need advice.”

“I wasn’t going to offer any.”

“Excellent.”

“Be nice,” said Elowen from the sofa.

“I am always nice.”

Zhao coughed. Chen Si studied the ceiling beams. Lin Jian, who had been watching his daughter’s face, smiled into his tea. “Wenwen,” he said, “let her lose on her own.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia had not lost at mahjong since she was nineteen. Her grandfather had taught her at his kitchen table in Milan, with the windows open on the courtyard, and had taught her properly: she counted. She remembered every discard. She watched for the half-second when somebody’s fingers paused over a tile, and could usually tell what a player was waiting for before the player knew it herself.

Evangeline was doing something very strange.

She discarded tiles that Aurelia had already ruled out of her hand. A tile that ought to have been useful to Raiden turned up in Jia’s discards instead. The one tile Aurelia was waiting for vanished from the wall at exactly the wrong moment. Evangeline didn’t look at her. She simply played, unhurried, her black ribbon bow very straight, her pale hands resting between turns on the edge of the table.

On the eighth turn she laid down her last tile. “Mahjong.”

Silence. Lin Jian leaned forward. Raiden checked the hand. Jia looked at Evangeline as if she had grown a second head. It was a perfect hand.

Aurelia smiled. “Well played.”

Evangeline gave a small nod. “Thank you.”

Thirteen words, Aurelia thought. Possibly fourteen.

Chen Si’s hand came to rest on her shoulder. She looked up at him. “Don’t.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“Your face has.”

“I’m very proud of you.”

“You’re enjoying this.”

“A little,” said Chen Si.

The second round went worse. Evangeline won again. The third ended with Aurelia discarding the exact tile Evangeline needed, and Evangeline taking it with a soft “Pung” that seemed to land in Aurelia’s chest like a pebble. The fourth was a disaster. By the fifth Aurelia had lost enough that Lin Jian stopped counting the score out loud.

“Perhaps we should lower the stakes,” he said.

“No,” said Aurelia.

Evangeline began quietly building her wall. “Again?”

“Again.”

Behind her, Chen Si’s thumb moved once on her shoulder. He was enjoying this far, far too much.

The fifth round was the worst of all. Aurelia had counted every discard. She had tracked every suit. She had noticed every pause. And she was still walked straight into it. Evangeline threw out a tile that looked perfectly harmless. Aurelia took it. Three turns later Evangeline laid down her hand.

Five rounds. Five, in a row. Aurelia had not lost five rounds in a row in her whole adult life.

And then, staring at the tiles, she saw it. It hadn’t been luck. Evangeline had been feeding her false information all night. Not with obvious mistakes. With carefully chosen discards, one after another, that made Aurelia believe certain tiles were safe; that let her settle into a pattern and grow sure of it; and then broke the pattern at the precise moment she became confident. It had been done on purpose. It had been done beautifully.

Aurelia looked up slowly. Evangeline was watching her. For the first time all evening, she smiled. Not much. A very small smile, at the corners.

Aurelia began to laugh. Everyone turned. She laughed again, and leaned back in her chair, and put her hand over her eyes.

“Oh,” she said. “You little menace.”

Evangeline looked down at the tiles. “Sorry.”

“No. Don’t you dare apologise. That was brilliant.”

Chen Si bent down. “Are you all right?”

“I’m fine.”

“You’ve lost five rounds.”

“I can count.”

“Just checking,” he said, and she reached back without looking and caught his free hand.

“Stop looking so pleased.”

“I can’t help it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The money came back before they left. Aurelia was gathering her coat in the hall when Evangeline appeared at her elbow and put an envelope into her hand.

“What’s this?”

“Your money.”

“You won it.”

Evangeline shook her head. “I only wanted to see if I could beat you.”

Aurelia stared at her, and then laughed. “You made me lose five rounds in a row to find out if you could?”

Evangeline nodded.

“Why?”

Evangeline thought about it with the seriousness she gave everything. “Everyone says you never lose.”

“And?”

“I wanted to see what you’d do.”

Aurelia tilted her head. “What did I do?”

The small smile came back. “You laughed.”

For a moment Aurelia didn’t say anything. Then she put the envelope back into Evangeline’s hands and closed the girl’s fingers over it. “Keep it.”

“I can’t.”

“You earned it. Next time I’ll win it back.”

Evangeline looked at her, startled, and then, without warning, laughed. It was a small sound and it changed her whole face, and across the hall Elowen, who was helping their father on with his scarf, looked round with an expression of pure delight. Zhao looked at Chen Si. Chen Si gave one small nod. The two men understood each other perfectly. Aurelia had acquired another rival.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the car he was unusually quiet. She watched the New Year lanterns slide past on the old streets, and then turned. “You’re still smiling.”

“Am I?”

“Yes.”

“You played well.”

“I lost.”

“You enjoyed it.”

She thought about that, and sighed. “I did. That’s what’s so irritating. Apparently I’m capable of losing without ruining my entire evening.”

He took her hand and slid her three rings back onto her fingers one at a time, in the right order. “That’s progress.”

“Don’t sound so pleased.”

“I’m proud of you.”

“You’re only saying that because you won nothing.”

He laughed.

At home she found his diary for the next day open on the dining table, which Qian had sent up so he could look it over before bed. Three meetings in the morning, a call with the docks at two, dinner with a senior partner. She picked up his pen. He came in from the hall loosening his collar.

“What are you doing?”

“Changing your schedule.”

“Why?”

She looked at him. “Pung.”

He stopped. Then smiled. “That isn’t how mahjong works.”

“It is tonight.” She drew a line through the morning, and then through the call at two. “I take your discard.”

“Am I allowed to object?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because I’ve won.”

“You lost five rounds.”

“At mahjong.” She put the pen down and came round the table. “This is a different game.”

He caught her round the waist. “What’s the prize?”

“Your time.”

His face softened. “How much?”

“All of tomorrow.”

He kissed her forehead. “Done.” He began to turn away, and she caught him by the end of his loosened tie and pulled him back and kissed him slowly, and when she let him go she said into his mouth, “You may call me lucky.”

“I wouldn’t dare,” said Chen Si.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning Elowen sent a photograph. Evangeline at the mahjong table in the Lin kitchen, holding a cup of tea, and beside her a small note in neat schoolgirl characters.

Round six?

Aurelia: Tell her I’m coming.

Elowen sent back a laughing face, and then another message.

Elowen: She’s been practising since six this morning.

Aurelia looked across the bed at Chen Si, who was lying on his back with his eyes shut, enjoying the rare and possibly unprecedented luxury of having nowhere at all to be.

“Chen Si?”

“Mm.”

“Cancel the day after as well.”

He opened one eye. “Why?”

“I have a rematch.”

He sighed. “Of course you do.”

She slid back under the covers and stole his pillow, and he pulled her in against him.

“At least let me watch.”

“Absolutely not.”

“Why?”

“Because you make a terrible face when I’m losing.”

He kissed her hair. “I’ll work on it.”

She shut her eyes. She had lost five rounds in a row. She had found a new rival who said fourteen words a year and played like a knife. And, most annoying of all, she had discovered that losing could be fun.

She still intended to win next time. Naturally.

chapters.title: The Sewer, Nineteen Years Ago
chapters.desc: Chen Si has told this story once, to nobody, in his head, every night for nineteen years. Tonight his wife asks about the scar on his arm, and he tells it out loud. Block C. The riot. A boy who came down off the top bunk without deciding to. And half a kilometre of freezing water in the dark.
chapters.epigraph: “Brothers.”
chapters.content:
It had been raining since the middle of the afternoon. The rain ticked on the windows and made the flat unusually quiet. Aurelia lay on her side facing Chen Si. He was reading, or pretending to.

Her fingers had found the scar on his forearm. It ran from just below the elbow almost to the wrist, a long pale patch of skin with a puckered edge, the kind of mark that only comes from heat. She traced the edge of it.

“How did you get this?”

He glanced down. “An old injury.”

“I know it’s old.”

“Then why ask?”

“Because you’ve never told me. Zhao told me some of it, nine years ago, outside a door on the ninth floor. You told me the road.”

He put the book down on the blanket. For a moment he looked at the scar as though he hadn’t seen it in a long while. Then he turned on his side to face her.

“Block C.”

Her fingers stopped.

“Nineteen years ago,” he said. “Zhao was there.” He took her hand and turned it palm up and rubbed his thumb across the middle of it. “I’ve told this once. In my head. Most nights, for nineteen years.”

She moved closer. “Tell it out loud.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He had been sixteen. Block C was a place where boys learned to sleep lightly and never sit with their backs to a door. He had come in in October with a split lip, a cracked rib, and the watch his father had given him on his fifteenth birthday, three weeks before the men came up the stairs. The watch was the only thing he had managed to keep. It was also the only thing he owned worth enough to interest a guard.

He found the man by the laundry corridor and told him he wanted the drainage plans.

The guard laughed. “Why?”

“Because I need them.”

“You’re sixteen.”

“I know.”

The guard looked at the watch, and then at him. “That belonged to somebody?”

“My father.”

The guard held out his hand. Chen Si hesitated for less than a second, and then unbuckled it and gave it to him, and the man put it in his pocket and walked away. Three days later a folded sheet of paper came to him inside a library book: a rough plan of the old storm drains under the block, drawn in pencil by someone who had been down there. He learned it by heart and burned it in the washroom. He had no intention of going alone.

In January a new boy came. Fifteen, and already very large, and silent, and impossible to provoke; he took the top bunk in Chen Si’s row and slept through shouting like a cat. Chen Si started sitting next to him for one reason only. Because he was big, and the others might think twice.

The new boy looked down at him from the bunk. “What?”

“Nothing.”

“Then move.”

Chen Si didn’t move. Zhao stared at him for a while, and then went back to the book he was holding. A battered paperback with no cover, half the pages loose, the spine held together with tape. Journey to the West. Chen Si knew it at once. His father had owned a copy: a very different one, old and heavy and kept on the high shelf above the desk, that Chen Si had been allowed to touch only with clean hands. He watched Zhao’s finger moving along the line.

“You’re reading it wrong.”

Zhao’s eyes narrowed. “Am I.”

“Yes.”

“Then you read it.”

Chen Si took the book and read the page aloud, quietly, so no one else would hear. Zhao listened without moving. When it was finished he held out his hand for the book. The next evening Chen Si sat beside him again, and read another chapter. For a while that was all there was. A boy who needed someone big to sit next to. A boy who needed someone to read. Neither of them said so.

✦ ✦ ✦

The riot started just after midnight at the end of the month: shouting on the lower floor, and then the crash of something heavy hitting a door, again and again. Chen Si was awake before the first bell. He had spent three months learning what trouble sounded like. When he swung down off the bunk Zhao was already standing in the dark with his shoes on.

“Stay behind me,” said Zhao.

“There’s another way.”

“Where?”

“Down.”

Zhao looked at him, and for the first time seemed to understand that Chen Si hadn’t been sitting beside him all month only because he was frightened.

They went by the service passage. The corridor was filling with smoke and noise. And at the corner a boy called Gao was waiting, who had been waiting for Chen Si since October for reasons that were never very clear, with a bed slat he had spent a month sharpening on the concrete.

Chen Si saw it too late. Zhao didn’t. He came down off his feet as if he hadn’t decided to, shoved Chen Si into the wall, and the slat went into Zhao’s side instead.

For a moment everything became very small. The splinter of wood. The blood. Zhao’s hand flat against the wall. Chen Si heard himself say his name a long way off. Then Gao came again, and Zhao caught him, and what followed was brutal and very fast, and when Chen Si finally got his hands on Zhao’s arm and dragged him back, the slat was on the floor and Zhao was white to the lips.

“You’re loud,” said Zhao.

“You’re bleeding.”

“I noticed.”

“Can you walk?”

Zhao looked down at his shirt, and then at Chen Si. “Can you?”

The drain was sealed with an iron grate, as the plan had said. The lock was rusted and the frame had gone soft with damp, as the plan had said. What the plan hadn’t said was that the boiler-room steam main ran along the wall beside it, and that someone had set the lagging on fire that evening, and that the iron had been sitting in the heat for hours.

Chen Si wrapped his hand in his shirt and lifted. Nothing. Zhao was leaning on the wall with his hand pressed to his side and his breath whistling. “Move,” he said. Chen Si said wait. Zhao said his name. Chen Si said wait, again, and put his forearm against the edge of the grate and leaned his whole weight into it. The shirt burned through. He felt the skin go. He didn’t let go. The frame shifted, and shifted again, and opened a gap.

“Your arm,” said Zhao.

“Later.”

He pulled the gap wide enough and got Zhao through it, and went in after him, and the drain swallowed them both.

✦ ✦ ✦

The water was so cold it stopped his breath. Waist deep at first, then chest deep, a narrow brick tunnel stinking of rust and worse, with no light at all. He kept one hand on the wall. With the other he held Zhao up. Half a kilometre, the plan had said.

They went very slowly. Zhao stumbled, and Chen Si hauled him up. After a while Chen Si couldn’t feel his fingers. Once, Zhao stopped and leaned his head against the bricks.

“Don’t,” said Chen Si.

“I’m not stopping.”

“You are.”

“Catching my breath.”

Chen Si got in front of him in the black water. “Look at me. You’re getting out of here.”

Zhao laughed, very weakly. “You’re bossy.”

“Yes.”

“Annoying.”

“Yes.”

“Keep talking.”

So he did. He told him about the monkey king, and the chapter they hadn’t finished, and when the water got too loud for talking he recited the next chapter from memory, the way his father used to read it to him at bedtime, every word, until his throat was raw. And Zhao kept moving.

They came out just before dawn, onto a concrete spillway with rainwater sheeting down it into the harbour. Chen Si dragged Zhao out first and then crawled after him, and they lay on their backs on the wet concrete for a long time, breathing, under a grey sky. Zhao turned his head.

“Your arm.”

The sleeve had burned away. The skin under it was raw and blistered from elbow to wrist.

“It’ll heal.”

“You need a doctor.”

“After you.”

Zhao shut his eyes, and opened them. “You’re an idiot.”

Chen Si laughed, once, and it came out almost like a sob.

✦ ✦ ✦

There was a doctor in the old town, behind a dried-goods shop, who would stitch anyone without asking their name, if they could pay. He kept Zhao on a camp bed in his back room for three days. On the third day he named his price, and Chen Si had nothing. The watch was gone. That afternoon he went out without saying where, and came back after dark with something wrapped in a cloth under his coat, and put it on the doctor’s table, and unwrapped it. It was the heavy old book from the shelf above his father’s desk. He had walked in through the back door of his mother’s flat, and she had been sitting in the kitchen, and she had looked at him, and at his arm, and at his face, and had asked nothing at all, and had gone and taken it down off the shelf herself and put it in his hands.

The doctor opened the cover and looked at the flyleaf and closed it again, and said that would do.

Zhao tried to sit up. “No.”

“Be quiet.”

“That’s your father’s—“

“I know.”

“You can’t—“

“I know,” said Chen Si, and pushed the book across the table.

Zhao looked at him as though he had done something unforgivable. Chen Si sat on the floor beside the camp bed until the stitching was done, and then until Zhao could stand. And when they finally went out into the street, Zhao held out his hand.

“What?”

“Your hand.”

Chen Si gave it to him. Zhao took the doctor’s little blade from his pocket, where he had evidently put it while nobody was looking, and drew it across his own palm, and held it out. Chen Si understood. He cut his own. They pressed their palms together in the alley behind the dried-goods shop, blood on blood. No ceremony. No witnesses. No speech. Two boys who had come out of the dark alive.

“Brothers,” said Zhao.

“Brothers.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia didn’t say anything for a long time when he had finished. The rain went on against the glass. Her hand had moved from the scar on his arm to the old white line across his palm.

“You told me it was the road,” she said at last. “For twelve years.”

“I didn’t want to remember it every time someone asked.”

“And now?”

“Now I don’t mind remembering.”

“Because Zhao lived?”

“Because we both did.”

She lifted his hand and kissed the middle of the palm, and then the scar on his arm, and then the inside of his wrist. He watched her. “You don’t have to be gentle with it.”

“I know. I want to be.” She lay with her cheek on his chest. After a while she said, very quietly, “Do you still miss it? The book?”

He looked across the room. On the shelf by the window, between his mother’s recipe book and the black jade queen, stood the 1592 Journey to the West with his father’s name inside the cover.

“I missed it for nineteen years.”

“Would you read it to me?”

“Now? All of it?”

She smiled. “Twice.”

He laughed and got up and fetched it, and they settled against the headboard, and she tucked herself under his arm with her fingers over the scar, and he opened it with great care, because the pages were very old, and began to read. His voice was low and even, the same voice that had read to a fifteen-year-old on a top bunk so nobody would hear. When the first chapter ended she lifted her head.

“Again.”

“Already?”

“You promised.”

“I don’t remember promising.”

“Clause nine.”

He looked at her. “That isn’t what clause nine means.”

“It means I set the terms,” said Aurelia, and he laughed and turned back to the first page.

Halfway through the second time, she kissed the scar on his arm again, and he stopped reading.

“Say it,” she said. “That you’re here.”

“I’m here.”

She kissed him. “Again.”

“I’m here, Aurelia.”

He held her face and kissed her back, slowly, and when they came apart he rested his forehead on hers and asked whether she wanted him to go on, and she said yes. Outside the rain went on. Inside, Chen Si read his father’s book aloud for the second time that night, and for once the story didn’t end in a tunnel. It ended with his wife asleep against him, her hand over the scar he had carried for nineteen years. He turned one more page, and kept reading.

chapters.title: Her Rules for Galas
chapters.desc: The Shen Foundation gala, December 2025, from the other side of the room. Eleven rules, written on cream paper in red ink and slipped into her husband’s pocket at six o’clock. He has annotated every one. In black. In the car.
chapters.epigraph: “I am never bored when you are talking.”
chapters.content:
At six o’clock on the twentieth of December, Aurelia slipped a folded sheet of cream paper into the breast pocket of her husband’s dinner jacket.

He looked down. “What’s this?”

“Instructions.”

“For what?”

“Your behaviour.”

He unfolded it. Eleven rules, in her red ink. He read them once and looked at her. “Eleven?”

“I was being generous.”

He smiled and put the paper back in his pocket. “Of course, sweetheart.”

She straightened his lapel. “Don’t make me regret marrying you.”

“Six years too late for that.”

She kissed his cheek and went to finish her hair. He waited until she had left the room. Then he took out a black pen.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty past seven, in the back of the car, while she was checking her lipstick in the little mirror, he gave the paper back to her. Every rule had been annotated.

1. You will not intimidate the donors. Only if they behave.

2. You will not discuss business unless asked. Define business.

3. You will not have Qian cancel anyone’s invitation because you dislike them. I dislike very few people.

4. You will not stand behind me like a bodyguard. Impossible.

5. You will not stare at my champagne. I don’t trust champagne.

6. You will not answer questions put to me. Unless the question is stupid.

7. You will not threaten anyone who compliments my dress. Depends on the compliment.

8. You will not look at Miles Wei like that. Like what?

9. You will not interrupt my conversations because you are bored. I am never bored when you are talking.

10. You will not pretend you don’t know me when I am talking to someone important. I have never once pretended not to know you.

11. You will not make me regret bringing you. You won’t.

She lowered the paper and stared at him. “You annotated my rules.”

“Naturally.”

“In black.”

“I thought red would be confusing.”

She looked at number eight again, and then at him. “Chen Si.”

“Yes, sweetheart?”

“Behave.”

He folded the paper and put it back over his heart. “I’ll try,” he said, which she knew meant nothing whatsoever.

✦ ✦ ✦

The Shen Foundation’s winter gala was in the ballroom of the Harbour Hotel, the same room where their old school had held its sixtieth birthday dinner five years before. Crystal chandeliers, white roses, a great curving staircase at one end where the Shen family stood at eight o’clock to receive their guests like a painting of themselves. At 7:42 Elowen stepped out of a car at the kerb in deep green, with Zhao beside her in black. At 7:44 Zhao glanced towards the doors and lifted two fingers, and Aurelia, still in her own car, understood at once. Cloakroom, two minutes.

“You’re two minutes behind her,” said Chen Si, looking at his watch.

“Thank you for the report.”

She went in two minutes after Elowen, in ivory silk with a sculpted neckline, her hair loose at the nape, a necklace of old-cut diamonds at her collarbone. Chen Si followed. Four metres behind her. Exactly four.

He didn’t look at her all the time. He didn’t need to. His attention went round the room like a lighthouse beam: the doors, the waiters, the service corridor, the men drifting towards his wife. A tray of champagne came towards her from the left, and the waiter carrying it changed direction before he reached her, without quite knowing why. Another came from the right; Qian appeared out of nowhere and steered it smoothly towards a group of trustees. Aurelia noticed. She didn’t turn round. She lifted her own glass an inch, without looking back, and Chen Si, four metres away, watched her over the rim of his. Rule four, he thought, was going to be difficult.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 8:16, Miles Wei came over.

He had been two years above them at school. He had been handsome then, in a pale, absent, entirely unconscious way, and was handsome still, with his soft fringe and his thin round glasses and the air of a man who would rather be in a laboratory. He had also been, in their last year, the boy on whom Aurelia Song and Elowen Lin had both wasted an embarrassing quantity of energy, and who had preferred physics to either of them and never noticed that he was being competed for. Chen Si knew this because Aurelia had told him. Voluntarily. Which was why he considered himself to be behaving remarkably well.

“Aurelia.”

“Miles. It’s been years. Dr. Wei, now.”

“Only on paper.” He touched his bow tie. “Is this crooked? I’ve been told it’s crooked.”

“Turn.”

She straightened it with two neat movements, the way she straightened everything. “There.”

“Still rescuing people from their own clothes.”

She laughed. Behind her, Chen Si was there. He hadn’t hurried. He wasn’t angry. He was simply, suddenly, present.

“Chen Si,” said Miles, holding out his hand. “Good to see you.”

“Dr. Wei.”

The handshake was perfectly civil. Chen Si’s eyes went to the bow tie his wife had just straightened, and back to Miles’s face. “Your tie looks better.”

Miles laughed uncertainly. “Thank you.” Then his gaze slid past them both to the foot of the great staircase, where the Shen family was standing, and stayed there a moment too long, and something in his face that had been absent all evening came suddenly awake. He excused himself very politely and went.

Aurelia watched him go, and then she watched where he was going, and said, quite softly, “Oh.” Then she turned on her husband. “That was unnecessary.”

“I shook his hand.”

“You appeared.”

“I was already nearby.”

“You were four metres behind me.”

“Now I’m closer.”

She tried not to smile and failed. He leaned towards her ear. “I wanted him to know I know.”

“Know what?”

“That he used to be the one.”

“Used to be.”

“I know.”

“And?”

“And I wanted him to know I know.”

She stared at him, and let out a laugh of pure disbelief. “You’re impossible.”

“Only at galas.”

“Rule eight.”

He looked genuinely thoughtful. “I haven’t done anything.”

“Your face.”

“My face is my own.”

“And for your information, he didn’t notice either of us at seventeen and he isn’t noticing me now. Did you see where he was looking?”

“Yes,” said Chen Si. “That’s why I let him keep his hand.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Across the ballroom, Zhao was standing behind Elowen.

Aurelia noticed because the likeness was almost comic. Elowen was talking to one of the trustees about the children’s garden on the hospital roof; Zhao stood just behind her shoulder with his attention moving quietly round the room. When a waiter came towards her with champagne, Zhao stepped half a pace and the tray went somewhere else. When a man cut into her conversation, Zhao waited until Elowen had finished her sentence before he offered his hand. When she turned, he was already looking at her. Not possessively. Not impatiently. Just there.

Aurelia watched them for a while, and then looked round. Chen Si was doing exactly the same thing. Four metres had become two. She sighed.

“You’re both ridiculous.”

He followed her look. “Zhao’s worse.”

“He’s your brother. Of course he’s worse.”

Elowen came over a minute later. Her eyes went from one to the other of them, and then settled on Aurelia’s throat. “Your necklace was crooked,” she said pleasantly.

Aurelia blinked. “What?”

“Earlier. In the cloakroom. Before you came in. I straightened it while you were looking for your lipstick.” She smiled. “One point.”

“For what?”

“For noticing something your husband didn’t.”

Aurelia looked at Chen Si. He looked away.

“That isn’t a point.”

“It is.”

“Since when?”

“Since I decided.”

Zhao appeared at his wife’s elbow. “Don’t argue with her.”

“You’re supposed to be on my side,” said Aurelia.

“I’m on my wife’s side.”

Chen Si nodded. “A very sensible policy.”

Aurelia looked at the two of them standing shoulder to shoulder. “Blood brothers,” she said. “Of course.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They left at 10:35. By then Aurelia had spoken to all the trustees who mattered, secured a donation for the foundation’s jewellery apprentice scheme, and survived a second conversation with Miles Wei, during which he looked over her shoulder at the staircase eleven times. Chen Si had intimidated no donors. He had threatened nobody. He had redirected seven trays of champagne, interrupted one conversation, and looked at Miles Wei, by her count, twice. She considered it a qualified success.

The lift doors closed. They were alone. He loosened his tie.

“Well?” she said. “How many did you break?”

He thought about it. “Three.”

“Four. You stood behind me.”

“I was two metres away.”

“Still behind me.”

“That isn’t a rule. It’s a preference.”

She stepped close. “Rule eleven.”

“Yes?”

“You didn’t make me regret bringing you.”

“No.”

“Good.”

He took the paper out of his pocket. She held out her hand for it. He didn’t give it to her. He unfolded it and put his finger on the last rule, and his own black words beside it. You won’t.

“There’s something you should know about rule eleven,” he said.

“What?”

“It reverses clause nine.”

The lift went on down. She looked at him for a long time. “Explain.”

“At the gala you set the rules. You decided where I stood, what I said, who I spoke to. You gave me eleven instructions, and I followed them.”

“Mostly.”

“Mostly.” He smiled. “Now we’re going home.”

“Are we?”

“Nearly.” He folded the paper and put it back over his heart. “So tonight I set the terms. Unless you say otherwise.”

She studied his face. “You’re very confident.”

“I married a woman who writes rules in red ink and expects me to follow them.”

“An excellent decision.”

“The best one I ever made.”

The lift slowed. He held out his hand, and she put hers in it.

“Then tell me your terms.”

He ran his thumb across her knuckles. “First, you let me take that necklace off.”

“Why?”

“Because it’s been crooked all night.”

She laughed. “Elowen straightened it.”

“I know. It’s crooked now.” He leaned closer. “Second, you stop pretending you don’t know how much I wanted to kiss you when you were straightening Miles Wei’s tie.”

She burst out laughing. The doors opened. She stepped out first, and turned round, and took hold of the end of his loosened tie. “Come along, Mr. Chen.”

He came. And the eleven rules, written in red and answered in black, stayed folded in his breast pocket. He meant to keep them. He had always liked having something of hers close to his heart.

chapters.title: He Reads Her Reviews
chapters.desc: Every review. Every one. Since 2019. In a folder on his laptop called “Rotterdam (Q3)” so that nobody will ever open it. And one night she finds out that he does not only read them. He answers them. Under a name she would recognise anywhere.
chapters.epigraph: “I do what she asks.”
chapters.content:
The folder was called ROTTERDAM (Q3). It contained no documents about Rotterdam and no quarterly anything. It contained two thousand four hundred and six comments defending Aurelia Chen, and Chen Si had been keeping it for seven years without once considering it embarrassing. Until his wife found it.

It happened on a Wednesday night in February. He was in the shower. She had borrowed his laptop to find a photograph Qian had sent him of the new Harbour Road window, and opened the list of recent folders, and saw ROTTERDAM (Q3), and clicked, because nobody in the history of the world has ever been able to leave a folder called Rotterdam alone in that house.

The first file was a screenshot of a review from the spring of 2019. The second was a thread on a jewellery forum. The third was a comment. So was the fourth. She leaned closer, and saw the name.

LiftedAtEveryTurn.

She stopped. She knew that name. Everyone who followed her work knew that name. For years an account called LiftedAtEveryTurn had turned up under reviews, newspaper pieces, auction-house threads and the occasional particularly vicious post about her, and taken them apart. It was sharp. It was sometimes very funny. It was frequently terrifying. And it knew things about her work that only a handful of people in the world could know.

She scrolled. Two thousand four hundred and six. Seven years.

She opened the most recent. That afternoon Desmond Holt, the critic, had published a long piece under the headline The Gangster’s Wife Plays at Jewellery. It described her new collection as expensive decoration, raised doubts about whether she designed her own work, and suggested her reputation owed rather more to her husband’s influence than to her hands. Underneath it, posted at 4:12 p.m.:

LiftedAtEveryTurn: Mr. Holt appears to have confused access with understanding. If he cannot tell the construction of a piece from the circumstances of its maker’s marriage, he may wish to consider a different profession.

Her mouth twitched. She scrolled down. Someone had asked how this person could possibly know so much about the new collection, Inverno.

LiftedAtEveryTurn: The interior engravings were not in the press photographs. They were visible at the private viewing. That you missed them does not make them imaginary.

She went very still. Only the bench men and nine invited guests had seen inside those pieces. She looked at the name again. Then at the bathroom door.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came out ten minutes later with a towel round his neck and his hair wet, and stopped. She was sitting on the bed with his laptop open on her knees.

“Hello,” she said.

He looked at the screen, and then at her. “Hello.”

“Rotterdam?”

A pause. “Yes.”

“Q3?”

“Yes.”

She turned the laptop round so he could see. “Would you like to explain?”

His expression changed very slightly. Not guilt. Recognition. He came and sat beside her. “You found it.”

“All of it.”

“That’s unfortunate.”

“Unfortunate?”

“I meant to tell you eventually.”

“When?”

He considered. “At three thousand.”

She laughed once, in disbelief. “Chen Si. Are you LiftedAtEveryTurn?”

“Yes.”

She stared at him, and then she started to laugh properly, the helpless kind that folds you in half, and put her face in her hands. He watched her with great patience.

“My husband,” she managed, “has been fighting strangers on the internet for seven years.”

“They were wrong.”

“All of them?”

“Most.”

“Two thousand four hundred and six comments?”

“Some were replies.”

“That isn’t an answer.” She wiped her eyes. Then her laughter softened, and went. “Why?”

He didn’t answer at once. “The first one was Desmond Holt.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It had been the spring before the wedding. Before the boat. Before her name appeared in foreign papers. Holt had written a short, contemptuous piece calling her first collection an expensive hobby paid for by a powerful man’s affection. Chen Si had read it at his desk, twice. Qian had been standing by the door.

“Do you want me to deal with it?”

Chen Si had been thinking, at that moment, about a very particular kind of dealing with it. Then he had remembered her across the table at Uncle Fan’s, telling him that she wanted her work to stand up without his name anywhere near it. He had closed the article.

“No.”

“Then what?”

He had opened a new account instead, and chosen a name, and written three paragraphs. Qian had read them later over his shoulder and described them as the most restrained thing Chen Si had ever done while angry.

“You wanted him killed,” said Aurelia.

“I considered it.”

“Chen Si.”

“I didn’t.”

“That isn’t very reassuring.”

“I know.” He looked at her. “So I wrote comments instead.”

“On jewellery forums.”

“Yes.”

“To strangers.”

“Yes.”

“Did you even know anything about jewellery?”

He looked offended. “I know enough.”

“Enough to argue about pavé?”

“Yes.”

“Natural against heated sapphires?”

“Yes.”

“The Inverno engravings?”

“Apparently.”

She fell back against the pillows, laughing again. And then, scrolling back through the years, she saw a date, and a time, and stopped laughing.

3:07 a.m. Early January, 2020.

The thread was a gossip column. Someone had written that the jeweller was using her husband’s mysterious illness to drum up sympathy for her business. The reply was four words long.

LiftedAtEveryTurn: I do what she asks.

She read it again. “Three in the morning.”

“Yes.”

“You were on the ninth floor. You couldn’t hold a spoon.”

“Qian held the phone. I told him what to type.”

“Why? Of all the things to spend your strength on.”

He was quiet. “Because they were talking about you as if you were waiting for me to die.”

Her throat tightened. She closed the laptop and put it aside and took his hand. “You know I don’t need you to defend every review. Some criticism is useful. Some of it’s right.”

“I know.”

“You don’t have to fight the whole internet for me.”

“I don’t.”

She raised an eyebrow.

“Not the whole internet,” he amended, and she laughed, and put her forehead against his.

“Thank you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning she was reading the papers in bed while he dressed, and suddenly began to read aloud. A long review, in a newspaper in New York, of Inverno. “Her understanding of restraint, of proportion, and of the emotional language of precious material places her among the most compelling designers now working anywhere.” She lowered the paper. “Well?”

He fastened his cuff in the mirror. “I agree.”

“Why?”

“Because it’s accurate.”

She read the rest. At the end there was a small photograph of her wearing one of the pieces. She looked at it for a long moment, and then at him. “I want to answer.”

“The review?”

“The comments.”

He came and sat beside her. She found the thread on her phone, under the review, where the arguments had already started. And for the first time in seven years she wrote under her own name.

Aurelia Chen: Thank you to everyone who has taken the time to look closely at the work, whether you liked it or not. I make jewellery because I have something to say with it. I’m grateful to anyone who engages with the work itself. As for the rest, I think the pieces can speak for themselves.

She pressed post. He read it over her shoulder.

“Good.”

“Only good?”

“Very good.”

“You’re not going to reply underneath me?”

“No,” he said. “The last word should be yours.”

She turned and kissed him, and he caught her round the waist and pulled her closer, and when they came apart he murmured that he still had the first comment.

“Of course you do.”

“And the second.”

“Chen Si.”

“And the third—“

She kissed him again to stop him. It worked for about four seconds.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday he took her to Uncle Fan’s. There was a thick brown envelope on the table. She opened it. Printed pages. Hundreds of them, held with a black clip, with a cover sheet: LiftedAtEveryTurn. Complete. The last page number was 2,407.

“Two thousand four hundred and seven?”

“I printed one more.”

“Why?”

“Because you replied.”

She lifted the first page. Spring, 2019. If you intend to criticise her work, you might at least have the decency to understand it first. She read it twice. “You were very angry.”

“Yes.”

“And very formal.”

“I was trying to be polite.”

She laughed, and turned to the last page. Not a defence of anything. Someone on the thread had asked LiftedAtEveryTurn why on earth he cared so much about a designer he had never met.

LiftedAtEveryTurn: I have watched her work for seven years. I know what goes into every piece, what she gives up for it, and what she will not compromise. I don’t need to know her to see that she deserves to be taken seriously.

Aurelia looked across the table. “That isn’t true.”

He lifted his eyes. “What isn’t?”

“You know her.”

He smiled. “Yes.”

“And you know exactly how much she hates being defended by strangers.”

“I do.”

She reached across the table. “Then I suppose you’ll have to find something else to do.”

“Such as?”

“Read my next collection before the critics do.”

He took her hand. “Gladly.”

She picked up his pen from beside his bowl and wrote on the last page, under his comment: For the man who has always looked closely. She signed her name, and gave it back to him. He read it, and put his thumb over her signature, and for once had nothing at all to add.

Uncle Fan came out with the fish, saw the stack of paper, and stopped. “What’s all that?”

Chen Si calmly folded the top page over. “Work.”

Uncle Fan looked at Aurelia.

“He’s been arguing with strangers,” she said.

Uncle Fan considered this. Then he put Chen Si’s fish in front of him, already boned. “Eat,” he said. “You look tired.”

Aurelia laughed. Chen Si picked up his chopsticks, and under the table, where nobody could see, he kept hold of her hand.

chapters.title: Milan in August
chapters.desc: The city is empty. Everyone who matters has gone to the lakes. The palazzo where they were married is closed for the summer and she has the only key. There is a problem, though, and it is clause ten: the safe word is the name of the city they are standing in, and every waiter in Milan keeps saying it.
chapters.epigraph: “Only if necessary.”
chapters.content:
The first problem occurred at passport control. The second happened outside the airport. The third was the name badge on the hotel receptionist. By then Chen Si had begun to suspect that bringing his wife to Milan in August had been a mistake.

“Buongiorno. Benvenuti a Milano.”

Aurelia stopped walking. He looked round. She pointed, without a word, at the sign above the passport desks. MILANO. Then at the officer’s shoulder flash. Then at the enormous lit advertisement on the wall behind him, for a fashion house, in which the name of the city was written in letters a metre high.

“Your safe word,” she said, “is everywhere.”

He stared at the advertisement. She began to laugh.

“Don’t.”

“I’m not doing anything.”

“You’re enjoying it.”

“Very much.”

Clause ten of their agreement was perfectly clear. The word was Milan. If either of them said it, everything stopped. No questions, no argument, no hesitation. It had seemed an entirely sensible choice when they were sitting on the forty-fourth floor of a building half a world away. It was considerably less sensible standing in Milan. At baggage reclaim a recorded voice said the name of the city three times in two languages. Aurelia nearly dropped her handbag. Chen Si closed his eyes.

At the hotel desk she took a blank room-service card and a red pen out of her bag.

Temporary amendment to Clause 10. For the duration of our stay in Milan, the word shall be ROTTERDAM.

She signed it and handed it to him. He read it. “Rotterdam?”

“We’re not in Rotterdam.”

He looked at her for a moment, then signed beneath her name. “Agreed.” She slid the card into his wallet behind his driving licence.

“Legally binding.”

“Of course,” he said gravely. “I’ve always wanted a contractual amendment witnessed by a hotel receptionist,” and the receptionist, whose name badge said MILENA, looked from one to the other of them and decided not to ask.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her grandparents’ Milan wasn’t the one in the guidebooks. In August it was hardly there at all. The families who owned the old shops had gone to the lakes. The cafés opened late, if they opened. By noon the streets in the old quarter were nearly empty, the shutters down, the heat lying on the stone like a cat. Even the palazzo on the Naviglio where they had been married was shut for the summer, and the only spare key in the world was in her handbag.

She took him through streets tourists never found. A bakery with a blue door that had sold her grandfather the same loaf every morning for forty years. A courtyard where the fountain hadn’t worked since she was a child and nobody had ever thought of mending it. A tiny grocer’s where the woman behind the counter still called her piccolina, though she hadn’t been in for nine years, and pressed a paper twist of sugared almonds into her hand without being asked.

At a corner an old man sat outside a café with a small glass of something amber and a pack of cards on the table.

“Signor Bruno!”

He looked up. For a second he didn’t know her. Then his whole face rearranged itself. “Ah! La piccola Aurelia!” He stood up, kissed her on both cheeks, and immediately began to talk at enormous speed in the old Milanese of her grandmother’s kitchen, the dialect hardly anyone under seventy used any more. She answered in Italian. He waved that away as beneath him, and turned to Chen Si. “And this is the husband.”

Chen Si greeted him in old Milanese. Bruno’s eyebrows went up into his hair. Then he laughed out loud and slapped the table. “Ah! You talk like my grandfather!”

Aurelia turned very slowly. “You speak Milanese?”

Chen Si shrugged. “Some.”

“Since when?”

“Enzo.”

“Enzo taught you old Milanese?”

“He thought it might be useful.”

Bruno pulled out a chair. “Sit. We play.”

“Scopa?” said Aurelia, looking at the cards.

“Scopa.”

Chen Si sat. Within twenty minutes he had won twice. Aurelia watched him sweep the table with an expression of deep personal betrayal. “You’re showing off.”

“Only a little.”

Bruno laughed until he had to take off his glasses and wipe his eyes. When they got up to go he pressed a packet of biscuits from the café into Aurelia’s hands and nodded at Chen Si. “For your husband. He looks thin.”

“He is not thin.”

Bruno waved a hand. “All husbands are thin.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The palazzo smelled of dust and cool stone and summer. She unlocked the side door herself. The mirror room was exactly as she remembered: tall windows onto the canal, pale walls, a long glass in a dark carved frame, and the afternoon sun lying across the floorboards in a long gold oblong. Five years ago she had stood here in her dress and checked her veil while he waited in the corridor outside, pretending to Zhao that he wasn’t nervous.

She walked to the mirror and turned. “Do you remember?”

“Everything.”

“Even my dress?”

“Especially your dress.”

She came back to him. One by one she began to take off her jewellery. Her earrings first. Then her bracelet. Then the rings from her right hand. She put each piece into his palm until his hand was full of her gold, and then she closed his fingers over it and moved his hand to her waist.

“Your turn,” she said.

He looked at her in the long glass. “Aurelia.”

“Don’t look so serious.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.” He bent and kissed her bare shoulder, and she turned round in his arms, and for a moment they only looked at each other in the dusty gold light.

Then he took the room card out of his wallet and glanced at the red ink. “Rotterdam,” he said.

She blinked. “What?”

“Testing.”

She laughed out loud, and the empty room gave it back to her. “You’re impossible.”

He put the card away and leaned in until his mouth was against her ear. “Otherwise,” he said, very quietly, and her laughter went soft.

She reached up and touched his face. “Yes,” said Aurelia, and he kissed her, slowly, in the room where she had once checked her veil. He turned her to face the glass and undid her dress down the back, hook by hook, and let it fall round her feet, and stood behind her with his mouth on her shoulder and his hands moving over her where she could watch them, until she reached back and pulled his belt open herself. He took her there against the old gilt frame with the late sun on the dust and her palms flat on the cool mirror, slowly, his arm round her waist holding her up when her knees went, and somewhere in it the reflection stopped mattering, and after that neither of them was looking at the mirror at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

By sunset the canal was nearly empty. They sat on the broad stone sill outside the palazzo’s water door with their shoes off beside them and their feet above the slow green water. He had taken off his watch. She had lost count of the number of times she had asked him to kiss her, and stopped counting. She wore only her wedding ring. The rest of her gold was in his jacket pocket.

“You’re missing something,” he said, and held up her necklace between two fingers.

“Keep it.”

He put it back in his pocket and took her hand. The city was warm and still around them.

“Do you know why I wanted to come?” she said.

“Because your grandmother loved it.”

“Partly. And because this is where we got married, and I wanted to see it without anybody else. No guests. No photographer hiding behind a pillar. No schedule. Just us.”

He kissed her temple. “Then we should come every August.”

“Every August?”

“Even when we’re old. Especially then.”

She smiled. “Good.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The first call came at twelve minutes past eight the next morning. Chen Si answered it in bed.

“Qian.”

“Mr. Chen. Rotterdam has brought the meeting forward.”

Beside him, Aurelia began to laugh into the pillow. He shut his eyes. “Tell them I’ll ring back.”

The second call came twelve minutes later. “Mr. Chen, Rotterdam needs your approval on—“ He hung up. The third came at 8:41, by which time Aurelia was laughing so hard she had pulled the pillow over her head.

He rang Qian back. “Change the contact name.”

“To what, sir?”

“Dental.”

A pause of perfect professionalism. “Understood.”

“And don’t ring me again today.”

“Of course, sir.”

Aurelia came out from under the pillow and took the phone out of his hand and typed, with great care, a message to Qian: For scheduling purposes, all Rotterdam matters are postponed until further notice. She showed it to him before she sent it.

“You’re making it worse,” he said.

“Good,” said Aurelia, and sent it.

At home, half a world away, Qian opened the shared calendar and created a new category, DENTAL (AUGUST), and blocked out three days. Then he added a note for the senior staff: Mr. and Mrs. Chen are in Milan. Do not use the word Rotterdam in any communication unless absolutely unavoidable. He looked at it for a long time. Then he added one more line. Do not ask why.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening she stood at the open window of the mirror room with the canal going violet below. He came up behind her and put his arms round her waist.

“Ready?”

She nodded. He kissed her cheek. “Rotterdam?”

“Only if necessary,” she said, and turned round in his arms and kissed him.

Outside, the city was still empty. The shops were shut. The streets were quiet. Milan belonged to nobody in particular, and for three days it belonged to them. They hadn’t come back to celebrate a wedding. They had come back to remember the two people who had chosen it. And, as Aurelia reminded Qian in writing on the morning they left, to make absolutely certain that next August nobody booked them anything at all.

chapters.title: The Ring She Designed Herself
chapters.desc: For three weeks, her husband gets out of bed at two in the morning and comes back at five smelling of polish. Aurelia Chen does not do jealousy. Aurelia Chen follows him anyway, in silk pyjamas and a coat, with a gun in her bag, and finds him somewhere she never expected: at her own bench.
chapters.epigraph: “Then it is perfect.”
chapters.content:
At seven minutes past two in the morning, Chen Si got out of bed. Again.

Aurelia didn’t open her eyes. She knew the order of it by now: the mattress lifting, his bare feet on the floor, the very quiet click of the bedroom door. Then nothing. At four minutes to five he came back. He showered before he got into bed, but not before she had caught it on his shirt in the dark, faint and unmistakable. Polishing compound.

It had been three weeks. Three weeks of leaving at two and coming back at five. Three weeks of meetings that didn’t appear in Qian’s calendar, of excuses that were getting more careful every day, of a husband who had apparently developed a private life that smelled like a jeweller’s bench.

Aurelia Chen did not do jealousy. She did, however, have an imagination. And it was becoming extremely unpleasant.

On the Tuesday she told Dr. Ho, whom she still saw on the first Tuesday of every month, in the same room with the same two armchairs and the trees outside the window grown taller. “He leaves at two. He comes back at five. And he smells of polish.”

Dr. Ho waited. “Have you asked him?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

Aurelia thought about it. “Because if he’s having an affair I’d rather know before I ask him to lie to me.”

“And if he isn’t?”

She looked out at the trees. “Then I’ll feel foolish.”

“Would that be worse?”

“No,” said Aurelia, and smiled without any humour. She knew it wouldn’t. That was the problem. She could read a room full of hostile men, find a dishonest account in forty-one minutes, and tell from the back of a setting whether a stone had been lied about. She had no idea at all what to do with the possibility that her husband was keeping something from her.

On the twenty-first night, she followed him.

Silk pyjamas. The long charcoal coat. Flat shoes. A small clutch with her phone and her keys and the little pistol that lived in the drawer of her bedside table. She hadn’t told Chen Si. She hadn’t told Qian. It was, by any reasonable standard, a terrible decision.

His car went down the hill, across the old atelier quarter, and stopped in a lane she knew better than her own hand. He got out and let himself into a narrow building with a key. Her building. Her workshop.

She stood in the lane in her pyjamas for a full minute. Then she let herself in with her own key. There was light under the workroom door at the top of the stairs. She heard Enzo’s voice, low and patient. Then her husband’s.

“Again.”

She pushed the door open. “Would someone like to explain why my husband is meeting another man at my bench at three o’clock in the morning?”

Both men turned. Enzo held a file. Chen Si held a ring. Neither said anything at all.

Chen Si was wearing one of her old leather aprons, his sleeves rolled to the elbow, a fine grey line of polish across the inside of one wrist. She lowered the clutch slowly.

“You’re making jewellery?”

Enzo cleared his throat. “Technically,” he said, “he is attempting it.”

Chen Si gave him a look. Enzo put the file down, very wisely, and stepped back.

✦ ✦ ✦

The ring on the bench was unfinished. A plain gold band, slightly irregular, with a carefully shaped claw setting standing empty at the top. She knew the design at once. Not from any of her collections. From another life.

Beside it lay a small sketchbook, open. The paper had gone yellow. The pencil lines were faint. At the top of the page, in her own sixteen-year-old handwriting, was a date. Under the drawing, in a different hand, in red, was a single word.

Second-rate.

She stopped breathing. She knew that hand. She had forgotten the sketchbook existed. No. That wasn’t true. She hadn’t forgotten. She had buried it.

“I found them at the house,” said Chen Si, coming to stand beside her. “In your old room. When the builders took the wardrobe out to do the wall behind it. There were five of them, behind the bottom drawer.”

She turned a page. Another ring. A necklace. A pair of earrings so ambitious it made her face hot to look at them. Her schoolgirl notes filled the margins; some of the designs were crossed out and some redrawn and some had small hopeful lists of metals and weights beside them. She remembered making them. She remembered the afternoon her mother had gone through them at the kitchen table with a red pen, and every word. Second-rate. Unfinished. You don’t understand proportion. She had never stopped designing after that day. But she had stopped letting herself make anything just for herself, without first knowing who would approve of it.

She looked at the ring. “You made this?”

“Not entirely.”

“He has been learning to file a band,” said Enzo. “I corrected the proportions. He made several mistakes.”

“Several?” said Chen Si.

“Many,” said Enzo. “But he insisted on doing all the work himself.”

She looked at her husband. “Why?”

He looked at the sketchbook. “Because you drew it.”

He had found them three weeks before, he said. He had opened the first one sitting on the floor of her old room among the builders’ dust sheets, and known the handwriting at once, and read every page. Every crossed-out idea. Every small, hopeful note in the margin. Then he had found the red word. He had shut the book. He had wanted to bring it straight to her. But he knew her. He knew that handing her those words without giving her anything else to hold might open something she had spent years learning to live beside. So he had taken the sketchbook to Enzo instead, and asked him to teach him. Not how to design; not how to be a jeweller. How to finish one small thing. A ring she had drawn when she was sixteen. He had wanted to give her something that began with her own hands, before she knew what those hands would become.

“Also,” he said, “I wanted it to be a surprise. I didn’t plan on being followed by a woman with a gun.”

She looked at the empty claws. “Why is there no stone?”

His face softened. “I thought you should choose it.”

She ran her thumb along the band for a long time. Then she put her clutch down on the bench and took off the charcoal coat.

“Move.”

Enzo moved at once. Chen Si didn’t. “What are you doing?”

“Finishing it.” She tied her hair back with a bench elastic and pulled the lamp down and looked at the ring through the loupe. The band needed work. The setting was very slightly out of true. None of it was beyond saving. She picked up a file.

“You’re not angry?” he said.

She glanced up. “I followed my husband across the city at three in the morning in my pyjamas with a pistol in my bag, because I thought he was having an affair.”

“Yes.”

“I’m deciding exactly how angry.”

“That seems fair.”

She went back to the band. Then, quietly, without looking up: “Thank you for finding them.”

He came round the bench. “I wish I’d found them sooner.”

“You found them when you found them.” She looked at the sketchbook, and then at the ring in her fingers. “Let’s finish it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They worked until it was light. Enzo set the angle of the claws. Aurelia trued the band. Chen Si filed the edges under her direction and took every correction she gave him with an expression of steadily increasing patience. Once she took the file out of his hand altogether.

“You’re pressing too hard.”

“I know.”

“Then stop.”

He smiled. “Yes, ma’am.”

“Don’t.”

He laughed. Enzo went home a little before five, with his coat over his arm and the face of a man who had given up his nights for three weeks and would do it again tomorrow. By six the ring was finished. It wasn’t perfect. Where Chen Si had gone too deep with the file there was a faint unevenness in the band, a soft little dip you could feel with your thumb, and she had decided to keep it. The claws stood empty. The design had survived exactly as a sixteen-year-old had drawn it.

She held it up under the lamp. “I’d have made the band thinner.”

“I know.”

“And used a different setting.”

“I know.”

She turned to him. “But I think I like it this way.”

“So do I,” said Chen Si.

He gave it to her that evening, at home, after dinner, with the rain beginning again on the windows. He put a small box into her palm.

“Clause thirteen.”

She looked at him. The yearly gift, with no price and no account owed of its worth. She opened the box. Her ring lay in it, finished by the two of them, with one small stone now standing in the claws, a pale old-mine diamond she had chosen that afternoon from the tray at the back of her own safe.

“Three weeks,” she said. “At two in the morning.”

“Yes.”

“With Enzo.”

“Unfortunately.”

She laughed, and then looked down at it, and didn’t. “Why didn’t you just tell me?”

“I wanted you to see it finished.”

“I’d have helped.”

“I know.” He took her hand. “I wanted to make something for you. Not buy it. Not commission it. Make it.”

He slid it onto her finger. It fitted, of course; he had taken the measurement from the sketch and from the ring she wore on that hand. She turned it under the lamp.

“Do you know what I’d call this, if it were a collection?”

“Second Chance?”

“No.” She touched the soft dip in the band. “First Draft. Because I was sixteen and I didn’t know what I was doing. I was learning. And I deserved to be allowed to go on learning.”

He lifted her hand and kissed the ring. “You did.”

“Next time you want to surprise me,” she said, “tell me you’re learning something.”

“That would ruin the surprise.”

“It would also stop me bringing a pistol to my own workshop.”

He considered that. “That’s fair.”

She took his face in both hands and kissed him, and he held her waist and kissed her back slowly, and when she drew away she kept her forehead on his. “And you’re sleeping in tomorrow.”

“I have a meeting.”

“Cancel it.”

“Under which clause?”

She held up her hand with the new ring on it. “Thirteen.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning Enzo received a photograph. Aurelia’s hand flat on Chen Si’s chest, the ring on her finger. Under it she had written:

Aurelia: First Draft. Finished together.

Enzo: The band is still uneven.

Aurelia: I know.

Then she sent another. Chen Si asleep beside her, very late into the morning for him, his hand over hers.

Aurelia: He made it.

Enzo didn’t answer for some time. When he did, it was only four words.

Enzo: Then it is perfect.

She put the phone down and looked at the ring. The red word in her mother’s hand was still there in the old sketchbook, in the drawer of her desk, where she had put it last night with the other four. She hadn’t needed to rub it out. She had made the thing anyway. And this time, when she looked at her own work, she didn’t see a sixteen-year-old waiting to be told whether it was good enough. She saw the beginning of a woman who had finally understood that her first draft had always been worth keeping.

chapters.title: A Normal Evening, Attempted
chapters.desc: Elowen and Aurelia book their husbands six hours off, and Eliana diverts every call to either man until eleven. Zhao and Chen Si go bowling, walk out of half a film, and eat noodles at the stall at the mouth of the old-town alley where they came out with cut palms in January 2010.
chapters.epigraph: “He’s allowed to watch a film.”
chapters.content:
At four minutes to five on a Friday in January, Zhao Zhendong’s phone lit up on the arm of Chen Si’s sofa.

Mrs. Zhao: Don’t make plans tonight. And don’t answer your phone.

He read it twice, which was once more than he read most things. Across the office, high above the harbour, Chen Si finished a call to Rotterdam, put the receiver down and looked at his own screen.

Mine: Six hours. Don’t argue.

He had saved her that way on the night of the wedding in Milan and never changed it. He turned the phone round so Zhao could see. Zhao turned his. They studied each other across the carpet like two men comparing ransom notes.

“What did you do?” said Zhao.

“Nothing. You?”

“Nothing.”

Someone knocked once and came in without waiting, which in that office only Qian and Aurelia ever did, and this was neither. Eliana Lin had her husband’s grey jumper on with the sleeves pushed up, a laptop under one arm and a paper bag in her hand, and the face of a woman who had been given a job she thought was beneath her and was going to enjoy anyway.

She held out her free hand. “Phones.”

Neither of them moved.

“Elowen and Aurelia want six hours,” she said. “Until eleven, every call to either of you comes to me. Work, family, numbers you don’t know. If someone’s bleeding or something’s on fire, I’ll find you. Anything else waits for tomorrow.”

“And if it’s urgent?” said Zhao.

“Then it’s urgent tomorrow.”

Chen Si gave his up first, which surprised all three of them. Zhao gave his with the expression of a man surrendering a weapon at a border. Eliana sat on the edge of the desk, plugged both into the laptop, typed for about ninety seconds and handed them back.

“They’ll ring your wives. That’s all they’ll do.” She put the paper bag down. “Peanut biscuits. Elowen says you forget to eat when you’re busy. She said other things. They were ruder.”

At the door she turned round.

“Don’t come back early. If you come back early, they’ll know it didn’t work.”

The door shut. Chen Si looked at the bag, and then at the window, where the lights were coming on along the water.

“Bowling,” he said.

Zhao looked at him the way he looked at a contract with a clause missing.

“I haven’t bowled since I was twenty.”

“I’ve never bowled.”

“Then it’s fair.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The alley was on the east side, up a ramp from a car park, loud with students and birthday parties and children dragging balls too heavy for their arms. Zhao stood at the shoe counter holding a pair of rental shoes at arm’s length, as if they had been served on him.

Chen Si tested three balls before he chose one. He stepped up, swung and watched it trundle down the lane, drift left and knock down six pins. He turned round with his arms out.

“Six.”

“There are ten,” said Zhao.

His second ball took two more. Zhao got up, picked a ball off the rack without weighing it, walked to the line and rolled it once, barely bending. It went down the middle as if it had been told where to go. All ten pins went over.

Chen Si was on his feet before the last one stopped rolling, clapping with both hands over his head.

“Brother! Did you see that?”

The family in the next lane turned round to look. Zhao put the ball back on the rack.

“Sit down.”

“That was textbook.”

“Si.”

Zhao sat, took a biscuit out of the bag and ate it.

“I’m finished.”

“You’ve bowled once.”

“I won’t do better than that.”

Chen Si laughed so hard he had to sit down on the bench. Then he bowled every frame himself for the next hour. He complained that the lane pulled left. He put both arms in the air for a spare, a thing nobody who had seen him in a black suit and gloves would have believed, and the children in the next lane started cheering with him. Zhao kept the score with the little pencil and did not bowl again.

On the last frame Chen Si knocked down all ten. Zhao tapped the table twice with the pencil.

“Good.”

Chen Si had been praised by bankers, by ministers and once by a judge who hadn’t meant to. He grinned about that one all the way down the ramp to the car.

✦ ✦ ✦

The film was Chen Si’s choice too. Zhao objected to the film, to the time and to the price of the popcorn, and then paid for all three. They sat in the back row with nobody behind them, out of habit.

Forty minutes in, a man two rows down turned to reach for his drink, and his eyes went past Zhao and stopped on Chen Si.

Zhao watched the colour leave his face. He knew that look. He had put it on men’s faces himself. The man turned to the front, then back, then whispered to the woman beside him, and she turned too.

Chen Si didn’t move. His hands were folded and his eyes stayed on the screen, where somebody was falling into a swimming pool and three hundred people were laughing. But Zhao had known him since a top bunk in Block C, and he knew the difference between Chen Si being still and Chen Si listening.

He leaned over. “Who?”

“He borrowed from us in 2021 and tried to leave the city instead of paying. He got as far as the ferry pier.” Chen Si’s voice didn’t change. “I know his name, his wife’s name and what floor they live on. So does he.”

“And?”

“He paid.”

The man two rows down had stopped watching the film. He was sitting with his shoulders up round his ears, the way men sit when they think a hand is about to land on them.

Chen Si stood up.

“Let’s go.”

“We’ve paid,” said Zhao.

“So has he. He’s allowed to watch a film.”

They went out along the back of the row without making anyone stand. In the corridor, under a poster for something with explosions, Chen Si stopped and put his hands in his pockets.

“His wife didn’t know,” he said. “She does now.”

Zhao stood beside him and didn’t say anything, because there was nothing in it that needed answering. After a while he took the biscuit bag out of his coat and held it out, and Chen Si took one.

“Noodles,” said Zhao.

✦ ✦ ✦

The stall was at the mouth of the alley in the old town, where eighteen years ago a doctor in a back room had stitched anyone who could pay. The doctor was long gone. His back door was a counter for mending phones now, shuttered for the night. But the stall was still there under its faded awning, four plastic stools and a pot that had been on the boil since before either of them was born, and the broth smelled the same as it had in January 2010.

They had come out of this alley at dusk on the third day with nothing. No watch and no book, Zhao’s stitches pulling, a fresh cut across each of their left palms. They had stopped at this stall because of the smell. The woman who ran it had looked at the stitches, at Chen Si’s burned sleeve and at the blood on their hands, and put two bowls on the counter.

“Sit.”

Chen Si had sat. Zhao had stood there. He’d been fed before by a man who made him pay for it afterwards, and he hadn’t moved until Chen Si took his wrist and pulled him down onto the stool.

She was eighteen years older now and had the same forearms. She came over with her notepad and looked at them over the top of it.

“Same?”

“Same,” said Zhao.

The bowls came. Zhao reached for the chilli oil and Chen Si for the vinegar, and neither had to ask the other to pass it.

They ate. A scooter went by. Somebody in a flat above them was arguing with a television. Chen Si put his chopsticks down halfway through.

“You didn’t sit.”

“I sat.”

“I had to pull you.”

“You were bossy,” said Zhao. “You still are.”

“You were fifteen and the size of a door.”

“You read to me like a schoolteacher.”

“Somebody had to.” Chen Si picked his chopsticks up again. “You were reading it wrong.”

Zhao ate for a while. Then, without looking up, he said, “The old copy. You’ve still got it?”

“On the shelf by the window. Aurelia found it.”

“Read me a chapter some time.”

Chen Si looked at him.

“You can read,” he said.

“Not the way you do it.”

Chen Si said nothing to that. He ordered another plate of greens, because it gave him something to do with his face. When the woman brought the bill he had his money under the bowl before Zhao could get his hand inside his coat. In 2010 she wouldn’t take anything. Now she took it without a word, as if eighteen years of it were just one long tab that had finally been paid.

At 10:52 Zhao’s phone buzzed on the table.

Mrs. Zhao: Alive?

Zhao: Yes.

Mrs. Zhao: Fun?

He looked across the table. Chen Si was trying to fold a paper napkin into a crane. It looked like a crane that had been run over.

Zhao: Yes.

Mrs. Zhao: Good.

✦ ✦ ✦

They rang their wives from the car, at eleven exactly, one in each front seat, which meant each of them heard every word of the other’s call and pretended not to.

Elowen answered on the second ring.

“Hm.”

“I bowled,” said Zhao.

“And?”

“Once.”

“And?”

“Strike.”

She laughed, low and warm and only for him, and he looked out at the dark alley so Chen Si wouldn’t see his face.

“So you stopped,” she said.

“Yes.”

“Of course you did. Come home, Zhendong. Thank you for going.”

Aurelia picked up before Chen Si’s phone had finished ringing once.

“Liar.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“You said you’d hate it. You said it on Tuesday, in bed, in two languages.”

“I did say that.”

“Where did you go?”

“Bowling. Half a film. The stall in the old town.”

There was a pause on the line. She knew which stall. She had kissed the scar on his palm on a rainy Sunday and heard all of it.

“Did you eat?”

“Two bowls.”

“Then come home and tell me about the bowling. Just the bowling.” Then, lower: “I’ll hear the rest in bed.”

Zhao drove him back along the harbour without braking for anything, the way he always had, and stopped outside Chen Si’s tower. Chen Si got out, then leaned back in through the window.

“Next Friday,” he said.

“No cinema.”

“No cinema. You can bowl.”

“I’m not bowling.”

Chen Si straightened up with the run-over crane in his hand and went in. Zhao sat with the engine running until the lights came on at the top of the tower. Then he drove up the hill to the house where his wife had left the porch light on.

extras.title: Lo Prometto
extras.line: Eleven pages in red, signed at her counter. Then thirty-seven nights of learning to promise in Italian, without her knowing.

extras.title: Eleven Days
extras.line: The night he lost the argument. He hands her his phone and doesn’t tell her the code. He says she already knows it.
